title: Network tomography based on 1-D projections
abstract: Network tomography has been regarded as one of the most promising methodologies for performance evaluation and diagnosis of the massive and decentralized Internet. This paper proposes a new estimation approach for solving a class of inverse problems in network tomography, based on marginal distributions of a sequence of one-dimensional linear projections of the observed data. We give a general identifiability result for the proposed method and study the design issue of these one dimensional projections in terms of statistical efficiency. We show that for a simple Gaussian tomography model, there is an optimal set of one-dimensional projections such that the estimator obtained from these projections is asymptotically as efficient as the maximum likelihood estimator based on the joint distribution of the observed data. For practical applications, we carry out simulation studies of the proposed method for two instances of network tomography. The first is for traffic demand tomography using a Gaussian Origin-Destination traffic model with a power relation between its mean and variance, and the second is for network delay tomography where the link delays are to be estimated from the end-to-end path delays. We compare estimators obtained from our method and that obtained from using the joint distribution and other lower dimensional projections, and show that in both cases, the proposed method yields satisfactory results.
technical_mechanism: Selected 1-D projections of end-to-end path-delay observations are used to estimate latent per-link queuing-delay distributions from the routing matrix, rather than fitting the full joint distribution. The projections are designed for identifiability and statistical efficiency.
why_it_works: Paths combine delays from different subsets of links, so their joint observations contain clues about which link distributions contribute to the measured end-to-end delays. The method retains information through selected marginal projections; for the paper’s simple Gaussian model, it proves asymptotic efficiency comparable to joint-distribution maximum likelihood. This offers a concrete way to diagnose shared versus path-specific link delay with a lower-dimensional estimator, though it does not establish fewer raw delay samples or guarantee tail-event localization.
root_seam: Attach to request-correlated end-to-end delay samples across paths with known routing, ideally simultaneous measurements over paths sharing some links. Apply the routing matrix and selected projections to infer link queuing-delay distributions. This could localize network-side delay contributions without access to Reflex’s private infrastructure. It does not distinguish network delay from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application unless those are separately timestamped or excluded.
experiment: In a controlled network with known routes, inject a queuing-delay distribution on one link and collect end-to-end delay samples for paths that share or avoid that link. Compare selected-projection estimates with joint-distribution and arbitrary-projection estimates as the number of projections and samples are varied. Measure link-distribution estimation error and localization of the injected delay; separately timestamp server queueing, GPU compute, and action application to check attribution boundaries.
evidence_quote: The network delay tomography problem is to infer the distribution of X from independent samples of Y.
evidence_location: Retrieved passage, Section 4.2, “Network delay tomography using mixture modeling of link delays”; the same passage defines Y = AX and specifies that X contains internal link delays.
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: Joint-distribution estimation and other lower-dimensional projections; the abstract reports comparison but gives no quantitative gain.
uncertainty: The paper supports link-delay distribution inference and gives a Gaussian-model efficiency result, with simulation evidence that selected projections perform satisfactorily. It does not show that the method needs fewer raw samples, quantify tail-localization performance, or test Root or robot inference. Its estimated delays are queuing delays, not a complete end-to-end attribution across network and compute.

title: Proposition and validation of an original MAC layer with simultaneous medium accesses for low latency wireless control/command applications
abstract: Control/command processes require a transmission system with some characteristics like high reliability, low latency and strong guarantees on messages delivery. Concerning wire networks, field buses technologies like FIP offer this kind of service (periodic tasks, real time constraints...). Unfortunately, few wireless technologies can propose a communication system which respects such constraints. Indeed, wireless transmissions must deal with medium characteristics which make impossible the direct translation of mechanisms used with wire networks. The purpose of this paper is to present an original Medium Access Control (MAC) layer for a real time Low Power-Wireless Personal Area Network (LP-WPAN). The proposed MAC-layer has been validated by several complementary methods; in this paper, we focus on the specific Simultaneous Guaranteed Time Slot (SGTS) part.
technical_mechanism: Cross-correlate per-receiver outcomes during simultaneous transmissions with measured synchronization offsets, then equalize node timing as a control. This tests whether a small timing lead, rather than received signal strength alone, explains asymmetric packet reception or collision-related delivery failures.
why_it_works: The paper connects a node's reception advantage to its measured temporal advance and then repeats measurements with equalized synchronization. This is more diagnostic than logging losses alone: it offers a testable way to distinguish timing-skew-related interference from signal-strength effects. Applied to Root, packet/ACK timing and loss observations could reveal a wireless cause of delayed or missing requests, separately from server queueing, GPU compute, and action application.
root_seam: At the robot-side wireless transport boundary, attach request or packet identity to transmit timestamps, receiver ACK/reception outcomes, and available synchronization offset. Correlate tail requests with overlapping transmissions and timing leads; this adds a causal test for radio timing/interference without requiring Reflex's private infrastructure.
experiment: In a controlled wireless test, induce rare delayed or missing request deliveries under overlapping transmissions. Record packet identities, transmit/receive and ACK timestamps, receiver outcomes, signal strength, and node clock offset. Compare natural offset against a timing-equalized condition while holding traffic and signal conditions fixed; test whether tail events track the leading node or collisions and whether the association changes when the offset is removed.
evidence_quote: We have made a cross-comparison of these two studies and determined that the favourite node in the SGTS study is the one which takes the temporal advance in the synchronisation study.
evidence_location: Supplied passage, SGTS hardware-prototyping results, discussion immediately before the equal-synchronization follow-up study.
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The paper reports reception-success and collision-related tests, not tail-latency measurements or remote-inference results. Its equal-synchronization follow-up reports equalized node behavior, but the supplied text does not establish a measured latency improvement. Root would need to test whether this timing-offset diagnostic applies to its wireless transport and tail events.

title: Boolean Compressed Sensing and Noisy Group Testing
abstract: The fundamental task of group testing is to recover a small distinguished subset of items from a large population while efficiently reducing the total number of tests (measurements). The key contribution of this paper is in adopting a new information-theoretic perspective on group testing problems. We formulate the group testing problem as a channel coding/decoding problem and derive a single-letter characterization for the total number of tests used to identify the defective set. Although the focus of this paper is primarily on group testing, our main result is generally applicable to other compressive sensing models. The single letter characterization is shown to be order-wise tight for many interesting noisy group testing scenarios. Specifically, we consider an additive Bernoulli(q) noise model where we show that, for N items and K defectives, the number of tests T is O(KN1-q) for arbitrarily small average error probability and O(K²N1-q) for a worst case error criterion. We also consider dilution effects whereby a defective item in a positive pool might get diluted with probability u and potentially missed. In this case, it is shown that T is O(KN(1-u)²) and O(K²N(1-u)²) for the average and the worst case error criteria, respectively. Furthermore, our bounds allow us to verify existing known bounds for noiseless group testing including the deterministic noise-free case and approximate reconstruction with bounded distortion. Our proof of achievability is based on random coding and the analysis of a Maximum Likelihood Detector, and our information theoretic lower bound is based on Fano's inequality.
technical_mechanism: Non-adaptive noisy group testing: assign candidate causes to coded pools, record each pool's binary outcome, then use maximum-likelihood decoding to recover a sparse set of causes.
why_it_works: Each pooled measurement covers multiple candidates, and distinct codewords make sparse cause sets distinguishable from their combined outcomes. The paper explicitly models false-positive and missed-positive test noise, so the decoder need not treat every pool result as infallible. This is a concrete route to distinguishing sparse causes with fewer measurements, although it diagnoses only when Root can define meaningful pool tests with interpretable binary outcomes.
root_seam: Attach at a controlled diagnostic-probe or fault-injection harness: define candidate network causes (separately from server queueing, GPU compute, and action application), assign them to non-adaptive probe pools, and retain each pool's tail/non-tail outcome. Decode the sparse cause set rather than measuring each cause independently. The paper does not supply a mapping from network causes to pool outcomes; Root must establish that experimentally.
experiment: In a controlled testbed, select a known sparse subset of injected network impairments and compare individually tested causes with randomized coded pools and maximum-likelihood decoding. Repeat with false-positive and missed-positive outcomes, and measure cause-identification accuracy and number of probes at matched error rates. Include server-queue and GPU-load controls to test whether outcomes distinguish network causes rather than merely flagging slow requests.
evidence_quote: The outcome of a test is positive if and only if the second item is a member of that test.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, introduction, description of the group-testing example; noisy models and maximum-likelihood decoding are described in the abstract and selected PDF text.
reported_gain: Theoretical test-count bounds for noisy group testing; no empirical or Root-specific gain is reported.
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The coded pooling and sparse decoding operation is explicit and directly addresses reducing measurements for cause identification. The paper does not establish that network tail causes can be tested as pooled Boolean outcomes, nor does it demonstrate network-delay localization; the controlled Root experiment must validate that transfer.

title: Precise Request Tracing and Performance Debugging for Multi-tier Services of Black Boxes
abstract: As more and more multi-tier services are developed from commercial components or heterogeneous middleware without the source code available, both developers and administrators need a precise request tracing tool to help understand and debug performance problems of large concurrent services of black boxes. Previous work fails to resolve this issue in several ways: they either accept the imprecision of probabilistic correlation methods, or rely on knowledge of protocols to isolate requests in pursuit of tracing accuracy. This paper introduces a tool named PreciseTracer to help debug performance problems of multi-tier services of black boxes. Our contributions are two-fold: first, we propose a precise request tracing algorithm for multi-tier services of black boxes, which only uses application-independent knowledge; secondly, we present a component activity graph abstraction to represent causal paths of requests and facilitate end-to-end performance debugging. The low overhead and tolerance of noise make PreciseTracer a promising tracing tool for using on production systems.
technical_mechanism: Correlate kernel TCP SEND/RECEIVE activity into per-request causal graphs. The method matches activity using endpoint and message-size information, along with process/thread context and event order, then compares component and interaction latency shares across request paths.
why_it_works: The graph attributes time to either work within a component or an interaction between components, so a changed interaction share can flag a transport boundary for investigation. The paper reports this exposing a network problem in an injected Ethernet-driver case. This is transferable request-to-transport causal reconstruction, though not packet-, ACK-, or loss-level diagnosis; cross-node interaction timing is also vulnerable to clock skew.
root_seam: On robot and inference-server hosts, collect request-associated TCP send/receive events with timestamps, endpoint tuples, message sizes, and process/thread context. Build per-request interaction timelines and compare tail requests with healthy requests. This could localize an anomalous transport interaction without requiring application protocol knowledge, but would not alone separate network transit from endpoint waiting, server queueing, GPU compute, or action application.
experiment: Replay matched remote-inference requests with controlled network delay or loss, and separately inject server queueing and GPU delay. Correlate request-linked TCP events into causal graphs; test whether tail-request interaction shares identify the affected boundary and distinguish network perturbations from server-side delays. Measure localization accuracy, clock-skew sensitivity, missing-event effects, and collection overhead.
evidence_quote: Our experiments show we can pinpoint performance problems by using CAGs to calculate changes in observed latency percentages of components.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section 2 overview; network-injection diagnostic example in Section 5.4.2, “Identifying performance bottleneck.”
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The method correlates TCP SEND/RECEIVE activities, not individual packets or ACK/loss sequences, and does not establish a sparse packet-trace representation. Cross-node interaction latency is inaccurate without clock-skew correction. The reported network diagnosis uses latency percentages and does not demonstrate network-tail diagnosis in Root.

title: Tight Bounds for Lp Samplers, Finding Duplicates in Streams, and Related Problems
abstract: In this paper, we present near-optimal space bounds for Lp-samplers. Given a stream of updates (additions and subtraction) to the coordinates of an underlying vector x ∈ Rⁿ, a perfect Lp sampler outputs the i-th coordinate with probability |xi|p/||x||pp. In SODA 2010, Monemizadeh and Woodruff showed polylog space upper bounds for approximate Lp-samplers and demonstrated various applications of them. Very recently, Andoni, Krauthgamer and Onak improved the upper bounds and gave a O(ε-p log³ n) space ε relative error and constant failure rate Lp-sampler for p ∈ [1,2]. In this work, we give another such algorithm requiring only O(ε-p log² n) space for p ∈ (1,2). For p ∈ (0,1), our space bound is O(ε⁻¹ log² n), while for the p=1 case we have an O(log(1/ε)ε⁻¹ log² n) space algorithm. We also give a O(log² n) bits zero relative error L0-sampler, improving the O(log³ n) bits algorithm due to Frahling, Indyk and Sohler. As an application of our samplers, we give better upper bounds for the problem of finding duplicates in data streams. In case the length of the stream is longer than the alphabet size, L1 sampling gives us an O(log² n) space algorithm, thus improving the previous O(log³ n) bound due to Gopalan and Radhakrishnan. In the second part of our work, we prove an Omega(log² n) lower bound for sampling from 0, ± 1 vectors (in this special case, the parameter p is not relevant for Lp sampling). This matches the space of our sampling algorithms for constant ε > 0. We also prove tight space lower bounds for the finding duplicates and heavy hitters problems. We obtain these lower bounds using reductions from the communication complexity problem augmented indexing.
technical_mechanism: Precision-sampling sketch: maintain a compact CountSketch of randomly scaled per-request signal values, then output a coordinate sampled with probability proportional to its magnitude raised to p.
why_it_works: The sampling distribution deliberately favors large-magnitude coordinates, while the streaming sketch avoids retaining every coordinate. Applied to per-request network-delay values, it could preserve a compact set of tail-request identities and estimates for follow-up inspection. This exposes and localizes candidate slow requests, but does not by itself distinguish transport delay from server queueing or preserve packet-level causal evidence.
root_seam: At request completion, update a streaming sketch keyed by request identity with a network-specific delay value derived from robot/server transport timestamps. Retain sampled request IDs and estimates, then use them to retrieve detailed traces if available. This could reduce always-on trace retention while keeping weighted tail exemplars; it does not require Reflex-private infrastructure.
experiment: On controlled Root replays, stream request-keyed transport-delay values into the sampler and compare its retained identities and estimates against full trace retention and ordinary random sampling. Inject transport-tail regressions separately from server-queueing, GPU-compute, and action-application slowdowns. Measure whether sampled records identify the transport-tail requests and whether the signal separates those cases; do not treat the paper's space result as a Root gain.
evidence_quote: Roughly speaking, the idea of precision sampling is to scale the input vector with random coefficients so that the i-th coordinate becomes the maximum with probability roughly proportional to |xi| p. Moreover the maximum (heavy) coordinate is found through a small-space heavy hitter algorithm.
evidence_location: selected_pdf_text, paragraph beginning “bring down the space upper bounds”
reported_gain: For p in (1,2), the paper reports O(ε^-p log² n) space, saving a log factor over the cited O(ε^-p log³ n) sampler; this is a streaming-space result, not a Root diagnostic gain.
baseline: For p in [1,2], the cited prior sampler uses O(ε^-p log³ n) space.
uncertainty: The sampler's weighted-coordinate output is supported, but the paper does not evaluate request-level network signals, causal attribution, or whether sampled records retain enough detail for diagnosis. Root must validate that the chosen signal and sampling distribution reliably surface injected transport tails.

title: Link Delay Estimation via Expander Graphs
abstract: One of the purposes of network tomography is to infer the status of parameters (e.g., delay) for the links inside a network through end-to-end probing between (external) boundary nodes along predetermined routes. In this work, we apply concepts from compressed sensing and expander graphs to the delay estimation problem. We first show that a relative majority of network topologies are not expanders for existing expansion criteria. Motivated by this challenge, we then relax such criteria, enabling us to acquire simulation evidence that link delays can be estimated for 30% more networks. That is, our relaxation expands the list of identifiable networks with bounded estimation error by 30%. We conduct a simulation performance analysis of delay estimation and congestion detection on the basis of l1 minimization, demonstrating that accurate estimation is feasible for an increasing proportion of networks.
technical_mechanism: Use the known routing matrix to model end-to-end probe delays as sums of link delays, then apply expander-graph conditions and l1 sparse recovery to estimate per-link delays and identify congested links.
why_it_works: When only a small number of links have large delays, end-to-end measurements across overlapping paths provide a sparse linear system. The expander conditions establish when those measurements can distinguish and recover the elevated link delays, even with fewer measurements than links. Relaxing the expansion bound makes more given routing matrices eligible, at the cost of a bounded estimation error.
root_seam: Attach probe timing to request-correlated paths between robot and server, form a routing matrix for the traversed network, and recover likely high-delay links from path-delay sums. This could localize a shared network bottleneck across requests, but would require known routes or a defensible path-to-link model; the paper does not attribute delay to off-path flows or separate network delay from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application.
experiment: On a controlled robot-inference path, inject delay on a known small set of network links while collecting end-to-end probe delays over known overlapping routes. Compare recovered link delays and congestion locations against ground truth and a non-sparse tomography baseline; separately vary the number of probes to test recovery with fewer measurements. Keep server queueing and compute timings separately instrumented.
evidence_quote: We exploit the LP optimization in Eq. (8) to estimate link delays for k-identifiable expander networks.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section IV-C, “Delay Estimation: Simulation Experiments”
reported_gain: Simulation reports that relaxing the expansion bound increases the number of networks satisfying the expansion property by almost 30%; it also reports lower estimation-error CDF than the CF-estimator baseline.
baseline: CF-estimator (Chen, Cao, and Bu) for the estimation-error comparison; the expansion-property comparison uses the prior bound ε < 1/6.
uncertainty: The method assumes a given routing matrix and sparse link-delay vector. The context does not establish that these assumptions hold for robot-inference paths or provide evidence about noisy, changing routes, off-path-flow attribution, or separation of network delay from compute and queueing.

title: Sparsity without the Complexity: Loss Localisation using Tree Measurements
abstract: We study network loss tomography based on observing average loss rates over a set of paths forming a tree -- a severely underdetermined linear problem for the unknown link loss probabilities. We examine in detail the role of sparsity as a regularising principle, pointing out that the problem is technically distinct from others in the compressed sensing literature. While sparsity has been applied in the context of tomography, key questions regarding uniqueness and recovery remain unanswered. Our work exploits the tree structure of path measurements to derive sufficient conditions for sparse solutions to be unique and the condition that ℓ₁ minimization recovers the true underlying solution. We present a fast single-pass linear algorithm for ℓ₁ minimization and prove that a minimum ℓ₁ solution is both unique and sparsest for tree topologies. By considering the placement of lossy links within trees, we show that sparse solutions remain unique more often than is commonly supposed. We prove similar results for a noisy version of the problem.
technical_mechanism: Sparse loss tomography on a tree: use path-level loss estimates and their shared-link structure, then apply UpSparse to recover a compact link-level loss explanation. For finite-probe uncertainty, allow path measurements to vary within confidence intervals and recover a sparse consistent explanation.
why_it_works: Overlapping paths constrain which link-loss patterns can explain the observations. Under the paper's tree and sparsity assumptions, UpSparse efficiently selects a link-level explanation and has stated conditions for uniqueness and recovery of the true losses. At Root, localized loss could expose a network cause of tail events involving retransmission or recovery, rather than merely correlating tails with an end-to-end path. It does not itself diagnose latency or distinguish network delay from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application.
root_seam: Attach to robot/server probe or transport loss observations, mapping measured paths onto a tree of shared network segments. Root would gain candidate lossy links from sparse path measurements without requiring instrumentation at every link. The paper does not establish that Root can observe a suitable tree or that loss explains its latency tails.
experiment: In a controlled tree-shaped test network, inject loss at known links and collect finite-probe path-loss estimates with confidence intervals. Run UpSparse and compare its localized links with link-instrumented ground truth and with dense measurements. For Root requests, separately record transport/network timing, retransmissions or loss, server queueing, GPU time, and action-application time; test whether localized loss corresponds to network-attributed tail events. Do not treat the paper's results as a Root gain.
evidence_quote: We define the ‘UpSparse’ algorithm, a fast single-pass linear-time algorithm which outputs the minimal ‘1 solution.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Introduction, contributions on recovery; noisy-measurement treatment in Section V.
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: The paper compares UpSparse with SCFS, a binary path/link failure-set method; it reports higher recovery success for UpSparse in its described experiments, but a quantified gain is UNKNOWN.
uncertainty: The method localizes loss rates, not tail latency. Transfer depends on Root having usable path-loss observations and a tree-like measurement topology; the paper does not show that localized loss causes Root's tails or establish separation from other latency sources.

title: Stealthy Traffic Analysis of Low-Latency Anonymous Communication Using Throughput Fingerprinting
abstract: Anonymity systems such as Tor aim to enable users to communicate in a manner that is untraceable by adversaries that control a small number of machines. To provide efficient service to users, these anonymity systems make full use of forwarding capacity when sending traffic between intermediate relays. In this paper, we show that doing this leaks information about the set of Tor relays in a circuit (path). We present attacks that, with high confidence and based solely on throughput information, can (a) reduce the attacker's uncertainty about the bottleneck relay of any Tor circuit whose throughput can be observed, (b) exactly identify the guard relay(s) of a Tor user when circuit throughput can be observed over multiple connections, and (c) identify whether two concurrent TCP connections belong to the same Tor user, breaking unlinkability. Our attacks are stealthy, and cannot be readily detected by a user or by Tor relays. We validate our attacks using experiments over the live Tor network. We find that the attacker can substantially reduce the entropy of a bottleneck relay distribution of a Tor circuit whose throughput can be observed-the entropy gets reduced by a factor of 2 in the median case. Such information leaks from a single Tor circuit can be combined over multiple connections to exactly identify a user's guard relay(s). Finally, we are also able to link two connections from the same initiator with a crossover error rate of less than 1.5% in under 5 minutes. Our attacks are also more accurate and require fewer resources than previous attacks on Tor.
technical_mechanism: Concurrent-flow throughput fingerprinting: measure a target flow and ordinary probe flows through candidate paths, then correlate their throughput time series to identify a shared bottleneck resource.
why_it_works: Flows sharing a capacity-constrained relay experience common throughput variation, so correlation can implicate a shared network bottleneck without deliberately congesting it. This provides a concrete way to narrow the candidate shared-resource causes of a request tail; it does not by itself distinguish network delay from server queueing or compute.
root_seam: At the robot/server transport boundary, associate request identity and synchronized throughput samples with the suspect request and candidate concurrent flows or paths. A correlated probe can point to a shared network bottleneck; separately timestamp server queueing, GPU execution, and action application to avoid attributing those delays to the network.
experiment: Replay controlled robot-inference requests while varying whether candidate probe flows share a known constrained network link with the request. Measure synchronized per-flow throughput and request latency. Test whether correlation localizes shared-link cases against disjoint paths and server-only queue/GPU-delay controls, and report false positives and detection time.
evidence_quote: We found that the throughput values for the two circuits were highly correlated, measured using the Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, experimental results for the All-Common scenario.
reported_gain: Median factor-of-2 reduction in bottleneck-relay entropy; connection linking crossover error rate below 1.5% in under 5 minutes.
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The experiments concern Tor circuits, not remote robot inference, and do not establish that throughput correlation separates network delay from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application. The proposed Root experiment must validate that transfer; no Root-measured gain is available.

title: Reflection Scan: an Off-Path Attack on TCP
abstract: The paper demonstrates how traffic load of a shared packet queue can be exploited as a side channel through which protected information leaks to an off-path attacker. The attacker sends to a victim a sequence of identical spoofed segments. The victim responds to each segment in the sequence (the sequence is reflected by the victim) if the segments satisfy a certain condition tested by the attacker. The responses do not reach the attacker directly, but induce extra load on a routing queue shared between the victim and the attacker. Increased processing time of packets traversing the queue reveal that the tested condition was true. The paper concentrates on the TCP, but the approach is generic and can be effective against other protocols that allow to construct requests which are conditionally answered by the victim. A proof of concept was created to assess applicability of the method in real-life scenarios.
technical_mechanism: Conditionally trigger victim responses with a sequence of spoofed TCP segments while sending ping probes through a shared router queue; increased probe RTT or loss reveals whether the victim responded.
why_it_works: The victim's responses add traffic to the shared queue, increasing the delay of probes that traverse it. Repeating queries and retrying ambiguous spikes helps distinguish a response-related signal from incidental spikes.
root_seam: A controlled Root experiment could send probes through a suspected shared transport bottleneck while inducing or observing a known competing flow, then compare probe RTT/loss with request-tail events. This could indicate shared-queue interference, but the paper does not reconstruct request-to-packet causality or separate network delay from other inference stages.
experiment: The authors tested idle, saturated-downlink, and saturated-uplink scenarios on a shared edge router. They sent pings to a router beyond the edge router while spoofed segments elicited TCP responses from the victim, and measured ping RTT and loss.
evidence_quote: At the same time, the attacker sends ping probes that share an outbound queue with segments from the victim. Increased round trip time reveals the positive answer to the query.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section 1 Introduction, Figure 1 caption
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The method assumes the probes and induced responses share a queue, and its experiments use favorable network conditions. The context does not establish how reliably this would identify shared-resource causes of remote robot inference tails or distinguish them from other delay sources.

title: Caracterizac~ao de tempos de ida-e-volta na Internet
abstract: Round-trip times (RTTs) are an important metric for the operation of many applications in the Internet. For instance, they are taken into account when choosing servers or peers in streaming systems, and they impact the operation of fault detectors and congestion control algorithms. Therefore, detailed knowledge about RTTs is important for application and protocol developers. In this work we present results on measuring RTTs between 81 PlanetLab nodes every ten seconds, for ten days. The resulting dataset has over 550 million measurements. Our analysis gives us a profile of delays in the network and identifies a Gamma distribution as the model that best fits our data. The average times observed are below 500 ms in more than 99% of the pairs, but there is significant variation, not only when we compare different pairs of hosts during the experiment, but also considering any given pair of hosts over time. By using a clustering technique, we observe that links can be divided in five distinct groups based on the distribution of RTTs over time and the losses observed, ranging from groups of near, well-connected pairs, to groups of distant hosts, with lower quality links between them.
technical_mechanism: Periodically probe host pairs for RTT and loss, then cluster links by their RTT distributions over time and observed losses.
why_it_works: Repeated RTT and loss observations characterize link variability over time and distinguish broad link-quality profiles. They can reveal whether elevated request latency coincides with a degraded network path, but do not identify retransmissions or endpoint stalls.
root_seam: Add timestamped active probes between robot and inference-server endpoints, and compare their RTT/loss series with request latency. This supplies a network-path signal alongside request timing, without assuming access to private infrastructure.
experiment: In a controlled Root test, inject network delay and loss separately from server queueing or compute delays. Compare request-latency changes with periodic robot-to-server RTT/loss measurements and assess whether the measurements distinguish network degradation from server-side delay.
evidence_quote: we present results on measuring RTTs between 81 PlanetLab nodes every ten seconds, for ten days.
evidence_location: Abstract
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The supplied context supports periodic RTT/loss measurement and clustering, but gives no packet- or ACK-level event sequences, method details for the clustering, or evidence that it separates network delay from endpoint stalls. The n13 transfer to robot-to-cloud action loops is plausible but not demonstrated.

title: Nearly Optimal Change-Point Detection with an Application to Cybersecurity
abstract: We address the sequential change-point detection problem for the Gaussian model where baseline distribution is Gaussian with variance σ² and mean μ such that σ²=aμ, where a>0 is a known constant; the change is in μ from one known value to another. First, we carry out a comparative performance analysis of four detection procedures: the CUSUM procedure, the Shiryaev-Roberts (SR) procedure, and two its modifications - the Shiryaev-Roberts-Pollak and Shiryaev-Roberts-r procedures. The performance is benchmarked via Pollak's maximal average delay to detection and Shiryaev's stationary average delay to detection, each subject to a fixed average run length to false alarm. The analysis shows that in practically interesting cases the accuracy of asymptotic approximations is "reasonable" to "excellent". We also consider an application of change-point detection to cybersecurity - for rapid anomaly detection in computer networks. Using real network data we show that statistically traffic's intensity can be well-described by the proposed Gaussian model with σ²=aμ instead of the traditional Poisson model, which requires σ²=μ. By successively devising the SR and CUSUM procedures to "catch" a low-contrast network anomaly (caused by an ICMP reflector attack), we then show that the SR rule is quicker. We conclude that the SR procedure is a better cyber "watch dog" than the popular CUSUM procedure.
technical_mechanism: Sequential Shiryaev–Roberts likelihood-ratio change-point detection on sampled packet rate: accumulate evidence for a modeled distribution shift and alarm at a threshold calibrated to a target average run length to false alarm.
why_it_works: Evidence from successive samples accumulates, allowing a sustained low-contrast change to trigger profiling even when no individual sample is decisive. Calibrating the threshold gives a way to control false-alarm frequency. This is more than logging or a single-sample threshold and transfers as a cheap trigger for richer diagnosis; the paper does not show that packet-rate shifts predict inference tail latency.
root_seam: Apply the detector to time-binned packet-rate or transport-event measurements at the robot/server boundary, retaining request IDs and timestamps so alarms can trigger richer traces. Compare alarms with end-to-end latency and separately measured transport, server-queue, GPU, and action-application times to determine whether the trigger identifies network-related regressions.
experiment: In a controlled Root replay or testbed, inject known network-delay/loss regressions and non-network regressions while collecting packet-rate or transport signals. Compare SR-triggered trace retention with no trigger and a simple-threshold trigger at matched false-trigger rates. Measure regression detection delay, false triggers, retained profiling volume, and whether alarms associate with transport delay rather than server queueing, GPU compute, or action application.
evidence_quote: The detection delay for the SR procedure is roughly 15 seconds (or 30 samples), and that for the CUSUM procedure is about 18 seconds (or 36 samples).
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section 6, discussion of Figure 7 and the diminished ICMP reflector attack.
reported_gain: SR detected the diminished attack in roughly 15 seconds versus roughly 18 seconds for CUSUM; both procedures raised three false alarms along the way.
baseline: CUSUM, with both methods calibrated to an average run length to false alarm of approximately 1000.
uncertainty: The demonstrated signal is aggregate packet rate during a cybersecurity volume anomaly, not request-level latency or transport delay in remote robot inference. The paper does not establish that packet-rate changes predict inference tail regressions or localize their cause. Root gains are unknown.

title: Efficient and reliable network tomography in heterogeneous networks using BitTorrent broadcasts and clustering algorithms
abstract: In the area of network performance and discovery, network tomography focuses on reconstructing network properties using only end-to-end measurements at the application layer. One challenging problem in network tomography is reconstructing available bandwidth along all links during multiple source/multiple destination transmissions. The traditional measurement procedures used for bandwidth tomography are extremely time consuming. We propose a novel solution to this problem. Our method counts the fragments exchanged during a BitTorrent broadcast. While this measurement has a high level of randomness, it can be obtained very efficiently, and aggregated into a reliable metric. This data is then analyzed with state-of-the-art algorithms, which reliably reconstruct logical clusters of nodes inter-connected by high bandwidth, as well as bottlenecks between these logical clusters. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed two-phase approach efficiently solves the presented problem for a number of settings on a complex grid infrastructure.
technical_mechanism: Run synchronized BitTorrent broadcasts across multiple peers, count fragments exchanged between peers over repeated broadcasts, aggregate these measurements into a weighted connectivity graph, and use modularity-based clustering to identify high-bandwidth groups and bottlenecks between them.
why_it_works: During parallel bulk transfer, peers naturally exchange more data over higher-bandwidth paths. Repeated broadcasts reduce the impact of randomness in individual fragment counts; clustering the aggregated graph exposes groups connected by strong paths and bottlenecks separating groups, including shared constraints that emerge under collective load.
root_seam: As a controlled diagnostic, attach peer identities and timestamps to robot–server or robot–robot transfer measurements, then compare fragment/byte exchange patterns and inferred clusters with request-tail events. This could reveal shared or off-path bottlenecks under concurrent load, but would diagnose network structure rather than directly attribute an individual inference request’s delay; network delay would still need separation from server queueing, GPU compute, and action application.
experiment: Evaluate on a controlled robot-inference testbed with known shared and independent network paths. Generate concurrent bulk transfers during inference, repeat broadcasts, infer clusters and bottlenecks, and compare detections against known topology and request-tail timings. Measure localization accuracy and diagnostic overhead against pairwise bandwidth probing and ordinary request tracing.
evidence_quote: The measurement metric is the number of exchanged fragments between peers during a synchronized BitTorrent broadcast
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Introduction, description of the two phases
reported_gain: The paper reports that its approach requires only a few minutes and achieves high accuracy; it says existing methods would take hours or days.
baseline: Existing active bandwidth-tomography methods that saturate links and test pairs or node triplets iteratively; described as taking hours or days.
uncertainty: The experiments reconstruct logical bandwidth clusters on Grid’5000, not request-level inference tails or robot networks. The method does not itself distinguish network delay from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application.

title: Multipath Routing With Novel Packet Scheduling Approach In Wireless Sensor Networks
abstract: Wireless sensor networks sense and monitor real-time events. They supervise a geographic area where a phenomenon is to be monitored. The data in sensor networks have different levels of priority and hence their criticality differs. In order to keep up the real time commitment, the applications need higher transmission rates and reliability in information delivery. In this work we propose a multipath routing algorithm which enables the reliable delivery of data. By controlling the scheduling rate, it is possible to prevent congestion and packet loss in the network. The algorithm provides an efficient way to prevent the packet loss at each node. This results in congestion management in the sensor networks. This protocol prevents packet clustering and provides smoothness to the traffic. Through monitoring and controlling the scheduling rate the flow control and congestion control are managed.
technical_mechanism: Per-hop queue/service telemetry piggybacked in packet headers, coupled with service-ratio and queue-threshold feedback. A node reports its queue length, scheduling rate, and service rate; falling service ratio with a growing queue identifies a local service bottleneck and can trigger parent-rate reduction.
why_it_works: The per-node queue and service signals offer more than an end-to-end delay observation: they can show that delay is accumulating at a particular forwarding node. In Root, correlating those signals with request timestamps could expose transport-queue buildup as a contributor to a tail while separating it from transit delay, server queueing, GPU compute, and action application. The paper describes rate control as the intervention, but its per-node telemetry is the transferable diagnostic operation.
root_seam: At robot-side and server-side transport queues, attach timestamped request or packet identity to queue length and enqueue/dequeue or service-rate events. Preserve per-hop reports where available and correlate them with end-to-end request timing to locate queue buildup rather than attributing all excess latency to network transit.
experiment: Use controlled Root runs with injected transport congestion that creates queue buildup at a known hop, alongside controls that add server queueing or GPU delay. Compare request-level tail localization with per-hop queue/service telemetry enabled versus disabled. Check whether the reported bottleneck identifies the injected transport queue and does not misclassify server or compute delay; evaluate rate reduction separately as a mitigation.
evidence_quote: Each node also calculates the originating rate of the packets.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section II, paragraph beginning “The scheduling unit sends the packets to the MAC layer”; the same paragraph states that nodes piggyback queue length, scheduling rate, and service rate. For the queue trigger, it says: “When the packet sevice ratio falls below certain value the queue starts building up at the node.”
reported_gain: Simulation reports packet drop decreasing from 80% at packet service ratio 0.5 to 60% at 3.0; no Root gain is reported.
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The paper provides a per-node queue/service signal that can support bottleneck localization, but does not evaluate tail-delay diagnosis or establish that the signal distinguishes all network transit delay from local queueing. Its reported packet-drop figures are not evidence of a Root latency improvement.

title: Generalized Network Tomography
abstract: For successful estimation, the usual network tomography algorithms crucially require i) end-to-end data generated using multicast probe packets, real or emulated, and ii) the network to be a tree rooted at a single sender with destinations at leaves. These requirements, consequently, limit their scope of application. In this paper, we address successfully a general problem, henceforth called generalized network tomography, wherein the objective is to estimate the link performance parameters for networks with arbitrary topologies using only end-to-end measurements of pure unicast probe packets. Mathematically, given a binary matrix A, we propose a novel algorithm to uniquely estimate the distribution of X, a vector of independent non-negative random variables, given only IID samples of the components of the random vector Y = AX. This algorithm, in fact, does not even require any prior knowledge of the unknown distributions. The idea is to approximate the distribution of each component of X using linear combinations of known exponential bases and estimate the unknown weights. These weights are obtained by solving a set of polynomial systems based on the moment generating function of the components of Y. For unique identifiability, it is only required that every pair of columns of the matrix A be linearly independent, a property that holds true for the routing matrices of all multicast tree networks. Matlab based simulations have been included to illustrate the potential of the proposed scheme.
technical_mechanism: Unicast delay-distribution tomography: use end-to-end delay samples from paths with known, overlapping link routes to infer the delay distribution of each independent link component.
why_it_works: Different path sums constrain the components they share. Given an identifiable routing matrix and the independent additive-delay model, the method estimates component distributions and matches them to links. A changed tail can therefore be localized to a modeled link, rather than merely observed in an end-to-end request. This does not identify which off-path flow caused the link delay.
root_seam: Collect timestamped probe or request delays over multiple known routes between robot and server, and use the route-incidence matrix to infer link-level delay distributions. Align results with inference-stage timestamps to separate network contribution from server queueing, GPU compute, and action application. This requires route diversity and the paper's independent additive-link assumptions; it does not require access to Reflex's private infrastructure.
experiment: In a controlled Root test, collect IID delay samples on identifiable overlapping routes, then inject delay or contention on one selected link. Test whether tomography localizes the changed delay distribution to that link and whether its inferred tail contribution tracks end-to-end request tails. Compare against injection ground truth and available per-link telemetry. Treat this as a Root experiment proposal, not a measured Root gain.
evidence_quote: The idea is to approximate the distribution of each component of X using linear combinations of known exponential bases and estimate the unknown weights.
evidence_location: Abstract; Section IV, “Distribution Tomography Scheme,” describes estimating path MGFs from IID samples, constructing polynomial systems, and matching inferred weights to components using the routing matrix.
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The transfer supports localizing a delay contribution to a modeled link, not attributing it to a particular off-path flow or proving contention caused it. The method depends on known routes, identifiability, independent additive link delays, and sufficient samples; the paper's examples use one million probe samples per path. No Root experiment or Root-measured gain is reported. Lane n10 is not promoted: the supplied text does not establish fewer measurements or a measurement-efficiency advantage.

title: How to sample if you must: on optimal functional sampling
abstract: We examine a fundamental problem that models various active sampling setups, such as network tomography. We analyze sampling of a multivariate normal distribution with an unknown expectation that needs to be estimated: in our setup it is possible to sample the distribution from a given set of linear functionals, and the difficulty addressed is how to optimally select the combinations to achieve low estimation error. Although this problem is in the heart of the field of optimal design, no efficient solutions for the case with many functionals exist. We present some bounds and an efficient sub-optimal solution for this problem for more structured sets such as binary functionals that are induced by graph walks.
technical_mechanism: Optimize allocation of end-to-end path probes to minimize the trace of the covariance of per-link delay-mean estimates. For exponentially many graph paths, restrict sampling to product distributions over node exits and compute the information matrix by dynamic programming.
why_it_works: Each path measurement is a sum of the delays on that path, so different paths constrain different combinations of link means. Choosing probes to improve estimator information can avoid wasting a fixed probe budget on paths that leave important links poorly observed. This is a concrete tomography operation for distinguishing link-delay contributions with fewer measurements, rather than ordinary logging or thresholding. Its model estimates Gaussian means, however, and does not itself identify tail behavior.
root_seam: At the robot/server transport boundary, record probe path identity and end-to-end transport delay, then use the optimized path allocation to estimate link-delay means. This could help localize a persistent network-delay regression with fewer probes. It does not by itself separate transport from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application; those require separately scoped timestamps or measurements.
experiment: On a controlled network with known per-link delays, inject link-delay regressions and compare the paper's optimized path-probe allocation with uniform path sampling under the same probe budget. Measure per-link mean-estimation error and probes needed to localize the changed link. Separately test a tail-only perturbation to establish whether mean-based estimates miss it. This is a proposed Root experiment, not a reported Root result.
evidence_quote: The only measurement obtained for each probe is the sum of delays along the path.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section 1, Introduction. The structured optimization is described in Section 5.1, “The product distribution,” including dynamic programming to compute the matrix.
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The operation and its link-localization rationale are explicit, and a controlled equal-budget Root experiment is feasible. The method targets estimator covariance for Gaussian delay means, not tail quantiles or tail-event causes; transfer is therefore to efficient diagnosis of link-delay contributions, not a demonstrated solution for network tail latency.

title: Efficient Touch Based Localization through Submodularity
abstract: Many robotic systems deal with uncertainty by performing a sequence of information gathering actions. In this work, we focus on the problem of efficiently constructing such a sequence by drawing an explicit connection to submodularity. Ideally, we would like a method that finds the optimal sequence, taking the minimum amount of time while providing sufficient information. Finding this sequence, however, is generally intractable. As a result, many well-established methods select actions greedily. Surprisingly, this often performs well. Our work first explains this high performance -- we note a commonly used metric, reduction of Shannon entropy, is submodular under certain assumptions, rendering the greedy solution comparable to the optimal plan in the offline setting. However, reacting online to observations can increase performance. Recently developed notions of adaptive submodularity provide guarantees for a greedy algorithm in this online setting. In this work, we develop new methods based on adaptive submodularity for selecting a sequence of information gathering actions online. In addition to providing guarantees, we can capitalize on submodularity to attain additional computational speedups. We demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods in simulation and on a robot.
technical_mechanism: Adaptive hypothesis-pruning measurement selection: maintain weighted candidate causes, update them from each measurement outcome, and greedily select the next measurement expected to disprove the most remaining hypotheses. Lazy-greedy evaluation avoids rescoring every candidate at each step.
why_it_works: Each observation eliminates or downweights causes inconsistent with the result. Choosing the next measurement using the updated candidate set makes the process adaptive, so informative measurements can be selected based on what earlier measurements revealed. The paper establishes adaptive-submodularity guarantees for its hypothesis-pruning objectives. Transferred to Root, this offers a concrete way to seek cause-discriminating measurements rather than collect a fixed set of diagnostics.
root_seam: Attach at Root's incident/request identity and its candidate-cause model. Treat available measurements—such as robot/server transport timestamps, packet or ACK/loss evidence, queue/NIC signals, and server-side queue or GPU timings—as candidate actions with predicted outcomes under each cause. Update the cause weights after each result, then select the next measurement by expected hypothesis pruning. This transfer requires Root to define candidate causes and measurement outcome models; the paper supplies neither network signals nor a way to distinguish network delay from queueing, compute, or action application.
experiment: On replayed Root requests with controlled, separately injected network delay/loss, server queueing, GPU compute delay, and action-application delay, compare adaptive hypothesis-pruning measurement selection with fixed-order and random measurement selection. Use identical candidate causes and measurement availability, and measure diagnostic accuracy and number of measurements needed to identify the injected cause. Include mixed-cause cases to test whether adaptive follow-up measurements help.
evidence_quote: The latter two maximize the expected number of hypotheses they disprove. We show these metrics are adaptive submodular.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section I (Introduction); the measurement and observation framework is described in Section III, and experiments in Section V.
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: Simulation compares against random action selection and a human-designed orthogonal-approach scheme; the robot task compares against no touch localization. No Root or network-diagnosis baseline or gain is reported.
uncertainty: The active hypothesis-pruning operation is explicit and supports a controlled Root experiment, but the paper evaluates tactile localization, not network diagnosis. Root would need to supply a cause model and establish that its available measurements have outcomes that discriminate those causes.

title: Locating Disruptions on Internet Paths through End-to-End Measurements
abstract: In backbone networks carrying heavy traffic loads, unwanted and unusual end-to-end delay changes can happen, though possibly rarely. In order to understand and manage the network to potentially avoid such abrupt changes, it is crucial and challenging to locate where in the network lies the cause of such delays so that some corresponding actions may be taken. To tackle this challenge, the present paper proposes a simple and novel approach. The proposed approach relies only on end-to-end measurements, unlike literature approaches that often require a distributed and possibly complicated monitoring / measurement infrastructure. Here, the key idea of the proposed approach is to make use of compressed sensing theory to estimate delays on each hop between the two nodes where end-to-end delay measurement is conducted, and infer critical hops that contribute to the abrupt delay increases. To demonstrate its effectiveness, the proposed approach is applied to a real network. The results are encouraging, showing that the proposed approach is able to locate the hops that have the most significant impact on or contribute the most to abrupt increases on the end-to-end delay.
technical_mechanism: Aggregate end-to-end delays into anomalous time bins, build a binary route-incidence matrix from traceroutes, then use iterative hybrid counting and candidate-set fusion to identify likely critical hops. This combines sparse end-to-end measurements with route information rather than requiring per-hop monitoring.
why_it_works: If a small number of hops contribute disproportionately to anomalous delays, those hops recur across anomalous routes. Counting route incidence, eliminating routes covered by selected candidates, and fusing candidates across delay groups can narrow the likely contributors without full tracing or distributed per-hop telemetry.
root_seam: Associate timestamped robot-to-server delay measurements with route identities and attach the route-incidence analysis to anomalous request windows. Root could gain candidate network-hop localization while avoiding continuous per-hop tracing. This does not by itself attribute delay to individual inference requests or distinguish network delay from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application.
experiment: In a controlled testbed with known routes, inject sparse queueing delays at selected network hops and collect end-to-end timestamped probes plus traceroutes. Compare the method's inferred hops against injected locations and against end-to-end thresholding alone; separately measure server queueing and compute time to check whether network delay is being isolated.
evidence_quote: The core of the counting technique is to count the number of traceroutes that pass from each node; the number of 1s in each column of the matrix R.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section IV, “The CS Algorithm”
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The paper demonstrates real-network localization, but does not provide a controlled Root experiment or establish request-level attribution. Its method assumes route stability within aggregation bins and sparse, recurring critical hops; traceroute artifacts, load balancing, and RTT ambiguity can limit localization. The paper notes that traceroute delays are RTTs and do not identify which one-way path caused a disruption.

title: Lingering Issues in Distributed Scheduling
abstract: Recent advances have resulted in queue-based algorithms for medium access control which operate in a distributed fashion, and yet achieve the optimal throughput performance of centralized scheduling algorithms. However, fundamental performance bounds reveal that the "cautious" activation rules involved in establishing throughput optimality tend to produce extremely large delays, typically growing exponentially in 1/(1-r), with r the load of the system, in contrast to the usual linear growth. Motivated by that issue, we explore to what extent more "aggressive" schemes can improve the delay performance. Our main finding is that aggressive activation rules induce a lingering effect, where individual nodes retain possession of a shared resource for excessive lengths of time even while a majority of other nodes idle. Using central limit theorem type arguments, we prove that the idleness induced by the lingering effect may cause the delays to grow with 1/(1-r) at a quadratic rate. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first mathematical results illuminating the lingering effect and quantifying the performance impact. In addition extensive simulation experiments are conducted to illustrate and validate the various analytical results.
technical_mechanism: Detect lingering shared-resource ownership: correlate resource ownership with an empty active queue and nonempty waiting queues.
why_it_works: This signature shows the resource is still held even though its current owner has no work to serve while other queues wait. It can expose a shared-resource scheduling bottleneck that ordinary request timing would not identify. The paper analyzes this effect rather than proposing a runtime diagnostic tool, but the modeled signal and its interpretation are concrete and transferable.
root_seam: At the robot-side network interface, attach request timestamps to available MAC/driver ownership or channel-access events and per-queue occupancy or waiting signals. Compare these with packet/ACK timing to test for network resource retention, separately from server queueing, GPU compute, and action application. This requires no assumed access to Reflex’s private infrastructure.
experiment: In a controlled Root test, add competing traffic to a shared wireless resource and compare healthy and tail requests. Retain packet/ACK timestamps alongside available resource-ownership and queue-activity signals. Test whether long request tails coincide with the resource remaining assigned to an empty queue while other queues wait, and verify that this signature is absent when tails are induced by server queueing or GPU compute alone.
evidence_quote: individual nodes retain possession of a shared resource for excessive lengths of time even while a majority of other nodes idle
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, abstract
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The paper establishes and quantifies lingering in a queueing model, not a practical runtime diagnosis procedure. Root would need observable resource-ownership and queue-activity signals; the paper does not establish that these are available in Root or distinguish this signature from every other network bottleneck.

title: Decision-Theoretic Troubleshooting: A Framework for Repair and Experiment
abstract: We develop and extend existing decision-theoretic methods for troubleshooting a nonfunctioning device. Traditionally, diagnosis with Bayesian networks has focused on belief updating---determining the probabilities of various faults given current observations. In this paper, we extend this paradigm to include taking actions. In particular, we consider three classes of actions: (1) we can make observations regarding the behavior of a device and infer likely faults as in traditional diagnosis, (2) we can repair a component and then observe the behavior of the device to infer likely faults, and (3) we can change the configuration of the device, observe its new behavior, and infer the likelihood of faults. Analysis of latter two classes of troubleshooting actions requires incorporating notions of persistence into the belief-network formalism used for probabilistic inference.
technical_mechanism: Decision-theoretic configuration intervention: select a configuration change and follow-up observation by expected troubleshooting cost, then update fault probabilities with a persistence Bayesian network that shares the causal mapping across pre- and post-intervention states.
why_it_works: Changing the configuration can isolate which part of a system is exercised; the resulting observation provides counterfactual evidence about competing fault causes. The persistence network represents that the causal relationship remains the same across the intervention, so the pre-change evidence can be combined with the post-change result rather than treated as an unrelated observation. This offers a way to distinguish causes with a targeted intervention instead of collecting more passive measurements.
root_seam: Attach the intervention, configuration, request identity, and timestamped outcome to Root’s request record. A controlled alternate-path inference or network-path probe could provide evidence about whether a tail follows the network path while the causal model retains other request-stage evidence. The paper does not itself measure latency or separate transport delay from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application.
experiment: On matched reproducible requests with a suspected network tail, compare the normal inference path with a controlled alternate route or path-bypass configuration, then restore the original configuration. Record request identity, configuration, end-to-end latency, and available transport, queue, GPU, and action-stage timings. Use a persistence-network model to update probabilities for path-related versus local-stage causes, and compare the number of interventions or measurements needed to identify the cause against passive diagnosis and a planner without configuration changes. Do not treat the paper’s reported result as a Root gain.
evidence_quote: By setting the configuration node to one value or the other, we isolate part of the system for inspection.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section 3, canonical configurable-device discussion.
reported_gain: 13.4 minutes average time to resolution with configuration changes versus 14.4 minutes without them; simulation on the printing network.
baseline: Planner that did not suggest configuration changes.
uncertainty: The paper’s method is demonstrated for device troubleshooting, not network latency diagnosis. It does not specify network-event or latency measurements, and its example does not distinguish network delay from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application. The proposed Root experiment is a transfer, not a reported Root result.

title: FRANTIC: A Fast Reference-based Algorithm for Network Tomography via Compressive Sensing
abstract: We study the problem of link and node delay estimation in undirected networks when at most k out of n links or nodes in the network are congested. Our approach relies on end-to-end measurements of path delays across pre-specified paths in the network. We present a class of algorithms that we call FRANTIC. The FRANTIC algorithms are motivated by compressive sensing; however, unlike traditional compressive sensing, the measurement design here is constrained by the network topology and the matrix entries are constrained to be positive integers. A key component of our design is a new compressive sensing algorithm SHO-FA-INT that is related to the prior SHO-FA algorithm for compressive sensing, but unlike SHO-FA, the matrix entries here are drawn from the set of integers 0, 1, ..., M. We show that O(k log n /log M) measurements suffice both for SHO-FA-INT and FRANTIC. Further, we show that the computational complexity of decoding is also O(k log n/log M) for each of these algorithms. Finally, we look at efficient constructions of the measurement operations through Steiner Trees.
technical_mechanism: FRANTIC uses topology-aware end-to-end path-delay measurements to recover a sparse vector of congested-link or node delays. It designs weighted paths using local loops, subtracts paired path measurements to cancel unwanted-link contributions, then applies an integer compressive-sensing decoder that iteratively peels off congested elements.
why_it_works: When only a small number of network elements are congested, path delays are additive measurements of a sparse delay vector. Carefully weighted, correlated paths create distinguishable signatures for those elements, while subtraction isolates the intended measurements. This can identify shared congested links from multiple end-to-end paths without measuring every link separately, and the sparse decoder reduces the number of measurements needed. The inferred delay is network-element delay under the paper’s additive model; it does not by itself separate network delay from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application.
root_seam: Attach measurements to identifiable Root requests and collect end-to-end probe delays over known network paths. Reconstruct which shared links have elevated delay, potentially localizing a network tail without direct telemetry from every link. Root would need a usable path topology and sufficiently controlled measurements; the method does not identify off-path flows directly.
experiment: In a controlled Root testbed, inject delay on a known sparse set of links shared by selected request paths. Collect the designed end-to-end path-delay measurements and compare FRANTIC’s recovered links and delays with ground truth and per-link instrumentation. Separately record server queueing, GPU, and action-application times to check whether the diagnosed tail is actually attributable to the network. Vary the number of congested links and measurement count to test localization and measurement efficiency.
evidence_quote: by considering correlated measurements, we can cancel out the contribution of the undesired links and nodes in a given measurement.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section IV, “Idea 1: Cancellation enables selecting disconnected subsets of links and nodes.”
reported_gain: The paper claims O(ρk log n / log M) path measurements and decoding steps; it states that with M = O(n), these can be O(k). It also describes improvement over the cited Xu et al. approach from O(TN k log n) measurements and recovery steps. These are paper-reported theoretical results, not Root measurements.
baseline: The cited Xu et al. random-walk compressive-sensing approach, with O(TN k log n) measurements and recovery steps.
uncertainty: The supplied text provides theoretical guarantees, not an empirical Root evaluation. Transfer depends on known topology, sparse congestion, additive path delays, and the feasibility of collecting the designed weighted paths. It does not establish performance under noisy or time-varying delays or distinguish network delay from other components without additional measurements.

title: Near Optimal Bayesian Active Learning for Decision Making
abstract: How should we gather information to make effective decisions? We address Bayesian active learning and experimental design problems, where we sequentially select tests to reduce uncertainty about a set of hypotheses. Instead of minimizing uncertainty per se, we consider a set of overlapping decision regions of these hypotheses. Our goal is to drive uncertainty into a single decision region as quickly as possible. We identify necessary and sufficient conditions for correctly identifying a decision region that contains all hypotheses consistent with observations. We develop a novel Hyperedge Cutting (HEC) algorithm for this problem, and prove that is competitive with the intractable optimal policy. Our efficient implementation of the algorithm relies on computing subsets of the complete homogeneous symmetric polynomials. Finally, we demonstrate its effectiveness on two practical applications: approximate comparison-based learning and active localization using a robot manipulator.
technical_mechanism: Hyperedge Cutting (HEC) adaptively selects the next test to drive the remaining hypotheses into one decision region, rather than selecting tests merely to reduce overall uncertainty. For Root, the transferable chain is candidate network measurement -> HEC-selected measurement based on its ability to separate diagnosis regions -> fewer observations needed to identify a latency-regression cause.
why_it_works: A measurement is valuable when its possible outcomes distinguish hypotheses that imply different decisions. Sequentially choosing tests for that purpose can reach a diagnosis with fewer measurements than non-adaptive collection or uncertainty reduction that ignores the decision. The abstract identifies HEC and states conditions for correctly identifying a decision region.
root_seam: Attach to Root's diagnosis stage after defining candidate causes and available measurements. Supply hypotheses such as transport delay, server queueing, GPU compute, or action-application delay, and candidate measurements such as endpoint timestamps, packet/ACK/loss observations, queue signals, and GPU timings. HEC could choose which measurement to collect next; the paper does not establish that these Root signals or decision regions are available.
experiment: On controlled inference-delay regressions with known injected causes, compare HEC-selected measurements against a fixed non-adaptive measurement schedule. Measure observations required to identify the correct cause and diagnosis accuracy, keeping the candidate measurements and diagnosis regions the same. This is a proposed Root experiment, not a reported result.
evidence_quote: Instead of minimizing uncertainty per se, we consider a set of overlapping decision regions of these hypotheses. Our goal is to drive uncertainty into a single decision region as quickly as possible.
evidence_location: Abstract
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The abstract supports adaptive, decision-directed test selection and reports a robot-manipulator application, but provides no network-specific measurements, diagnosis regions, or network-tail evaluation. Transfer to Root remains to be tested.

title: Millions of Little Minions: Using Packets for Low Latency Network Programming and Visibility (Extended Version)
abstract: This paper presents a practical approach to rapidly introduce new dataplane functionality into networks: End-hosts embed tiny programs into packets to actively query and manipulate a network's internal state. We show how this "tiny packet program" (TPP) interface gives end-hosts unprecedented visibility into network behavior, enabling them to work with the network to achieve a common goal. Our design leverages what each component does best: (a) switches forward and execute tiny packet programs (at most 5 instructions) at line rate, and (b) end-hosts perform arbitrary computation on network state, which are easy to evolve. Using a hardware prototype on a NetFPGA, we show our design is feasible, at a reasonable cost. By implementing three different research proposals, we show that TPPs are also useful. And finally, we present an architecture in which they can be made secure.
technical_mechanism: Attach a tiny packet program to selected packets; at each switch hop, read and append local state such as queue occupancy, port, or switch ID to the packet. The destination returns the executed packet state to the sender, giving a per-packet record of network conditions along its path.
why_it_works: The state is sampled as the packet traverses each hop, so transient queueing is tied to a specific packet rather than inferred from slow, averaged counters. Per-hop snapshots can expose where network queueing accumulated and distinguish congestion on the path from delay elsewhere, though the paper does not provide server or GPU measurements.
root_seam: At the robot/server transport boundary, associate sampled inference request packets with request IDs and timestamps, and attach TPP-style per-hop queue and path metadata. This could localize network queueing on a tailed request without relying on network-wide periodic counters. The paper does not establish that Root can access or deploy TPP-capable switches.
experiment: The paper instruments packets in a six-node Mininet dumbbell topology and collects executed TPPs to plot queue evolution at six queues. It also reports a NetFPGA prototype and a CONGA* software prototype that queries link utilization every millisecond.
evidence_quote: As the packet traverses each hop, the packet memory has snapshots of queue sizes at each hop.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, passage beginning “TPPs can provide fine-grained per-RTT, or even per-packet visibility into queue evolution inside the network.”
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The mechanism measures in-network state but does not itself identify which off-path flow caused a busy queue, retain traces only when a regression occurs, or separate network delay from server queueing and GPU compute using server-side signals. The supplied text also does not report a controlled diagnostic-accuracy gain.

title: NaNet: a Low-Latency, Real-Time, Multi-Standard Network Interface Card with GPUDirect Features
abstract: While the GPGPU paradigm is widely recognized as an effective approach to high performance computing, its adoption in low-latency, real-time systems is still in its early stages.
