Although GPUs typically show deterministic behaviour in terms of latency in executing computational kernels as soon as data is available in their internal memories, assessment of real-time features of a standard GPGPU system needs careful characterization of all subsystems along data stream path. The networking subsystem results in being the most critical one in terms of absolute value and fluctuations of its response latency. Our envisioned solution to this issue is NaNet, a FPGA-based PCIe Network Interface Card (NIC) design featuring a configurable and extensible set of network channels with direct access through GPUDirect to NVIDIA Fermi/Kepler GPU memories. NaNet design currently supports both standard - GbE (1000BASE-T) and 10GbE (10Base-R) - and custom - 34 Gbps APElink and 2.5 Gbps deterministic latency KM3link - channels, but its modularity allows for a straightforward inclusion of other link technologies. To avoid host OS intervention on data stream and remove a possible source of jitter, the design includes a network/transport layer offload module with cycle-accurate, upper-bound latency, supporting UDP, KM3link Time Division Multiplexing and APElink protocols. After NaNet architecture description and its latency/bandwidth characterization for all supported links, two real world use cases will be presented: the GPU-based low level trigger for the RICH detector in the NA62 experiment at CERN and the on-/off-shore data link for KM3 underwater neutrino telescope.
technical_mechanism: Common-clock communication/compute interval decomposition: use the x86 TSC to measure packet-send-to-receive-buffer-ready time, then measure the serialized CUDA-kernel interval separately.
why_it_works: The two intervals identify whether delay occurs before GPU input is available or during kernel execution, rather than treating end-to-end latency as one number. The paper demonstrates this on a system-loopback path; it does not isolate server queueing or prove that the communication interval is pure network delay.
root_seam: At the server, correlate a request ID with timestamps for send/transport events, NIC receive or buffer-ready, queue admission, kernel start, and kernel end. This decomposition would show whether a tail occurs before GPU data readiness, in server queueing, or during GPU compute. The paper's loopback measurement is not evidence about a robot-to-server path.
experiment: Replay identical inference requests while injecting controlled transport delay and, separately, server queueing and GPU workload. Capture synchronized per-request transport/buffer-ready, queue, and kernel timestamps; test whether the communication interval rises under transport injection while queue and kernel intervals remain stable, and whether the other injections produce their respective interval changes.
evidence_quote: Exploiting the x86 Time Stamp Counter (TSC) register as a common time reference, it was possible in a single process test application to measure latency as time difference between when a received buffer is signalled to the application and the moment before the first UDP packet of a bunch (needed to fill the receive buffer) is sent through the host GbE port. Communication and kernel processing tasks were serialized in order to perform the measure
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, section II-B, “Results”
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The measurement supports separating communication from kernel processing in the stated loopback benchmark, but does not distinguish network transit from host-side receive or queueing delay. It reports no per-request tail diagnosis and does not establish performance on a remote robot-inference path.

title: Trading off Worst and Expected Cost in Decision Tree Problems and a Value Dependent Model
abstract: We study the problem of evaluating a discrete function by adaptively querying the values of its variables until the values read uniquely determine the value of the function. Reading the value of a variable is done at the expense of some cost, and the goal is to design a strategy (decision tree) for evaluating the function incurring as little cost as possible in the worst case or in expectation (according to a prior distribution on the possible variables assignments). Except for particular cases of the problem, in general, only the minimization of one of these two measures is addressed in the literature. However, there are instances of the problem for which the minimization of one measure leads to a strategy with a high cost with respect to the other measure (even exponentially bigger than the optimal). We provide a new construction which can guarantee a trade-off between the two criteria. More precisely, given a decision tree guaranteeing expected cost E and a decision tree guaranteeing worst cost W our method can guarantee for any chosen trade-off value ρ to produce a decision tree whose worst cost is (1 + ρ)W and whose expected cost is (1 + 1ρ)E. These bounds are improved for the relevant case of uniform testing costs. Motivated by applications, we also study a variant of the problem where the cost of reading a variable depends on the variable's value. We provide an O(n) approximation algorithm for the minimization of the worst cost measure, which is best possible under the assumption P ≠ NP.
technical_mechanism: Adaptive cost-aware test selection: DividePairs chooses a test based on the maximum, over its possible outcomes, of outcome-specific test cost divided by the number of separable object pairs that outcome eliminates, then recurses on each resulting group.
why_it_works: The test sequence adapts to earlier outcomes and targets distinctions between different-class candidates, rather than collecting a fixed set of measurements. Accounting for outcome-dependent costs can prioritize measurements that separate more plausible competing causes per unit cost. This provides a concrete diagnostic operation for the lane, though it does not itself model noisy probes or network-layer causes.
root_seam: Represent candidate regression causes as objects or classes and available Root-side measurements as tests, with observed outcomes and costs. Attach at request identity and collect only the tests selected by the current candidate set. Tests could include robot/server transport timestamps or packet/ACK/loss observations, queue/NIC signals, and server or action-stage timings. Their outcomes can narrow causes, while stage-specific tests help avoid conflating network delay with queueing, GPU compute, or action application. No access to Reflex private infrastructure is assumed.
experiment: Create controlled Root replays with known regression causes and an explicit candidate-cause-to-test outcome model. Compare DividePairs' adaptive measurements with a fixed measurement set and a non-adaptive sequence. Measure diagnostic cost, number of measurements to identify the cause, worst-case cost, and identification accuracy; separately check whether network-tail causes are distinguished from server queueing, GPU compute, and action application.
evidence_quote: Our algorithm, called DividePairs, chooses the test t that minimizes:
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section 3, “A logarithmic approximation for value dependent testing costs”; the following displayed objective is max_i c^i(t)/(P(S) − P(S_t^i)).
reported_gain: Theoretical O(log n) approximation for binary tests with value-dependent costs; no Root or network-diagnosis gain reported.
baseline: Theoretical comparison is to the minimum worst testing cost for the abstract decision-tree problem; no Root diagnostic baseline is reported.
uncertainty: Transfer depends on having a useful cause-to-test outcome model and meaningful test costs. The paper analyzes abstract discrete-function testing, not network telemetry or noisy causal diagnosis; Root gains and diagnostic accuracy are unknown.

title: RepNet: Cutting Tail Latency in Data Center Networks with Flow Replication
abstract: Data center networks need to provide low latency, especially at the tail, as demanded by many interactive applications. To improve tail latency, existing approaches require modifications to switch hardware and/or end-host operating systems, making them difficult to be deployed. We present the design, implementation, and evaluation of RepNet, an application layer transport that can be deployed today. RepNet exploits the fact that only a few paths among many are congested at any moment in the network, and applies simple flow replication to mice flows to opportunistically use the less congested path. RepNet has two designs for flow replication: (1) RepSYN, which only replicates SYN packets and uses the first connection that finishes TCP handshaking for data transmission, and (2) RepFlow which replicates the entire mice flow. We implement RepNet on node.js, one of the most commonly used platforms for networked interactive applications. node's single threaded event-loop and non-blocking I/O make flow replication highly efficient. Performance evaluation on a real network testbed and in Mininet reveals that RepNet is able to reduce the tail latency of mice flows, as well as application completion times, by more than 50%.
technical_mechanism: For mice flows, RepSYN opens two TCP connections with distinct five-tuples and sends a SYN on each; it sends data only on the connection whose TCP handshake completes first, closing the other. The first handshake acts as an active probe: SYN delay reflects congestion on that path. RepFlow instead duplicates the entire mice flow and uses the first copy to complete.
why_it_works: With ECMP, connections with different five-tuples can take different paths, and congestion is often transient and isolated to a subset of paths. Racing the handshakes makes it more likely that the selected connection avoids a congested path; full-flow replication can additionally tolerate losses. This reduces exposure to network-path delay, but does not by itself distinguish network delay from server queueing, compute, or action-application delay.
root_seam: A plausible Root experiment is to race two robot-to-cloud transport connections for a request, timestamp both SYN/handshake completion events, and use the winning connection for inference traffic. This could reveal whether an occasional slow path explains request tails and reduce tail exposure without access to private infrastructure. Transfer depends on the robot/cloud transport and routing allowing distinct connections to traverse meaningfully different paths; the paper does not establish this for robot action loops.
experiment: The paper evaluates RepFlow and RepSYN against Linux TCP Cubic on a real testbed and in Mininet, measuring mice-flow completion time and distributed bucket-sort job completion time under varying loads. It also evaluates incast behavior. A controlled Root test could compare ordinary transport with RepSYN-style handshake racing under injected or naturally occurring path congestion, recording per-connection handshake and request timestamps and separating transport time from server inference and action-application time.
evidence_quote: The idea is simple: Before transmitting data, we establish two TCP connections as in RepFlow. However data is only transmitted using the first established connection, and the other is ended immediately. Essentially SYN is used to probe the network and find a better path. The delay experienced by the SYN reflects the latest congestion condition of the corresponding path.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, section II.C, “RepNet Design” (RepSYN description).
reported_gain: The abstract reports more than 50% reduction in tail latency of mice flows and application completion times. In the bucket-sort experiment, the 99.9th-percentile job completion time is reported reduced by 45%, and the 99th percentile by 50%.
baseline: Linux TCP Cubic / stack TCP.
uncertainty: The supplied context demonstrates latency reduction, not diagnostic accuracy or localization of a particular tail cause. It does not establish whether robot-to-cloud connections can select sufficiently diverse paths, or how replication overhead and duplicate-request semantics would interact with remote inference.

title: An Adaptive Load Balancing to Provide Quality of Service
abstract: In order to utilize network resources and provide a more reliable delivery of information, multipath routing algorithms are used with a higher priority than single path routing. But providing the quality of service (QoS) requirements while load balancing is done among multiple paths is still a challenge. In this paper a new load balancing algorithm is proposed by using an explicit endpoint admission control (EEAC) to achieve a dynamic load balancing algorithm, with the ability to guarantee the end-to-end QoS for a variety of service classes. The simulation results for non deterministic network conditions show that the proposed algorithm increases the utilization of network resources and also decreases the end-to-end delay.
technical_mechanism: Periodic probes carry compact, per-service-class congestion state: routers exponentially smooth arrival rate and buffer length, calculate remaining buffer space, and compare it with the prior router's value. The path bottleneck is recorded in the probe and returned to the destination. This is a lightweight queue-hotspot localization signal, not merely end-to-end delay logging or load balancing.
why_it_works: Remaining buffer space is a router-local congestion indicator. Comparing it along the path identifies where buffer pressure is greatest, while smoothing makes the observation less sensitive to bursts. Root could use that compact signal to test whether a network queue hotspot accompanies a tail-latency regression, without retaining a full packet trace. It does not by itself attribute delay to a specific inference request or separate network delay from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application.
root_seam: Attach a probe or flow identity and timestamp to robot/server transport events, and collect the probe's bottleneck-router annotation plus compact per-class buffer observations. Compare these with request latency and transport timestamps; do not assume access to the paper's network infrastructure.
experiment: During remote inference, inject a controlled queue bottleneck at a known network hop, then compare probe-localized bottlenecks and their timing against packet-level transport timestamps or a full trace. Include a server-queueing-only control. Measure localization accuracy for network-tail requests and telemetry volume, and check whether probe identity and cadence permit useful correlation.
evidence_quote: As the probing packet goes through the path, the remaining buffer spaces of all classes in each router are compared to the values of previous router and the bottleneck of the network is detected and inserted in the probing packets.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section 2.2, “Decision function and load balancing parameter.”
reported_gain: The abstract reports increased network utilization and decreased end-to-end delay; numeric gain is UNKNOWN. No diagnostic-accuracy gain is reported.
baseline: The simulations compare a single-path scenario with a two-path load-balancing scenario; this is not a diagnostic baseline.
uncertainty: The method gives periodic path-probe congestion localization, not per-inference-request attribution. The paper does not evaluate tail-latency diagnosis, correlation with request identity, or separation of network delay from server-side and application delays. Root gains are UNKNOWN.

title: On Crowdsourced Interactive Live Streaming: A Twitch.TV-Based Measurement Study
abstract: Empowered by today's rich tools for media generation and collaborative production, the multimedia service paradigm is shifting from the conventional single source, to multi-source, to many sources, and now toward crowdsource. Such crowdsourced live streaming platforms as Twitch.tv allow general users to broadcast their content to massive viewers, thereby greatly expanding the content and user bases. The resources available for these non-professional broadcasters however are limited and unstable, which potentially impair the streaming quality and viewers' experience. The diverse live interactions among the broadcasters and viewers can further aggravate the problem. In this paper, we present an initial investigation on the modern crowdsourced live streaming systems. Taking Twitch as a representative, we outline their inside architecture using both crawled data and captured traffic of local broadcasters/viewers. Closely examining the access data collected in a two-month period, we reveal that the view patterns are determined by both events and broadcasters' sources. Our measurements explore the unique source- and event-driven views, showing that the current delay strategy on the viewer's side substantially impacts the viewers' interactive experience, and there is significant disparity between the long broadcast latency and the short live messaging latency. On the broadcaster's side, the dynamic uploading capacity is a critical challenge, which noticeably affects the smoothness of live streaming for viewers.
technical_mechanism: Controlled source-uplink capacity step-down and restoration, correlated with source-side dropped frames and viewer-side broadcast latency.
why_it_works: The intervention changes broadcaster upload capacity while observing both a source-side symptom (dropped frames) and an end-to-end outcome (viewer broadcast latency). Their stepwise worsening as capacity falls, followed by only slight latency reduction after capacity is restored, supports a causal contribution from the source uplink and exposes possible lingering effects. This is more diagnostic than passive latency logging, though it does not fully decompose network delay from platform processing.
root_seam: At the robot upload and server receipt boundaries, correlate request IDs and timestamps with transport or upload-capacity signals, server queueing, GPU compute, and action-application timings. The paper’s controlled uplink intervention transfers as a way to test whether an inference tail begins in transport without access to Twitch’s infrastructure.
experiment: Replay equivalent remote-inference requests under randomized, controlled robot-uplink bandwidth steps, including an unconstrained condition and restoration. Record per-request upload/receipt times, packet or transport signals, queueing, GPU, and action-application durations; compare tail latency and dropped or delayed requests across conditions and after restoration.
evidence_quote: the number of total dropped frames consistently grows with decreasing the uploading bandwidth on the broadcaster’s side. In the meantime, the broadcast latency on the viewer’s side also suffers the stepwise rise
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section IV-D, “Impacts of Broadcaster’s sources”
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: Controlled conditions include No Limit; the paper reports latency rises as upload bandwidth decreases, not a numerical improvement over that condition.
uncertainty: The intervention supports a source-uplink diagnosis, but the reported viewer broadcast latency is not decomposed into transport, platform queueing, and processing. The study does not report inference request tails or a Root-measured gain.

title: Scalability and Dimensioning of Network-Capacity Measurement System using Reflecting Servers
abstract: In a class of methods for measurement of available path capacity and other capacity-related metrics in a network, trains of probe packets are transmitted from a sender to a receiver across a network path, and the sequences of time stamps at sending and reception are analyzed. In large-scale implementations there may potentially be interference between the probe-packet trains corresponding to several concurrent measurement sessions, due to congestion in the network and common measurement end points. This paper outlines principles for large-scale deployments of network capacity measurement methods using standardized network functionality. Further, the paper provides an in-depth study of dimensioning and scalability challenges related to the measurement end-points of such systems. The main result is a framework for dimensioning of large-scale network capacity measurement systems based on TWAMP. The framework is based on a method for explicit calculation of queuelength and waiting-time distributions, where results from M/G/1 queuing theory are combined with Monte Carlo integration.
technical_mechanism: Use TWAMP probe trains with sender- and reflector-side timestamps, then model the reflector’s non-interleaving output queue as an M/G/1 system and compute queue-length and waiting-time distributions using Monte Carlo integration. This estimates endpoint queueing separately from path delay.
why_it_works: The timestamped probes provide measurements across the path, while the queue model quantifies waiting caused by overlapping trains at a shared reflector. Comparing measured delay with the modeled reflector waiting-time distribution could expose whether a tail is consistent with endpoint queue buildup rather than network-path delay. The model does not identify which competing flow caused the buildup.
root_seam: Attach TWAMP-like probes and timestamping at the robot and inference server, with transport or reflector-side timestamps where available. Compare end-to-end delay against measured endpoint queue occupancy and the modeled waiting-time distribution to separate network and endpoint queueing; retain request identity to align probes with inference requests.
experiment: In a controlled Root test, vary concurrent probe or request-train intensity and train service times at a shared endpoint while holding path conditions and inference workload constant. Compare predicted M/G/1 queue-length and waiting-time quantiles with observed endpoint queueing and request-delay tails; separately record path timestamps to check whether the excess delay is network or endpoint queueing.
evidence_quote: we compute the cumulative distribution functions for the out queue length and the waiting time for a train in the queue, for different values of the critical parameters.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section IV, “The Node Scalability Challenge.”
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The paper studies capacity-measurement reflector scalability and queue dimensioning, not diagnosis of robot inference requests. It does not establish per-request attribution to competing flows, tail-triggered retention, or a streaming diagnosis result. The proposed Root experiment is a transfer, not a reported evaluation.

title: PCS: Predictive Component-level Scheduling for Reducing Tail Latency in Cloud Online Services
abstract: Modern latency-critical online services often rely on composing results from a large number of server components. Hence the tail latency (e.g. the 99th percentile of response time), rather than the average, of these components determines the overall service performance. When hosted on a cloud environment, the components of a service typically co-locate with short batch jobs to increase machine utilizations, and share and contend resources such as caches and I/O bandwidths with them. The highly dynamic nature of batch jobs in terms of their workload types and input sizes causes continuously changing performance interference to individual components, hence leading to their latency variability and high tail latency. However, existing techniques either ignore such fine-grained component latency variability when managing service performance, or rely on executing redundant requests to reduce the tail latency, which adversely deteriorate the service performance when load gets heavier. In this paper, we propose PCS, a predictive and component-level scheduling framework to reduce tail latency for large-scale, parallel online services. It uses an analytical performance model to simultaneously predict the component latency and the overall service performance on different nodes. Based on the predicted performance, the scheduler identifies straggling components and conducts near-optimal component-node allocations to adapt to the changing performance interferences from batch jobs. We demonstrate that, using realistic workloads, the proposed scheduler reduces the component tail latency by an average of 67.05% and the average overall service latency by 64.16% compared with the state-of-the-art techniques on reducing tail latency.
technical_mechanism: Estimate component service time from measured resource-contention signals, then use request arrival rate and service-time statistics in an M/G/1 model to estimate latency including queueing. This creates separate service-time and queueing contributions rather than treating observed latency as one undifferentiated cause.
why_it_works: When predicted service time rises with contention, the model points to resource interference; when service time is stable but the modeled queueing contribution rises with arrival rate and utilization, it points to queue buildup. The paper applies this model to scheduling rather than validating tail-cause diagnosis, but the separation itself is testable for Root.
root_seam: Join request identity and robot/server timestamps to server-side arrival-rate measurements, per-component service-time observations, and resource-contention counters. Compare observed latency against estimated service and queueing contributions. This could help distinguish server queue buildup from resource-related service slowdown, but does not by itself isolate network delay from GPU compute or action application.
experiment: Replay identical inference requests in a controlled factorial test: vary server arrival rate while holding resource contention low, then hold arrival rate steady while introducing measured network-bandwidth contention. Record request-level queue wait, service time, network events, and end-to-end latency. Test whether the model attributes queue-dominated tails to arrival-rate-driven queueing and contention-dominated tails to service-time changes; include an uncongested baseline.
evidence_quote: The extended model further considers the request queueing delay and estimates the latency of the whole service based on its implementation topology.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, introduction, contributions describing the extended performance model.
reported_gain: 67.05% reduction in component 99th-percentile latency and 64.16% reduction in average overall service latency.
baseline: Request redundancy and request reissue techniques (RED-3, RED-5, RI-90, and RI-99).
uncertainty: The model is evaluated for prediction and scheduling, not for request-level tail-cause diagnosis. Its queueing estimate depends on an M/G/1 assumption and monitored arrival rate and service-time statistics. Although network bandwidth is included among shared-resource signals, the paper does not identify individual off-path flows or separate network delay from other service-time causes; therefore n02 is not promoted.

title: YTrace: End-to-end Performance Diagnosis in Large Cloud and Content Providers
abstract: Content providers build serving stacks to deliver content to users. An important goal of a content provider is to ensure good user experience, since user experience has an impact on revenue. In this paper, we describe a system at Yahoo called YTrace that diagnoses bad user experience in near real time. We present the different components of YTrace for end-to-end multi-layer diagnosis (instrumentation, methods and backend system), and the system architecture for delivering diagnosis in near real time across all user sessions at Yahoo. YTrace diagnoses problems across service and network layers in the end-to-end path spanning user host, Internet, CDN and the datacenters, and has three diagnosis goals: detection, localization and root cause analysis (including cascading problems) of performance problems in user sessions with the cloud. The key component of the methods in YTrace is capturing and discovering causality, which we design based on a mix of instrumentation API, domain knowledge and blackbox methods. We show three case studies from production that span a large-scale distributed storage system, a datacenter-wide network, and an end-to-end video serving stack at Yahoo. We end by listing a number of open directions for performance diagnosis in cloud and content providers.
technical_mechanism: YTrace records causal relationships and timestamps at RPC request/response edges, uses those relationships to compute a session’s latency critical path, and estimates variable RPC network delay by subtracting the minimum observed one-way delay in a recent time window. It flags RPCs whose estimated queueing delay is significant relative to end-to-end latency, then associates them with possible network problems using device syslogs and topology.
why_it_works: The critical path identifies RPCs that contributed to a slow session, while the recent-window minimum estimates relatively constant delay and leaves variable delay as a candidate queueing component. This offers a way to focus diagnosis on transport-involved RPCs rather than treating total session latency as a single cause. Syslog correlation can add candidate network-device problems, but does not establish that a device problem caused the RPC delay.
root_seam: Attach request identity and edge timestamps at the robot and inference service, then apply the variable-delay estimate to transport events for critical-path requests. Compare transport delay with server queueing, GPU execution, and action-application timestamps. YTrace's device-syslog correlation is only suggestive; it does not prove a network-device problem caused a slow RPC, and it relies on infrastructure-specific syslogs and topology.
experiment: Replay matched remote-inference requests while independently injecting network queueing and server-side queueing or compute delay. Record request/response edge timestamps and the minimum one-way delay over a recent window; test whether flagged variable delay rises for network-injected tails but not for server-only tails. Separately measure whether correlated network syslogs identify candidate devices without treating correlation as causal proof.
evidence_quote: YTrace estimates queueing delay during the RPC as dAB(e) = CfB(e) − CfA(e) − min∆(dAB), where the min is taken over the recent ∆ time window
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, datacenter network diagnosis section.
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The supplied text gives a concrete variable-delay estimate and critical-path operation, but does not report a controlled diagnostic accuracy or gain. It explicitly says the relationship between network problems and RPC performance remains to be established; syslog-based results list possible problems. Applicability to robot-to-cloud action loops and streaming is plausible but not demonstrated for those settings.

title: Micro-burst in Data Centers: Observations, Implications, and Applications
abstract: Micro-burst traffic is not uncommon in data centers. It can cause packet dropping, which results in serious performance degradation (e.g., Incast problem). However, current solutions that attempt to suppress micro-burst traffic are extrinsic and ad hoc, since they lack the comprehensive and essential understanding of micro-burst's root cause and dynamic behavior. On the other hand, traditional studies focus on traffic burstiness in a single flow, while in data centers micro-burst traffic could occur with highly fan-in communication pattern, and its dynamic behavior is still unclear. To this end, in this paper we re-examine the micro-burst traffic in typical data center scenarios. We find that evolution of micro-burst is determined by both TCP's self-clocking mechanism and bottleneck link. Besides, dynamic behaviors of micro-burst under various scenarios can all be described by the slope of queue length increasing. Our observations also implicate that conventional solutions like absorbing and pacing are ineffective to mitigate micro-burst traffic. Instead, senders need to slow down as soon as possible. Inspired by the findings and insights from experimental observations, we propose S-ECN policy, which is an ECN marking policy leveraging the slope of queue length increasing. Transport protocols utilizing S-ECN policy can suppress the sharp queue length increment by over 50%, and reduce the 99th percentile of query completion time by 20%.
technical_mechanism: Embed a timestamp and switch output-queue length in each packet, then analyze per-packet queue-length evolution and its slope to characterize microbursts and aggregation at a bottleneck.
why_it_works: Fine-grained queue samples expose rapid queue growth that coarse switch monitoring can miss. Queue-growth patterns reflect aggregated traffic behavior; the paper reports that their slopes vary with fan-in and background-flow scenarios, helping distinguish queue buildup and possible upstream hidden-buffer effects from other causes.
root_seam: At a robot-side or server-side transport event, correlate request timing or packet identity with per-packet switch queue samples. This could show whether a slow request coincided with bottleneck queue growth, including growth intensified by background traffic or an upstream hidden buffer. The context does not establish direct per-request attribution.
experiment: In a controlled remote-inference test, retain packet timestamps and queue lengths at a candidate bottleneck while varying fan-in concurrency and adding background traffic. Compare queue-slope patterns for tail requests against request latency and separately measured server queueing, GPU compute, and action-application time.
evidence_quote: whenever a packet is passing through the switch, we let it carry the timestamp and current queue length in its payload.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, paragraph beginning “cause the queue length changes every a few microseconds.”
reported_gain: S-ECN suppresses sharp queue-length increment by over 50% and reduces 99th-percentile query completion time by 20%.
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The paper measures data-center switch queues and proposes a congestion-control policy, not remote robot inference. It does not establish request-level attribution or show that queue telemetry alone can separate network delay from server-side queueing, GPU compute, or action application. No sketch or compact sufficient-summary mechanism is described.

title: Performance Characterization of a Commercial Video Streaming Service
abstract: Despite the growing popularity of video streaming over the Internet, problems such as re-buffering and high startup latency continue to plague users. In this paper, we present an end-to-end characterization of Yahoo's video streaming service, analyzing over 500 million video chunks downloaded over a two-week period. We gain unique visibility into the causes of performance degradation by instrumenting both the CDN server and the client player at the chunk level, while also collecting frequent snapshots of TCP variables from the server network stack. We uncover a range of performance issues, including an asynchronous disk-read timer and cache misses at the server, high latency and latency variability in the network, and buffering delays and dropped frames at the client. Looking across chunks in the same session, or destined to the same IP prefix, we see how some performance problems are relatively persistent, depending on the video's popularity, the distance between the client and server, and the client's operating system, browser, and Flash runtime.
technical_mechanism: Join client- and CDN-side measurements per video chunk, decompose first-byte delay into network, server, backend, and client-stack components, and sample the server TCP connection’s RTT, RTT variability, retransmissions, and congestion window every 500 ms. Aggregate RTT samples by session and client prefix to distinguish transient from persistent high-latency paths.
why_it_works: The joined measurements prevent client-observed delay from being automatically attributed to the network: server-side service timing and TCP-stack signals help separate network behavior from CDN and client download-stack delay. Repeated measurements across chunks and prefixes reveal whether a high RTT is persistent rather than a one-off spike.
root_seam: Attach request or inference identity and timestamps to robot-side and server-side transport events; collect available TCP RTT, variation, retransmission, and congestion-window signals alongside server queue and compute timings. Aggregate comparable requests by robot or path to identify persistent network tails without conflating them with server queueing or inference execution.
experiment: On a fixed set of remote inference requests, compare existing end-to-end latency monitoring with per-request joined client/server timing and periodic transport-state snapshots. Blindly classify injected network delay, server queueing, and client-side buffering, then compare tail attribution accuracy and localization; also test whether grouping repeated requests by robot/path distinguishes persistent from transient network tails.
evidence_quote: To isolate network performance from end-host performance, we measure the end-to-end network path at the CDN host kernel’s TCP stack.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, instrumentation and TCP measurement discussion following the end-to-end latency decomposition.
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The context supports the diagnostic operation and its network-versus-end-host rationale, but does not report a controlled diagnostic-accuracy comparison. Transfer to Root depends on access to corresponding transport signals and reliable request identity across robot and server measurements.

title: Near-optimal Bayesian Active Learning with Correlated and Noisy Tests
abstract: We consider the Bayesian active learning and experimental design problem, where the goal is to learn the value of some unknown target variable through a sequence of informative, noisy tests. In contrast to prior work, we focus on the challenging, yet practically relevant setting where test outcomes can be conditionally dependent given the hidden target variable. Under such assumptions, common heuristics, such as greedily performing tests that maximize the reduction in uncertainty of the target, often perform poorly. In this paper, we propose ECED, a novel, computationally efficient active learning algorithm, and prove strong theoretical guarantees that hold with correlated, noisy tests. Rather than directly optimizing the prediction error, at each step, ECED picks the test that maximizes the gain in a surrogate objective, which takes into account the dependencies between tests. Our analysis relies on an information-theoretic auxiliary function to track the progress of ECED, and utilizes adaptive submodularity to attain the near-optimal bound. We demonstrate strong empirical performance of ECED on two problem instances, including a Bayesian experimental design task intended to distinguish among economic theories of how people make risky decisions, and an active preference learning task via pairwise comparisons.
technical_mechanism: Dependency-aware adaptive test selection: after each noisy test, ECED selects the next test by maximizing a surrogate objective that accounts for dependencies among test outcomes.
why_it_works: When candidate measurements are correlated given the hidden cause, treating them as independent can waste tests on redundant evidence. Selecting with those dependencies in view can yield more diagnostic information per measurement and help distinguish causes with fewer tests.
root_seam: Attach to Root's choice of follow-up measurements for a regressed request. Candidate tests could include robot/server transport timestamps, packet or ACK/loss evidence, queue and NIC signals, and compute timings. Their outcome dependencies would need to be modeled; this could help select a compact set of measurements to distinguish network delay from queueing, GPU compute, or action application.
experiment: On controlled requests with injected network and non-network regressions, compare ECED-selected diagnostic measurements with greedy uncertainty-reduction and random selection under equal measurement budgets. Measure cause-identification accuracy and tests needed to identify the cause, using held-out requests and a fixed candidate-test set.
evidence_quote: at each step, ECED picks the test that maximizes the gain in a surrogate objective, which takes into account the dependencies between tests.
evidence_location: Supplied abstract
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The abstract supports dependency-aware adaptive test selection and reports empirical evaluation on two other tasks, but provides no details here about the surrogate, measured gains, or applicability to network-tail diagnosis. Root would need suitable candidate tests and a model of their conditional dependencies.

title: Adaptive Submodular Ranking and Routing
abstract: We study a general stochastic ranking problem where an algorithm needs to adaptively select a sequence of elements so as to "cover" a random scenario (drawn from a known distribution) at minimum expected cost. The coverage of each scenario is captured by an individual submodular function, where the scenario is said to be covered when its function value goes above a given threshold. We obtain a logarithmic factor approximation algorithm for this adaptive ranking problem, which is the best possible (unless P=NP). This problem unifies and generalizes many previously studied problems with applications in search ranking and active learning. The approximation ratio of our algorithm either matches or improves the best result known in each of these special cases. Furthermore, we extend our results to an adaptive vehicle routing problem, where costs are determined by an underlying metric. This routing problem is a significant generalization of the previously-studied adaptive traveling salesman and traveling repairman problems. Our approximation ratio nearly matches the best bound known for these special cases. Finally, we present experimental results for some applications of adaptive ranking.
technical_mechanism: Adaptive scenario-aware probe selection: after each probe outcome, update the compatible scenarios and select the next probe using a score combining expected progress toward coverage with information gain about the realized scenario.
why_it_works: Probe outcomes eliminate incompatible causes, so subsequent measurements can be chosen to distinguish the remaining candidates while also advancing a stopping objective. This is more than logging or thresholding: it provides a principled way to select measurements adaptively when probes have different costs and diagnostic value. The paper describes the selection rule and applies it to optimal decision trees, making a controlled Root test plausible, though not establishing network-specific performance.
root_seam: At a request or inference-stage boundary, record probe identity, outcome, and cost against a request ID. Represent candidate causes—such as transport delay, server queueing, GPU compute, or action application—as scenarios with predicted outcomes for available probes. Root could use the observed outcomes to select the next measurement and obtain a diagnosis with fewer or lower-cost probes. The paper does not supply a network-specific scenario model.
experiment: On controlled remote-inference requests, inject known causes spanning transport delay, server queueing, GPU compute, and action application. Compare the paper-style adaptive selection rule with a fixed probe sequence under the same probe budget and costs. Measure cause-identification accuracy and number/cost of probes, and verify that network delay is distinguished from non-network stages.
evidence_quote: Our algorithm for ASR involves repeatedly selecting an element that maximizes a combination of (i) the expected increase in function value relative to the target of one, and (ii) a measure of gain in identifying the realized scenario.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, “Outline of key techniques.”
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The operation and its scenario-identification purpose are explicit, and the paper reports experiments on optimal decision trees. It does not show that its probes are network measurements, validate a network-cause model, or report gains in a Root setting.

title: Randomised Relevance Model
abstract: Relevance Models are well-known retrieval models and capable of producing competitive results. However, because they use query expansion they can be very slow. We address this slowness by incorporating two variants of locality sensitive hashing (LSH) into the query expansion process. Results on two document collections suggest that we can obtain large reductions in the amount of work, with a small reduction in effectiveness. Our approach is shown to be additive when pruning query terms.
technical_mechanism: Index historical request signatures with locality-sensitive hashing, then use multi-probe lookup to retrieve signatures in nearby buckets as candidates for comparison. The operation is approximate similar-request retrieval, not network-tail detection by itself.
why_it_works: Hashing avoids an exhaustive search through the history; probing nearby buckets can recover similar candidates missed by the exact query bucket, while trading probe count against retrieval work. For Root, comparing a regressed request with retrieved healthy counterparts could expose which transport or runtime events differ, provided the indexed signatures preserve those events.
root_seam: Attach at historical trace lookup: build signatures from request identity and available robot/server timestamps, transport events, and queue or compute spans; retrieve comparable healthy requests before doing a full history scan. This could reduce baseline-search work and supply concrete comparison traces, but the paper does not show how to construct useful robot-inference signatures or distinguish network delay from other delay sources.
experiment: Create a fixed corpus of healthy Root traces and held-out requests, then inject network-tail delays into a controlled subset. Compare multi-probe LSH retrieval with exhaustive nearest-neighbor search using the same trace signatures. Measure lookup work and latency, whether retrieved healthy traces are comparable, and whether those comparisons localize the injected network delay separately from queueing, GPU compute, and action application. Treat all Root outcomes as experimental, not as gains established by this paper.
evidence_quote: The probing sequence is directed by the shortest hamming distance between the hash-code of the query and hash-codes corresponding with adjacent bucket.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section 3, “Multi Probe Randomised Relevance Model”
reported_gain: MP-RRM reduces complexity by 37.5% on TDT1 and 42.24% on TREC-ROBUST versus RRM; these are paper-reported retrieval results, not Root gains.
baseline: Standard Relevance Model (RM); MP-RRM is also compared with RRM.
uncertainty: The paper supports faster approximate retrieval of similar objects, but does not evaluate historical robot-request traces, define a signature that preserves diagnostic information, or demonstrate network-tail localization. Root gains and diagnostic accuracy are unknown.

title: A New Queue Discipline for Reducing Bufferbloat Effects in HetNet Concurrent Multipath Transfer
abstract: Heterogeneous wireless networks have evolved to reach application requirements for low latency and high throughput on Internet access. Recent studies have improved network performance employing the Multipath TCP, which aggregates flows from heterogeneous wireless interfaces in a single connection. Although existing proposals are powerful, coupled congestion control algorithms are currently limited because of the high variation in path delays, bandwidth and loss rate, typical from heterogeneous wireless networks, even more over concurrent multipath transmissions. These transmissions experience bufferbloat, i.e., high delays caused by long queues. Hence, to cope with the current limitations, this work presents CoDel-LIFO, a new active queue management (AQM) discipline to reduce the dropped packet ratio in the Multipath TCP congestion control mechanism. Differently from other approaches, CoDel-LIFO gives priority to the most recent packets, being then promising. This paper provides a detailed simulation analysis over congestion control algorithms by comparing CoDel-LIFO to CoDel and DropTail disciplines. Results indicate that CoDel-LIFO reduces queue drops, diminishing the impact on congestion control; improving substantially the goodput; and keeping RTT low.
technical_mechanism: Measure packet sojourn time from enqueue and dequeue timestamps, then use persistent delay above a configured target to identify queue buildup. The transferable diagnostic operation is per-packet queue-residence measurement with a persistence rule—not CoDel-LIFO’s LIFO forwarding or forgiveness policy.
why_it_works: Queue residence time measures delay at the queue itself, rather than inferring its source from end-to-end latency. At an instrumented bottleneck, elevated residence time aligned with a request’s packets would expose network queueing as a contributor to a tail event, separately from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application. The paper describes the signal and congestion rule, though it uses them for queue control rather than request-tail diagnosis.
root_seam: Instrument enqueue and dequeue timestamps at a robot-path gateway or other accessible bottleneck, and correlate packet identity or transport-flow timestamps with Root request identity and end-to-end timing. This would add a direct measurement of delay at that queue; Root's ability to instrument such a point is unknown.
experiment: In a controlled Root test, add a bottleneck queue and record per-packet enqueue/dequeue times alongside request identity, transport timing, server queueing, GPU, and action-application timings. Compare queue residence during tail and non-tail requests, and test whether persistent above-target residence identifies queue-driven tails when the other timings do not. Do not treat the paper's simulation results as a Root gain.
evidence_quote: CoDel uses the packet sojourn time on queue as a metric to predict a congestion and control the queue size.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section III, “Path Delay Management with CoDel.”
reported_gain: Average goodput is reported as at least 20% higher with CoDel-LIFO than with CoDel; RTT is reported to remain low. Simulation results, not Root results.
baseline: CoDel; the evaluation also compares against DropTail.
uncertainty: The text supports queue-residence measurement as a congestion signal, but does not evaluate it as a retained diagnostic trace or correlate it with inference requests. Whether Root can instrument and correlate an on-path queue is unknown.

title: Dapper: Data Plane Performance Diagnosis of TCP
abstract: With more applications moving to the cloud, cloud providers need to diagnose performance problems in a timely manner. Offline processing of logs is slow and inefficient, and instrumenting the end-host network stack would violate the tenants' rights to manage their own virtual machines (VMs). Instead, our Dapper system analyzes TCP performance in real time near the end-hosts (e.g., at the hypervisor, NIC, or top-of-rack switch). Dapper determines whether a connection is limited by the sender (e.g., a slow server competing for shared resources), the network (e.g., congestion), or the receiver (e.g., small receive buffer). Emerging edge devices now offer flexible packet processing at high speed on commodity hardware, making it possible to monitor TCP performance in the data plane, at line rate. We use P4 to prototype Dapper and evaluate our design on real and synthetic traffic. To reduce the data-plane state requirements, we perform lightweight detection for all connections, followed by heavier-weight diagnosis just for the troubled connections.
technical_mechanism: At the network edge, Dapper tracks TCP flow state from packet headers, sequence numbers, ACKs, and timestamps. It first collects lightweight metrics for every connection and uses flow rate as a badness signal; troubled connections receive heavier diagnosis. For those flows, it infers loss and retransmission type, passive RTT, flight size and congestion-window behavior, receive-window limits, and sender reaction time, then uses these signals to classify sender-, network-, or receiver-limited performance.
why_it_works: Observing both directions of a flow near the sender allows Dapper to relate data packets to ACKs and infer transport state without modifying the tenant’s host stack. Its cross-layer heuristics help separate sender delay from network loss or path latency and receiver constraints. The lightweight-first, heavy-diagnosis-second design focuses per-flow state on connections flagged as troubled.
root_seam: Attach packet timestamps and request/flow identity at the robot-side or server-side transport boundary, or at an accessible network edge. Compare send-to-ACK RTT, retransmissions, and flight/window behavior for slow versus healthy requests. This could reveal transport loss or elevated path latency and help distinguish those from sender-side delay; it does not directly measure remote inference queues or GPU execution.
experiment: Replay matched healthy and slow remote-inference requests while collecting edge packet/ACK timestamps and flow state. Use a lightweight per-flow rate trigger to retain heavier transport metrics only for flagged requests. Inject network loss or latency separately from server queueing and GPU delay, then test whether the retained signals classify network-limited tails and distinguish them from non-network causes. Measure classification accuracy and monitoring state/CPU overhead against always-on detailed collection.
evidence_quote: To reduce the data-plane state requirements, we perform lightweight detection for all connections, followed by heavier-weight diagnosis just for the troubled connections.
evidence_location: Abstract; selected PDF text, Introduction and Section 5 discussion of two-phase monitoring.
reported_gain: Average diagnosis accuracy of 94% in controlled tests with known sender-, receiver-, and network-limited problems.
baseline: Ground-truth diagnoses in the controlled tests; no comparative system baseline reported in the supplied text.
uncertainty: The supplied text describes rate-based lightweight detection and a two-phase design, but does not provide the exact trigger rule or measured state savings for the two-phase prototype. Dapper diagnoses TCP bottlenecks, not request-level inference latency, and its RTT signal alone does not establish that delay came from queue buildup.

title: Testing, Verification and Improvements of Timeliness in ROS processes
abstract: This paper addresses the problem of improving response times of robots implemented in the Robotic Operating System (ROS) using formal verification of computational-time feasibility. In order to verify the real time behaviour of a robot under uncertain signal processing times, methods of formal verification of timeliness properties are proposed for data flows in a ROS-based control system using Probabilistic Timed Programs (PTPs). To calculate the probability of success under certain time limits, and to demonstrate the strength of our approach, a case study is implemented for a robotic agent in terms of operational times verification using the PRISM model checker, which points to possible enhancements to the operation of the robotic agent.
technical_mechanism: Instrument service lifecycle events at the requester and provider, then estimate separate distributions for request communication, service execution, and answer communication times. This stage decomposition can distinguish communication-side delay from provider execution time; the paper also uses the distributions in probabilistic deadline analysis.
why_it_works: A slow end-to-end request alone does not identify which stage is responsible. Separately measuring communication intervals and service execution gives Root a way to test whether a tail grows in the communication portion or in server execution, rather than attributing the whole regression to inference. The communication intervals include middleware and scheduling effects, so they are not a pure measurement of network delay or its cause.
root_seam: For each inference request, retain its identity and record robot-side send and response-receive timestamps plus server-side request-arrival and execution start/end timestamps. Compare the resulting communication and execution distributions with healthy requests. Validate clock alignment for cross-host intervals; same-host round-trip timing and server execution timing can also provide a communication-versus-compute comparison without assuming synchronized clocks.
experiment: Run a robot-to-cloud inference loop with matched request identities and stage timestamps. Hold inference load constant while separately injecting network delay or loss and server-side queueing or compute delay. Test whether the communication and execution distributions identify which stage's tail changed, and compare localization against an independently instrumented transport baseline. Treat clock alignment and middleware/scheduling contributions as explicit measurement controls.
evidence_quote: Probability distribution of the request communication times
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, §4.2, “Estimation of operations”; §4.1 describes the requester- and provider-side service timestamps.
reported_gain: The case study reports deadline-success probability increasing from 0.91 to 0.9724 after changing image processing to begin on the first image; this is not a Root or network-diagnostic gain.
baseline: The case-study baseline waits for two images before processing; no network-diagnostic baseline is reported.
uncertainty: The paper does not establish cross-host clock synchronization or show that its communication intervals isolate network delay from ROS middleware and scheduling. It estimates timing distributions and supports stage-level separation, but does not diagnose specific network causes such as loss, retransmission, or queueing.

title: Dynamic Network Probes: A Stepping Stone to Omni Network Visibility
abstract: Effective SDN control relies on the network data collecting capability as well as the quality and timeliness of the data. As open programmable data plane is becoming a reality, we further enhance it with the support of runtime interactive programming in order to cope with application dynamics, optimize data plane resource allocation, and reduce control-plane processing pressure. Based on the latest technologies, we propose the Dynamic Network Probes (DNP) as a means to support real-time and on-demand network visibility. DNPs serve as an important building block of an integrated networking data analytics platform which involves the network data plane as an active component for in-network computing. In this paper, we show the types of DNPs and their role in the big picture. We have implemented an NP-based hardware prototype to demonstrate the feasibility and efficiency of DNPs. We lay out the research challenges and our future work to realize the omni network visibility based on DNPs.
technical_mechanism: Dynamically install passive data-plane probes at selected queues and flows; use queue-depth watermark events and flow counters or timestamps to report network state on demand or when a condition fires.
why_it_works: A request tail can be compared with queue-threshold crossings and competing-flow activity at a shared network resource. This exposes evidence of shared-resource contention that request timing alone cannot provide; it does not independently prove which off-path flow caused the delay.
root_seam: At an accessible transport-path switch, correlate Root request identity and timestamps with queue watermark reports and counters for other flows sharing the queue. This adds data-plane evidence about network contention, distinct from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application.
experiment: Run identified inference requests with and without controlled competing flows on a shared queue. Dynamically enable queue-depth watermark and per-flow probes, then compare probe reports with request-tail intervals and a no-contention run. Check whether network queue events distinguish injected contention from server-side queueing or compute delay.
evidence_quote: Every time when an enqueue or a dequeue event happens, the queue depth is compared with the marks and a report packet is generated when a mark is crossed.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section 5, “Dynamic Network Probes,” register/queue-monitoring example
reported_gain: DNP deployment latency is reported as reduced by 40 times versus static programming for the prototype; no Root gain is reported.
baseline: Static programming requiring source editing, recompilation, and configuration download.
uncertainty: The paper supports queue and flow observation, including dynamic event reports, but does not demonstrate attributing an inference request's tail to a particular off-path flow. Transfer also depends on access to programmable data-plane devices.

title: Deconstructing the Tail at Scale Effect Across Network Protocols
abstract: Network latencies have become increasingly important for the performance of web servers and cloud computing platforms. Identifying network-related tail latencies and reasoning about their potential causes is especially important to gauge application run-time in online data-intensive applications, where the 99th percentile latency of individual operations can significantly affect the the overall latency of requests. This paper deconstructs the "tail at scale" effect across TCP-IP, UDP-IP, and RDMA network protocols. Prior scholarly works have analyzed tail latencies caused by extrinsic network parameters like network congestion and flow fairness. Contrary to existing literature, we identify surprising rare tails in TCP-IP round-trip measurements that are as enormous as 110x higher than the median latency. Our experimental design eliminates network congestion as a tail-inducing factor. Moreover, we observe similar extreme tails in UDP-IP packet exchanges, ruling out additional TCP-IP protocol operations as the root cause of tail latency. However, we are unable to reproduce similar tail latencies in RDMA packet exchanges, which leads us to conclude that the TCP/UDP protocol stack within the operating system kernel is likely the primary source of extreme latency tails.
technical_mechanism: Controlled protocol-path differential diagnosis: measure many request/response RTTs on an isolated link over TCP, UDP, and RDMA; similar TCP/UDP tails but much smaller RDMA tails implicate the conventional OS networking path, by elimination.
why_it_works: Isolation reduces the likelihood that switch congestion, scheduling, or load balancing caused the tails; UDP tests whether TCP-specific operations explain them; RDMA provides a contrasting path that bypasses the OS. The resulting comparison supports broad attribution to OS networking, not localization to a particular kernel component. Repeated RTT sampling also exposes rare tail events.
root_seam: At a robot-to-server inference request boundary, retain request identity and client RTT timestamps, plus server-side receive/response and queue/compute timings. Under matched payload and load, compare tail distributions across available transport or OS-networking configurations. This can flag whether a tail follows the conventional networking path while the server/GPU stages remain stable; RTT alone cannot separate outbound from return-path delay.
experiment: Issue many matched remote-inference requests under controlled load and record client RTT and server-side queue, inference, and response timestamps. Compare tail behavior across transport or OS-networking configurations while holding payload, offered load, and server/GPU work constant. Check whether tails persist across TCP/UDP but change on an OS-bypassing path, and whether server/GPU timings remain stable.
evidence_quote: As RDMA style communication completely bypasses the operating system, the RDMA experiments allow us to distinguish latency tails in TCP and UDP that are likely attributable to software.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, §4.3 RDMA
reported_gain: TCP tails reported up to 11 ms, UDP tails up to 2.5 ms, and RDMA read worst-case RTT of 150 µs. These are paper observations, not a Root-measured gain.
baseline: TCP-IP and UDP-IP socket-based RTT measurements compared with RDMA read/write RTT measurements on an isolated two-machine network.
uncertainty: Attribution is by controlled comparison, not per-request causal localization. RTT combines both network traversals and endpoint effects; the paper does not isolate individual OS-stack components or separate network delay from server processing within each RTT. Root would need server-side timing to distinguish network delay from queueing, GPU compute, and action application.

title: Ending the Anomaly: Achieving Low Latency and Airtime Fairness in WiFi
abstract: With more devices connected, delays and jitter at the WiFi hop become more prevalent, and correct functioning during network congestion becomes more important. However, two important performance issues prevent modern WiFi from reaching its potential: Increased latency under load caused by excessive queueing (i.e. bufferbloat) and the 802.11 performance anomaly. To remedy these issues, we present a novel two-part solution: We design a new queueing scheme that eliminates bufferbloat in the wireless setting. Leveraging this queueing scheme, we then design an airtime fairness scheduler that operates at the access point and doesn't require any changes to clients. We evaluate our solution using both a theoretical model and experiments in a testbed environment, formulating a suitable analytical model in the process. We show that our solution achieves an order of magnitude reduction in latency under load, large improvements in multi-station throughput, and nearly perfect airtime fairness for both TCP and downstream UDP traffic. Further experiments with application traffic confirm that the solution provides significant performance gains for real-world traffic.We develop a production quality implementation of our solution in the Linux kernel, the platform powering most access points outside of the managed enterprise setting. The implementation has been accepted into the mainline kernel distribution, making it available for deployment on billions of devices running Linux today.
technical_mechanism: The method moves flow-aware FQ-CoDel queue management into the lower WiFi MAC/driver layers, maintaining per-TID queues and applying per-queue CoDel; it then schedules stations by airtime deficit. Comparing latency with this integrated queue structure against upper-layer queue management alone provides an intervention for testing whether unmanaged lower-layer WiFi queues drive the tail.
why_it_works: Upper-layer queue management cannot control packets already queued in lower WiFi stack layers. Collapsing queue management across those layers limits that unmanaged buildup; airtime scheduling also prevents slow stations from monopolizing the shared medium. A latency reduction under the integrated-queue intervention supports queue buildup at the WiFi hop as a contributor, though it does not by itself distinguish queueing from every other possible network delay.
root_seam: Attach at the robot-side or access-point WiFi transmit path: correlate request latency with queue residence or queue depth across qdisc, MAC, and driver layers, and compare against an integrated-queue intervention. This would help localize WiFi queueing rather than attribute delay to server compute or action application; the paper does not provide request-level causal reconstruction.
experiment: Under repeatable robot-inference traffic and competing WiFi load, compare default FIFO, upper-layer FQ-CoDel, and integrated FQ-MAC queueing. Record request-correlated WiFi queue residence and end-to-end latency distributions, while separately measuring server/GPU time. Test whether the integrated queue intervention selectively reduces network-side tail latency.
evidence_quote: The reason for the limited effect of prior solutions is queueing in the lower layers of the wireless network stack.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section 2.1, “Bufferbloat in the context of WiFi.”
reported_gain: Order-of-magnitude reduction in latency under load, as reported in the abstract and evaluation summary; this is the paper’s result, not a Root gain.
baseline: Default FIFO queueing in the unmodified kernel; the experiments also compare upper-layer FQ-CoDel.
uncertainty: The work mitigates WiFi queueing rather than providing a request-level diagnostic. Its intervention can support a queueing-cause test, but the context does not show direct instrumentation that separates queue residence from other WiFi-hop delays.

title: Latency and Reliability-Aware Task Offloading and Resource Allocation for Mobile Edge Computing
abstract: While mobile edge computing (MEC) alleviates the computation and power limitations of mobile devices, additional latency is incurred when offloading tasks to remote MEC servers. In this work, the power-delay tradeoff in the context of task offloading is studied in a multi-user MEC scenario. In contrast with current system designs relying on average metrics (e.g., the average queue length and average latency), a novel network design is proposed in which latency and reliability constraints are taken into account. This is done by imposing a probabilistic constraint on users' task queue lengths and invoking results from extreme value theory to characterize the occurrence of low-probability events in terms of queue length (or queuing delay) violation. The problem is formulated as a computation and transmit power minimization subject to latency and reliability constraints, and solved using tools from Lyapunov stochastic optimization. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, while examining the power-delay tradeoff and required computational resources for various computation intensities.
technical_mechanism: Fit a generalized Pareto distribution to queue-length excesses above a high threshold, then use the fitted tail to estimate rare queue-length or queue-delay violations. This is a queue-specific tail detector, not a method for assigning all end-to-end delay to its cause.
why_it_works: Queue length is a direct signal of buildup at the queue being measured, and modeling conditional excesses focuses on rare events that averages can hide. For Root, request-correlated tail estimates from robot-side and server-side queues could reveal whether queue buildup accompanies a regression; comparing them with transport and compute timings would help distinguish queueing from other sources. The paper does not itself perform that cross-layer attribution.
root_seam: Attach request identity and timestamps to observable robot-side and inference-server queue enqueue/dequeue events; retain queue depth and residence-time samples. Fit the exceedance tail separately for each queue and compare its violations with transport, GPU, and action-application timing.
experiment: In a controlled Root workload, first vary queue load while holding network and compute conditions fixed, then introduce network impairment while holding queue load fixed. Record per-request queue depth and residence time at each observable queue, plus transport, compute, and end-to-end timings. Test whether queue-specific exceedance tails rise under queue loading and remain low under network-only impairment.
evidence_quote: Once convergence is achieved, we can estimate the statistics of the extreme queue length/queuing delay which enables us to proactively deal with the occurrence of extreme events.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section V, Numerical Results, discussion of Figures 6–7.
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: Average queue length and average latency metrics, described as insufficient for low-latency reliability constraints.
uncertainty: The paper demonstrates queue-tail estimation, including a GPD fit to queue exceedances, but does not test diagnosis against transport, computation, or action-application delays. Root transfer and the proposed controlled experiment are not evaluated in the paper.

title: On Spectral Analysis of the Internet Delay Space and Detecting Anomalous Routing Paths
abstract: Latency is one of the most critical performance metrics for a wide range of applications. Therefore, it is important to understand the underlying mechanisms that give rise to the observed latency values and diagnose the ones that are unexpectedly high. In this paper, we study the Internet delay space via robust principal component analysis (RPCA). Using RPCA, we show that the delay space, i.e. the matrix of measured round trip times between end hosts, can be decomposed into two components - the expected latency between end hosts with respect to the current state of the Internet and the inflation on the paths between the end hosts. Using this decomposition, first we study the well-known low-dimensionality phenomena of the delay space and ask what properties of the end hosts define the dimensions. Second, using the decomposition, we develop a filtering method to detect the paths which experience unexpected latencies and identify routing anomalies. We show that our filter successfully identifies an anomalous route even when its observed latency is not obviously high in magnitude.
technical_mechanism: Apply robust PCA to a matrix of RTTs between endpoint pairs, separating low-rank expected latency from sparse path inflation, then rank candidate anomalies by inflation relative to expected latency. This provides differential path diagnosis against the structure of comparable paths rather than relying on an absolute RTT threshold.
why_it_works: A path can be anomalous relative to comparable endpoint pairs even when its RTT is not unusually large in absolute terms. The method uses the matrix’s shared latency structure as its comparison baseline and identifies paths whose residual inflation is substantial. The paper also reports detecting anomalies when all paths in a region are inflated and with missing measurements.
root_seam: Attach RTT samples to source and destination identities, such as robot/server or network-region pairs, and retain enough comparable pairs to form a latency matrix. The decomposition could provide Root with a path-level anomaly signal beyond per-request timing comparisons. It flags candidate paths, but does not attribute an individual inference’s total delay to networking versus server queueing, GPU compute, or action application.
experiment: In a controlled Root test, collect RTT matrices across comparable robot/server endpoint pairs under healthy conditions and during injected route detours or path-delay inflation. Test whether RPCA and the inflation-to-expected-latency filter identify affected pairs, including cases where absolute RTT is not an outlier. Compare with absolute-RTT thresholding and correlate candidate paths with traceroute or transport evidence; record queueing, inference, and action-application times separately. Treat these as candidate diagnostics, not measured Root gains.
evidence_quote: We show that our filter successfully identifies an anomalous route even when its observed latency is not obviously high in magnitude.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Abstract; also section “Detecting Inflated Paths via Ratio Filtering” and Case 3.
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The method operates on RTT matrices between end hosts, not individual robot requests or packet traces. Root needs sufficiently comparable endpoint measurements to form a useful baseline. It identifies anomalous paths for investigation rather than independently localizing the responsible hop or separating network delay from server-side delay. The supplied evidence does not establish a Root-relevant gain.

title: Sketching Linear Classifiers over Data Streams
abstract: We introduce a new sub-linear space sketch---the Weight-Median Sketch---for learning compressed linear classifiers over data streams while supporting the efficient recovery of large-magnitude weights in the model. This enables memory-limited execution of several statistical analyses over streams, including online feature selection, streaming data explanation, relative deltoid detection, and streaming estimation of pointwise mutual information. Unlike related sketches that capture the most frequently-occurring features (or items) in a data stream, the Weight-Median Sketch captures the features that are most discriminative of one stream (or class) compared to another. The Weight-Median Sketch adopts the core data structure used in the Count-Sketch, but, instead of sketching counts, it captures sketched gradient updates to the model parameters. We provide a theoretical analysis that establishes recovery guarantees for batch and online learning, and demonstrate empirical improvements in memory-accuracy trade-offs over alternative memory-budgeted methods, including count-based sketches and feature hashing.
technical_mechanism: Train a compact linear classifier over labeled tail and healthy request-feature streams by sketching its gradient updates, then recover the largest-magnitude discriminative feature weights. The active-set variant stores high-weight features exactly and updates their sketch contribution lazily, reducing collision error.
why_it_works: Unlike frequency summaries, classifier weights favor features that distinguish the two labeled groups—even when those features are not frequent overall. The recovered features can therefore reveal candidate correlates of tail requests under a fixed memory budget. This is a diagnostic lead, not causal attribution.
root_seam: At request completion, join a request identity and latency outcome to available features such as transport events, packet/ACK/loss summaries, queue or NIC signals, server queue time, GPU time, and action-application time. Label tail versus healthy requests and maintain the sketch over that stream; recovered weights identify which recorded features distinguish the groups. Root would gain a compact retained summary instead of keeping every high-dimensional feature record, but must still collect the features and cannot infer network causality from weights alone.
experiment: Replay the same labeled Root request-feature stream into the Weight-Median/active-set sketch and an uncompressed classifier, with memory-matched frequency sketches as controls. Vary memory budgets and compare top-feature recovery and tail-versus-healthy classification; check whether transport features remain identifiable and whether they are distinguishable from server, GPU, and action-application features.
