evidence_quote: the Weight-Median Sketch captures the features that are most discriminative of one stream (or class) compared to another.
evidence_location: Abstract; also selected PDF text, opening paragraph.
reported_gain: Over 4x recall versus the paired Count-Min baseline at the same memory budget for relative-deltoid detection; this is the paper's result, not a Root-measured gain.
baseline: Paired Count-Min at the same memory budget and at 8x the memory budget; the relative-deltoid evaluation also compared against memory-unconstrained logistic regression.
uncertainty: The paper demonstrates feature discrimination and recovery, including relative differences between concurrent network traffic streams, not diagnosis of remote-robot inference latency tails. Root transfer depends on having request-linked features and latency labels; recovered associations do not establish causes or separate network delay from compute and other stages.

title: Toward Metric Indexes for Incremental Insertion and Querying
abstract: In this work we explore the use of metric index structures, which accelerate nearest neighbor queries, in the scenario where we need to interleave insertions and queries during deployment. This use-case is inspired by a real-life need in malware analysis triage, and is surprisingly understudied. Existing literature tends to either focus on only final query efficiency, often does not support incremental insertion, or does not support arbitrary distance metrics. We modify and improve three algorithms to support our scenario of incremental insertion and querying with arbitrary metrics, and evaluate them on multiple datasets and distance metrics while varying the value of k for the desired number of nearest neighbors. In doing so we determine that our improved Vantage-Point tree of Minimum-Variance performs best for this scenario.
technical_mechanism: Build an incrementally updated Vantage-Point tree whose splits minimize the weighted variance of distances to the vantage point, improving branch pruning during nearest-neighbor retrieval.
why_it_works: The tree uses distance bounds to prune branches that cannot contain a nearer neighbor, reducing distance computations compared with brute-force search. Root could index prior healthy inference requests by request or runtime features and retrieve comparable baselines without scanning the full history.
root_seam: Attach the index to Root's healthy-request baseline lookup: represent requests with a consistent feature vector and distance metric, then incrementally add requests as they become available. This provides a faster way to find comparable historical requests; it does not itself identify network delay.
experiment: Replay a stream of Root request features and interleave baseline lookups with insertions. Compare indexed lookup against brute-force retrieval, measuring lookup latency, nearest-neighbor agreement, and insertion cost, including tail latency as the history grows.
evidence_quote: we find the split that minimizes the weighted variance of each split
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, VP-tree improvement discussion.
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: Brute-force search is identified as the baseline for maximum distance computations in the interleaved insertion/query evaluation.
uncertainty: The paper evaluates metric-index performance on malware and other datasets, not Root request traces. It does not establish which Root features or distance metric would yield useful healthy-request matches.

title: Homa: A Receiver-Driven Low-Latency Transport Protocol Using Network Priorities (Complete Version)
abstract: Homa is a new transport protocol for datacenter networks. It provides exceptionally low latency, especially for workloads with a high volume of very short messages, and it also supports large messages and high network utilization. Homa uses in-network priority queues to ensure low latency for short messages; priority allocation is managed dynamically by each receiver and integrated with a receiver-driven flow control mechanism. Homa also uses controlled overcommitment of receiver downlinks to ensure efficient bandwidth utilization at high load. Our implementation of Homa delivers 99th percentile round-trip times less than 15μs for short messages on a 10 Gbps network running at 80% load. These latencies are almost 100x lower than the best published measurements of an implementation. In simulations, Homa's latency is roughly equal to pFabric and significantly better than pHost, PIAS, and NDP for almost all message sizes and workloads. Homa can also sustain higher network loads than pFabric, pHost, or PIAS.
technical_mechanism: Packet-trace-based queue attribution: analyze detailed packet traces to associate tail latency with receiver-downlink queueing; instrument the simulator to decompose tail delay into causes such as link-level preemption lag.
why_it_works: A request's packet timing can reveal delay at a shared link even when the competing traffic is not part of the request's own inference path. The paper uses this analysis to distinguish downlink queueing from other causes of transport delay, exposing a shared-resource explanation for tails. This transfers to n02's shared-resource diagnosis, though the evidence does not establish identification of a specific off-path culprit flow.
root_seam: Correlate Root request IDs with robot- and server-side packet timestamps or captures, and attribute the network portion of request delay to observed shared-link queueing or preemption. Keep transport delay separate from server queueing, GPU compute, and action application. This could reveal a contended link without assuming access to Homa's private infrastructure.
experiment: Replay the same inference requests with controlled competing traffic on a candidate shared link, recording packet timestamps and queue or NIC telemetry where available. Compare packet-trace-based attribution against known injected contention and separately timestamp server queueing, GPU execution, and action application. Test whether the method localizes the affected shared link and distinguishes it from non-network delay.
evidence_quote: By analyzing detailed packet traces we determined that Basic’s high latency is caused by queuing delays at the receiver’s downlink
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, section 5 Evaluation, paragraph discussing Basic transport and Figure 8.
reported_gain: The paper reports 5–15x higher tail latency in Basic than Homa and attributes Basic's high latency to receiver-downlink queueing; this is a paper result, not a Root-measured gain.
baseline: Basic transport, which is receiver-driven but does not use priorities and has no limit on overcommitment.
uncertainty: The paper reports the diagnostic finding but does not detail a general trace-analysis algorithm or demonstrate attribution of an individual off-path culprit flow. Its receiver-downlink and datacenter assumptions may not match Root's topology.

title: Link and code: Fast indexing with graphs and compact regression codes
abstract: Similarity search approaches based on graph walks have recently attained outstanding speed-accuracy trade-offs, taking aside the memory requirements. In this paper, we revisit these approaches by considering, additionally, the memory constraint required to index billions of images on a single server. This leads us to propose a method based both on graph traversal and compact representations. We encode the indexed vectors using quantization and exploit the graph structure to refine the similarity estimation. In essence, our method takes the best of these two worlds: the search strategy is based on nested graphs, thereby providing high precision with a relatively small set of comparisons. At the same time it offers a significant memory compression. As a result, our approach outperforms the state of the art on operating points considering 64-128 bytes per vector, as demonstrated by our results on two billion-scale public benchmarks.
technical_mechanism: Use hierarchical graph traversal to find nearby indexed vectors with relatively few comparisons, and compact quantized codes with neighbor-based regression to refine candidate similarity estimates. For Root, this is a candidate mechanism for retrieving comparable healthy requests efficiently; it is not itself a network-tail detector.
why_it_works: The nested graph guides search toward promising neighbors without comparing every indexed item, while regression from connected neighbors improves estimates of candidate vectors. This provides a concrete approximate-retrieval operation for a Root experiment, though its effectiveness depends on choosing useful request representations and does not distinguish network delay from other latency sources.
root_seam: Attach at Root's comparable-request retrieval stage: index representations of requests and query the index for similar healthy requests. The paper supplies the graph-based retrieval and code-refinement operation, but not request features or a method for attributing latency to the network.
experiment: On a fixed collection of request representations with known comparable healthy requests, compare L&C retrieval against Root's existing retrieval method at matched recall and memory budgets. Measure retrieval latency and whether the returned healthy comparables aid regression localization. Separately retain network, server-queue, GPU, and action-application timing so retrieval success is not mistaken for network attribution.
evidence_quote: The search strategy is based on nested graphs, thereby providing high precision with a relatively small set of comparisons.
evidence_location: Abstract; also supported by Section 4, “Graph-based structure” and “Vector approximation.”
reported_gain: The paper reports outperforming the state of the art at 64–128 bytes per vector on two public billion-scale benchmarks; selected text also reports 2.5 times faster attainment of recall@1 of 50% on Deep1B. These are paper results, not Root measurements.
baseline: State-of-the-art methods on two public billion-scale benchmarks; the selected text identifies Faiss IMI as the experimental baseline.
uncertainty: The paper establishes approximate-neighbor retrieval over image descriptors, not retrieval over inference requests. Root must validate request representations, comparable-request recall, and diagnostic usefulness; the method supplies no network-specific signal or causal attribution.

title: Reducing Property Graph Queries to Relational Algebra for Incremental View Maintenance
abstract: The property graph data model of modern graph database systems is increasingly adapted for storing and processing heterogeneous datasets like networks. Many challenging applications with near real-time requirements -- e.g. financial fraud detection, recommendation systems, and on-the-fly validation -- can be captured with graph queries, which are evaluated repeatedly. To ensure quick response time for a changing data set, these applications would benefit from applying incremental view maintenance (IVM) techniques, which can perform continuous evaluation of queries and calculate the changes in the result set upon updates. However, currently, no graph databases provide support for incremental views. While IVM problems have been studied extensively over relational databases, views on property graph queries require operators outside the scope of standard relational algebra. Hence, tackling this problem requires the integration of numerous existing IVM techniques and possibly further extensions. In this paper, we present an approach to perform IVM on property graphs, using a nested relational algebraic representation for property graphs and graph operations. Then we define a chain of transformations to reduce most property graph queries to flat relational algebra and use techniques from discrimination networks (used in rule-based expert systems) to evaluate them. We demonstrate the approach using our prototype tool, ingraph, which uses openCypher, an open graph query language specified as part of an industry initiative. However, several aspects of our approach can be generalised to other graph query languages such as G-CORE and PGQL.
technical_mechanism: Use compound, constraint-based indexes to narrow lookup candidates, and retain intermediate query results for reuse with incremental updates.
why_it_works: The indexer supports lookups using IDs and labels, and the paper states that adding constraints makes lookups cheaper. The Rete network also caches intermediate results and updates them when data changes. Applied to retained Root traces, these operations could speed retrieval of comparable healthy requests without rescanning the full corpus. This is a retrieval optimization, not a mechanism for identifying network delay by itself.
root_seam: Attach the operation to Root’s retained trace store: index request identity and comparison metadata such as robot, model, and workload; use compound constraints to retrieve candidates, then compare timestamped transport events separately from server queueing, inference, and action application. The paper does not supply those network signals.
experiment: For the same held-out Root requests, compare scan-based retrieval with compound indexed retrieval for latency and retrieval quality. Separately measure lookup work when retained-trace metadata changes, comparing recomputation with cached intermediate results updated incrementally. Keep the candidate corpus and comparison criteria identical across methods.
evidence_quote: In general, lookups are cheaper when more constraints are provided, e.g. it is cheaper to get the set of edges when both the edge type and the source/target labels are specified compared to when only the edge type is known.
evidence_location: Section 5.3, “Data representation and indexing”
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The paper establishes constraint-based indexing and incremental reuse for property-graph queries, but does not evaluate retrieval of comparable healthy requests or Root trace data. The Root experiment is a proposed transfer, not a reported result.

title: Understanding Differences among Executions with Variational Traces
abstract: One of the main challenges of debugging is to understand why the program fails for certain inputs but succeeds for others. This becomes especially difficult if the fault is caused by an interaction of multiple inputs. To debug such interaction faults, it is necessary to understand the individual effect of the input, how these inputs interact and how these interactions cause the fault. The differences between two execution traces can explain why one input behaves differently than the other. We propose to compare execution traces of all input options to derive explanations of the behavior of all options and interactions among them. To make the relevant information stand out, we represent them as variational traces that concisely represents control-flow and data-flow differences among multiple concrete traces. While variational traces can be obtained from brute-force execution of all relevant inputs, we use variational execution to scale the generation of variational traces to the exponential space of possible inputs. We further provide an Eclipse plugin Varviz that enables users to use variational traces for debugging and navigation. In a user study, we show that users of variational traces are more than twice as fast to finish debugging tasks than users of the standard Eclipse debugger. We further show that variational traces can be scaled to programs with many options.
technical_mechanism: Synchronous variational execution merges executions into a conditional trace, recording control-flow splits and data-state differences without aligning separate logs.
why_it_works: The shared execution context identifies where behavior splits, while choice values retain state differences across executions. This offers a concrete differential-diagnosis operation beyond ordinary per-request logging: a trace can highlight the earliest differing instrumented event between a tail request and a comparable healthy request.
root_seam: Attach request identity and timestamps to robot-side and server-side transport events, plus queue, compute, and action-application events. Compare a tail request with a matched healthy request using a shared differential trace. Root would gain a compact view of where their instrumented behavior first differs; the paper itself supplies no transport signal or network-delay attribution.
experiment: For matched remote-inference requests, record timestamped transport, queue, compute, and action-application events, then build differential traces for tail and healthy pairs. Inject network delay separately from server queueing and compute delay. Test whether the earliest differing event correctly localizes the injected cause, and compare diagnosis accuracy and time with ordinary per-request traces.
evidence_quote: As variational execution synchronizes the executions among configurations, there is no need to align the executions of the program. Instead, we directly generate the variational trace by recording how variational execution runs the program.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, section “Generating Variational Traces.”
reported_gain: More than twice as fast to finish debugging tasks versus the standard Eclipse debugger, as reported in the abstract.
baseline: Standard Eclipse debugger for the user study.
uncertainty: The paper compares program configurations, not tail and healthy requests, and does not model transport timing or distinguish network delay from queueing or compute. Root transfer depends on adding timestamped network and runtime events; the paper reports no Root-measured gain.

title: Optimal design of experiments to identify latent behavioral types
abstract: Bayesian optimal experiments that maximize the information gained from collected data are critical to efficiently identify behavioral models. We extend a seminal method for designing Bayesian optimal experiments by introducing two computational improvements that make the procedure tractable: (1) a search algorithm from artificial intelligence that efficiently explores the space of possible design parameters, and (2) a sampling procedure which evaluates each design parameter combination more efficiently. We apply our procedure to a game of imperfect information to evaluate and quantify the computational improvements. We then collect data across five different experimental designs to compare the ability of the optimal experimental design to discriminate among competing behavioral models against the experimental designs chosen by a "wisdom of experts" prediction experiment. We find that data from the experiment suggested by the optimal design approach requires significantly less data to distinguish behavioral models (i.e., test hypotheses) than data from the experiment suggested by experts. Substantively, we find that reinforcement learning best explains human decision-making in the imperfect information game and that behavior is not adequately described by the Bayesian Nash equilibrium. Our procedure is general and computationally efficient and can be applied to dynamically optimize online experiments.
technical_mechanism: Select experimental settings that maximize KL divergence between candidate models’ predicted outcome distributions; use parameter-sampled likely datasets to estimate information value and Gaussian Process Upper Confidence Bound Pure Exploration to search the design space adaptively.
why_it_works: Settings where candidate models make more divergent predictions are more informative, so fewer observations can distinguish them. Adaptive search concentrates evaluations on promising settings while exploring uncertain regions, reducing the cost of finding an informative design.
root_seam: The paper does not diagnose network delays. A Root experiment could adapt the same design principle: define candidate causes such as transport delay, server queueing, GPU compute, or action application, then select controlled workload or network conditions where their predicted measurements diverge most. This could reduce measurements needed to distinguish causes, but the paper provides no network-specific signals or validation.
experiment: The authors compared data from five experimental designs, including an optimal design and designs chosen by experts, to assess how well they distinguished behavioral models. They also evaluated computational improvements to the design search.
evidence_quote: We find that data from the experiment suggested by the optimal design approach requires significantly less data to distinguish behavioral models (i.e., test hypotheses) than data from the experiment suggested by experts.
evidence_location: Abstract; selected PDF text, Abstract
reported_gain: Significantly less data required to distinguish behavioral models than with the expert-suggested experiment; the selected text gives no quantitative measurement.
baseline: Expert-suggested experimental designs (“wisdom of experts” prediction experiment).
uncertainty: The method and its fewer-data result are supported for behavioral-model experiments, not network-tail diagnosis. Its transfer to Root would require candidate network-cause models and controlled measurements, which the paper does not specify.

title: Real-time Linux communications: an evaluation of the Linux communication stack for real-time robotic applications
abstract: As robotics systems become more distributed, the communications between different robot modules play a key role for the reliability of the overall robot control. In this paper, we present a study of the Linux communication stack meant for real-time robotic applications. We evaluate the real-time performance of UDP based communications in Linux on multi-core embedded devices as test platforms. We prove that, under an appropriate configuration, the Linux kernel greatly enhances the determinism of communications using the UDP protocol. Furthermore, we demonstrate that concurrent traffic disrupts the bounded latencies and propose a solution by separating the real-time application and the corresponding interrupt in a CPU.
technical_mechanism: Under controlled concurrent TX/RX traffic, prioritize the real-time UDP flow and map it to a hardware queue, then pin its application and corresponding NIC IRQ thread to the same CPU (or isolate that CPU). Compare round-trip latency across kernel and affinity configurations to test whether shared CPU/IRQ processing contributes to tails.
why_it_works: The intervention separates real-time packet processing from competing work. Changes in worst-case RTT under matched background traffic provide evidence that CPU and interrupt contention, rather than only link-layer queuing, contributes to delay. This is a transferable controlled experiment for robot-cloud loops, though RTT alone does not identify which endpoint or network segment caused an individual tail.
root_seam: Attach request timestamps and identity at the robot and server transport boundaries, then run matched background-traffic tests while varying CPU/IRQ affinity and queue priority. This could reveal whether tail changes track endpoint packet-processing contention; additional per-hop or transport-event timestamps would be needed to separate network delay from server queueing, GPU compute, and action application.
experiment: Replay a fixed-rate UDP control-loop workload on a robot-side and server-side test setup for the paper's 3-hour duration, comparing baseline scheduling with prioritized traffic and pinned application/NIC IRQ threads. Repeat under idle, CPU stress, and controlled concurrent TX/RX traffic; record per-request RTT distributions, maxima, packet loss, and missed deadlines, with synchronized endpoint timestamps to localize delay.
evidence_quote: Separating the real-time application and the corresponding interrupt in a CPU seems to be an effective approach to avoid high latencies.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section V, Conclusion and Future Work
reported_gain: For 100 Mbps TX traffic, maximum RTT fell from 25727 µs (RT Normal) to 568 µs (RT, CPU Affinity); missed deadlines fell from 20/600000 to 0/600000.
baseline: RT Normal: PREEMPT-RT kernel without binding the round-trip programs and network IRQs to any CPU.
uncertainty: The experiment measures round-trip latency and does not provide per-request one-way or per-hop attribution. The reported benefit is specific to the tested embedded Linux devices and configuration. At 200 Mbps RX traffic, the paper reports high latency spikes even with CPU isolation.

title: Towards a distributed and real-time framework for robots: Evaluation of ROS 2.0 communications for real-time robotic applications
abstract: In this work we present an experimental setup to show the suitability of ROS 2.0 for real-time robotic applications. We disclose an evaluation of ROS 2.0 communications in a robotic inter-component (hardware) communication case on top of Linux. We benchmark and study the worst case latencies and missed deadlines to characterize ROS 2.0 communications for real-time applications. We demonstrate experimentally how computation and network congestion impacts the communication latencies and ultimately, propose a setup that, under certain conditions, mitigates these delays and obtains bounded traffic.
technical_mechanism: Use controlled concurrent network and system load, then raise the priority of Ethernet IRQ, ROS/DDS, and ksoftirqd threads and compare ROS ping-pong round-trip latency, missed deadlines, and message loss. The improvement under this intervention implicates delayed packet processing in low-priority ksoftirqd, rather than merely recording an end-to-end latency.
why_it_works: Under high traffic and system stress, receive processing may switch from the Ethernet IRQ thread to ksoftirqd, which is easily preempted. Prioritizing that processing path and observing whether tail latency and deadline misses improve provides a causal test for network-stack scheduling delay. The RTT measurement alone does not separate each direction or network processing from other endpoint work.
root_seam: At each robot/server transport endpoint, correlate request identity and send/receive timestamps with Ethernet IRQ and ksoftirqd scheduling or packet-processing events. A controlled priority or load intervention can test whether endpoint receive scheduling contributes to the tail; this would not, by itself, distinguish network transit from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application.
experiment: On a robot-to-server request loop, collect request-level RTT and deadline/loss outcomes while varying concurrent traffic and CPU stress; repeat with network IRQ and receive-processing thread priorities changed. Compare tail latency and misses across matched conditions, and separately timestamp endpoint transport events to check whether the implicated scheduling delay coincides with the tail.
evidence_quote: Comparing to Test2.F (Figures6fand8) we observe a clear improvement with the new configuration. We observe almost no missed deadlines, nor message loss for a 10 minutes duration test.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Experimental Setup and Results, B.4 Test 4: Tuning the kernel threads priorities.
reported_gain: Qualitative: almost no missed deadlines or message loss during a 10-minute test after kernel-thread priority tuning.
baseline: Test2.F: system under load with 80 Mbps concurrent traffic, before the new thread-priority configuration.
uncertainty: No packet/ACK sequence signatures, request-level differential diagnosis, or full cross-layer timestamps are reported. Experiments are ROS 2 inter-component Ethernet communication, not robot-to-cloud action loops; reported improvement is not a Root result.

title: Time Synchronization in modular collaborative robots
abstract: A new generation of robot systems which are modular, flexible and safe for human-robot interaction are needed. Existing cobots seem to meet only the later and require a modular approach to improve their reconfigurability and interoperability. We propose a new sub-class of cobots named M-cobots which tackle these problems. In particular, we discuss the relevance of synchronization for these systems, analyze it and demonstrate how with a properly configured M-cobot, we are able to obtain a) distributed sub-microsecond clock synchronization accuracy among modules, b) timestamping accuracy of ROS 2.0 messages under 100 microseconds and c) millisecond-level end-to-end communication latencies, even when disturbed with networking overloads of up to 90% of the network capacity.
technical_mechanism: Use PTP-synchronized clocks to timestamp each message before publish and at the start of the receiver's subscription callback; subtract the timestamps to estimate one-way send-to-callback delay. Under controlled link saturation, compare this signal with and without traffic prioritization to test whether delay is congestion-sensitive.
why_it_works: A common clock makes timestamps on different nodes comparable, so the send-to-arrival interval exposes delay that unsynchronized clocks would confound with offset and drift. The congestion and priority comparison provides a diagnostic intervention: if the delay changes with competing traffic or prioritization, that supports a network-contention cause. The measured interval includes receiver-stack and callback-entry time, so it is not a pure wire-delay measurement.
root_seam: Attach synchronized timestamps and request/message identity at robot-side send and server-side receive, plus timestamps around server queueing and inference and at the return/action boundary. This would give Root a send-to-receive interval to compare with server-side intervals, helping distinguish transport tail from queueing, compute, or action application without assuming access to the paper's infrastructure.
experiment: For Root, collect synchronized send/receive timestamps and per-request identity on a controlled remote inference path. Introduce competing network traffic, compare delay distributions with and without a traffic-priority intervention, and separately timestamp server queueing and inference. Check whether the send-to-receive tail responds to the intervention while server-side intervals remain stable.
evidence_quote: When the system clocks have been synchronized, the publishing and arrival timestamps can be compared and the transport delay calculated
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, section III, experimental setup and results; timing-measurement description.
reported_gain: The paper reports that under 90% link saturation, prioritizing sensor and actuator traffic almost eliminates delays caused by low-priority traffic; it does not provide a numerical tail-percentile gain.
baseline: Communication under 90% link saturation without prioritization, compared with prioritization under the same congestion condition.
uncertainty: The experiment is on robot Ethernet and ROS 2, not robot-to-cloud inference. Its one-way interval ends at callback entry and can include receiver network-stack and software-path delay; Root would need additional timestamps to separate those from network transit and cloud queueing. No Root-measured gain is established.

title: Pulser: Fast Congestion Response using Explicit Incast Notifications for Datacenter Networks
abstract: Datacenter applications frequently cause incast congestion, which degrades both flow completion times of short flows and throughput of long flows. Without isolating incast, existing congestion control schemes (e.g., DCTCP) rely on existing ECN signal to react to general congestion, and they lose performance due to their slow, cautious, and inaccurate reaction to incast. We propose to isolate incast using Explicit Incast Notifications (EIN) that are generated by switches, similar to ECN. Our incast detection is fast and accurate. Further, we present our congestion control scheme, called Pulser, which drastically backs off during incast based on EIN, but restores sending rate once incast ends. Our real experiments and ns-3 simulations show that Pulser outperforms prior schemes, DCTCP and ICTCP, in both flow completion times and throughput.
technical_mechanism: At each switch output port, measure queue-length gradients on packet-dequeue events, average recent samples in a sliding window, and mark packets with an Explicit Incast Notification (EIN) when the average exceeds a threshold; retain the mark above a high-water mark for hysteresis. This identifies rapid incast-driven queue buildup rather than treating it as undifferentiated congestion.
why_it_works: Incast causes queue length to rise steeply over a short interval. The queue-gradient signal detects that buildup quickly, whereas ordinary ECN threshold marking and gradual end-host window adaptation may react too slowly. For Root, equivalent per-request or per-flow transport/queue measurements could show whether a latency tail coincides with network queue buildup; this would not by itself identify GPU compute or action-application delay.
root_seam: Attach queue-depth samples or queue-gradient/EIN-like events to request identity and timestamps at the relevant switch output port, then correlate them with robot-side send/receive and server-side inference timestamps. This localizes a network-queue contribution without treating all end-to-end latency as network delay; the paper's switch-generated signal requires suitable network instrumentation.
experiment: In a controlled remote-inference workload, create matched requests with and without induced competing bursts on the transport path. Record per-output-port queue depth/gradient and request send/receive plus inference timestamps. Test whether queue-gradient events predict network-attributable tail latency, and compare localization against end-to-end timing alone while separately accounting for server inference time.
evidence_quote: We present a novel algorithm for detecting incasts in a short time interval by monitoring the gradient of queue length over small time windows.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Introduction; algorithm and implementation details in sections 3.1 and 4.
reported_gain: Simulations: average 50% reduction in 99th-percentile flow completion time versus DCTCP and ICTCP for loads greater than 20%, with up to 70% at higher loads. Real testbed: about 26% lower 99th-percentile flow completion time than DCTCP.
baseline: DCTCP and ICTCP for simulation results; DCTCP for real-testbed results.
uncertainty: The mechanism detects incast-related switch queue buildup, not every cause of network tail latency. The paper does not evaluate remote robot inference or establish that its switch instrumentation is available in Root's deployment.

title: Link Delay Estimation Using Sparse Recovery for Dynamic Network Tomography
abstract: When the scale of communication networks has been growing rapidly in the past decades, it becomes a critical challenge to extract fast and accurate estimation of key state parameters of network links, e.g., transmission delays and dropped packet rates, because such monitoring operations are usually time-consuming. Based on the sparse recovery technique reported in [Wang et al. (2015) IEEE Trans. Information Theory, 61(2):1028--1044], which can infer link delays from a limited number of measurements using compressed sensing, we particularly extend to networks with dynamic changes including link insertion and deletion. Moreover, we propose a more efficient algorithm with a better theoretical upper bound. The experimental result also demonstrates that our algorithm outperforms the previous work in running time while maintaining a similar recovery performance, which shows its capability to cope with large-scale networks.
technical_mechanism: Use topology-constrained compressed sensing: form additive end-to-end path-delay measurements, choose connected dominating-set hub links using a maximum matching, and recover sparse per-link delays from far fewer measurements than measuring every path/link. Maintain the hub set incrementally as links are inserted or deleted.
why_it_works: If only a small number of links have large delays, the per-link delay vector is sparse. Path measurements are sums of link delays, so sparse recovery can infer individual link delays from a limited set of measurements. The matching-based hub construction supports connected measurements, while incremental hub maintenance avoids rebuilding the measurement structure after each link change. This could help Root distinguish which transport links contribute to an end-to-end tail with fewer probes, but the paper does not identify off-path flows or shared-resource contention.
root_seam: Attach probe-path identity and end-to-end delay measurements to the robot/server transport path, with known topology and additive link delays; apply sparse recovery to estimate anomalous link delays. This could reduce probe count, but would not by itself attribute delay to competing flows or distinguish network delay from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application.
experiment: On a controlled robot-inference network with injected delay on a small subset of links, compare sparse-recovery link estimates using limited path probes against per-link ground truth and exhaustive measurement. Repeat after link insertion/deletion and compare incremental maintenance with rebuilding. Track localization accuracy, probe count, and runtime; separately timestamp server queueing and compute to avoid attributing those delays to the network.
evidence_quote: Based on that, they can take N measurements, N ≪ m for sparse signal recovery
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section II, Problem Model
reported_gain: The paper reports that its algorithm runs at least thousand times faster than Wang et al.’s approach in the reported hub-selection experiment, and that the dynamic strategy runs ten times faster than rerunning the static algorithm. Recovery performance is described as similar overall and better under low to moderate sparsity in the reported experiments.
baseline: Wang et al.’s [18] static hub-selection and sparse-recovery approach; for dynamic updates, rerunning the proposed static algorithm without the dynamic strategy.
uncertainty: The paper studies network tomography and sparse link-delay recovery, not robot inference or off-path/shared-resource diagnosis. The supplied text does not specify a Root-ready probe placement or show separation of network delay from other inference stages. Reported gains are the paper’s own algorithmic comparisons, not Root measurements.

title: Machine Learning-based Link Fault Identification and Localization in Complex Networks
abstract: With the proliferation of network devices and rapid development in information technology, networks such as Internet of Things are increasing in size and becoming more complex with heterogeneous wired and wireless links. In such networks, link faults may result in a link disconnection without immediate replacement or a link reconnection, e.g., a wireless node changes its access point. Identifying whether a link disconnection or a link reconnection has occurred and localizing the failed link become a challenging problem. An active probing approach requires a long time to probe the network by sending signaling messages on different paths, thus incurring significant communication delay and overhead. In this paper, we adopt a passive approach and develop a three-stage machine learning-based technique, namely ML-LFIL that identifies and localizes link faults by analyzing the measurements captured from the normal traffic flows, including aggregate flow rate, end-to-end delay and packet loss. ML-LFIL learns the traffic behavior in normal working conditions and different link fault scenarios. We train the learning model using support vector machine, multi-layer perceptron and random forest. We implement ML-LFIL and carry out extensive experiments using Mininet platform. Performance studies show that ML-LFIL achieves high accuracy while requiring much lower fault localization time compared to the active probing approach.
technical_mechanism: Passively collect aggregate flow rate, end-to-end RTT, and packet loss at ingress and egress nodes, then use a three-stage trained ML pipeline to detect and localize link faults. A delay regressor additionally distinguishes disconnection alone from disconnection with reconnection.
why_it_works: Different link faults produce characteristic changes in normal traffic measurements. The classifier maps those signatures to a tentative failed link; the delay regressor checks whether observed delays match the disconnection-only case, and a final classifier can localize a reconnection. This can localize a fault without injecting probe traffic or retaining full traces.
root_seam: Attach passive flow-rate, RTT, and loss measurements to request or flow identities at robot-side and server-side network boundaries. Test whether their fault signatures localize network-path tail regressions; compare with healthy requests and separate network delay from server queueing, GPU compute, and action application.
experiment: The paper evaluates the three-stage method in Mininet on two random complex networks and a 100-node Interroute topology, using normal and fault-scenario traffic measurements. A Root experiment could inject controlled link disconnections, reconnections, and tail-delay faults, then compare localization accuracy and overhead using these passive signals against full tracing and active probing.
evidence_quote: The traffic features used for machine learning model include the aggregate flow rate, packet loss and round-trip time delay of traffic packets among the monitored nodes.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, overview of ML-LFIL and its traffic features; also Section III.A, “Traffic Features.”
reported_gain: Up to 97% fault-detection accuracy; localization time reported as microseconds for ML-LFIL versus longer ping-based probing. No Root gain reported.
baseline: Ping-based active probing, which pings network nodes and analyzes the results to localize link faults.
uncertainty: The method targets trained link-fault scenarios, not arbitrary inference tail regressions. The context does not establish that its measurements distinguish network delay from server queueing or compute, or that models transfer across changing topologies and workloads.

title: Dynamic Space-Time Scheduling for GPU Inference
abstract: Serving deep neural networks in latency critical interactive settings often requires GPU acceleration. However, the small batch sizes typical in online inference results in poor GPU utilization, a potential performance gap which GPU resource sharing can address. In this paper, we explore several techniques to leverage both temporal and spatial multiplexing to improve GPU utilization for deep learning inference workloads. We evaluate the performance trade-offs of each approach with respect to resource-efficiency, latency predictability, and isolation when compared with conventional batched inference. Our experimental analysis suggests up to a 5x potential for improved utilization through the exploration of more advanced spatial and temporal multiplexing strategies. Our preliminary prototype of a dynamic space-time scheduler demonstrates a 3.23x floating-point throughput increase over space-only multiplexing and a 7.73x increase over time-only multiplexing for convolutions, while also providing better isolation and latency predictability.
technical_mechanism: Per-kernel latency monitoring to identify GPU-side stragglers, paired with request-level transport and end-to-end timestamps in Root.
why_it_works: Kernel timings provide a direct measure of part of server-side GPU execution. Correlating those timings with Root's request and transport events can show whether a slow request's tail coincides with GPU execution or instead lies outside the measured GPU interval. The paper also describes evicting degraded workers, but that is a response to the diagnosis, not the key transfer.
root_seam: At the inference server, attach per-kernel timing to request identity and the server inference span; correlate it with robot/server transport timestamps and queue timings. This adds a GPU-compute measurement that can help distinguish compute delay from network delay, while avoiding an assumption that the paper itself measures network latency.
experiment: Under controlled GPU contention, collect per-request kernel timings, transport-event timestamps, queue timings, and end-to-end latency. Compare whether kernel timing identifies GPU-side tail requests when network conditions are fixed, then impose network impairment with GPU conditions fixed and test whether the measured GPU interval remains distinct from the network-related residual.
evidence_quote: We preserve predictability and isolation during virtualization by monitoring inference latencies per-kernel.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section 4, “A new hope? Dynamic space-time scheduling”
reported_gain: 3.23x throughput increase over space-only multiplexing and 7.73x over time-only multiplexing for convolutions.
baseline: Space-only multiplexing and time-only multiplexing.
uncertainty: The paper measures per-kernel inference latency and discusses stragglers, but does not describe correlating kernel timings with request identities, transport events, or end-to-end latency. The proposed separation and experiment are a Root transfer, not a reported paper result or measured Root gain.

title: Analysis of Large-Scale Multi-Tenant GPU Clusters for DNN Training Workloads
abstract: With widespread advances in machine learning, a number of large enterprises are beginning to incorporate machine learning models across a number of products. These models are typically trained on shared, multi-tenant GPU clusters. Similar to existing cluster computing workloads, scheduling frameworks aim to provide features like high efficiency, resource isolation, fair sharing across users, etc. However Deep Neural Network (DNN) based workloads, predominantly trained on GPUs, differ in two significant ways from traditional big data analytics workloads. First, from a cluster utilization perspective, GPUs represent a monolithic resource that cannot be shared at a fine granularity across users. Second, from a workload perspective, deep learning frameworks require gang scheduling reducing the flexibility of scheduling and making the jobs themselves inelastic to failures at runtime. In this paper we present a detailed workload characterization of a two-month long trace from a multi-tenant GPU cluster in a large enterprise. By correlating scheduler logs with logs from individual jobs, we study three distinct issues that affect cluster utilization for DNN training workloads on multi-tenant clusters: (1) the effect of gang scheduling and locality constraints on queuing, (2) the effect of locality on GPU utilization, and (3) failures during training. Based on our experience running a large-scale operation, we provide design guidelines pertaining to next-generation cluster schedulers for DNN training workloads.
technical_mechanism: Controlled shared-resource intervention: compare a workload with background jobs that share the RDMA network against a baseline placement, then use GPU utilization and training throughput changes to expose interference attributable to that shared network resource.
why_it_works: The controlled placement comparison changes whether background traffic shares the RDMA network while measuring the workload under study. The resulting utilization drop, alongside the reported training slowdown, is evidence that the shared resource can impair performance—not merely that low utilization and network use coincide. This offers a concrete way to test whether competing traffic on Root’s path contributes to a tail, although it does not identify an individual off-path flow or directly measure network delay.
root_seam: At the robot-server transport or NIC, associate request identities and timestamps with a controlled competing-traffic condition. Compare matched requests with and without that traffic, while recording transport timing and NIC or queue signals. This would test for shared-path contention and help distinguish network effects from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application.
experiment: Replay a fixed remote-inference workload under randomized or paired conditions with and without competing traffic on the relevant shared link. Measure per-request tail latency, transport events, NIC/queue signals, server queueing, GPU compute, and action-application time. Test whether the competing-traffic condition changes network-attributed delay and request tails, rather than relying on GPU utilization alone.
evidence_quote: For this setup we use two DiffServer jobs instead of two SameServer jobs as background traffic, so that all the jobs are distributed across two servers and share the RDMA network. In this case, we see a 13.1% decrease in utilization compared to the baseline.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, controlled ResNet-50 placement experiment, paragraph beginning “study. Thus, these jobs interfere”.
reported_gain: 13.1% decrease in GPU utilization under shared RDMA traffic versus the paper’s baseline; no Root gain reported.
baseline: The controlled experiment compares two DiffServer background jobs sharing the RDMA network with two SameServer background jobs.
uncertainty: The study measures GPU utilization and training throughput, not per-request network delay, tail latency, or individual-flow attribution. Its aggregate and per-minute telemetry cannot by itself establish where a Root request’s delay occurred; the proposed Root experiment would need direct transport and request-level measurements.

title: User Space Network Drivers
abstract: The rise of user space packet processing frameworks like DPDK and netmap makes low-level code more accessible to developers and researchers. Previously, driver code was hidden in the kernel and rarely modified, or even looked at, by developers working at higher layers. These barriers are gone nowadays, yet developers still treat user space drivers as black-boxes magically accelerating applications. We want to change this: every researcher building high-speed network applications should understand the intricacies of the underlying drivers, especially if they impact performance. We present ixy, a user space network driver designed for simplicity and educational purposes to show that fast packet IO is not black magic but careful engineering. ixy focuses on the bare essentials of user space packet processing: a packet forwarder including the whole NIC driver uses less than 1,000 lines of C code. This paper is partially written in tutorial style on the case study of our implementations of drivers for both the Intel 82599 family and for virtual VirtIO NICs. The former allows us to reason about driver and framework performance on a stripped-down implementation to assess individual optimizations in isolation. VirtIO support ensures that everyone can run it in a virtual machine. Our code is available as free and open source under the BSD license at https://github.com/emmericp/ixy
technical_mechanism: Vary NIC ring size under load and measure packet latency with hardware timestamps to test whether buffering in the ring contributes to delay.
why_it_works: A controlled change to ring size changes available buffering; the observed latency response can expose queueing delay attributable to the NIC ring rather than relying on full request tracing.
root_seam: At the robot or server NIC, associate packet timestamps with the configured RX ring size and, if available, ring occupancy. This would help Root identify transport-side buffering as a contributor to tail latency, separately from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application.
experiment: Under repeatable inference traffic, vary RX ring size while holding workload and other settings constant. Collect packet-level hardware timestamps and compare latency distributions across configurations; correlate tail changes with ring settings to test for NIC-ring queueing.
evidence_quote: The results show a linear dependency between ring size and latency when the system is overloaded, but the effect under lower loads are negligible.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, passage beginning “ware timestamping ... with different ring sizes”
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The text reports an experimental relationship between configured ring size and latency, but does not establish a request-to-packet mapping or report ring occupancy as a measured signal. Its transfer to remote robot inference therefore requires packet identity/timestamp integration at Root.

title: Computing Extremely Accurate Quantiles Using t-Digests
abstract: We present on-line algorithms for computing approximations of rank-based statistics that give high accuracy, particularly near the tails of a distribution, with very small sketches. Notably, the method allows a quantile q to be computed with an accuracy relative to (q, 1-q) rather than absolute accuracy as with most other methods. This new algorithm is robust with respect to skewed distributions or ordered datasets and allows separately computed summaries to be combined with no loss in accuracy. An open-source Java implementation of this algorithm is available from the author. Independent implementations in Go and Python are also available.
technical_mechanism: Build a compact, mergeable t-digest by clustering streaming values into weighted centroids, with a scale function that constrains cluster sizes to be small near distribution tails and larger near the center; estimate quantiles from the resulting summary.
why_it_works: Small tail clusters preserve finer rank resolution for extreme quantiles, while larger central clusters keep the sketch compact. Digests from separate streams or partitions can be merged, supporting summarized latency distributions without retaining every sample.
root_seam: Attach a digest to timestamped request or transport-event latency samples, partitioned by robot, server, or network stage, and merge digests across intervals or workers. This would preserve tail-quantile summaries at low storage cost, but does not itself distinguish network delay from queueing, compute, or action-application delay; those require separately identified measurements.
experiment: For the same labeled request traces, compare per-stage t-digest tail quantiles against exact quantiles while varying compression and partition/merge structure. Measure quantile error and storage, and check whether the summaries preserve detection of known network-tail regressions.
evidence_quote: Importantly, we force clusters near both ends to be small while allowing sub-sequences in middle to be larger in order to get fairly constant relative accuracy.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section 2.2, “A simple start”
reported_gain: The paper reports that t-digest errors are more than an order of magnitude smaller than Q-digest errors across q values in the described comparison, and 3–5 orders of magnitude smaller in absolute error near q = 0.
baseline: Q-digest
uncertainty: The paper evaluates quantile-summary accuracy, not network-regression diagnosis. It does not establish which latency signals or request identities Root can collect, nor whether the reported quantile gains preserve detection of network-specific tails.

title: COP2: Continuously Observing Protocol Performance
abstract: As enterprises move to a cloud-first approach, their network becomes crucial to their daily operations and has to be continuously monitored. Although passive monitoring can be convenient from a deployment viewpoint, inferring the state of each connection can cause them to miss important information (e.g., starvation). Furthermore, the increasing usage of fully encrypted protocols (e.g., QUIC encrypts headers), possibly over multiple paths (e.g., MPTCP), keeps diminishing the applicability of such techniques to future networks. We propose a new monitoring framework, Flowcorder, which leverages information already maintained by the end-hosts and records Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) from their transport protocols. More specifically, we present a generic approach which inserts lightweight eBPF probes at runtime in the protocol implementations. These probes extract KPIs from the per-connection states, and eventually export them over IPFIX for analysis. We present an application of this technique to the Linux kernel TCP stack and demonstrate its generality by extending it to support MPTCP. Our performance evaluation confirms that its overhead is negligible. Finally, we present live measurements collected with Flowcorder in a campus network, highlighting some insights provided by our framework.
technical_mechanism: Install lightweight eBPF probes in the end-host transport implementation and read per-connection KPIs at selected lifecycle transitions and unexpected events, rather than on every packet. Summarize KPI changes between events as connection performance profiles and export them with connection and path identifiers over IPFIX.
why_it_works: Transport state exposes signals passive packet monitoring can miss, including encrypted or multipath traffic, and event-based sampling avoids recording every packet. RTT evolution, loss, retransmissions, reordering, and stalls can reveal transport/path degradation; profiles associated with connection transitions can help separate network symptoms from server compute or action-application time when paired with request timing.
root_seam: Attach probes at the robot-side and inference-server transport stacks, then correlate connection/path identifiers and profile timestamps with request IDs and application-stage timestamps. This would add transport-level evidence—such as RTT changes, loss, retransmissions, or progress stalls—without requiring full packet tracing. The paper does not itself provide request-to-packet correlation.
experiment: In a controlled Root workload, correlate request IDs and application-stage timestamps with event-based transport KPI profiles from both endpoints. Inject network delay, jitter, and loss separately from server queueing and GPU delay; test whether profiles distinguish network-induced tail requests from compute-induced tails. Compare diagnostic accuracy and collection overhead against no probes and per-packet KPI collection.
evidence_quote: Instead, we aim at recording the evolution of kpis between key events in the connection life-cycle.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, section 3.3, Creating performance profiles
reported_gain: Flowcorder adds less than 1% to executed instructions on a perfect link; the reported median completion-time increase for a one-segment HTTP response is about 0.017%.
baseline: No instrumentation and a naive eBPF instrumentation that updates KPIs on each incoming segment; application-performance tests also compare against no instrumentation.
uncertainty: The paper measures transport monitoring overhead and reports campus-network observations, but does not demonstrate request-level tail localization or correlation to robot inference stages. Its profiles are event-based, not tail-triggered, and the text does not establish off-path flow attribution.

title: An SDN-Based Transmission Protocol with In-Path Packet Caching and Retransmission
abstract: In this paper, a comprehensive software-defined networking (SDN) based transmission protocol (SDTP) is presented for fifth generation (5G) communication networks, where an SDN controller gathers network state information from the physical network to improve data transmission efficiency between end hosts, with in-path packet retransmission. In the SDTP, we first develop a new two-way handshake mechanism for connection establishment between a pair of end host. With the aid of SDN control module, signaling exchanges for establishing E2E connections are migrated to the control plane to improve resource utilization in the data plane. A new SDTP packet header format is designed to support efficient data transmission with in-path packet caching and packet retransmission. Based on the new data packet format, a novel in-path receiver-based packet loss detection and caching-based packet retransmission scheme is proposed to achieve in-path fast recovery of lost packets. Extensive simulation results are presented to validate the effectiveness of the proposed protocol in terms of low connection establishment delay and low end-to-end packet transmission delay.
technical_mechanism: Adaptive sequence-gap and interarrival loss detection with retransmission-event timing: in-path nodes track received sequence windows and expected packets, compare observed interarrival time and out-of-order counts with adaptive thresholds, then record retransmission requests and retransmission RTTs. The node that detects a gap and the recovery events can expose where a packet drought and its repair occurred.
why_it_works: A sequence gap or interarrival interval exceeding a predictor-based expectation is a concrete packet-level signal, while the trigger type, request, and recovery time add a temporal signature of loss recovery. Observing these events at multiple points can help distinguish a network packet drought and its location from delay that occurs after packet delivery. This supports n05's search for compact drought/recovery signatures. The paper does not establish that these signatures distinguish jitter from endpoint stalls, so n08 is not promoted.
root_seam: At an accessible robot-side or server-side transport boundary, correlate request identity with packet sequence numbers, receive timestamps, loss-detection trigger, retransmission request/response, and recovery time. If intermediate instrumentation is available, compare the same events across points to narrow the affected network segment. Root would gain packet-level evidence of gaps and recovery timing to compare against inference, server-queue, GPU, and action-application timestamps; it need not assume access to the paper's SDN infrastructure.
experiment: Replay identical inference traffic under separately controlled packet loss, jitter without loss, and endpoint stalls. Collect request-linked sequence numbers, packet receive times, adaptive-threshold triggers, retransmission events, and inference-stage timestamps. Test whether gap and recovery signatures detect and localize loss-related tails, and whether they separate those cases from jitter and endpoint stalls. Compare with ordinary end-to-end timing; do not treat the paper's simulation results as a Root gain.
evidence_quote: The expected interarrival time, denoted by ∆TE, can be obtained by linear prediction based on sampled interarrival time
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, section C.2, “Interarrival Timeout”
reported_gain: Qualitative simulations report lower average end-to-end packet delay and lower delay jitter than TCP, with the difference increasing as packet loss rises; no numerical gain is stated in the supplied text.
baseline: TCP
uncertainty: The evidence supports a concrete loss-detection and recovery-event chain, but the paper evaluates transport performance in simulation rather than diagnostic accuracy for inference tails. It does not validate that the event signatures distinguish ordinary jitter from endpoint stalls, nor establish Root performance.

title: Fifty Shades of Congestion Control: A Performance and Interactions Evaluation
abstract: Congestion control algorithms are crucial in achieving high utilization while preventing overloading the network. Over the years, many different congestion control algorithms have been developed, each trying to improve in specific situations. However, their interactions and co-existence has, to date, not been thoroughly evaluated, which is the focus of this paper. Through head-to-head comparisons of representatives from loss-based, delay-based and hybrid types of congestion control algorithms, we reveal that fairness in resources claimed is often not attained, especially when flows sharing a link have different RTTs.
technical_mechanism: Detect ACK-path compression or loss by comparing ACK spacing/rate at the receiver with ACK arrivals at the sender, then correlate that distortion with sender-observed RTT and transport performance.
why_it_works: ACKs arriving in bursts or being lost can make a sender misestimate the network state and change its sending rate. The paper connects distorted ACK timing and increased sender-observed delay to queues on the ACK path, exposing a shared network resource that can affect a flow even when the congestion is not on its forward data path. This is more diagnostic than observing request latency alone, though it does not identify the competing flow.
root_seam: For a request-associated transport flow, retain ACK send/arrival timing or packet-level ACK spacing alongside RTT and request timestamps. This could distinguish reverse-path queueing or ACK compression from server queueing, GPU compute, and action application, without assuming access to Reflex infrastructure.
experiment: Replay a representative inference workload with a controlled competing flow that queues or compresses ACKs on the reverse path, and compare against an otherwise identical no-contention run. Record request timing, sender-side RTT, and ACK timing at both ends where available; separately record server queueing, GPU compute, and action application. Test whether ACK-spacing distortion and sender-observed delay identify the network contribution to the tail.
evidence_quote: If ACKs spend any time in queues or get lost, the sender might be misled into sending more data than the network can accept (if ACKs arrive in bursts), or will detect congestion even if bandwidth is available on its path to the sender.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, section on sensitivity to ACK-compression.
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: The paper compares scenarios with and without cross-traffic and reports transport metrics; it does not report a Root comparison.
uncertainty: The paper supports diagnosing ACK-path distortion and shared bottleneck effects in controlled tests, but does not establish a method for identifying an unknown off-path flow in production or attributing an individual Root request tail. Root-measured gain is UNKNOWN.

title: Leveraging Deep Learning to Improve the Performance Predictability of Cloud Microservices
abstract: Performance unpredictability is a major roadblock towards cloud adoption, and has performance, cost, and revenue ramifications. Predictable performance is even more critical as cloud services transition from monolithic designs to microservices. Detecting QoS violations after they occur in systems with microservices results in long recovery times, as hotspots propagate and amplify across dependent services. We present Seer, an online cloud performance debugging system that leverages deep learning and the massive amount of tracing data cloud systems collect to learn spatial and temporal patterns that translate to QoS violations. Seer combines lightweight distributed RPC-level tracing, with detailed low-level hardware monitoring to signal an upcoming QoS violation, and diagnose the source of unpredictable performance. Once an imminent QoS violation is detected, Seer notifies the cluster manager to take action to avoid performance degradation altogether. We evaluate Seer both in local clusters, and in large-scale deployments of end-to-end applications built with microservices with hundreds of users. We show that Seer correctly anticipates QoS violations 91% of the time, and avoids the QoS violation to begin with in 84% of cases. Finally, we show that Seer can identify application-level design bugs, and provide insights on how to better architect microservices to achieve predictable performance.
technical_mechanism: Cross-layer queue and stage-time comparison with on-demand hardware diagnosis: Seer combines per-request RPC-stage timing and per-microservice outstanding-request counts with NIC and software queue measurements. It uses the lightweight signals to identify an impending QoS violation and likely initiating service, then collects detailed hardware diagnostics for that service.
why_it_works: Separating time spent handling network requests from application computation, and comparing NIC queues with software queues, provides evidence about where delay is accumulating without requiring detailed hardware tracing everywhere. The paper also compares network-only and application-only queue signals, supporting a controlled test of whether combining layers improves localization. This can identify network-side queueing, but does not by itself distinguish every transport cause, such as loss versus congestion.
root_seam: At Root's robot/server RPC boundaries, retain request identity and stage timestamps, plus available NIC/transport and application-queue measurements. Compare network-side and server-side queue buildup for the same request; collect more expensive host diagnostics only when the lightweight signals flag a likely culprit. This adds cross-layer localization evidence beyond end-to-end latency alone and may reduce continuous detailed-trace collection.
experiment: Inject network delay or drops, server queueing, and compute contention separately on Root workloads. Compare end-to-end timing alone, network-side signals alone, application-side signals alone, and the combined signals. Measure tail-regression detection and layer-localization accuracy, lead time, and collection overhead; do not treat Seer's reported results as Root results.
evidence_quote: To distinguish between the time spent processing network requests, and the time that goes towards application computation, we instrument the application to report the time it sees a new request (post- RPC processing).
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section 4.2, “Distributed Tracing” → “Instrumentation.”
reported_gain: Seer reports correctly identifying 90.6% of upcoming QoS violations and avoiding 84% in the large-scale Social Network deployment.
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The supplied text supports cross-layer signal collection and a comparison of network-only versus application-only queues, but gives no numerical comparison results for those variants. Root's available NIC/transport instrumentation and the resulting localization accuracy are unknown; the paper's reported performance is not a Root-measured gain.

title: Measuring and simulating latency in interactive remote rendering systems
abstract: Background: The computationally intensive task of real-time rendering can be offloaded to remote cloud systems. However, due to network latency, interactive remote rendering (IRR) introduces the challenge of interaction latency (IL), which is the time between an action and response to that action. Objectives: to model sources of latency, measure it in a real-world network and to use this understanding to simulate latency so that we have a controlled platform for experimental work in latency management. Method: we present a seven-parameter model of latency for a typical IRR system; we describe new, minimally intrusive software methods for measuring latency in a 3D graphics environment and create a novel latency simulator tool in software. Results: We demonstrate our latency simulator is comparable to real-world behavior and confirm that real-world latency exceeds the interactive limit of 70ms over long distance connections. We also find that current approaches to measuring IL are not general enough for most situations and therefore propose a novel general-purpose solution. Conclusion: to ameliorate latency in IRR systems we need controllable simulation tools for experimentation. In addition to a new measurement technique, we propose a new approach that will be of interest to IRR researchers and developers when designing IL compensation techniques.
technical_mechanism: Correlate a client interaction with its server response by attaching a unique GUID to the request and response, timing from client registration until the matching response arrives; separately model end-to-end latency as input, client, network, server, and display components. The paper also provides a tunable asynchronous latency simulator for controlled latency experiments.
why_it_works: The GUID identifies which returning response belongs to an interaction, enabling per-interaction timing rather than confusing unrelated frame updates with its result. Measuring at pipeline boundaries can distinguish network transit from client, server, and display delays. The simulator allows controlled latency changes without synchronous backlog growth, supporting repeatable tests; however, the evidence does not establish a method for diagnosing rare network tails or separating queue buildup within the network.
root_seam: Attach request IDs and timestamps at robot action creation/send and server receipt/response/send, then match them at the robot on response arrival. This would give per-action end-to-end and boundary timings to separate transport delay from server processing, while the simulator offers a controlled test platform. The supplied evidence does not describe packet/ACK-level signals or a queue-specific diagnostic.
experiment: In a robot inference loop, correlate action requests and returned results with unique IDs and record timestamps at client send, server receive, server response, and client receive. Inject controlled network delays using asynchronous processing, then compare the inferred network component against known injected delay and separately measure server time. Test repeated runs with ordinary delays and rare injected spikes to evaluate detection and localization; the paper itself does not report this Root experiment.
evidence_quote: The GUID should be included in the interaction message sent to the rendering server. The first result message from the server must include the initiating GUID when sent back to the client.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, integrated measurement approach
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The context supports request-response correlation, a latency-component model, and a controllable simulator, but gives no detailed quantitative evidence for queue discrimination or rare-tail localization. The simulator validates against real-world measurements in remote rendering, not robot inference.

title: Approximate Quantiles for Datacenter Telemetry Monitoring
abstract: Datacenter systems require efficient troubleshooting and effective resource scheduling so as to minimize downtimes and to efficiently utilize limited resources. In doing so, datacenter operators employ streaming analytics for collecting and processing datacenter telemetry over a temporal window. The quantile operator is key to these systems as it can summarize the typical and abnormal behavior of the monitored system. Computing quantiles in real-time is resource-intensive as it requires processing hundreds of millions of events in seconds while providing high accuracy. We overcome these challenges in real-time quantile computation through workload-driven approximation, motivated by three insights in our study: (i) values are dominated by a set of recurring small values, (ii) distribution of small values is consistent across different time scales, and (iii) tail values are dominated by a small set of large values. That is, we propose AOMG, an efficient and accurate quantile approximation algorithm that capitalizes on these insights. AOMG minimizes memory footprint of the quantile operator via compression and frequency-based summarization of small values. While these summaries are stored and processed at sub-window granularity for memory efficiency, they can extend to compute quantiles on user-defined temporal windows. Low value error for tail quantiles is achieved by retaining a few tail values per subwindow. AOMG estimates quantiles with high throughput and less than 5% relative value error across a wide range of use cases while state-of-the-art algorithms either have a high relative value error (9.3-137.0%) or deliver lower throughput (15-92%).
technical_mechanism: AOMG compresses and frequency-summarizes recurring small values, while retaining a few tail values per subwindow to estimate high quantiles. It uses top-k merging when subwindows have too few observations for statistically robust high quantiles, and sample-k merging to represent bursty tails; burst detection compares sampled large values across adjacent subwindows.
why_it_works: The method allocates memory according to observed workload structure: recurring small values need compact summaries, while a small number of large values dominate high quantiles. Explicit tail retention protects estimates from sparse or bursty extremes. This can provide low-error summaries of network-latency tails at lower cost than exact quantiles, but it does not identify which request or network event caused a tail.
root_seam: Attach the method to a stream of timestamped robot inference request RTTs or other transport-latency measurements, grouped into temporal subwindows. Root could obtain lower-cost, accurate aggregate tail quantiles and detect subwindows with bursty tails; this does not itself separate network delay from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application.
experiment: Replay timestamped healthy and tail-latency measurements through AOMG and exact quantile computation over the same windows. Compare high-quantile relative value error, throughput, and memory use; inject a tail burst into selected subwindows and evaluate whether burst detection and sample-k merging preserve the resulting window quantiles. The paper reports datacenter and synthetic workload evaluations, not a Root experiment.
evidence_quote: AOMG explicitly records tail values to better approximate the high quantiles
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, section on high quantiles.
reported_gain: On the evaluated workloads, average relative value error for different quantiles is below 5%; compared with prior approximate quantile algorithms, space usage is around 5–20 times lower. Relative to exact quantiles, throughput is 2.4–4.8 times higher for a 10K-element window and up to 62 times higher for a 1M-element window.
baseline: Exact quantile computation and prior approximate quantile algorithms, including CMQS, AM, Random, and Moment.
uncertainty: The context demonstrates aggregate quantile accuracy and resource benefits, but not per-request differential diagnosis, causal localization, or tail-triggered trace retention with measured overhead savings. Transfer to Root depends on having a suitable timestamped latency stream; the method alone cannot attribute delay to network versus other inference stages.

title: Streaming Quantiles Algorithms with Small Space and Update Time
abstract: Approximating quantiles and distributions over streaming data has been studied for roughly two decades now. Recently, Karnin, Lang, and Liberty proposed the first asymptotically optimal algorithm for doing so. This manuscript complements their theoretical result by providing a practical variants of their algorithm with improved constants. For a given sketch size, our techniques provably reduce the upper bound on the sketch error by a factor of two. These improvements are verified experimentally.
