Our modified quantile sketch improves the latency as well by reducing the worst case update time from O(1/ε) down to O((1/ε)). We also suggest two algorithms for weighted item streams which offer improved asymptotic update times compared to na"ive extensions. Finally, we provide a specialized data structure for these sketches which reduces both their memory footprints and update times.
technical_mechanism: Maintain a bounded-space KLL quantile sketch of streaming latency measurements: compact buffered items into weighted representatives, then estimate quantiles with rank-error guarantees. Root could attach sketches to network-stage timings to retain tail-distribution summaries without storing every request.
why_it_works: The sketch preserves approximate rank information while discarding most individual measurements, making high quantiles measurable under a memory limit. Comparing sketches for transport, server queueing, GPU compute, and action application could show which stage's latency distribution develops a tail, though the sketch does not establish causality by itself.
root_seam: Attach a separate sketch to timestamped per-request durations at robot-side send/receive and server-side transport, queue, compute, and action-application boundaries. This would provide bounded-memory stage-level tail summaries; request-level traces or additional signals would still be needed to localize individual causes.
experiment: Replay the same timestamped remote-inference requests through a full-data quantile calculation and bounded-memory KLL sketches at several space limits. Compare p95/p99 estimates and rank error for each pipeline-stage duration, including during injected network-delay episodes, and compare memory use against retaining all samples.
evidence_quote: For a given sketch size, our techniques provably reduce the upper bound on the sketch error by a factor of two.
evidence_location: Abstract; also selected PDF text, Abstract.
reported_gain: The paper reports a factor-of-two reduction in the upper bound on sketch error for a given sketch size; it also reports reducing worst-case update time from O(1/ε) to O(log(1/ε)). These are paper results, not Root measurements.
baseline: KLL algorithm of Karnin, Lang, and Liberty; the abstract does not specify the exact experimental comparison baseline for the factor-of-two error bound.
uncertainty: The supplied text supports approximate quantile sketches and experimental evaluation, but does not report network-tail diagnosis or stage-specific measurements. Quantile sketches summarize distributions; they do not preserve request identities or directly distinguish network delay from server queueing without separate stage signals.

title: Model based Level Shift Detection in Autocorrelated Data Streams using a moving window
abstract: Standard Control Chart techniques to detect level shift in data streams assume independence between observations. As data today is collected with high frequency, this assumption is seldom valid. To overcome this, we propose to adapt the off-line test procedure for detection of outliers based on one-step prediction errors proposed by Tsay (1988) into an on-line framework by considering a moving window. Further, we present two algorithms, that in combination, estimate an appropriate test value for our control chart. We test our method on AR(1) processes exposed to level shifts of different sizes and compare it to CUSUM applied to one-step prediction errors. We find that, even though both methods perform comparable when tuned correctly, our method has higher probability of identifying the correct change point of the process. Furthermore, for more complicated processes our method is easier to tune, as the range of window size to be tested is independent of the process.
technical_mechanism: Use a moving-window, model-based level-shift detector on one-step prediction errors from an autocorrelated latency stream. The window tests candidate shift times, and a critical value calibrated to a target in-control average run length controls alarms. An alarm can trigger richer profiling.
why_it_works: Prediction errors account for the stream’s autocorrelation, while testing candidate change points within a bounded window can both flag a sustained mean shift and locate its onset. This provides a concrete trigger beyond a raw latency threshold; Root can evaluate it as an alarm for increased transport latency, distinct from server queueing, GPU compute, or action-application delay.
root_seam: Attach the detector to timestamped, per-request transport latency measurements, preserving request identity and separating transport duration from server queueing, GPU time, and action application. Use an alarm to retain or collect richer traces around the suspected change.
experiment: Replay timestamped Root request traces with autocorrelated baseline variation and injected sustained network-delay level shifts. Compare the moving-window detector with a simple threshold and CUSUM at matched false-alarm rates. Measure detection delay, change-point localization, false triggers, and monitoring overhead; test whether alarms selectively trigger expensive profiling. Do not treat transient tail spikes as equivalent to the paper’s level shifts.
evidence_quote: To convert the method by Tsay into an on-line application, we only consider a moving window of observations.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section 2, Method
reported_gain: On simulated AR(1) level shifts, the paper reports 39% better overall performance than CUSUM setting 1 and comparable performance to tuned CUSUM setting 2; it also reports a higher probability of identifying the correct change point. These are paper results, not Root-measured gains.
baseline: CUSUM applied to one-step prediction errors on simulated AR(1) processes with level shifts.
uncertainty: The evaluation is on simulated level shifts, not network latency tails or remote robot inference. The paper does not establish runtime overhead, performance on transient tail spikes, or whether alarms reduce profiling cost.

title: DDSketch: A fast and fully-mergeable quantile sketch with relative-error guarantees
abstract: Summary statistics such as the mean and variance are easily maintained for large, distributed data streams, but order statistics (i.e., sample quantiles) can only be approximately summarized. There is extensive literature on maintaining quantile sketches where the emphasis has been on bounding the rank error of the sketch while using little memory. Unfortunately, rank error guarantees do not preclude arbitrarily large relative errors, and this often occurs in practice when the data is heavily skewed. Given the distributed nature of contemporary large-scale systems, another crucial property for quantile sketches is mergeablility, i.e., several combined sketches must be as accurate as a single sketch of the same data. We present the first fully-mergeable, relative-error quantile sketching algorithm with formal guarantees. The sketch is extremely fast and accurate, and is currently being used by Datadog at a wide-scale.
technical_mechanism: Encode each latency observation into a fixed logarithmic bucket, increment its count, and merge sketches by summing matching bucket counts. Query the merged counts for quantiles with relative-error guarantees, retaining useful tail-latency summaries without storing every observation.
why_it_works: Logarithmic bucket widths preserve relative accuracy even for heavily skewed latency distributions, where rank-error sketches can give large relative errors at high quantiles. Mergeability lets summaries from distributed sources be combined while retaining quantile accuracy. For Root, applying this to separately measured transport intervals could expose changes in network p95/p99 without shipping every request sample; the sketch itself would summarize delay, not identify its cause.
root_seam: Attach the sketch to request-correlated robot-side and server-side transport interval measurements, with network time separated from server queueing, GPU compute, and action application. Compare per-stage quantiles across time windows or robot/server groups. The paper does not provide request-level causal localization, so timestamps or request identities and stage-specific measurements must be collected separately.
experiment: In a controlled Root replay or test deployment, record per-request network-stage latency and exact values as ground truth. Build and periodically merge DDSketch summaries at robot and server collectors; compare estimated p50/p95/p99 and relative error against exact quantiles under normal traffic and injected network-tail conditions. Also measure bytes retained or transmitted versus raw samples, and confirm that non-network stages are summarized separately.
evidence_quote: We present the first fully-mergeable, relative-error quantile sketching algorithm with formal guarantees.
evidence_location: Abstract; selected PDF text, Section 2.1 describes logarithmic buckets and merging.
reported_gain: The paper reports that on heavy-tailed data DDSketch's relative-accuracy improvement over GK can be measured in orders of magnitude, and that merging can be more than an order of magnitude faster than GKArray or HDR Histogram in some comparisons. No Root gain is reported.
baseline: GKArray (Greenwald–Khanna), HDR Histogram, and Moments sketch in the paper's evaluation; exact Root baseline is UNKNOWN.
uncertainty: The paper sketches observed values such as request or trace durations; it does not establish that those values isolate network delay. Root must instrument stage-specific transport intervals, and the proposed Root experiment has not been reported.

title: Tiny Buffer TCP for Data Center Networks
abstract: A low and stable buffer occupancy is critical to achieve high throughput, low packet drop rate, low latency, and low jitter for data center networks. It also allows switch chips to support higher port density, larger lookup tables, or richer functions. Tiny Buffer TCP creatively uses the common RED-based ECN with two novel congestion-window adjustment schemes to significantly reduce the required buffer size. Aiming to eliminate the residual packets in the bottleneck queue, Queue Canceling Decrease amortizes the ideal window reduction to the same number of flows so as to minimize the impact to active flows. In order to keep the buffer occupancy low and stable, Reduced Additive Increase recovers the flow window at a slower pace than normal. We implemented TBTCP in Linux kernel and conducted ns2-based simulations and real network-based tests. Our results show that compared to DCTCP, TBTCP reduces the switch buffer requirement by more than 80%, increases the bandwidth utilization by up to 15%, improves the FCT performance by up to 39%, and achieve a 71% better RTT fairness index.
technical_mechanism: RED-based ECN marks packets according to bottleneck queue depth. Queue Canceling Decrease spreads one-MSS congestion-window reductions across marked flows to drain residual queued packets; Reduced Additive Increase restores windows slowly to stabilize occupancy.
why_it_works: The queue-dependent ECN signal ties congestion feedback to bottleneck buffering, a direct indicator of network queueing rather than server or GPU delay. The mechanisms actively reduce and stabilize that queue, so a Root experiment can compare transport queue signals with end-to-end latency and separate queue buildup from non-network latency. This is congestion control, not a standalone diagnostic method.
root_seam: At the robot/server transport boundary, associate request timestamps with TCP ECN feedback and, where available, bottleneck queue-depth telemetry. This would provide evidence of transport queueing during a slow inference request, distinct from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application. The paper's mechanism assumes a controllable TCP sender and RED/ECN-capable switches, which may not be available on a robot-to-cloud path.
experiment: In a controlled Root test, induce transport contention while holding inference workload constant; record request latency, ECN marks, RTT, and queue depth where accessible. Compare latency tails with and without TBTCP-style queue control, and check whether elevated network queue signals precede slow requests while server/GPU timings remain stable.
evidence_quote: The buffer occupancy, which is reflected in queue depth, is a direct signal for network congestion status.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, paragraph beginning “The buffer occupancy, which is reflected in queue depth”.
reported_gain: Compared to DCTCP, the paper reports over 80% lower switch buffer requirement, up to 15% higher bandwidth utilization, up to 39% better FCT performance, and a 71% better RTT fairness index.
baseline: DCTCP
uncertainty: The paper evaluates data-center TCP congestion control, not robot-to-cloud inference diagnosis. Whether the relevant path exposes ECN or queue-depth telemetry, permits sender-side TCP changes, or exhibits comparable bottleneck behavior is unknown.

title: Accurate and Fast Retrieval for Complex Non-metric Data via Neighborhood Graphs
abstract: We demonstrate that a graph-based search algorithm-relying on the construction of an approximate neighborhood graph-can directly work with challenging non-metric and/or non-symmetric distances without resorting to metric-space mapping and/or distance symmetrization, which, in turn, lead to substantial performance degradation. Although the straightforward metrization and symmetrization is usually ineffective, we find that constructing an index using a modified, e.g., symmetrized, distance can improve performance. This observation paves a way to a new line of research of designing index-specific graph-construction distance functions.
technical_mechanism: Build an approximate neighborhood graph over stored items, optionally using a modified distance for graph construction, then retrieve similar items by graph traversal using the query distance.
why_it_works: The graph links nearby items so search can explore promising neighborhoods rather than exhaustively compare the query with the full collection. The paper reports that a construction distance different from the retrieval distance can sometimes improve the index.
root_seam: Index feature representations of prior robot-inference requests and retrieve comparable requests when investigating a regression. This could accelerate healthy-baseline lookup, but does not itself identify whether delay came from network transport, server queueing, GPU compute, or action application.
experiment: On a fixed corpus of prior requests, compare graph-index retrieval with exhaustive nearest-neighbor retrieval for baseline lookup. Measure lookup latency and recall of the same comparable requests; test original versus modified graph-construction distances while keeping query-time distance fixed.
evidence_quote: indexing can dramatically speed up retrieval
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section 2.1, Retrieval Algorithms
reported_gain: Up to 10× speedup in some index-time symmetrization cases; the paper also reports up to an order-of-magnitude performance loss for full symmetrization in many high-dimensional cases.
baseline: Brute-force search is the reported speedup comparison; the paper also compares graph-index variants.
uncertainty: The paper evaluates nearest-neighbor retrieval on non-metric data, not robot requests or network-tail diagnosis. Whether request features support useful comparable-baseline retrieval, and whether that helps localize network delay, is untested.

title: Optimal experimental design via Bayesian optimization: active causal structure learning for Gaussian process networks
abstract: We study the problem of causal discovery through targeted interventions. Starting from few observational measurements, we follow a Bayesian active learning approach to perform those experiments which, in expectation with respect to the current model, are maximally informative about the underlying causal structure. Unlike previous work, we consider the setting of continuous random variables with non-linear functional relationships, modelled with Gaussian process priors. To address the arising problem of choosing from an uncountable set of possible interventions, we propose to use Bayesian optimisation to efficiently maximise a Monte Carlo estimate of the expected information gain.
technical_mechanism: Actively select the next controlled intervention to maximize expected information gain about competing causal graphs: estimate graph-posterior entropy reduction from interventional outcomes, approximate it with Monte Carlo under GP models, and use Bayesian optimization to search intervention targets and values.
why_it_works: Competing causal graphs predict different outcome distributions under interventions. Choosing the intervention expected to make their posterior beliefs diverge can distinguish causes with fewer measurements than fixed or random experiments. For Root, this is a diagnostic experiment-design method, not passive network telemetry or a latency mitigation.
root_seam: In a controlled Root testbed, represent network conditions, server queueing, GPU compute, and end-to-end or stage-level request latency as variables. Apply interventions such as injected transport delay/loss or controlled server load, then record request-identified outcomes and update competing causal hypotheses. This could guide which controlled condition to test next; the paper does not supply Root instrumentation or establish that its model assumptions fit production network tails.
experiment: With an equal number of request measurements, compare the method's information-gain-selected interventions against random and fixed intervention schedules. In a testbed, vary transport delay/loss and server load independently and measure transport, queueing, GPU, and end-to-end latency for identified requests. Evaluate how quickly each schedule distinguishes injected network-tail causes from server-side causes and whether it identifies the responsible intervention. Treat as a proposed Root experiment, not a reported Root result.
evidence_quote: we follow a Bayesian active learning approach to perform those experiments which, in expectation with respect to the current model, are maximally informative about the underlying causal structure.
evidence_location: Abstract; Section 4, “Proposed approach,” specifies maximizing information gain over intervention target and value, with a Monte Carlo objective and Bayesian optimization.
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The active intervention-selection mechanism and its causal-discrimination rationale are supported, making n10 transferable to controlled Root diagnosis. The paper studies causal discovery in small Gaussian-process networks, not network-performance diagnosis; it does not establish that Root's latency variables satisfy its assumptions or report a comparison demonstrating fewer measurements.

title: Root Cause Detection Among Anomalous Time Series Using Temporal State Alignment
abstract: The recent increase in the scale and complexity of software systems has introduced new challenges to the time series monitoring and anomaly detection process. A major drawback of existing anomaly detection methods is that they lack contextual information to help stakeholders identify the cause of anomalies. This problem, known as root cause detection, is particularly challenging to undertake in today's complex distributed software systems since the metrics under consideration generally have multiple internal and external dependencies. Significant manual analysis and strong domain expertise is required to isolate the correct cause of the problem. In this paper, we propose a method that isolates the root cause of an anomaly by analyzing the patterns in time series fluctuations. Our method considers the time series as observations from an underlying process passing through a sequence of discretized hidden states. The idea is to track the propagation of the effect when a given problem causes unaligned but homogeneous shifts of the underlying states. We evaluate our approach by finding the root cause of anomalies in Zillows clickstream data by identifying causal patterns among a set of observed fluctuations.
technical_mechanism: Residual-state temporal alignment: fit a state-space model to each anomalous metric series, discretize its residuals into ordered states, then apply shifted DTW to align and cluster lagged state-propagation patterns and score candidate causal groups.
why_it_works: The method compares local anomaly-state patterns rather than raw values, making differently scaled metrics comparable. Shifted temporal alignment can expose a metric entering an anomalous state before related metrics, while clustering narrows which dimensions need investigation. For Root, this offers a candidate way to localize lagged cross-layer propagation from sparse timestamped metrics rather than requiring full request traces. It identifies candidate relationships, not definitive causation, and does not inherently distinguish network delay from server queueing or compute.
root_seam: Attach the method to timestamped, per-window robot/server metrics: transport send/receive or ACK/loss timing, queue/NIC signals, and inference-stage timings. Use already-detected anomalous windows to compare discretized residual-state sequences, cluster similar propagation patterns, and rank which signals precede the tail. No Reflex private infrastructure is assumed.
experiment: In an isolated remote-inference test, inject network delay or loss separately from server queueing and GPU load. Collect timestamped metrics across those layers, identify anomalous windows, and compare state-alignment clusters and causality scores with the known injected cause and full traces. Measure localization accuracy and the number of signals required against a full-tracing baseline; do not interpret paper results as Root gains.
evidence_quote: we perform a DTW based temporal alignment to group the similar residual state propagations into clusters.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section I (Introduction); method details in Section III, “Temporal Alignment.”
reported_gain: Lower empirical clustering classification error for SAC-DTW than C-DTW in the simulation study; numeric gain unavailable in supplied text. No Root-measured gain.
baseline: C-DTW, a DTW-based causality detection method.
uncertainty: The method assumes anomalies are already detected and metrics are granular enough for temporal lags to be identifiable. Evidence is from simulations and Zillow clickstream data, not remote robot inference. Whether sparse transport and inference metrics yield stable clusters, and whether the method can separate network delay from queueing or compute, requires controlled validation.

title: Indoor Localization System of ROS mobile robot based on Visible Light Communication
abstract: In this paper, an indoor robot localization system based on Robot Operating System (ROS) and visible light communication (VLC) is presented. On the basis of our previous work, we innovatively designed a VLC localization and navigation package based on Robot Operating System (ROS), which contains the LED-ID detection and recognition method, the video target tracking algorithm and the double-lamp positioning algorithm. This package exploited the principle of double-lamp positioning and the loose coupling characteristics of the ROS system, which is implemented by loosely coupled ROS nodes. Consequently, this paper combines ROS and VLC, aiming at promoting the application of VLC positioning in mature robotic systems. Moreover, it pushed forward the development of localization application based on VLC technology and lays a foundation for transplanting to other ROS robot platforms. Experimental results show that the proposed system can provide indoor localization within 1 cm and possesses a good real-time performance which takes only 0.4 seconds for one-time positioning. And if a high-performance laptop is used, the single positioning time can be reduced to 0.08 seconds. Therefore, this study confirms the practical application and the superior performance of VLC technology in ROS robot, showing the great potential of VLC localization. T he video demo of the proposed robot positioning system based on VLC can be seen in *
technical_mechanism: Payload-size and placement differential: vary image resolution, then compare cross-device ROS publish-subscribe with same-device execution to identify delay associated with transferring large images.
why_it_works: The payload-size intervention changes the amount sent, while same-device execution acts as a control for effects that do not require cross-device transfer. The paper reports a two-second transfer for full-resolution images and says the effect is absent on the same device. This provides a minimal diagnostic contrast for transfer-related delay, though it does not establish tail behavior or fully exclude network/runtime confounders.
root_seam: At the robot-to-server image handoff, record request identity, payload size, publish and receive timestamps, plus locator completion time. Compare remote and same-host runs at matched resolutions to tell whether a slow request accumulated delay before receipt or after it, without collecting a full trace.
experiment: Replay identical inference inputs at several payload sizes in remote and same-host configurations, holding processing workload constant. Record per-request publish, receive, and completion timestamps; compare transfer-stage and end-to-end latency distributions, including tail quantiles. Check that any remote-only size effect occurs before receipt rather than in server queueing, compute, or action application.
evidence_quote: When an image of this size is subscribed through ROS, it takes two seconds to transfer the image to another device.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, section 3.2.2.b, “Real-Time Performance.”
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: Cross-device transfer of 2048×1536 images is contrasted with smaller images and with same-device publish-subscribe; no controlled quantitative diagnostic gain is reported.
uncertainty: The paper reports average positioning times and a transfer-time observation, not per-request tail distributions or a detailed timing breakdown. Payload-size changes may also affect processing, so Root should use the placement control and handoff timestamps to separate transport delay from server queueing and computation.

title: A Survey of Approximate Quantile Computation on Large-scale Data (Technical Report)
abstract: As data volume grows extensively, data profiling helps to extract metadata of large-scale data. However, one kind of metadata, order statistics, is difficult to be computed because they are not mergeable or incremental. Thus, the limitation of time and memory space does not support their computation on large-scale data. In this paper, we focus on an order statistic, quantiles, and present a comprehensive analysis of studies on approximate quantile computation. Both deterministic algorithms and randomized algorithms that compute approximate quantiles over streaming models or distributed models are covered. Then, multiple techniques for improving the efficiency and performance of approximate quantile algorithms in various scenarios, such as skewed data and high-speed data streams, are presented. Finally, we conclude with coverage of existing packages in different languages and with a brief discussion of the future direction in this area.
technical_mechanism: Maintain compact approximate-quantile summaries of latency samples and merge summaries across nodes; query the merged summary for tail percentiles instead of retaining every sample.
why_it_works: Quantile summaries retain information about the latency distribution in bounded space, and their mergeability supports combining observations from distributed sources. Approximation bounds make it possible to assess tail percentiles while reducing trace-retention and transmission costs.
root_seam: Attach samples to request timestamps or identities and record per-stage durations at the robot and inference server. Summaries of transport-stage latency, kept separate from queueing, GPU compute, and action-application durations, could show whether a regression affects tail percentiles without storing every request trace.
experiment: On a fixed Root workload, compare full per-request latency traces with compact quantile summaries at matched memory and transmission budgets. Evaluate tail-percentile error and whether the summaries detect injected transport-delay tails; report collection overhead and distinguish transport from server-side stages.
evidence_quote: When a network node receives q-digest trees from other nodes, it merges them with its own tree by adding up count of nodes representing the same elements and applying COMPRESS.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section II.B, Distributed Model (q-digest description).
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: This is a survey of approximate quantile methods, not a Root or remote-inference evaluation. It supports compact, mergeable quantile summaries, but provides no evidence that such summaries preserve the diagnostic power needed to localize network tails in Root.

title: Combinatorial Group Testing and Sparse Recovery Schemes with Near-Optimal Decoding Time
abstract: In the long-studied problem of combinatorial group testing, one is asked to detect a set of k defective items out of a population of size n, using m ≪ n disjunctive measurements. In the non-adaptive setting, the most widely used combinatorial objects are disjunct and list-disjunct matrices, which define incidence matrices of test schemes. Disjunct matrices allow the identification of the exact set of defectives, whereas list disjunct matrices identify a small superset of the defectives. Apart from the combinatorial guarantees, it is often of key interest to equip measurement designs with efficient decoding algorithms. The most efficient decoders should run in sublinear time in n, and ideally near-linear in the number of measurements m. In this work, we give several constructions with an optimal number of measurements and near-optimal decoding time for the most fundamental group testing tasks, as well as for central tasks in the compressed sensing and heavy hitters literature. For many of those tasks, the previous measurement-optimal constructions needed time either quadratic in the number of measurements or linear in the universe size. Most of our results are obtained via a clean and novel approach which avoids list-recoverable codes or related complex techniques which were present in almost every state-of-the-art work on efficiently decodable constructions of such objects.
technical_mechanism: Non-adaptive sparse fault group testing: design disjunct or list-disjunct test matrices, run tests on selected combinations of candidate causes, then decode the positive/negative outcomes to identify the sparse cause set or a small superset. The decoder progressively extends candidate prefixes and discards prefixes that participate in negative tests.
why_it_works: A true cause cannot occur in a negative test, so negative outcomes prune candidates; the matrix construction lets a small number of tests distinguish a sparse set of causes, while the decoding procedure keeps recovery efficient. This is a concrete way to investigate fewer cause combinations than testing every cause individually, provided Root can define informative tests and outcomes.
root_seam: Attach at controlled Root fault-injection runs: treat candidate causes such as network delay/loss, server queueing, and GPU delay as items; apply designed combinations of those causes; and record whether a specified tail regression occurs. This could narrow the causes implicated in a regression with fewer runs. It does not itself localize delay within a request or distinguish transport from queueing/compute from passive telemetry; those require suitable test definitions and stage-specific signals.
experiment: In a controlled test environment, define candidate fault interventions and a fixed tail-regression outcome, construct a disjunct or list-disjunct test matrix, and run its prescribed combinations. Decode the outcomes and compare cause recovery, false positives, and number of runs against one-cause-at-a-time testing. Include network and server-side faults separately and in combinations; assess whether interactions or noisy outcomes violate the group-test assumptions.
evidence_quote: Our algorithm then starts from ℓ = log k and processes prefixes in increasing length ℓ, trying to gradually find the prefixes of all the defective items, by discarding prefixes that do not participate in a positive test.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, paragraph beginning “Our approach departs from previous work”; also the later paragraph beginning “Given the above definitions” describes checking prefixes for participation in a negative test.
reported_gain: The paper reports optimal measurement counts and near-optimal decoding time for stated constructions; the abstract says prior measurement-optimal constructions for many tasks required quadratic time in the number of measurements or linear time in the universe size. Root-measured gain: UNKNOWN.
baseline: Previous measurement-optimal constructions for many tasks, reported as requiring quadratic time in the number of measurements or linear time in the universe size.
uncertainty: The paper studies combinatorial group testing and sparse recovery, not network diagnosis. Applying it at Root depends on designing tests whose outcomes reliably indicate whether a cause subset produces the defined regression; interactions, stochastic tails, and cause dependence may complicate that encoding. It provides no network-tail results or Root experiment.

title: PINT: Probabilistic In-band Network Telemetry
abstract: Commodity network devices support adding in-band telemetry measurements into data packets, enabling a wide range of applications, including network troubleshooting, congestion control, and path tracing. However, including such information on packets adds significant overhead that impacts both flow completion times and application-level performance. We introduce PINT, an in-band telemetry framework that bounds the amount of information added to each packet. PINT encodes the requested data on multiple packets, allowing per-packet overhead limits that can be as low as one bit. We analyze PINT and prove performance bounds, including cases when multiple queries are running simultaneously. PINT is implemented in P4 and can be deployed on network devices. Using real topologies and traffic characteristics, we show that PINT concurrently enables applications such as congestion control, path tracing, and computing tail latencies, using only sixteen bits per packet, with performance comparable to the state of the art.
technical_mechanism: PINT probabilistically distributes in-band per-hop telemetry across multiple packets while enforcing a per-packet bit budget. For latency queries, switches contribute sampled per-hop latency values; per-switch sketches aggregate the samples to estimate flow latency quantiles, including the median and tail.
why_it_works: The collected packets provide sampled measurements associated with individual switches along a flow's path, so estimates can expose which network hops contribute latency without embedding every hop's measurements in every packet. This could give Root network-side evidence at the packet and switch level, while sketches and bounded packet overhead reduce collection and processing costs. The supplied context does not establish that this separates network delay from server or GPU time end to end.
root_seam: Instrument the robot-to-cloud transport path so switches attach PINT telemetry to packets associated with an inference request or flow. Preserve a request/flow identity at the endpoint, then compare per-switch latency estimates with endpoint request timings to localize network contributions; server queueing, GPU compute, and action application would require separate timestamps.
experiment: On a controlled remote-inference path, compare PINT-derived per-hop latency quantiles against full per-packet switch telemetry and endpoint timings during induced network congestion. Measure localization error for tail requests, packet overhead, and sketching/collection cost; separately timestamp server queueing and GPU execution to test whether network delay is distinguishable.
evidence_quote: we can estimate the median and tail latency of the (flow, switch) pair by finding the relevant quantile of the subsampled stream.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, PINT Encoding and Recording Module discussion (page 7 in the excerpt).
reported_gain: The abstract reports that PINT supports computing tail latencies using only sixteen bits per packet, with performance comparable to the state of the art. In the combined-query evaluation, median-latency relative error increases by 0.7% versus the baseline of running each query separately.
baseline: State-of-the-art approaches for the abstract's performance comparison; for the combined-query result, running each query separately.
uncertainty: The supplied text does not specify the precise switch-level latency measurement definition or show a robot-to-cloud deployment. Per-flow telemetry may require enough packets from that flow, and the paper notes that PINT is ineffective for some single-packet short flows. Request-to-packet association and separation from server/GPU delay are proposed transfer requirements, not demonstrated results.

title: Cloud-gaming:Analysis of Google Stadia traffic
abstract: Interactive, real-time, and high-quality cloud video games pose a serious challenge to the Internet due to simultaneous high-throughput and low round trip delay requirements. In this paper, we investigate the traffic characteristics of Stadia, the cloud-gaming solution from Google, which is likely to become one of the dominant players in the gaming sector. To do that, we design several experiments, and perform an extensive traffic measurement campaign to obtain all required data. Our first goal is to gather a deep understanding of Stadia traffic characteristics by identifying the different protocols involved for both signalling and video/audio contents, the traffic generation patterns, and the packet size and inter-packet time probability distributions. Then, our second goal is to understand how different Stadia games and configurations, such as the video codec and the video resolution selected, impact on the characteristics of the generated traffic. We also evaluate the ability of Stadia to adapt to different link capacity conditions, including cases where the capacity drops suddenly, as well as sudden increases in the network latency. Our results and findings, besides illustrating the characteristics of Stadia traffic, are also valuable for planning and dimensioning future networks, as well as for designing new resource management strategies. Finally, we compare Stadia traffic to other video streaming applications, showcasing the main differences between them, and introduce a traffic model using our captures. We show that this model can be used in simulations to further investigate the network performance in presence of Stadia traffic.
technical_mechanism: Controlled network-condition perturbation: add/remove latency or constrain bandwidth at the client, then correlate WebRTC RTT and jitter-buffer measurements with traffic and stream behavior.
why_it_works: The intervention provides a known change in network conditions, while transport metrics and observed stream changes show whether delay or capacity affects delivery. RTT and jitter-buffer delay offer distinct evidence about network round trips and client-side packet buffering, respectively.
root_seam: In a Root experiment, perturb the robot–server path and record synchronized request IDs and timestamps alongside transport RTT, packet loss/jitter, and client/server queue and compute timings. This could test whether a tail follows network delay or buffering rather than server queueing or inference. The paper’s Chrome WebRTC metrics may not be available in Root’s runtime.
experiment: Replay comparable inference requests under baseline conditions and under controlled added latency or reduced bandwidth. Compare end-to-end tails with transport RTT, packet-delivery or buffering signals, server queue time, and inference time; repeat after removing the perturbation to check whether the tail tracks the network change.
evidence_quote: Then, after 60 seconds, we add the same extra latency value to both incoming and outgoing packets from the client. We add 40 ms, 50 ms and 60 ms to each link
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section 11, “How Stadia reacts to latency changes”
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The study measures a cloud-gaming stream, not remote robot inference. Its RTT is derived from STUN request/response timing, and the excerpt does not establish that this metric isolates application request latency or one-way network delay.

title: Latency-aware and -predictable Communication with Open Protocol Stacks for Remote Drone Control
abstract: In order to create cooperating swarms of Unmanned Autonomous Vehicles (UAVs) that also interact with various other systems and devices, open and free communication systems are mandatory. This paper presents an implementation of such a communication system to incorporate the Crazyflie nano-drone as a UAV platform. The protocol stack leverages the open Predictably Reliable Real-time Transport (PRRT) protocol that adds latency-awareness and -predictability to stacks composed of standard Internet protocols. To enable the drone to receive and reply to control commands via Wi-Fi, it has been extended with a Raspberry Pi that runs two variants of the Crazybridge---a software to connect the control board to the network. To evaluate how practical this solution is for the use in control applications, the communication has been analysed with a focus on the latency properties. Our investigations show that despite using the open protocol stack---and hence opting out of specialised implementations---the resulting latencies are in the same order of magnitude (4 to 9 ms) as the latency of the proprietary link.
technical_mechanism: Cross-layer packet tracing (X-Lap) records how long each request-response packet pair spends in communication and processing steps, allowing end-to-end latency to be decomposed by stage.
why_it_works: Stage-level timing can distinguish network transmission delay from bridge processing and UART delay, so a tail can be localized rather than inferred from end-to-end RTT alone. The paper uses this analysis to identify the Raspberry Pi UART driver as a source of latency and jitter.
root_seam: Attach timestamps to request/response identity at the robot and server-side transport and processing boundaries. Retain per-stage timings for tail requests so Root can identify whether excess latency arose on the network path or in local queueing, bridge processing, or UART handling.
experiment: Replay the same remote-control request workload under baseline and controlled network impairment (such as injected delay, loss, or contention). Capture per-stage packet traces and compare tail RTTs and stage contributions; verify that network-induced tails increase network-stage time while local bridge or UART delays remain separable.
evidence_quote: X-Lap captures traces that allow to deduce how long a packet needed to be processed in a certain step in the communication and processing chain.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, section IV-D, “Cross-Layer Analysis using X-Lap”
reported_gain: The paper reports that replacing the Python bridge with the Rust bridge reduced RTT from about 18 ms to 9 ms; this is not a measured Root gain.
baseline: The communication-path comparison reports about 4 ms RTT for Crazyradio, 18 ms for PRRT with the Python bridge, and 9 ms for PRRT with the Rust bridge. For the Python-bridge trace, PRRT round-trip latency had a median below 7 ms, versus 17.50 ms median end-to-end latency.
uncertainty: The paper analyzes latency components but does not report a controlled rare-network-delay experiment. The Rust bridge lacks the logging required for the same in-depth X-Lap analysis.

title: Aggregate-Driven Trace Visualizations for Performance Debugging
abstract: Performance issues in cloud systems are hard to debug. Distributed tracing is a widely adopted approach that gives engineers visibility into cloud systems. Existing trace analysis approaches focus on debugging single request correctness issues but not debugging single request performance issues. Diagnosing a performance issue in a given request requires comparing the performance of the offending request with the aggregate performance of typical requests. Effective and efficient debugging of such issues faces three challenges: (i) identifying the correct aggregate data for diagnosis; (ii) visualizing the aggregated data; and (iii) efficiently collecting, storing, and processing trace data. We present TraVista, a tool designed for debugging performance issues in a single trace that addresses these challenges. TraVista extends the popular single trace Gantt chart visualization with three types of aggregate data - metric, temporal, and structure data, to contextualize the performance of the offending trace across all traces.
technical_mechanism: Overlay per-task latency distributions and millisecond-aligned counts of concurrent requests handled by the same process on a selected request trace; use the distributions and concurrency overlay to flag atypical task latency and potential server-side contention.
why_it_works: The selected trace gains comparison context from typical executions and concurrent work. A slow task aligned with high same-process concurrency supports a server-contention explanation; a slow task without that signal, especially around a communication edge, remains a candidate for network or other causes. This is a diagnostic cue, not packet-level proof of network delay.
root_seam: At the server-side spans for remote inference, attach the contemporaneous per-process active-request count and task-latency distribution to the request-correlated trace. This can expose server contention as an alternative to network tail delay without requiring packet-level instrumentation, though it cannot by itself distinguish network delay from every other cause.
experiment: Replay comparable inference requests with separately controlled network-delay and server-queueing perturbations. Compare task-latency distributions and same-process concurrency overlays for affected spans, and measure whether the cues distinguish queueing from network perturbation. Treat the result as a Root experiment; the paper reports no Root gain.
evidence_quote: Currently, TraVista uses the number of requests being handled by a process executing a task to approximate the contention during the execution of that task.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, §3.1, “Temporal Aggregation”; the following interface description says this data is gathered at millisecond granularity and plotted over spans.
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: Single-trace Gantt chart without aggregate context.
uncertainty: The concurrency count approximates contention but does not establish causality or identify packet-level network delay. The paper does not evaluate whether these cues distinguish network delay from server queueing, and its reported work is not a measured Root result.

title: Empirically Characterizing the Buffer Behaviour of Real Devices
abstract: All the routers include a buffer in order to enqueue packets waiting to be transmitted. The behaviour of the routers' buffer is of primary importance when studying network traffic, since it may modify some characteristics, as delay or jitter, and may also drop packets. As a consequence, the characterization of this buffer is interesting, especially when real-time flows are being transmitted: if the buffer characteristics are known, then different techniques can be used so as to adapt the traffic: multiplexing a number of small packets into a big one, fragmentation, etc. This work presents a preliminary study of how to determine the technical and functional characteristics of the buffer of a certain device (as e.g. behaviour, size, limits, input and output rate), or even in a remote Internet network node. Two different methodologies are considered, and tested on two real scenarios which have been implemented; real measurements permit the estimation of the buffer size, and the input and output rates, when there is physical or remote access to the "System Under Test". In case of having physical access, the maximum number of packets in the queue can be determined by counting. In contrast, if the node is remote, its buffer size has to be estimated. We have obtained accurate results in wired and wireless networks.
technical_mechanism: Actively flood a suspected bottleneck with sequenced UDP packets at an input rate above its output capacity, then use destination-side packet arrival times and sequence-number gaps to estimate output rate, losses, and buffer occupancy/size. With physical access, synchronized input/output captures instead count packets queued between arrival and departure.
why_it_works: Overload makes queue growth observable: output timing reflects packets draining at the bottleneck rate, while the first missing sequence number marks overflow. The remote method uses the delay until that loss, together with estimated input and output rates, to infer buffer size. This provides evidence of transport queue buildup rather than merely recording an end-to-end tail; it does not by itself distinguish that delay from server queueing or compute unless the measurement endpoints isolate the network.
root_seam: Attach sequence IDs and send/receive timestamps to robot-to-cloud requests, and capture transport events at the robot and inference server. A controlled, rate-limited overload probe on a test path could estimate whether a bottleneck queue contributes to tail latency; compare its arrival, loss, and queue-delay signature with request latency. This would add evidence about network buffering, but the paper's remote estimate relies on deliberate buffer flooding and does not establish a safe passive method for production action loops.
experiment: In a controlled Root testbed, replay identical robot requests over a path with a configurable bottleneck. Vary offered load around the bottleneck capacity; record request identity, sender/receiver timestamps, sequence gaps, and (where available) synchronized captures at both ends. Compare inferred queue delay/overflow against measured queue occupancy and end-to-end tail latency, with server queueing and GPU workload held fixed. Include an unloaded control and test whether the probe itself affects action-loop latency.
evidence_quote: The method is based on sending a continuous packet flow at a rate bigger than the output capacity. This will flood the buffer and cause packet loss.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section III.B, “Finding buffer size with remote access”
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The paper reports buffer-characterization tests on wired and wireless devices, not robot inference or rare control-loop tails. Remote estimates are less accurate than physical-access measurements and are reported as acceptable when input rate exceeds output rate by more than three times and large packets are used. The method's deliberate overload may be unsafe or unrepresentative for live robot traffic; n13 and n16 remain keep because direct action-loop applicability and rare-delay performance are not demonstrated.

title: A network analysis on cloud gaming: Stadia, GeForce Now and PSNow
abstract: Cloud gaming is a new class of services that promises to revolutionize the videogame market. It allows the user to play a videogame with basic equipment while using a remote server for the actual execution. The multimedia content is streamed through the network from the server to the user. This service requires low latency and a large bandwidth to work properly with low response time and high-definition video. Three of the leading tech companies, (Google, Sony and NVIDIA) entered this market with their own products, and others, like Microsoft and Amazon, are planning to launch their own platforms in the near future. However, these companies released so far little information about their cloud gaming operation and how they utilize the network. In this work, we study these new cloud gaming services from the network point of view. We collect more than 200 packet traces under different application settings and network conditions for 3 cloud gaming services, namely Stadia from Google, GeForce Now from NVIDIA and PS Now from Sony. We analyze the employed protocols and the workload they impose on the network. We find that GeForce Now and Stadia use the RTP protocol to stream the multimedia content, with the latter relying on the standard WebRTC APIs. They result in bandwidth-hungry and consume up to 45 Mbit/s, depending on the network and video quality. PS Now instead uses only undocumented protocols and never exceeds 13 Mbit/s.
technical_mechanism: Use packet-level retransmission activity as a loss-linked streaming signal, and validate its response under controlled packet-loss impairment.
why_it_works: For Stadia, the paper identifies a separate video-retransmission flow that becomes active alongside packet losses and bitrate adaptations. Controlled loss injection provides a way to check whether this signal responds to network impairment. This can expose loss-related streaming degradation, though it does not by itself localize end-to-end latency tails or distinguish network delay from server and compute time.
root_seam: Capture transport packets at a robot-side gateway and correlate loss or retransmission events with request IDs and action-loop timestamps. This adds a network-side signal that can be compared against server queueing, GPU completion, and action-application timestamps; it does not require Reflex's private infrastructure.
experiment: Replay the same Root workload while independently injecting packet loss and delay with tc-netem. Capture packet traces and correlate loss/retransmission sequences with request-level network time and end-to-end tail latency. In separate runs, vary server queueing or GPU load without network impairment; test whether the packet signal distinguishes network-linked regressions from those server-side causes.
evidence_quote: the ow becomes suddenly active, carrying large packets containing video content. Moreover, this behaviour co-occurs with packet losses and bi- trate adaptations on the video stream
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section 4.3, Multimedia streaming
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: Sessions with no packet loss are reported as a reference for the controlled loss experiments; a diagnostic-performance baseline is UNKNOWN.
uncertainty: The paper supports a loss-linked streaming indicator, not request-level tail diagnosis. It does not show that the indicator localizes latency or separates network delay from server queueing and compute. The cloud-gaming streaming setting is analogous to, but not identical to, a robot-to-cloud action loop.

title: Optimal Estimation of Link Delays based on End-to-End Active Measurements
abstract: Current IP based networks support a wide range of delay-sensitive applications such as live video streaming of network gaming. Providing an adequate quality of experience to these applications is of paramount importance for a network provider. The offered services are often regulated by tight Service Level Agreements that needs to be continuously monitored. Since the first step to guarantee a metric is to measure it, delay measurement becomes a fundamental operation for a network provider. In many cases, the operator needs to measure the delay on all network links. We refer to the collection of all link delays as the Link Delay Vector (LDV). Typical solutions to collect the LDV impose a substantial overhead on the network. In this paper, we propose a solution to measure the LDV in real-time with a low-overhead approach. In particular, we inject some flows into the network and infer the LDV based on the delay of those flows. To this end, the monitoring flows and their paths should be selected minimizing the network monitoring overhead. In this respect, the challenging issue is to select a proper combination of flows such that by knowing their delay it is possible to solve a set of a linear equation and obtain a unique LDV. We first propose a mathematical formulation to select the optimal combination of flows, in form of ILP problem. Then we develop a heuristic algorithm to overcome the high computational complexity of existing ILP solvers. As a further step, we propose a meta-heuristic algorithm to solve the above-mentioned equations and infer the LDV. The challenging part of this step is the volatility of link delays. The proposed solution is evaluated over real-world emulated network topologies using the Mininet network emulator. Emulation results show the accuracy of the proposed solution with a negligible networking overhead in a real-time manner.
technical_mechanism: Select a low-overhead set of routed active probe flows whose measured end-to-end delays form a solvable linear system, then infer per-link delays from the flow paths and delays.
why_it_works: Each probe reports the sum of delays along its known route. Combining measurements from selected routes allows the method to attribute elevated delay to individual links rather than leave it as an end-to-end symptom, while flow selection aims to use fewer probes. Repeating measurements can expose changing link delay, including queuing-related increases. This is a plausible way to distinguish network-path delay from server queueing or GPU compute, provided those server-side stages are measured separately.
root_seam: Attach probes and timestamps to the robot–server path, retaining each probe's route identity and end-to-end delay. Root would need a known topology and the ability to map or control probe paths; inferred link delay could then be compared with inference-request latency and separately measured server stages.
experiment: In a controlled Root setup with known probe routes, induce delay or queueing on one network link, then separately induce server queueing and GPU delay. Compare inferred per-link delays and end-to-end probe measurements with ground truth across repeated samples, including tail periods. Measure detection/localization accuracy and probe count and traffic overhead against a denser probing baseline.
evidence_quote: The number of flows and the selected path for each of them should be chosen in a way that by solving a system of linear equations the delays of desired links could be specified.
evidence_location: selected_pdf_text, Proposed Architecture discussion of flow selection and per-link delay inference.
reported_gain: The abstract reports accurate emulation results with negligible networking overhead in real time; quantitative gain is UNKNOWN.
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The method supports link-level delay localization, but the supplied text does not establish tail-specific accuracy or a Root result. Transfer depends on known topology and route identity, and the inferred link delay includes processing, transmission, queuing, and propagation components. Server queueing, GPU compute, and action application require separate measurements to distinguish them.

title: Latency Analysis of ROS2 Multi-Node Systems
abstract: The Robot Operating System 2 (ROS2) targets distributed real-time systems and is widely used in the robotics community. Especially in these systems, latency in data processing and communication can lead to instabilities. Though being highly configurable with respect to latency, ROS2 is often used with its default settings. In this paper, we investigate the end-to-end latency of ROS2 for distributed systems with default settings and different Data Distribution Service (DDS) middlewares. In addition, we profile the ROS2 stack and point out latency bottlenecks. Our findings indicate that end-to-end latency strongly depends on the used DDS middleware. Moreover, we show that ROS2 can lead to 50% latency overhead compared to using low-level DDS communications. Our results imply guidelines for designing distributed ROS2 architectures and indicate possibilities for reducing the ROS2 overhead.
technical_mechanism: Intra-layer message-path profiling: insert timestamps at ROS2 call-stack boundaries, then categorize elapsed time into DDS, ROS2 middleware-interface, common ROS2, and notification-to-retrieval intervals.
why_it_works: The timestamped intervals can distinguish time attributed to DDS transport and receive handling from ROS2 overhead and the delay between data-available notification and message retrieval. This provides a concrete cross-layer localization signal rather than an end-to-end latency alone.
root_seam: Attach request/message identity and timestamps at robot-side send and cloud-side receive boundaries, and retain comparable transport and application-layer events. This method suggests how to separate transport time from middleware or dispatch delay, but its evaluation used localhost, so it does not establish behavior on a robot-to-cloud network.
experiment: The paper evaluates ROS2 message pipelines while varying publisher frequency, payload, node count, DDS backend, and reliability; it reports 95th-percentile latency and profiles call-stack intervals. A Root experiment could apply equivalent boundary timestamps to remote inference requests and compare the transport interval with server-side queueing and compute intervals during tail events.
evidence_quote: It patches the ROS2 source tree to include timestamps into processed messages.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, §3.4 Evaluation Framework
reported_gain: Up to 50% ROS2 latency overhead compared to low-level DDS communications for small messages.
baseline: Low-level DDS communications
uncertainty: The profiling evaluation uses localhost rather than a distributed network, and reports the 95th percentile rather than analyzing latency distributions. It does not evaluate tail-versus-healthy request divergence, off-path flows, sampling, or robot-to-cloud inference.

title: ROS-NetSim: A Framework for the Integration of Robotic and Network Simulators
abstract: Multi-agent systems play an important role in modern robotics. Due to the nature of these systems, coordination among agents via communication is frequently necessary. Indeed, Perception-Action-Communication (PAC) loops, or Perception-Action loops closed over a communication channel, are a critical component of multi-robot systems. However, we lack appropriate tools for simulating PAC loops. To that end, in this paper, we introduce ROS-NetSim, a ROS package that acts as an interface between robotic and network simulators. With ROS-NetSim, we can attain high-fidelity representations of both robotic and network interactions by accurately simulating the PAC loop. Our proposed approach is lightweight, modular and adaptive. Furthermore, it can be used with many available network and physics simulators by making use of our proposed interface. In summary, ROS-NetSim is (i) Transparent to the ROS target application, (ii) Agnostic to the specific network and physics simulator being used, and (iii) Tunable in fidelity and complexity. As part of our contribution, we have made available an open-source implementation of ROS-NetSim to the community.
technical_mechanism: Synchronized, geometry-conditioned network co-simulation: capture the target application's IP packets, apply channel conditions derived from robot positions and environment, and record simulated packet delays alongside communication rates and robot state.
why_it_works: The operation enables controlled variation of network conditions on actual application traffic while keeping the robot and network simulations synchronized. Packet-delay tails can then be compared with channel state, rate drops, and retransmission conditions, helping test whether a regression is network-related rather than caused by inference compute or action application. The paper demonstrates a long delay tail and associates spikes with poor propagation conditions; it does not diagnose a deployed Root regression.
root_seam: At a request's transport boundary, retain request identity and packet timestamps, then compare observed or replayed traffic with synchronized robot/channel state and network-layer delay metrics. This could provide controlled attribution of tail changes to network conditions without treating end-to-end inference latency alone as network delay.
experiment: Replay a fixed request workload and robot-state trace through a network simulator, varying channel geometry or impairment settings while holding server queueing, GPU compute, and action application fixed. Compare packet-delay tail distributions with request-level end-to-end latency and rate/retransmission metrics; verify that induced network changes affect transport delay without changing the fixed compute portion.
evidence_quote: the average delay distribution has a main mode around 40 ms and a long exponential tail extending towards larger delays.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, numerical results following Figure 9 and Figure 10 discussion
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The paper supports controlled, simulation-based network-tail attribution, not a method for diagnosing live remote-inference regressions. It does not report a controlled rare-tail diagnostic experiment or separate inference-server queueing and compute from network delay.

title: A Comprehensive Survey and Experimental Comparison of Graph-Based Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
abstract: Approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) constitutes an important operation in a multitude of applications, including recommendation systems, information retrieval, and pattern recognition. In the past decade, graph-based ANNS algorithms have been the leading paradigm in this domain, with dozens of graph-based ANNS algorithms proposed. Such algorithms aim to provide effective, efficient solutions for retrieving the nearest neighbors for a given query. Nevertheless, these efforts focus on developing and optimizing algorithms with different approaches, so there is a real need for a comprehensive survey about the approaches' relative performance, strengths, and pitfalls. Thus here we provide a thorough comparative analysis and experimental evaluation of 13 representative graph-based ANNS algorithms via a new taxonomy and fine-grained pipeline. We compared each algorithm in a uniform test environment on eight real-world datasets and 12 synthetic datasets with varying sizes and characteristics. Our study yields novel discoveries, offerings several useful principles to improve algorithms, thus designing an optimized method that outperforms the state-of-the-art algorithms. This effort also helped us pinpoint algorithms' working portions, along with rule-of-thumb recommendations about promising research directions and suitable algorithms for practitioners in different fields.
technical_mechanism: Build an approximate nearest-neighbor graph index over feature vectors; for a query, start from seed vertices and greedily propagate through neighboring vertices with smaller query distance to retrieve similar items.
why_it_works: The graph encodes neighbor relationships, so search can evaluate fewer data points than a linear scan. Root could index request or trace features and retrieve comparable healthy requests more quickly, with approximate-search recall measured against exact retrieval.
root_seam: Attach the index to stored request or trace features and use a new request as the query. This could accelerate comparable-baseline lookup, but the paper does not define network-specific features or a Root integration.
experiment: On a fixed corpus of healthy request or trace feature vectors, compare graph-index lookup with exact linear-scan retrieval at matched recall; measure lookup latency and recall as corpus size varies.
evidence_quote: they only need to evaluate fewer points of dataset to receive more accurate results
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Introduction
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The paper surveys and compares graph-based approximate nearest-neighbor algorithms rather than proposing a network diagnostic method. Applying its retrieval mechanism to Root requires choosing request features and validating that approximate matches are diagnostically useful.

title: Theory meets Practice at the Median: a worst case comparison of relative error quantile algorithms
abstract: Estimating the distribution and quantiles of data is a foundational task in data mining and data science. We study algorithms which provide accurate results for extreme quantile queries using a small amount of space, thus helping to understand the tails of the input distribution. Namely, we focus on two recent state-of-the-art solutions: t-digest and ReqSketch. While t-digest is a popular compact summary which works well in a variety of settings, ReqSketch comes with formal accuracy guarantees at the cost of its size growing as new observations are inserted. In this work, we provide insight into which conditions make one preferable to the other. Namely, we show how to construct inputs for t-digest that induce an almost arbitrarily large error and demonstrate that it fails to provide accurate results even on i.i.d. samples from a highly non-uniform distribution. We propose practical improvements to ReqSketch, making it faster than t-digest, while its error stays bounded on any instance. Still, our results confirm that t-digest remains more accurate on the ``non-adversarial'' data encountered in practice.
technical_mechanism: Maintain a ReqSketch over streaming latency observations: sorted buffers are compacted using randomized promotion and level-dependent weights, yielding a bounded-size summary for relative-rank and tail-quantile queries.
why_it_works: The weighted summary retains information for estimating ranks without keeping every observation, and ReqSketch has a relative-error guarantee. This can expose a change in a measured boundary's tail distribution with bounded storage; unlike a single threshold, it supports tail-quantile comparisons. It summarizes the distribution, however, rather than identifying the cause of a delay.
root_seam: Attach sketches to timestamped request-level latency measurements at robot-side and server-side transport boundaries, keeping those measurements separate from server queueing, GPU compute, and action-application time. Root could retain bounded-space tail summaries at each boundary, but would still need request attribution or other signals to localize the cause.
experiment: Replay labeled Root request traces through ReqSketch, a t-digest, and an exact raw-sample reference. Inject controlled network-tail delays while holding queueing and compute fixed, then separately inject queueing and compute delays. Compare tail-quantile error, detection of distribution shifts, and retained bytes across stream orders and heavy-tailed inputs.
evidence_quote: The error in the rank estimate for any item is unbiased, that is, 0 in expectation, and since it is a weighted sum of a bounded number of independent uniform 1 random variables, its distribution is sub-Gaussian
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section 3.2, ReqSketch description and rank-estimation error.
reported_gain: The paper reports that ReqSketch's empirical standard deviation of error on randomly shuffled inputs is over 10 times smaller than predicted by its worst-case analysis; this is not a Root result.
baseline: t-digest is the paper's principal comparison baseline.
uncertainty: The paper evaluates quantile-summary accuracy, not network diagnostics. A sketch can reveal a tail shift only for the measurements supplied to it; it does not distinguish network delay from other latency components without suitable measurement placement and request attribution.

title: Automatic Cause Detection of Performance Problems in Web Applications
abstract: The execution of similar units can be compared by their internal behaviors to determine the causes of their potential performance issues. For instance, by examining the internal behaviors of different fast or slow web requests more closely and by clustering and comparing their internal executions, one can determine what causes some requests to run slowly or behave in unexpected ways. In this paper, we propose a method of extracting the internal behavior of web requests as well as introduce a pipeline that detects performance issues in web requests and provides insights into their root causes. First, low-level and fine-grained information regarding each request is gathered by tracing both the user space and the kernel space. Second, further information is extracted and fed into an outlier detector. Finally, these outliers are then clustered by their behavior, and each group is analyzed separately. Experiments revealed that this pipeline is indeed able to detect slow web requests and provide additional insights into their true root causes. Notably, we were able to identify a real PHP cache contention using the proposed approach.
technical_mechanism: Correlate user-space request boundaries with kernel scheduling, syscall, timer, and wakeup events; reconstruct each request’s cross-thread critical path and summarize its execution-state durations, including time blocked on network. Detect and cluster behavior outliers, then compare their features with normal requests to identify where time is spent.
why_it_works: Per-request execution-state durations and cross-thread wakeup relationships can distinguish network-blocked time from running or other blocked states, while comparison with normal requests highlights anomalous behavior. Root could attach request identities and timestamps to transport and runtime events, then test whether tail requests spend excess critical-path time blocked on network rather than in server queues, compute, or action application. The paper does not reconstruct packet-level causality.
root_seam: Join request start/end timestamps and request identity to robot-side and server-side transport events, then use scheduling and wakeup events to identify network-blocked intervals on the request’s critical path. This supplies a cross-layer localization signal without requiring full tracing; packet/ACK/loss attribution would require additional instrumentation.
experiment: On matched healthy and tail remote-inference requests, collect request boundaries plus minimal scheduling, syscall, timer, and wakeup events; reconstruct critical paths and compare network-blocked duration with queueing and compute states. Check whether identified network waits align with transport events, and measure localization accuracy and tracing overhead against full tracing and request-duration-only baselines.
evidence_quote: The following execution states are considered: Running in system call mode (RS) Running in user mode (RU) Blocked for disk I/O (BD) Blocked for network (BN)
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section III.A, Data Collection, execution states considered.
reported_gain: The paper reports minimal tracing overhead of 5.1–11.9% slowdown, compared with 29–62% for full tracing; it also reports identifying PHP OPcache contention. These are paper results, not Root gains.
baseline: No tracing and full tracing are the tracing-cost comparisons; for diagnosis, the method compares outlier request behavior with normal requests.
uncertainty: The reported network-blocked state and cross-thread critical path are transferable, but the supplied text does not show packet/ACK/loss attribution or validation on remote robot inference. The trace is not tail-triggered, so it does not support the tail-aware sampling lane.

title: Scouting the Path to a Million-Client Server
abstract: To keep up with demand, servers will scale up to handle hundreds of thousands of clients simultaneously. Much of the focus of the community has been on scaling servers in terms of aggregate traffic intensity (packets transmitted per second). However, bottlenecks caused by the increasing number of concurrent clients, resulting in a large number of concurrent flows, have received little attention. In this work, we focus on identifying such bottlenecks. In particular, we define two broad categories of problems; namely, admitting more packets into the network stack than can be handled efficiently, and increasing per-packet overhead within the stack. We show that these problems contribute to high CPU usage and network performance degradation in terms of aggregate throughput and RTT. Our measurement and analysis are performed in the context of the Linux networking stack, the the most widely used publicly available networking stack. Further, we discuss the relevance of our findings to other network stacks. The goal of our work is to highlight considerations required in the design of future networking stacks to enable efficient handling of large numbers of clients and flows.
technical_mechanism: Isolate Qdisc queueing through controlled interventions: compare baseline fair queuing with per-flow rate limiting that keeps aggregate demand below NIC capacity, then validate with CoDel configured to drop packets when queueing delay exceeds a target.
why_it_works: Rate limiting is intended to remove Qdisc queuing while preserving the workload, so a latency reduction implicates scheduler queue buildup. CoDel provides an independent check by constraining queueing delay. This helps distinguish queue delay from other stack overhead, though it does not identify every possible tail cause.
root_seam: At the server-side transport boundary, correlate request identity and end-to-end latency with Qdisc enqueue/dequeue timestamps or queue-delay measurements. A controlled comparison with and without egress shaping or an AQM can show whether a remote-inference tail comes from transport queueing rather than server queueing, GPU compute, or action application.
experiment: Replay comparable robot-inference requests while holding aggregate offered load and compute workload constant. Compare baseline scheduling with a rate-limited condition that avoids Qdisc queueing and a CoDel condition with a known delay target. Record per-request end-to-end latency and server-side Qdisc queue delay; test whether tail latency falls with queue delay while GPU and application timings remain stable.
evidence_quote: Latency drops by an order of magnitude in that scenario at 300k ows and by more at smaller numbers of ows, leading to the conclusion that hundreds of milliseconds of delay are added because of queuing delays at the Qdisc.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, discussion of Figure 2 and the comparison between baseline fq and per-flow rate limit.
reported_gain: At 300k flows, latency drops by an order of magnitude with per-flow rate limiting relative to baseline; CoDel delay is also reported as an order of magnitude below baseline.
