baseline: Baseline fq (fair queuing) with flows not rate limited.
uncertainty: The experiments use long-lived flows on a Linux testbed, not remote robot inference. The supplied text does not provide request-level event sequences or directly establish how much of a robot-inference tail this mechanism would explain.

title: AP-side WLAN Analytics
abstract: Monitoring the network performance experienced by the end-user is crucial for managers of wireless networks as it can enable them to remotely modify the network parameters to improve the end-user experience. Unfortunately, for performance monitoring, managers are typically limited to the logs of the Access Points (APs) that they manage. This information does not directly capture factors that can hinder station (STA) side transmissions. Consequently, state-of-the-art methods to measure such metrics primarily involve active measurements. Unfortunately, such active measurements increase traffic load and if used regularly and for all the STAs can potentially disrupt user traffic, thereby worsening performance for other users in the network and draining the battery of mobile devices. This thesis enables passive AP-side network analytics. In the first part of the thesis, I present virtual speed test, a measurement based framework that enables an AP to estimate speed test results for any of its associated clients solely based on AP-side observables. Next, I present Uplink Latency Microscope (uScope), an AP-side framework for estimation of WLAN uplink latency for any of the associated STAs and decomposition into its constituent components. Similar to virtual speed test, uScope makes estimations solely based on passive AP-side observations. We implement both frameworks on a commodity hardware platform and conduct extensive field trials on a university campus and in a residential apartment complex. In over 1 million tests, the two proposed frameworks demonstrate an estimation accuracy with errors under 10%.
technical_mechanism: Passive TCP virtual probing: correlate a downlink TCP segment with its returning uplink ACK to estimate WLAN uplink latency, then use intervening STA transmissions and 802.11 timing rules to decompose it into queueing and access delays, including retransmission and defer estimates.
why_it_works: TCP’s closed loop links the downlink segment to a later uplink ACK, so their timing reveals WLAN uplink delay without adding probe traffic. AP-observed STA transmissions help infer when the ACK reaches the STA queue, while 802.11 timing rules support further decomposition. This can expose WLAN delay as distinct from server queueing, GPU inference, or action application, though it does not diagnose those other delays.
root_seam: At a managed AP on the robot-cloud path, correlate per-robot downlink TCP segments with returning ACKs and retain AP packet and 802.11 transmission timestamps. Root could obtain passive estimates of WLAN uplink delay and its components without generating probe traffic or requiring robot-side logs. Access to suitable AP telemetry and TCP traffic is not established.
experiment: In a controlled robot-cloud WLAN test, collect AP-side TCP and 802.11 timestamps during inference requests and compare uScope-style latency and component estimates with synchronized robot- and server-side packet captures. Introduce controlled WLAN contention and retransmissions; separately time server queueing, GPU inference, and action application. Test whether the estimates identify WLAN-tail episodes without adding traffic.
evidence_quote: The duration between transmission of a TCP segment on the downlink to the reception of the TCP ACK on the uplink exposes the total WLAN uplink latency for that STA.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Chapter 4 uScope virtual-probing description.
reported_gain: Mean estimation errors under 10% across estimated parameters in 1,296,000 tests.
baseline: Ground-truth values collected from STA-side observations for evaluation.
uncertainty: The evidence supports WLAN uplink latency estimation and decomposition, not end-to-end inference-tail diagnosis specifically. Tail sensitivity, suitability of Root’s traffic, and access to AP-side telemetry remain unestablished; the reported accuracy is not a Root-measured gain.

title: Path-Aware OMP Algorithms for Provenance Recovery in Wireless Networks
abstract: Low-latency provenance embedding methods have received traction in vehicular networks for their ability to track the footprint of information flow. One such known method is based on Bloom filters wherein the nodes that forward the packets appropriately choose a certain number of hash functions to embed their signatures in a shared space in the packet. Although Bloom filter methods can achieve the required accuracy level in provenance recovery, they are known to incur higher processing delay since higher number of hash functions are needed to meet the accuracy level. Motivated by this behaviour, we identify a regime of delay-constraints within which new provenance embedding methods must be proposed as Bloom filter methods are no longer applicable. To fill this research gap, we present network-coded edge embedding (NCEE) protocols that facilitate low-latency routing of packets in vehicular network applications. First, we show that the problem of designing provenance recovery methods for the NCEE protocol is equivalent to the celebrated problem of compressed sensing, however, with additional constraints of path formation on the solution. Subsequently, we present a family of path-aware orthogonal matching pursuit algorithms that jointly incorporates the sparsity and path constraints. Through extensive simulation results, we show that our algorithms enjoy low-complexity implementation, and also improve the path recovery performance when compared to path-agnostic counterparts.
technical_mechanism: Compact in-packet route provenance with path-constrained sparse reconstruction: each forwarding node algebraically adds a pre-shared edge identity to the packet; the destination uses the encoded summary, hop count, and path-aware OMP to recover the traversed route.
why_it_works: The packet retains an encoded summary of the edges it traversed rather than a full forwarding trace. Path and sparsity constraints help reconstruct a valid route from that summary. For Root, attaching the recovered route to request identities could show whether tail requests use different paths or share route segments with other slow requests. This can narrow route-level investigation, but route provenance alone cannot identify which segment was slow or distinguish network delay from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application.
root_seam: At the robot/server transport boundary, attach request identity and compact edge provenance to packets or requests, then reconstruct the route at the receiver. Correlate recovered routes with transport timestamps and separately measured server/GPU/action timings. This could avoid retaining full packet traces when route variation is the diagnostic question.
experiment: In a controlled Root test, collect provenance and request identity for robot-to-server requests while independently recording transport timing and server, GPU, and action-application timing. Compare tail requests with healthy requests: test whether route summaries identify distinct paths or shared segments associated with network delay, and whether they retain that route-level diagnostic value with less trace storage. The paper does not evaluate Root or establish a Root-measured gain.
evidence_quote: the received provenance at the destination is
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, NCEE protocol description; followed by the formulation of recovery as a sparse solution whose nonzero edge identities form a path.
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: Path-agnostic OMP counterparts for path-recovery comparisons; Bloom-filter provenance embedding for the delay-profile comparison.
uncertainty: The paper demonstrates route recovery, not tail-latency diagnosis. It provides no timing for individual route segments, no attribution of shared-resource contention, and no Root evaluation. The Root experiment would need independent transport timing to associate route information with network delay and separate network delay from server-side and action-application time.

title: QWin: Enforcing Tail Latency SLO at Shared Storage Backend
abstract: Consolidating latency-critical (LC) and best-effort (BE) tenants at storage backend helps to increase resources utilization. Even if tenants use dedicated queues and threads to achieve performance isolation, threads are still contend for CPU cores. Therefore, we argue that it is necessary to partition cores between LC and BE tenants, and meanwhile each core is dedicated to run a thread. Expect for frequently changing bursty load, fluctuated service time at storage backend also drastically changes the need of cores. In order to guarantee tail latency service level objectives (SLOs), the abrupt changing need of cores must be satisfied immediately. Otherwise, tail latency SLO violation happens. Unfortunately, partitioning-based approaches lack the ability to react the changing need of cores, resulting in extreme spikes in latency and SLO violation happens. In this paper, we present QWin, a tail latency SLO aware core allocation to enforce tail latency SLO at shared storage backend. QWin consists of an SLO-to-core calculation model that accurately calculates the number of cores combining with definitive runtime load determined by a flexible request-based window, and an autonomous core allocation that adjusts cores at adaptive frequency by dynamically changing core policies. When consolidating multiple LC and BE tenants, QWin outperforms the-state-of-the-art approaches in guaranteeing tail latency SLO for LC tenants and meanwhile increasing bandwidth of BE tenants by up to 31x.
technical_mechanism: Queue-growth-triggered core-need diagnosis: within each request-based window, QWin snapshots queued work, estimates the cores required to meet the SLO using queue size, request waiting time, and storage service-time measurements, then compares that estimate with the current allocation. Within-window queue growth triggers a temporary-window recalculation.
why_it_works: The operation makes backlog an explicit runtime signal rather than inferring resource need only from past tail-latency percentiles. Its SLO-to-core estimate, informed by storage service time, provides a concrete test of whether queued work is consistent with insufficient processing capacity. This can expose backend queue buildup as a tail contributor, though it does not establish that a tail is network-caused or fully separate storage service delay from queue delay.
root_seam: Attach at the inference server’s request queue: retain request identity, queue depth or enqueue/dequeue timestamps, current worker capacity, and server-compute and transport-stage timestamps. These signals would let Root test whether backlog and insufficient server capacity precede a tail, rather than relying on end-to-end latency alone. The paper does not provide transport-event attribution.
experiment: Replay comparable remote-inference requests while independently injecting server queue/worker-capacity pressure, GPU-compute load, and network delay. Record queue depth and enqueue/dequeue, transport, compute, and action-application timestamps. Test whether queue-growth and core-need estimates identify server-side backlog under server pressure while remaining low under network-only delay; compare attribution against latency-only observation. This is a proposed Root experiment, not a reported paper result.
evidence_quote: In any case, insufficient cores cause queue to grow. Thus, the change of queue length indicates the changing need of cores.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, discussion of temporary windows and within-window core adjustment.
reported_gain: BE-tenant bandwidth increased by up to 31x without violating LC-tenant target SLOs.
baseline: Ceph-priority, Cake, and Shenango.
uncertainty: The paper uses queue growth to trigger core allocation, not to validate general tail-cause attribution. Its signals are from a storage backend; it provides no network-delay diagnostic or direct test of distinguishing network delay from backend queueing.

title: L, Q, R, and T -- Which Spin Bit Cousin Is Here to Stay?
abstract: Network operators utilize traffic monitoring to locate and fix faults or performance bottlenecks. This often relies on intrinsic protocol semantics, e.g., sequence numbers, that many protocols share implicitly through their packet headers. The arrival of (almost) fully encrypted transport protocols, such as QUIC, significantly complicates this monitoring as header data is no longer visible to passive observers. Recognizing this challenge, QUIC offers explicit measurement semantics by exposing the spin bit to measure a flow's RTT. Ongoing efforts in the IETF IPPM working group argue to expose further information and enable the passive quantification of packet loss. This work implements and evaluates four currently proposed measurement techniques (L-, Q-, R-, and T-bit). We find that all techniques generally provide accurate loss estimations, but that longer algorithmic intervals for Q and R, yet foremost for T, complicate detecting very small loss rates or loss on short connections. Deployment combinations of Q & R as well as Q & L, thus, have the best potential for accurately grasping the loss in networks.
technical_mechanism: Explicit in-band flow measurement: transport loss detections are encoded as L-bit marks on subsequent packets, while Q/R/T variants encode packet counts or loss through periodic marked-packet phases. A passive on-path observer counts or compares the marks to estimate packet loss.
why_it_works: The marks expose loss information to an observer even when encrypted transport headers hide ordinary semantics. Comparing observed marks or phase counts with expected counts can quantify loss without relying on application-level inference timing. The paper also finds that phase-based methods can miss loss when an entire phase is lost or flows are short.
root_seam: Attach a passive observer to the robot-cloud transport path and associate observed per-flow loss-mark counts with request timestamps or identities. This could reveal packet loss as a network contributor to slow inference requests, but does not by itself distinguish queueing, jitter, endpoint stalls, server queueing, GPU compute, or action application. The paper does not evaluate robot action loops.
experiment: The authors implemented L-, Q-, R-, and T-bit mechanisms in aioquic and evaluated them in a Mininet client-server testbed with a downstream observer. They induced random and burst loss using tc netem, varied download sizes, captured traffic with tcpdump, and compared inferred loss with ground truth derived from arbiter queue statistics and traffic captures.
evidence_quote: To convey the number of lost packets to an on-path observer, she sets the L-Bit (in the observable packet header) in the next packet
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section 2.2.1, “Loss Event Bit (L-Bit)”
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: Ground-truth packet loss derived from network-arbiter queue statistics and traffic captures; no scalar improvement over baseline reported.
uncertainty: The mechanism measures packet loss, not tail latency or queue buildup. The paper does not test event-sequence features for separating jitter, retransmission, and endpoint stalls, nor does it validate use in robot-to-cloud action loops. Its evaluation supports in-band loss summaries and a controlled Root experiment, but applicability to short robot requests is uncertain because phase-based mechanisms need sufficient flow length.

title: Improving Latency with Active Queue Management (AQM) During COVID-19
abstract: During the COVID-19 pandemic the Comcast network performed well in response to unprecedented changes in Internet usage and video communications applications that are sensitive to network latency have exploded in popularity. However, in today's typical networks-such as a home network-those applications often degrade if they are sharing a network link with other network traffic. This is a problem caused by a network design flaw often described using the term 'buffer bloat'. Several years ago, Comcast helped to fund research and development in the technical community into new Active Queue Management (AQM) techniques to eliminate this issue and AQM was later built into Data Over Cable Service Interface Specification (DOCSIS) standards. Just prior to the pandemic, Comcast also deployed a large-scale network performance measurement system that included a latency under load test. In addition, Comcast happened to deploy two otherwise identical cable modems; one with upstream AQM enabled, and the other without. This fortuitous confluence of events has enabled Comcast to perform a comparative analysis of the differences between cable modem gateways using AQM with those that lack that enhancement, at a unique level of scale across many months of time and millions of devices. The data reveals significantly better upstream latency under load performance when AQM is used. For the device with AQM, most of the latency under load tests resulted in 15-30 milliseconds of latency. In comparison, the device without AQM averaged roughly 250 milliseconds of latency, between 8-16 times higher, a highly significant difference to the end user quality of experience. These large-scale measurement comparisons should provide additional data to justify accelerated deployment of AQM in DOCSIS and other Internet Service Provider networks and user-purchased home network equipment.
technical_mechanism: Measure latency while iperf3 saturates the upstream link, then compare otherwise similar modem configurations with DOCSIS-PIE AQM enabled versus disabled. AQM manages the queue under load; reduced working latency with AQM indicates that queue buildup contributes to the observed delay.
why_it_works: The simultaneous load-and-latency test exposes delay that appears when traffic fills queues, while the AQM-on/off comparison tests whether managing that queue reduces latency. This can help distinguish queue-related network delay from inference compute or action-application delay, although the test measures end-to-end path latency rather than isolating every hop.
root_seam: Attach a latency-under-load probe to the robot-to-server transport path and correlate its result with request timestamps. A controlled AQM or queue-management comparison could reveal whether network queue buildup contributes to remote-inference tails, separately from server queueing and GPU execution. The paper does not provide packet-drought or loss-recovery signatures.
experiment: Run repeated remote-inference requests under controlled upstream background load, measuring request-path latency and inference/server timings. Compare queue-management enabled and disabled conditions while holding other factors constant; check whether network-path tail latency falls under load without a corresponding change in server or GPU time.
evidence_quote: To determine the impact to latency during periods when a data flow is causing queues to be filled to capacity the system uses a measurement that will simultaneously load the network and measure latency.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section 9, “Latency Testing.”
reported_gain: With AQM, most latency-under-load tests were 15–30 ms; without AQM, latency averaged roughly 250 ms, reported as 8–16 times higher.
baseline: XB6 modem variant without upstream AQM, using the older buffer-control configuration.
uncertainty: The comparison is between different XB6 hardware variants, and the context notes chipset differences; this may confound the AQM comparison. The measurement is path-level and does not independently separate access-network queueing from other network-path delays. No Root experiment or robot-inference result is reported.

title: ECO: Edge-Cloud Optimization of 5G applications
abstract: Centralized cloud computing with 100+ milliseconds network latencies cannot meet the tens of milliseconds to sub-millisecond response times required for emerging 5G applications like autonomous driving, smart manufacturing, tactile internet, and augmented or virtual reality. We describe a new, dynamic runtime that enables such applications to make effective use of a 5G network, computing at the edge of this network, and resources in the centralized cloud, at all times. Our runtime continuously monitors the interaction among the microservices, estimates the data produced and exchanged among the microservices, and uses a novel graph min-cut algorithm to dynamically map the microservices to the edge or the cloud to satisfy application-specific response times. Our runtime also handles temporary network partitions, and maintains data consistency across the distributed fabric by using microservice proxies to reduce WAN bandwidth by an order of magnitude, all in an application-specific manner by leveraging knowledge about the application's functions, latency-critical pipelines and intermediate data. We illustrate the use of our runtime by successfully mapping two complex, representative real-world video analytics applications to the AWS/Verizon Wavelength edge-cloud architecture, and improving application response times by 2x when compared with a static edge-cloud implementation.
technical_mechanism: Continuously monitor application- and network-level performance, and when the current microservice placement no longer meets its latency constraint, recompute an edge/cloud placement with a graph min-cut and reschedule the affected services.
why_it_works: Moving latency-critical services toward the edge can reduce dependence on a degraded WAN link. The method uses application-specific pipeline and communication information to select a placement under an end-to-end latency constraint, rather than treating network degradation as an isolated log signal.
root_seam: For a robot-cloud action loop, Root could attach network-performance measurements and action-loop latency to a placement-change event, then test whether moving inference or related services to the robot-side edge removes the tail. This is primarily a mitigation and causal intervention, not a method for separating network delay from server queueing or compute time.
experiment: In a 24-hour real-time monitoring deployment with a 250 ms latency constraint, compare dynamic mapping enabled versus disabled during observed drops in upload bandwidth between Wavelength and Availability Zone. The paper reports that services were temporarily moved to Wavelength when dynamic mapping was enabled.
evidence_quote: when dynamic mapping was turned ON, the spike was handled seamlessly by our runtime by moving FE and FM microservices temporarily from availability zone to the wavelength zone, thereby keeping the end-to-end application latency below 250 milliseconds
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section IV-D-2, “Impact on dynamic mapping”
reported_gain: End-to-end application latency stayed below the specified 250 ms constraint during three near-zero upload-bandwidth episodes; the abstract also reports 2x improved response time versus a static edge-cloud implementation.
baseline: Dynamic mapping OFF for the 24-hour experiment; for the reported 2x gain, a static, manually optimized edge-cloud implementation.
uncertainty: The context does not specify the network-performance signals or trigger thresholds used by the scheduler, nor does it report tail percentiles or isolate network delay from compute and queueing. The intervention is promising for Root but is not itself a fine-grained network-tail diagnosis.

title: Optimal Probing with Statistical Guarantees for Network Monitoring at Scale
abstract: Cloud networks are difficult to monitor because they grow rapidly and the budgets for monitoring them are limited. We propose a framework for estimating network metrics, such as latency and packet loss, with guarantees on estimation errors for a fixed monitoring budget. Our proposed algorithms produce a distribution of probes across network paths, which we then monitor; and are based on A- and E-optimal experimental designs in statistics. Unfortunately, these designs are too computationally costly to use at production scale. We propose their scalable and near-optimal approximations based on the Frank-Wolfe algorithm. We validate our approaches in simulation on real network topologies, and also using a production probing system in a real cloud network. We show major gains in reducing the probing budget compared to both production and academic baselines, while maintaining low estimation errors, even with very low probing budgets.
technical_mechanism: Use A- or E-optimal experimental design to allocate a fixed probe budget across network paths so path measurements best estimate per-edge latency or loss; compute scalable near-optimal probing distributions with Frank-Wolfe, then fit a model to estimate metrics for probed and unprobed paths.
why_it_works: Paths are represented by their constituent edges, allowing observed path metrics to inform estimates of edge metrics and, in turn, other path metrics. The design directs scarce probes toward measurements that reduce estimation error, rather than probing all paths uniformly. This could help identify which links contribute to elevated path latency, but the method estimates metrics such as mean latency and does not specifically diagnose tail events or separate network delay from server queueing or compute.
root_seam: A possible Root attachment is to treat robot-to-server or server-to-robot transport routes as paths and allocate probes across them, using path measurements to estimate shared-link contributions. Root would gain estimates for less-probed paths or links under a fixed probe budget. The paper does not establish how to map its cloud topology and probe observations to Root's request-level timing or isolate network delay from other inference stages.
experiment: On a fixed probe budget, compare optimal-design probing with uniform path probing and QR-selected paths in a controlled Root test. Estimate shared transport-link latency from measured path latencies, then compare estimation error and detection of injected link-delay regressions. Keep request-level network timing separate from server queueing, GPU compute, and action application.
evidence_quote: Our proposed algorithms produce a distribution of probes across network paths, which we then monitor; and are based on A- and E-optimal experimental designs in statistics.
evidence_location: Abstract; selected PDF text, Section 2 Framework
reported_gain: The paper reports lower estimation errors than QR and uniform-probing baselines at similar budgets, including real-cloud probing experiments. It describes major probing-budget gains but gives no specific budget-reduction figure in the supplied context.
baseline: QR path selection from Chua, Kolaczyk, and Crovella (2005), and Prod, which allocates probes evenly across all paths.
uncertainty: The supplied results concern metric-estimation error for latency and packet loss, not tail-latency diagnosis. The context does not establish request-level or robot-to-server deployment, tail-aware sampling, or attribution that separates transport delay from server-side delays.

title: Cross-layer Visualization and Profiling of Network and I/O Communication for HPC Clusters
abstract: Understanding and visualizing the full-stack performance trade-offs and interplay between HPC applications, MPI libraries, the communication fabric, and the file system is a challenging endeavor. Designing a holistic profiling and visualization method for HPC communication networks is challenging since different levels of communication coexist and interact with each other on the communication fabric. A breakdown of traffic is essential to understand the interplay of different layers along with the application's communication behavior without losing a general view of network traffic. Unfortunately, existing profiling tools are disjoint and either focus on only profiling and visualizing a few levels of the HPC stack, which limits the insights they can provide, or they provide extremely detailed information which necessitates a steep learning curve to understand. We target our profiling tool visualization to provide holistic and real-time insights into HPC communication stacks. In this paper, we propose and implement our visualization methods to enable holistic insight for representing the cross-stack metrics. Moreover, we propose and implement a low-overhead I/O profiling inside the communication library, collect and store the profiling information, and then study the correlation and evaluation of I/O traffic with MPI communication using a cross-stack approach by INAM. Through experimental evaluations and use cases, we demonstrate novel benefits of our cross-stack communication analysis in real-time to detect bottlenecks and understand communication performance.
technical_mechanism: Cross-layer route attribution of traffic: collect client-side Lustre I/O and MPI traffic statistics, map known endpoints through fabric routing tables, then correlate each traffic class with utilization on traversed links and visualize overlaps.
why_it_works: Route mapping connects communication-library and I/O measurements to specific fabric links. Link-level utilization and traffic-class breakdown can reveal a congested shared path and help distinguish network contention from application communication patterns. The paper’s example connects root-switch I/O traffic from a concurrent checkpoint-restart job with MPI performance variation. This offers a concrete streaming-diagnosis operation for n14, though it does not establish request-level inference attribution.
root_seam: Attach request timestamps or transport intervals to robot/server endpoints, then collect available NIC or switch link counters for their route. Correlate path utilization with request delay alongside server queue and GPU timing. This could identify a busy shared path without requiring packet-to-request identity; the paper does not establish that request-level correlation.
experiment: Replay identical inference traffic while injecting competing traffic on a known shared path, then on a disjoint path. Correlate request intervals with route-mapped link utilization and compare localization of induced network tails against server queue and GPU timings. Include a no-contention run as control.
evidence_quote: Considering we are gathering this information in real-time, we know how much traffic for MPI and I/O is going through each link and can see if they are colliding in the network.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section V implementation discussion on mapping traffic onto fabric routes.
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The evidence supports route-based, cross-layer localization of aggregate traffic contention in HPC, including a reported MPI performance-variation example. It does not show request-level or packet-level attribution, tail-latency detection, or performance on streaming robot inference; Root’s diagnostic value remains to be tested.

title: An Experimental Study of Latency for IEEE 802.11be Multi-link Operation
abstract: Will Multi-Link Operation (MLO) be able to improve the latency of Wi-Fi networks? MLO is one of the most disruptive MAC-layer techniques included in the IEEE 802.11be amendment. It allows a device to use multiple radios simultaneously and in a coordinated way, providing a new framework to improve the WLAN throughput and latency. In this paper, we investigate the potential latency benefits of MLO by using a large dataset containing 5 GHz spectrum occupancy measurements. Experimental results show that when the channels are symmetrically occupied, MLO can improve latency by one order of magnitude. In contrast, in asymmetrically occupied channels, MLO can sometimes be detrimental and increase latency. To address this case, we introduce Opportunistic Simultaneous Transmit and Receive (STR+) channel access and study its benefits.
technical_mechanism: Use real-world channel-occupancy traces to drive a Wi-Fi MAC state-machine emulation; compare channel-access modes under identical packet arrivals. The proposed STR+ runs backoff counters on both links in parallel and assigns a waiting packet to the interface whose counter expires first, avoiding assignment to a link whose backoff will be repeatedly paused by occupancy.
why_it_works: Parallel contention exposes which link offers the earliest actual transmission opportunity, rather than committing a packet to a temporarily idle but soon-busy link. The trace-driven comparison shows how asymmetric occupancy can create a tail through frozen backoff, and how opportunistic link selection avoids that particular delay. This diagnoses link contention, not server queueing, GPU work, or action application.
root_seam: At the robot or AP transport boundary, retain per-request packet timestamps plus per-link channel-busy/backoff-pause and transmission/ACK events. Associate them with request identity to distinguish wireless contention and link asymmetry from downstream inference time. The paper does not identify off-path flows or shared-resource owners, so transfer to n02 is only partial.
experiment: Replay matched remote-inference request traffic over a controlled two-link wireless setup with symmetric and asymmetric occupancy, comparing single-link, ordinary multi-link packet assignment, and parallel-backoff/first-expiring-link assignment. Record per-request tail latency and per-link busy, backoff, transmit, and ACK intervals; compare with a wired or otherwise uncongested control to separate network delay from server compute and queueing.
evidence_quote: When both interfaces are idle, one backoff instance is started on each. Packet allocation is deferred until either backoff counter expires, and the first waiting packet is allocated to the interface whose counter expires first.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, section IV.C, “Opportunistic MLO-STR” (mechanism); section III.B describes trace-based simulations.
reported_gain: Up to 70% delay reduction in the best observed case versus SLO; the paper also reports up to a 78% 95th-percentile reduction for MLO under symmetric occupancy.
baseline: SLO (single-link operation); for the STR+ mechanism, the paper also compares ordinary MLO-STR.
uncertainty: The work evaluates Wi-Fi MAC latency with trace-driven emulation, not remote robot inference or live streaming diagnosis. It demonstrates a transferable mechanism for link selection and controlled latency comparison, but does not measure whether the proposed Root instrumentation can identify off-path flows or shared-resource causes.

title: Slowing Down for Performance and Energy: An OS-Centric Study in Network Driven Workloads
abstract: This paper studies three fundamental aspects of an OS that impact the performance and energy efficiency of network processing: 1) batching, 2) processor energy settings, and 3) the logic and instructions of the OS networking paths. A network device's interrupt delay feature is used to induce batching and processor frequency is manipulated to control the speed of instruction execution. A baremetal library OS is used to explore OS path specialization. This study shows how careful use of batching and interrupt delay results in 2X energy and performance improvements across different workloads. Surprisingly, we find polling can be made energy efficient and can result in gains up to 11X over baseline Linux. We developed a methodology and a set of tools to collect system data in order to understand how energy is impacted at a fine-grained granularity. This paper identifies a number of other novel findings that have implications in OS design for networked applications and suggests a path forward to consider energy as a focal point of systems research.
technical_mechanism: Controlled NIC-interrupt-delay perturbation: sweep the NIC’s interrupt delay and observe per-request tail latency and per-interrupt events. A latency response to the setting provides evidence that delay in NIC-to-software packet handling contributes to the tail, rather than merely recording a correlation.
why_it_works: Interrupt delay controls when packet-arrival events are delivered to software. Changing it while holding the workload and other settings controlled is a causal probe of this receive-side processing stage. Per-interrupt timestamps and packet counters can help associate the latency response with NIC activity. This can localize interrupt batching or packet-processing delay, but does not by itself identify arbitrary network transit delay.
root_seam: At the robot or server transport boundary, correlate NIC interrupt timestamps and packet counters with request identity and request-stage timestamps. This could distinguish delayed NIC delivery/software handling from transport transit, server queueing, GPU compute, and action application; the paper does not establish those other stages.
experiment: Replay a fixed remote-inference workload with CPU frequency, workload, and other relevant settings controlled. Sweep NIC interrupt delay around the default while recording packet/NIC events and per-request transport and inference-stage timestamps. Test whether the tail changes with the intervention and whether the change aligns with receive-side handling; compare against an unchanged-setting control and report network, server, GPU, and action-application intervals separately.
evidence_quote: Figure 6(d) shows the direct effect of interrupt delay on tail latency.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, §5.2.1, Memcached discussion of interrupt-delay effects on tail latency.
reported_gain: The paper reports that Linux-tuned improved tail latency over Linux-default by 40% at 200K QPS and 25% at 600K QPS; this is not a Root-measured gain.
baseline: Linux-default, with interrupt delay and processor speed controlled dynamically by built-in policies.
uncertainty: The study concerns datacenter workloads, not robot inference or rare network-tail diagnosis. The proposed transfer is a controlled receive-side intervention, not a method for detecting unperturbed tails or measuring network transit independently. Request-identity correlation and stage-separated Root measurements are not established by the paper.

title: Rosebud: Making FPGA-Accelerated Middlebox Development More Pleasant
abstract: We introduce an approach to designing FPGA-accelerated middleboxes that simplifies development, debugging, and performance tuning by decoupling the tasks of hardware-accelerator implementation and software-application programming. Rosebud is a framework that links hardware accelerators to a high-performance packet processing pipeline through a standardized hardware/software interface. This separation of concerns allows hardware developers to focus on optimizing custom accelerators while freeing software programmers to reuse, configure, and debug accelerators in a fashion akin to software libraries. We show the benefits of the Rosebud framework by building a firewall based on a large blacklist and porting the Pigasus IDS pattern-matching accelerator in less than a month. Our experiments demonstrate that Rosebud delivers high performance, serving 200 Gbps of traffic while adding only 0.7-7 microseconds of latency.
technical_mechanism: Timestamp broadcast messages and compare sparse-load with saturated-load latency, then account for the added delay using the known FIFO depth and round-robin arbitration schedule. This is queueing-delay decomposition from sparse timing and queue structure, not full tracing.
why_it_works: The sparse-versus-saturated comparison exposes load-dependent delay, while the FIFO-slot and arbitration calculation attributes a large portion of that delay to a specific queueing mechanism. That gives a concrete path-localizing signal rather than an end-to-end RTT alone.
root_seam: At a robot or inference server NIC/transport queue, correlate request or packet timestamps with queue occupancy or known queue depth and scheduling policy. This could help identify network-side queueing as a contributor to tail latency without retaining full traces; it would not by itself separate network queueing from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application.
experiment: On a controlled Root test, timestamp request-correlated packets at transport ingress and egress and record the relevant NIC or transport queue signal. Compare sparse and saturated network load while holding server and GPU load fixed, then inject server queueing with network load fixed. Test whether the queue-based delay estimate tracks network-induced tails and distinguishes them from server-induced tails.
evidence_quote: This latency mostly comes from the 18 FIFO slots in each RPU—16 from actual FIFO and 2 from PR registers—which can be sent out every 16 cycles due to round-robin arbitration among cores
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section 6.3, “Inter-RPU Messaging Performance”
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The paper demonstrates attribution for an FPGA broadcast queue, not a network transport queue or robot-inference workload. Root would need access to relevant queue or scheduling signals, and the proposed controlled experiment must establish that these signals distinguish network queueing from server-side delay.

title: Monitoring Jitter in Software Defined Networks
abstract: End-to-end jitter of a flow is an important metric that indicates the Quality of Service a user is experiencing, particularly for real-time applications such as video streaming, cloud gaming, and so on. Monitoring the jitter can help controllers make routing decisions for certain flows. This paper discusses methods in which we can estimate/follow important patterns in the end-to-end jitter of a flow. Two main approaches are taken, one using a Software Defined Network controller and the other using P4 programmable data-planes. Results from the simulations of each method are discussed.
technical_mechanism: At programmable switches, timestamp packets and retain a window of one-way delays from the source; periodically estimate jitter from delay deviation (including a computationally cheaper mean absolute deviation). Comparing estimates at successive switches can indicate where along the path jitter grows. A separate SDN-controller method estimates per-port load/offload-time variation from packet counters polled over intervals and combines changes across path ports.
why_it_works: Delay variation is measured on packets rather than inferred only from application completion times. Switch-local estimates can expose jitter surges and, when compared across hops, help narrow where variation is added. The P4 approach also aligns estimates with packet arrivals, avoiding the SDN polling method’s time-series synchronization problem.
root_seam: Attach request or flow identity and packet timestamps at robot egress and successive transport observation points, retaining a bounded delay window and computing a jitter statistic. Compare estimates hop by hop to identify where network delay variation increases, separately from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application. Root would need suitable timestamping and clock alignment; the paper does not establish those for a robot/server deployment.
experiment: In a controlled Root replay, timestamp packets for matched inference requests at robot egress and available intermediate/server ingress points. Compute windowed delay-deviation estimates at each point and compare against synchronized per-request one-way network delay and end-to-end latency under induced network jitter and server-side queue/GPU-load changes. Test whether hop-to-hop changes flag network jitter without misclassifying server delays; compare with endpoint-only logging.
evidence_quote: the peaks of the estimate fall right in place with the peaks of the actual end-to-end jitter experienced in the network
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section 5.2, Euclidean Distance estimate (results at Switch S2).
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: Actual end-to-end jitter measured at the host; the paper compares estimated and actual jitter time series, including their peaks and distance measures.
uncertainty: The evidence is from Mininet simulations and does not demonstrate Root-like remote inference, tail-latency attribution, or cross-hop localization as a controlled result. SDN polling estimates are not time-synchronized with host jitter; P4 estimates depend on packet timestamps and a finite delay window. The paper reports estimate similarity, not a quantified Root diagnostic gain.

title: The Benefit of Hindsight: Tracing Edge-Cases in Distributed Systems
abstract: Today's distributed tracing frameworks are ill-equipped to troubleshoot rare edge-case requests. The crux of the problem is a trade-off between specificity and overhead. On the one hand, frameworks can indiscriminately select requests to trace when they enter the system (head sampling), but this is unlikely to capture a relevant edge-case trace because the framework cannot know which requests will be problematic until after-the-fact. On the other hand, frameworks can trace everything and later keep only the interesting edge-case traces (tail sampling), but this has high overheads on the traced application and enormous data ingestion costs. In this paper we circumvent this trade-off for any edge-case with symptoms that can be programmatically detected, such as high tail latency, errors, and bottlenecked queues. We propose a lightweight and always-on distributed tracing system, Hindsight, which implements a retroactive sampling abstraction: instead of eagerly ingesting and processing traces, Hindsight lazily retrieves trace data only after symptoms of a problem are detected. Hindsight is analogous to a car dash-cam that, upon detecting a sudden jolt in momentum, persists the last hour of footage. Developers using Hindsight receive the exact edge-case traces they desire without undue overhead or dependence on luck. Our evaluation shows that Hindsight scales to millions of requests per second, adds nanosecond-level overhead to generate trace data, handles GB/s of data per node, transparently integrates with existing distributed tracing systems, and successfully persists full, detailed traces in real-world use cases when edge-case problems are detected.
technical_mechanism: Retroactive symptom-triggered trace retrieval: record request trace data into local buffers across machines, then, when an outlier or queue symptom is detected, use its trace ID and breadcrumbs to retrieve a coherent distributed trace. For queue buildup, a QueueTrigger can retrieve the preceding N related request traces.
why_it_works: The trigger can use a cheap signal such as completed-request latency or queue latency without inspecting trace data. Retaining trace data locally until a trigger avoids eagerly sending every trace to a collector, while retroactive retrieval preserves evidence from before the symptom. Capturing related prior requests can expose work that contributed to a queue buildup.
root_seam: Attach a request identity and timestamps to robot-side and server-side transport events, and trigger retained trace retrieval when end-to-end action latency or queue latency crosses a threshold. The resulting trace could expose the request's cross-machine timeline and related queued requests without continuous centralized trace ingestion. The paper does not itself separate network delay from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application; Root would need explicit transport and compute timestamps to localize those intervals.
experiment: The paper evaluates percentile-triggered trace capture after ComposePost RPC completion with injected 20–30 ms slow requests, and a HDFS QueueTrigger configured to retrieve the 10 most recently dequeued lateral requests after high queue latency. It also evaluates tracing overhead and comparison tracing strategies.
evidence_quote: instead of eagerly ingesting and processing traces, Hindsight lazily retrieves trace data only after symptoms of a problem are detected.
evidence_location: Abstract; also selected PDF text, §3 Approach and §6.3 Case Studies
reported_gain: The paper reports nanosecond-level overhead to generate trace data and less than 3.5% impact on end-to-end application latency and throughput while tracing 100% of requests and generating over 200 MB/s per node. In its tail-latency case study, Hindsight specifically targets high-percentile latency traces. These are paper results, not measured Root gains.
baseline: OpenTelemetry with Jaeger under head-sampling (1% unless indicated) and tail-sampling; the tail-latency case study also contrasts captured requests with random head sampling.
uncertainty: Applicability to robot-to-cloud action loops is not evaluated. The method retrieves application-level traces rather than packet/ACK/loss histories, and the supplied context does not establish that its traces alone distinguish network delay from server queueing, GPU computation, or action application.

title: Graph-based Approximate NN Search: A Revisit
abstract: Nearest neighbor search plays a fundamental role in many disciplines such as multimedia information retrieval, data-mining, and machine learning. The graph-based search approaches show superior performance over other types of approaches in recent studies. In this paper, the graph-based NN search is revisited. We optimize two key components in the approach, namely the search procedure and the graph that supports the search. For the graph construction, a two-stage graph diversification scheme is proposed, which makes a good trade-off between the efficiency and reachability for the search procedure that builds upon it. Moreover, the proposed diversification scheme allows the search procedure to decide dynamically how many nodes should be visited in one node's neighborhood. By this way, the computing power of the devices is fully utilized when the search is carried out under different circumstances. Furthermore, two NN search procedures are designed respectively for small and large batch queries on the GPU. The optimized NN search, when being supported by the two-stage diversified graph, outperforms all the state-of-the-art approaches on both the CPU and the GPU across all the considered large-scale datasets.
technical_mechanism: Two-stage graph diversification for approximate nearest-neighbor retrieval: prune clearly redundant edges, then assign surviving edges occlusion factors that let search choose how many neighbors to visit.
why_it_works: The occlusion factors preserve a way to trade search cost against reachability at query time. One graph can therefore support different retrieval circumstances without maintaining multiple graphs. Root could use it to retrieve comparable historical requests more efficiently; it would speed baseline lookup, not itself identify the cause of a network tail.
root_seam: At request identity and feature-vector creation, index past requests together with their outcomes and timing evidence. Query the index for feature-similar healthy requests when a regression occurs, then inspect the retrieved cases' timing or transport evidence.
experiment: On the same historical request-feature corpus, compare this diversified graph with a full scan and a fixed-neighbor graph index at matched retrieval recall. Measure query latency and the quality of retrieved healthy comparables across query batch sizes. Separately assess whether those comparables help identify the regressed request's network-delay component.
evidence_quote: The second stage diversification associates an occlusion factor with each edge, which indicates the importance of an edge.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, section 2.2, “Graph-based Approaches”; query-time use is further described in section 3.3, “Soft Graph Diversification.”
reported_gain: For small-batch queries, the paper reports 2–10× faster NN search than state-of-the-art approaches.
baseline: State-of-the-art NN search approaches; the supplied text does not specify a single baseline for the 2–10× comparison.
uncertainty: The paper evaluates vector nearest-neighbor search, not retrieval of comparable robot requests or network-tail diagnosis. Whether Root request features produce useful healthy comparables, and any Root retrieval or diagnostic gain, remain unmeasured.

title: FogROS2: An Adaptive Platform for Cloud and Fog Robotics Using ROS 2
abstract: Mobility, power, and price points often dictate that robots do not have sufficient computing power on board to run contemporary robot algorithms at desired rates. Cloud computing providers such as AWS, GCP, and Azure offer immense computing power and increasingly low latency on demand, but tapping into that power from a robot is non-trivial. We present FogROS2, an open-source platform to facilitate cloud and fog robotics that is included in the Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2) distribution. FogROS2 is distinct from its predecessor FogROS1 in 9 ways, including lower latency, overhead, and startup times; improved usability, and additional automation, such as region and computer type selection. Additionally, FogROS2 gains performance, timing, and additional improvements associated with ROS 2. In common robot applications, FogROS2 reduces SLAM latency by 50 %, reduces grasp planning time from 14 s to 1.2 s, and speeds up motion planning 45x. When compared to FogROS1, FogROS2 reduces network utilization by up to 3.8x, improves startup time by 63 %, and network round-trip latency by 97 % for images using video compression. The source code, examples, and documentation for FogROS2 are available at https://github.com/BerkeleyAutomation/FogROS2, and is available through the official ROS 2 repository at https://index.ros.org/p/fogros2/.
technical_mechanism: Transparent H.264 streaming compression of robot image topics before cloud transmission, paired with cloud-side decompression; the paper measures round-trip time using an immediate acknowledgement.
why_it_works: Reducing image-stream bandwidth can reduce transmission delay when sending raw images is a bottleneck. Comparing compressed and uncompressed streams in a controlled robot-to-cloud setup can test whether image transfer contributes to a delay, though the measured round trip does not separately identify network delay from other components.
root_seam: Attach an A/B intervention at the robot image publisher and cloud subscriber, preserving request identity and recording send, receive, and acknowledgement timestamps. Compare raw and H.264 streams to learn whether image traffic contributes to Root's delay; separate transport timing from cloud processing where possible.
experiment: Publish images from a robot node to a cloud node under uncompressed and H.264 modes; have the cloud node immediately acknowledge each image, then measure round-trip time and received FPS. Root could repeat this comparison with its representative robot-to-cloud image workload and retain per-request timing.
evidence_quote: FogROS2 can setup transparent streaming compression between robot and cloud.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section E, “Streaming Image Compression”; evaluation in Section V.A.
reported_gain: H.264 reduced measured image round-trip latency from 1401 ms to 38 ms (97%); received FPS increased from 1.42 to 29.0.
baseline: Uncompressed image transmission.
uncertainty: The reported acknowledgement round-trip time is not a decomposition of network, queueing, or processing delay, and the context provides no tail-percentile measurements. The result is for image streams, not necessarily action-loop traffic.

title: Service Modeling and Delay Analysis of Packet Delivery over a Wireless Link
abstract: For delay analysis of packet delivery over a wireless link, several novel ideas are introduced. One is to construct an equivalent G/G/1 non-lossy queueing model to ease the analysis, enabled by exploiting empirical models of packet error rate, packet service time and packet loss rate obtained from measurement. The second is to exploit a classical queueing theory result to approximate the mean delay. For estimating the delay distribution, the newly developed stochastic network calculus (SNC) theory is made use of, forming the third idea. To enable this SNC based analysis, a stochastic service curve characterization of the link is introduced, relying on a packet service time model obtained from the empirical models. The focused link is a 802.15.4 wireless link. Extensive experimental investigation under a wide range of settings was conducted. The proposed ideas are validated with the experiment results. The validation confirms that the proposed approaches, integrating both empirical and analytical modes, are effective for service modeling and delay analysis. This suggests an integrated approach, now found previously, for quantitative understanding of the delay performance of packet delivery over a wireless link.
technical_mechanism: Use measurements to model packet error rate, packet service time, and packet loss; convert successful deliveries into an equivalent non-loss G/G/1 queue; then derive a stochastic service curve and apply stochastic network calculus to estimate the delay distribution.
why_it_works: The empirical service-time model incorporates retransmission variability, while the queueing and stochastic-network-calculus steps turn traffic and link-service variability into a predicted delay tail. Comparing that prediction with packet-level measurements can reveal whether observed tail delays are consistent with link service and load. This is a link-level estimate, not per-request causal reconstruction.
root_seam: Attach packet send/receive timestamps and request identities at the robot and server transport boundary; use observed traffic and link-service measurements to estimate a network-delay distribution, then compare it with measured end-to-end tails. Separately timestamp server queueing and compute so those delays are not attributed to the link.
experiment: In a controlled Root test, vary network conditions and request arrival load while recording per-request transport timestamps and end-to-end latency. Fit the paper’s empirical service-time and error models from a training run, predict delay distributions for held-out runs, and compare predicted and measured network-delay tails against server queueing and compute timings.
evidence_quote: To apply SNC results to delay distribution analysis of the wireless link, the discussion above indicates that we need to find a stochastic service curve for the link.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section V-B, “Service modeling of the wireless link”
reported_gain: Qualitative validation: predicted delay distributions are reported to agree approximately with measurements across tested settings; no numerical gain is supplied.
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The study concerns a measured 802.15.4 link, not remote robot inference. Its model predicts link-level delay distributions from empirical link and traffic characteristics; the supplied text does not show per-request packet-to-inference causal reconstruction or separation from server-side delays.

title: DWTCP: Ultra Low Latency Congestion Control Protocol for Data Centers
abstract: Congestion control algorithms rely on a variety of congestion signals (packet loss, Explicit Congestion Notification, delay, etc.) to achieve fast convergence, high utilization, and fairness among flows. A key limitation of these congestion signals is that they are either late in feedback or they incur significant overheads. An ideal congestion control must discover any available bandwidth in the network, detect congestion as soon as link utilization approaches full capacity, and react timely to avoid queuing and packet drops, without significant overheads. To this end, this work proposes Scout service that leverages priority queues to infer bandwidth availability and link busyness at the host. The key observation here is that as the high priority queue (HPQ) gets busier, the low priority queue (LPQ) is served less. Therefore, the state of the link can be observed from the LPQ and any congestion can be detected several RTTs earlier than observing the HPQ. We propose a new transport protocol, Double-Window Transmission Control Protocol (DWTCP) that builds upon the Scout service to dynamically adjust its congestion window. Our testbed and simulation-based evaluation demonstrates that Scout enables a data center transport to achieve high throughput, near-zero queues, lower latency, and high fairness.
technical_mechanism: Send low-priority Scout packets alongside normal traffic and analyze their ACK delay or loss: because switches serve them only when the link is idle, delayed or missing Scouts signal link busyness and congestion earlier than signals from the high-priority queue.
why_it_works: As normal traffic occupies more link capacity, low-priority Scouts get fewer opportunities to transmit. Their delay or loss therefore exposes network contention before ordinary traffic experiences comparable queueing or loss, helping distinguish a network-side tail from delays arising solely in inference computation.
root_seam: Attach a low-priority probe stream to the robot-to-server path and correlate Scout send/ACK timing and loss with request identity and inference-stage timestamps. This gives Root an early network-contention signal to compare against server queueing, GPU execution, and action-application time. A controlled experiment can vary network load while holding inference work fixed, then vary inference load while holding network conditions fixed.
experiment: Under fixed inference workload, increase competing traffic on the robot-server path and measure whether Scout delay/loss rises before request latency; then hold network load fixed and vary server/GPU load to test whether the Scout signal remains specific to network contention.
evidence_quote: The absence (loss) of, or a delay in serving Scout packets indicates a busy link
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Scout service description.
reported_gain: The paper reports congestion detection several RTTs earlier than observing the high-priority queue; it also reports DWTCP tail-latency improvements of up to 5x versus DCTCP/HPCC in stated workloads.
baseline: Existing congestion signals based on high-priority traffic, including packet loss, delay, and ECN; DWTCP is also compared with DCTCP and HPCC.
uncertainty: Scout delay/loss indicates path busyness but does not directly measure a particular queue or identify a specific hop; the supplied text does not establish how to separate forward-path delay from ACK-path delay.

title: Automated Cause Analysis of Latency Outliers Using System-Level Dependency Graphs
abstract: Detecting performance issues and identifying their root causes in the runtime is a challenging task. Typically, developers use methods such as logging and tracing to identify bottlenecks. These solutions are, however, not ideal as they are time-consuming and require manual effort. In this paper, we propose a method to automate the task of detecting latency outliers using system-level traces and then comparing them to identify the root cause(s). Our method makes use of dependency graphs to show internal interactions between threads and system resources. With these graphs, one can pinpoint where performance issues occur. However, a single trace can be composed of a large number of requests, each generating one graph. To automate the task of identifying outliers within the dataset, we use machine learning density-based models and statistical calculations such as -score. Our evaluation shows an accuracy greater than 97 % on outlier detection, making them appropriate for in-production servers and industry-level use cases.
technical_mechanism: Collect kernel-level system traces, extract per-request Waiting-Dependency Graphs that represent thread and resource waits, and detect outlier requests by graph embedding and clustering. Merge normal-request graphs into a representative graph and compare each outlier graph against it to highlight missing or quantitatively different nodes and dependencies.
why_it_works: The graph comparison exposes where an outlier diverges from normal executions, including resource waits and interacting threads. For Root, per-request graphs built from robot- and server-side execution traces could distinguish transport-related waiting from server-side waits or CPU contention when those events are represented in the trace. The paper demonstrates differential diagnosis against normal requests, but does not establish packet-level attribution.
root_seam: Attach request identity and timestamps to robot-side and server-side kernel events, construct per-request dependency graphs, and compare tail requests with a merged graph of healthy requests. This could localize whether extra waiting appears on the client, in network-related waits, or within server execution; it requires trace collection rather than sparse packet reconstruction.
experiment: For matched healthy and tail robot-inference requests, collect per-request kernel traces at the robot and inference server, construct waiting-dependency graphs, and compare each tail graph with a representative healthy graph. Check whether highlighted differences correctly identify injected network delay versus server queueing, CPU contention, GPU compute, or action-application delay.
evidence_quote: After detecting outliers, we can compare them with a group of normal DepGraphs to identify the root causes of the anomalies.
evidence_location: selected_pdf_text, introduction and method description
reported_gain: Outlier-detection accuracy greater than 97%; this is not a measured Root gain or a localization-accuracy result.
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The method uses system-level kernel tracing and graph comparison, not packet/ACK-level reconstruction. The supplied text does not show that its traces distinguish network-tail causes from all other delay sources, nor does it evaluate robot-to-cloud inference. The reported accuracy concerns outlier detection, not root-cause localization.

title: Hardware-in-the-Loop Simulation for Evaluating Communication Impacts on the Wireless-Network-Controlled Robots
abstract: More and more robot automation applications have changed to wireless communication, and network performance has a growing impact on robotic systems. This study proposes a hardware-in-the-loop (HiL) simulation methodology for connecting the simulated robot platform to real network devices. This project seeks to provide robotic engineers and researchers with the capability to experiment without heavily modifying the original controller and get more realistic test results that correlate with actual network conditions. We deployed this HiL simulation system in two common cases for wireless-network-controlled robotic applications: (1) safe multi-robot coordination for mobile robots, and (2) human-motion-based teleoperation for manipulators. The HiL simulation system is deployed and tested under various network conditions in all circumstances. The experiment results are analyzed and compared with the previous simulation methods, demonstrating that the proposed HiL simulation methodology can identify a more reliable communication impact on robot systems.
technical_mechanism: Hardware-in-the-loop network substitution: connect a simulated robot controller and robot model through real network devices, forward command and status traffic over UDP, and compare network conditions while observing robot outcomes. The system also integrates ET2000 timestamp-based network monitoring.
why_it_works: Real Ethernet or Wi-Fi communication exposes effects such as unstable delivery, packet loss, and connection interruption that static delay/loss models may miss. Comparing sent and executed motion loops or robot motion across network conditions links communication changes to control-loop effects.
root_seam: Attach request or action-cycle identity and timestamps at robot-side and server-side send/receive events, then correlate them with packet/ACK/loss telemetry and action execution. This would help distinguish network delay or loss from computation and action-application delay; the paper does not describe request-level tracing or its ET2000 measurement implementation in detail.
experiment: Run identical robot inference/action loops over Ethernet and controlled Wi-Fi conditions using a real network path. Synchronize request/action IDs with endpoint timestamps and packet-level telemetry; compare end-to-end tail latency and motion-loop loss against the network-segment measurements, while separately recording server compute and action-application time.
evidence_quote: The hardware interface for the network devices is designed and injected between the controller and the robot model, providing practical communication options.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section II.A, System Architecture
reported_gain: The paper reports that teleoperation motion loss rate was 0 under Ethernet, 0.008 under short-range Wi-Fi 6, and 0.03 under long-range Wi-Fi 6; it also reports more realistic coordination outcomes than static network modeling. These are paper results, not Root measurements.
baseline: Static network modeling for multi-robot coordination; Ethernet for the teleoperation comparison.
uncertainty: The paper does not provide compact temporal signatures of packet droughts or loss recovery, nor does it evaluate rare network-delay tails specifically. ET2000 timing resolution is stated, but its measurement software is not detailed and synchronized real-time network testing is described as future work.

title: SQP: Congestion Control for Low-Latency Interactive Video Streaming
abstract: This paper presents the design and evaluation of SQP, a congestion control algorithm (CCA) for interactive video streaming applications that need to stream high-bitrate compressed video with very low end-to-end frame delay (eg. AR streaming, cloud gaming). SQP uses frame-coupled, paced packet trains to sample the network bandwidth, and uses an adaptive one-way delay measurement to recover from queuing, for low, bounded queuing delay. SQP rapidly adapts to changes in the link bandwidth, ensuring high utilization and low frame delay, and also achieves competitive bandwidth shares when competing with queue-building flows within an acceptable delay envelope. SQP has good fairness properties, and works well on links with shallow buffers. In real-world A/B testing of SQP against Copa in Google's AR streaming platform, SQP achieves 27% and 15% more sessions with high bitrate and low frame delay for LTE and Wi-Fi, respectively. When competing with queue-building traffic like Cubic and BBR, SQP achieves 2-3X higher bandwidth compared to GoogCC (WebRTC), Sprout, and PCC-Vivace, and comparable performance to Copa (with mode switching).
technical_mechanism: Frame-coupled paced packet trains sample available bandwidth; adaptive one-way delay measurements detect queuing and trigger rate/bitrate reduction to drain self-induced queues.
why_it_works: The delay signal and per-frame delivery feedback reveal network queuing while pacing keeps probing at sub-frame timescales. For Root, attaching one-way transport-delay measurements and frame/request identity would help distinguish network-path delay growth from server-side inference or action-application time; the paced-train approach also provides an active bandwidth sample.
root_seam: At the robot/server transport boundary, correlate frame or request identity with send and delivery timestamps, and record one-way delay and per-frame delivery feedback. Compare these signals with inference and action timestamps to isolate transport queuing or bandwidth changes from compute delay.
experiment: In a controlled Root replay, hold inference workload constant while injecting bandwidth drops and queue-building cross traffic. Compare transport-tail detection using frame-coupled paced probes plus one-way delay feedback against ordinary request timing, and check whether it detects network delay changes without attributing server queueing or compute time to the network.
evidence_quote: SQP uses frame-coupled, paced packet trains to sample the network bandwidth, and uses an adaptive one-way delay measurement to recover from queuing
evidence_location: Abstract and selected PDF text, opening paragraph
reported_gain: The paper reports 27% and 15% more sessions with high bitrate and low frame delay than Copa in real-world LTE and Wi-Fi A/B tests, respectively; this is not a Root gain.
baseline: Copa for the real-world A/B tests; the paper also compares against other congestion-control algorithms in emulated scenarios.
uncertainty: SQP is a congestion-control intervention, not a standalone tail-diagnosis method. The context does not establish that its one-way delay signal separates network delay from all other sources of end-to-end delay, and it reports no Root evaluation.

title: Interference and Need Aware Workload Colocation in Hyperscale Datacenters
abstract: Datacenters suffer from resource utilization inefficiencies due to the conflicting goals of service owners and platform providers. Service owners intending to maintain Service Level Objectives (SLO) for themselves typically request a conservative amount of resources. Platform providers want to increase operational efficiency to reduce capital and operating costs. Achieving both operational efficiency and SLO for individual services at the same time is challenging due to the diversity in service workload characteristics, resource usage patterns that are dependent on input load, heterogeneity in platform, memory, I/O, and network architecture, and resource bundling. This paper presents a tunable approach to resource allocation that accounts for both dynamic service resource needs and platform heterogeneity. In addition, an online K-Means-based service classification method is used in conjunction with an offline sensitivity component. Our tunable approach allows trading resource utilization efficiency for absolute SLO guarantees based on the service owners' sensitivity to its SLO. We evaluate our tunable resource allocator at scale in a private cloud environment with mostly latency-critical workloads. When tuning for operational efficiency, we demonstrate up to 50% reduction in required machines; 40% reduction in Total-Cost-of-Ownership (TCO); and 60% reduction in CPU and memory fragmentation, but at the cost of increasing the number of tasks experiencing degradation of SLO by up to 25% compared to the baseline. When tuning for SLO, by introducing interference-aware colocation, we can tune the solver to reduce tasks experiencing degradation of SLO by up to 22% compared to the baseline, but at an additional cost of 30% in terms of the number of hosts. We highlight this trade-off between TCO and SLO violations, and offer tuning based on the requirements of the platform owners.
technical_mechanism: Controlled network-contention sensitivity testing: inject competing host traffic with iperf, measure the service SLI change in an A/B experiment, and derive a sensitivity score tied to the SLO.
why_it_works: The intervention tests whether added network bandwidth contention causes service degradation, rather than merely correlating host telemetry with a tail. The SLI response and SLO-based sensitivity score can implicate shared-host network bandwidth as a contributor. This can expose a resource-level cause of latency regression, though it does not identify the particular competing flow or attribute an individual request's delay.
root_seam: At the robot/server request path, retain request identity and timing alongside server-side network/runtime signals. In a controlled deployment, inject bounded competing traffic on the server host and compare request-tail latency and SLI with a no-injection control. Where available, separately measure transport delay, server queueing, GPU compute, and action-application time; the paper itself measures service SLI impact, not these per-request components.
experiment: Run randomized A/B trials with and without bounded competing host network traffic while holding inference load and other resources constant. Compare request-tail latency and network/runtime measurements, and check whether any change is attributable to transport or shared network contention rather than server queueing, GPU compute, or action application. Use no Root gain as assumed.
evidence_quote: Network Bandwidth: We use iperf [3] to add extra network bandwidth on hosts and see the impact it has on services running on it.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section III-C, Sensitivity Analysis.
reported_gain: Sensitivity scores reduced tasks experiencing interference by up to 22% relative to baseline, at an additional cost of 30% in host count.
baseline: Baseline placement without sensitivity scores.
uncertainty: The evidence supports a causal test of shared-host network-bandwidth contention using service-level SLI measurements, but not identification of specific off-path flows or localization of an individual request's network tail. The paper does not separate network delay from server queueing or compute, and reports no Root-measured gain.

title: Adaptive QoS of WebRTC for Vehicular Media Communications
abstract: Vehicles shipping sensors for onboard systems are gaining connectivity. This enables information sharing to realize a more comprehensive understanding of the environment. However, peer communication through public cellular networks brings multiple networking hurdles to address, needing in-network systems to relay communications and connect parties that cannot connect directly. Web Real-Time Communication (WebRTC) is a good candidate for media streaming across vehicles as it enables low latency communications, while bringing standard protocols to security handshake, discovering public IPs and transverse Network Address Translation (NAT) systems. However, the end-to-end Quality of Service (QoS) adaptation in an infrastructure where transmission and reception are decoupled by a relay, needs a mechanism to adapt the video stream to the network capacity efficiently. To this end, this paper investigates a mechanism to apply changes on resolution, framerate and bitrate by exploiting the Real Time Transport Control Protocol (RTCP) metrics, such as bandwidth and round-trip time. The solution aims to ensure that the receiving onboard system gets relevant information in time. The impact on end-to-end throughput efficiency and reaction time when applying different approaches to QoS adaptation are analyzed in a real 5G testbed.
technical_mechanism: Forward receiver-side RTCP path reports across the relay to the sender, restoring visibility into the otherwise hidden download path. The reported bandwidth, RTT, and jitter provide a path-specific signal that can expose whether network conditions coincide with a tail.
why_it_works: When a relay splits the connection, sender-side feedback may cover only the upload path, leaving receiver-side download degradation invisible. Forwarding the receiver's reports makes that missing path observable.
