In Root, request-correlated reports could help distinguish a degraded transport path from server-side queueing or inference compute, though the paper does not itself perform that separation.
root_seam: At a robot/server relay boundary, retain receiver-side RTCP metrics and associate them with request or time-window identifiers. Compare upload- and download-path reports with Root's request timestamps and server queue/GPU timings; the added signal would reveal download-path conditions unavailable from sender-side telemetry alone.
experiment: In a controlled Root replay or testbed, inject bandwidth and latency impairments independently on the robot-to-server and server-to-robot paths. Compare sender-only telemetry with receiver RTCP reports forwarded across the relay. Measure whether request-correlated reports identify the impaired path for tail requests, while separately recording server queueing, GPU compute, and action-application time.
evidence_quote: the relay server forwards the RTCP reports generated between the relay and the receiver towards the sender peer through a WebRTC data channel. This way, the relay provides awareness of the receiver download metrics to the sender.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section III, “Reporting Relay” paragraph.
reported_gain: Average sender reaction: 2.5 s for direct communication, 3.3 s for Simple Gateway, and 3.6 s for Janus Gateway; receiver encoding-update times: 0.7 s, 0.7 s, and 1.0 s, respectively. These are paper results, not Root gains.
baseline: The paper compares direct communication, a Simple Gateway with sender visibility limited to upload, and a Janus Gateway forwarding receiver RTCP reports to the sender.
uncertainty: The paper studies video adaptation, not inference-tail diagnosis. It does not establish request-level correlation or separate network delay from server queueing, GPU compute, and action application. The diagnostic transfer is plausible and testable, but its effectiveness for Root is unknown.

title: Waiting for QUIC: Passive Measurements to Understand QUIC Deployments
abstract: QUIC experiences a rapid adoption since its standardization in 2021, and hypergiants configure their infrastructure to optimize for QUIC performance. In this paper, we introduce a passive measurement method to study both the progressive rollout and individual hypergiant configurations during the last five years. By analyzing backscatter traffic of the UCSD network telescope, we are able to make the following observations. First, Meta, Google, and Cloudflare configure significantly different maximal retransmission numbers and timeouts. Second, we can identify different off-net deployments of hypergiants, using packet features, such as QUIC connection IDs, packet coalescence, and packet lengths. Third, we observe changing hypergiant deployment configurations during our different measurement periods. Fourth, connection IDs can allow further insights into load balancer deployments, such as the number of servers. We bolster our results using two orthogonal measurements: passive recording of QUIC flows and active probing.
technical_mechanism: Infer QUIC retransmission timing from packet timestamps, then compare observed intervals with an initial RTO and binary exponential backoff. For Root, applying this to packets associated with an individual request could expose transport retransmissions and their contribution to a long request delay.
why_it_works: A retransmission sequence with backoff intervals is a transport-level signal of missing acknowledgments and can distinguish network/ACK-path delay from server queueing or GPU compute when aligned with request-stage timestamps. The paper uses this signal to classify deployments, not to diagnose individual inference requests, so that per-request diagnostic effect remains a transfer to test.
root_seam: Correlate request identity and robot/server timestamps with QUIC packet, ACK, and retransmission events at the transport endpoints. Compare the transport interval with server queueing, GPU execution, and action-application timings to determine whether retransmission accounts for the tail.
experiment: Run controlled robot-to-cloud requests under healthy conditions, injected packet loss, and injected delay, alongside server-queueing and GPU-delay controls. Collect per-request QUIC packet/ACK/retransmission timestamps and stage timings. Test whether the inferred RTO/backoff sequence identifies network-affected tails and avoids attributing server-side delays to the network.
evidence_quote: The Retransmission Interval classifiers calculate the time since the reception of the first packet of a connection. We then use the determined value of the Initial RTO and perform binary exponential backoff on this value.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, §3.3/§6 excerpt, paragraph beginning “Retransmission Intervals.”
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The paper analyzes passive backscatter and uses retransmission intervals to classify server deployments; it does not validate per-request tail diagnosis or separation from inference-stage delays. Root applicability depends on having request-correlated endpoint transport events.

title: Dual Queue Coupled AQM: Deployable Very Low Queuing Delay for All
abstract: On the Internet, sub-millisecond queueing delay and capacity-seeking have traditionally been considered mutually exclusive. We introduce a service that offers both: Low Latency Low Loss Scalable throughput (L4S). When tested under a wide range of conditions emulated on a testbed using real residential broadband equipment, queue delay remained both low (median 100--300 μs) and consistent (99th percentile below 2 ms even under highly dynamic workloads), without compromising other metrics (zero congestion loss and close to full utilization). L4S exploits the properties of `Scalable' congestion controls (e.g., DCTCP, TCP Prague). Flows using such congestion control are however very aggressive, which causes a deployment challenge as L4S has to coexist with so-called `Classic' flows (e.g., Reno, CUBIC). This paper introduces an architectural solution: `Dual Queue Coupled Active Queue Management', which enables balance between Scalable and Classic flows. It counterbalances the more aggressive response of Scalable flows with more aggressive marking, without having to inspect flow identifiers. The Dual Queue structure has been implemented as a Linux queuing discipline. It acts like a semi-permeable membrane, isolating the latency of Scalable and `Classic' traffic, but coupling their capacity into a single bandwidth pool. This paper justifies the design and implementation choices, and visualizes a representative selection of hundreds of thousands of experiment runs to test our claims.
technical_mechanism: Timestamp packets on enqueue and measure their sojourn time at dequeue in a DualQ AQM; retain queue-specific delay signals and use them for congestion marking or dropping. The queue-sojourn measurement is the transferable diagnostic operation.
why_it_works: Sojourn time measures time spent waiting in the network queue, rather than total request latency. A tail that coincides with elevated bottleneck queue-sojourn measurements therefore has direct evidence of network queue buildup; low sojourn alongside a slow request points away from that queue as the cause. This helps separate queueing from server queueing, GPU compute, and action application, though correlation to a request is not supplied by the paper.
root_seam: At an instrumentable transport bottleneck, retain enqueue/dequeue timestamps or equivalent queue-sojourn samples and ECN marks, then associate packet events with robot/server request timestamps or request IDs. Compare those signals with server queue, GPU, and action-application timing. No Reflex-private infrastructure is assumed.
experiment: In a controlled Root test, create network queue buildup while holding server queueing, GPU compute, and action application constant; then introduce server-side delay while keeping the network queue shallow. Compare request-tail attribution using end-to-end timings alone against timings augmented with per-queue sojourn telemetry and ECN events. Check whether the telemetry identifies network-queue contribution in the first condition without misattributing the second.
evidence_quote: The function LEN() returns the the queue in bytes, while TIME() returns the duration since a packet was time-stamped (its sojourn time). On enqueue (not shown), packets are time-stamped
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, section III-E, Implementation, description of Algorithm 1.
reported_gain: Abstract reports median queue delay of 100–300 μs and 99th percentile below 2 ms under highly dynamic workloads. The paper also reports an order of magnitude lower queue delay for Prague over DualPI2 than other AQMs; this is a paper result, not a Root gain.
baseline: The paper names PIE and FQ-CoDel as comparison AQMs; the supplied text does not give a single numeric baseline for the abstract's reported delay.
uncertainty: The paper supports measuring queue-specific packet sojourn time, but does not provide request-level identity correlation or demonstrate causal attribution of remote-robot inference tails. Root would need to establish the packet-to-request attachment and validate that the monitored queue is on the relevant path.

title: Low latency communication over commercially available LTE and remote driving
abstract: In addition to autonomous car operation, in many cases it is desirable to let a human drive the vehicle remotely. To make remote operation possible, it is very critical to have a low and predictable latency to transmit video from the car cameras and receive control commands back. In this paper, we analyze the problem and present a communication and video streaming system that addresses the latency challenges and enables teleoperation of a real car over commercially available LTE network; demonstrating sub-50ms roundtrip latencies for 720p, 60FPS video, with average PSNR 36db.
technical_mechanism: Measure packet-delay autocorrelation across LTE links to expose persistent, correlated delay bursts; compare the correlation as the number of links changes.
why_it_works: A slow packet followed by more slow packets indicates a persistent network tail rather than isolated jitter. The paper reports that packet delays on a single last-mile link are highly correlated and that adding modems reduces autocorrelation, providing a measurable way to characterize whether delay tails cluster over time. This is diagnostic evidence, distinct from the paper’s separate mitigation using coding and multiple links.
root_seam: At the robot/server transport boundary, record packet sequence or request identity and send/receive timestamps, retaining the transport path or interface when available. Compute packet-delay autocorrelation and relate slow-packet runs to request completion tails. These measurements could show whether Root’s network delays are temporally clustered, separately from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application.
experiment: Replay or generate controlled inference-like traffic over a single path and over multiple paths under matched load. Capture per-packet send/receive times and request IDs; compare delay autocorrelation, runs of slow packets, and request-level tail latency. Keep server queue, inference, and action timestamps separate, and include a controlled network impairment with bursty versus independent delays.
evidence_quote: Experiments show that even using 2 modems the latency autocorrelation function decreases significantly (see Figure 6), and if the number of modems becomes 4, there is no correlation in packet latency at all.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section III.C, “Last mile connection with multiple LTE modems”; see also Section II’s discussion of correlated packet delays and Figure 3.
reported_gain: 8.5 ms latency gain at probability 0.95 in the two-modem experiment.
baseline: Hypothetical uncoded reconstructed latency based on individual-modem latency statistics measured at the start of the experiment.
uncertainty: The paper supports measuring packet-delay correlation, but does not establish that this analysis diagnoses Root inference regressions directly. The reported uncoded comparison is hypothetical, and no Root gain is measured.

title: Efficient Model Based Diagnosis
abstract: In this paper an efficient model based diagnostic process is described for systems whose components possess a causal relation between their inputs and their outputs. In this diagnostic process, firstly, a set of focuses on likely broken components is determined. Secondly, for each focus the most informative probing point within the focus can be determined. Both these steps of the diagnostic process have a worst case time complexity of O(n²) where n is the number of components. If the connectivity of the components is low, however, the diagnostic process shows a linear time complexity. It is also shown how the diagnostic process described can be applied in dynamic systems and systems containing loops. When diagnosing dynamic systems it is possible to choose between detecting intermitting faults or to improve the diagnostic precision by assuming non-intermittency.
technical_mechanism: Model-based fault focusing followed by entropy-guided probing: use causal dependency sets and observed conflicts/confirmations to focus on likely faulty components, then select the most informative component output to measure using the focus and its dependencies.
why_it_works: Confirmation and conflict observations narrow the likely fault set, while the probe-selection rule targets a measurement expected to divide that focus informatively. This can distinguish causes with fewer additional measurements than measuring every component output.
root_seam: Attach a causal component model to timestamped robot/server inference events and transport observations. Treat network-path stages, server queues, GPU execution, and action application as distinct components; use measured outputs and conflicts to focus diagnosis, then probe the most informative unmeasured event or counter. The paper provides no network-specific model or transport telemetry.
experiment: In a controlled Root replay or testbed, inject faults separately into transport delay/loss, server queueing, GPU execution, and action application. Compare the number of additional measurements needed to identify the injected cause using entropy-guided probing against measuring all component outputs and against a fixed probe order; also report cause-identification accuracy.
evidence_quote: Given a focus, the most informative new probing can be determined.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, abstract/overview paragraph beginning “The diagnostic process described in this paper is based on a careful determination…”
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: GDE is discussed as a qualitative comparison; no measured baseline gain is reported in the supplied context.
uncertainty: The context supports efficient fault focusing and probe selection, but does not demonstrate the method on network regressions or specify how to construct a Root transport/runtime causal model.

title: QStack: Re-architecting User-space Network Stack to Optimize CPU Efficiency and Service Quality
abstract: TCP/IP network stack is irreplaceable for Web services in datacenter front-end servers, and the demand for which is growing rapidly for emerging high concurrency network service applications (including Internet, Internet of Things, mobile Internet, etc.) especially. The existing network stack schemes often face the dilemma between the data center server resource utilization (i.e., high CPU efficiency) and application service quality (i.e., low tail latency). We break this dilemma via a flexible architectural design QStack, which simultaneously achieves CPU efficiency and low tail latency in user-space network stack for front-end datacenter server. QStack proposes elastic framework and application definable full-datapath priority, such that the network stack collaboration among CPU cores horizontally and coordination across network layers in fine grained vertically on demand. We prototype QStack on commodity servers. Testbed experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of QStack over state-of-the-art user-space network stack designs.
technical_mechanism: Timed fastcalldown checks interrupt long-running application coroutines to service overdue NIC receive checks, TCP processing, and packet sends; it can batch packet work and yield when a higher-priority event arrives. This exposes a server-side network-stack service delay by checking whether packet handling was postponed while application work occupied the core. It is a mitigation and diagnostic signal for endpoint processing stalls, not a detector of network-path delay.
why_it_works: The governing rule compares elapsed time since NIC and TCP processing with configured thresholds, then directly invokes the overdue network work. The paper connects long application execution on a shared core to NIC queue overflow and packet drops. Logging fastcalldown triggers alongside packet arrival, queue, and request timestamps could show whether a tail coincides with delayed server packet service; robot-send/server-receive timestamps would still be needed to separate path delay from server-side delay.
root_seam: At the server's user-space network stack, record request or packet identity, arrival time, NIC queue depth, fastcalldown check time and trigger reason, packet-processing time, and response-send time. Pair with robot-side send/receive timestamps to distinguish network transit from server NIC/service delay, server queueing, inference compute, and action application. This uses QStack's explicit timed checks as an attachment point; it does not require access to Reflex infrastructure.
experiment: Under a fixed mixed workload, compare fastcalldown enabled and disabled while varying the duration of application coroutines and injecting controlled network delay/loss separately. Retain per-request robot send, server packet arrival/service, inference queue/dequeue, compute completion, response send, and robot receive timestamps, plus NIC queue depth and fastcalldown trigger events. Test whether tails align with overdue server network service or queue buildup versus injected transit delay, and whether the instrumentation localizes those cases. Treat latency reduction as a separate mitigation result from diagnostic accuracy.
evidence_quote: If NIC check interval is timed out, fastcalldown would directly call the packet receiving function to collect data packets to the driver buffer for temporary storage.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Fastcalldown section; the following sentences describe timed-out TCP processing and application-coroutine runtime checks.
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The paper describes timed service checks and their role in avoiding delayed packet processing, but does not evaluate fastcalldown as a network-tail diagnostic or provide a localization-accuracy result. The extracted text does not give a Root experiment or Root-measured gain. This supports a controlled experiment for identifying server-side packet-service stalls; it cannot by itself diagnose delay on the network path.

title: Flow-Level Packet Loss Detection via Sketch Decomposition and Matrix Optimization
abstract: For cloud service providers, fine-grained packet loss detection across data centers is crucial in improving their service level and increasing business income. However, the inability to obtain sufficient measurements makes it difficult owing to the fundamental limit that the wide-area network links responsible for communication are not under their management. Moreover, millisecond-level delay jitter and clock synchronization errors in the WAN disable many tools that perform well in data center networks on this issue. Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop a new tool or method. In this work, we propose SketchDecomp, a novel loss detection method, from a mathematical perspective that has never been considered before. Its key is to decompose sketches upstream and downstream into several sub-sketches and builds a low-rank matrix optimization model to solve them. Extensive experiments on the test bed demonstrate its superiority.
technical_mechanism: Collect upstream and downstream count-min sketches by flow and time window, model each sketch as a sum of sub-sketches spanning possible jitter-shifted receive windows, then use low-rank matrix optimization to recover those sub-sketches and estimate per-flow, per-window packet loss.
why_it_works: The decomposition accounts for packets arriving in later windows because of delay jitter, rather than mistaking window misalignment for loss. The low-rank assumption—flows share similar delay distributions over short intervals—constrains the otherwise underdetermined reconstruction. Comparing recovered sent and received sub-sketches estimates loss without packet modification or visibility into the WAN.
root_seam: Attach sketches to robot-side and server-side transport boundaries, keyed by flow/request identity and time window. The method could expose loss hidden by jitter despite sparse summaries, but does not itself reconstruct request-to-packet causality or distinguish network delay from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application.
experiment: In a controlled Root replay, collect endpoint sketches while injecting known per-flow packet loss and variable delay that shifts packets across windows. Compare reconstructed per-flow, per-window loss with ground truth, and test sensitivity to sketch width/depth, jitter range, and violations of the shared-delay-distribution assumption.
evidence_quote: Given that packets sent may be branched to multiple receive windows due to delay jitter, we regard the sketches as the sum of several unknown sub-sketches.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section 1 Introduction; mechanism details in Sections 2.3–2.5.
reported_gain: On the test bed, reported error ratios (average error divided by average actual loss) were 0.019 for extremely severe loss, 0.070 for severe loss, and 0.073 for slight loss.
baseline: Ground-truth packet loss on the test bed.
uncertainty: The paper evaluates flow-level loss estimation, not remote robot inference or request-level tail latency. Root transfer depends on obtaining compatible sketches at both endpoints and on the assumed bounded jitter range and low-rank/shared-delay structure.

title: Enabling On-Demand Cyber-Physical Control Applications with UAV Access Points
abstract: Achieving cyber-physical control over a wireless channel requires satisfying both the timeliness of a single packet and preserving the latency reliability across several consecutive packets. To satisfy those requirements as an ubiquitous service requires big infrastructural developments, or flexible on-demand equipment such as UAVs. To avoid the upfront cost in terms of finance and energy, this paper analyzes the capability of UAV access points (UAVAPs) to satisfy the requirements for cyber-physical traffic. To investigate this, we perform a Gilbert-Eliott burst-error analysis that is analytically derived as a combination of two separate latency measurement campaigns and provide an upper-bound analysis of the UAVAP system. The analysis is centered around a UAVAP that uses its LTE connection to reach the backhaul, while providing service to ground nodes (GNs) with a Wi-Fi access point (AP). Thus, we combine both measurement campaigns to analyze the plausibility of the described setup in casual, crowded or mixed network settings.
technical_mechanism: Classify each hop's packet as timely or untimely against a latency deadline, fit a two-state Gilbert-Elliott model to consecutive packet outcomes, then combine the hop models to estimate end-to-end burst lengths.
why_it_works: The state-transition probabilities capture temporal correlation: a hop that enters a bad state may keep producing consecutive late or lost packets. Modeling Wi-Fi and LTE separately also indicates which hop contributes to a burst, rather than treating end-to-end latency as one undifferentiated measurement.
root_seam: Attach request identities and timestamps to robot-side and server-side transport events, classify per-hop network timeliness against deadlines, and fit transition probabilities to consecutive outcomes. This could expose whether a tail is a persistent network bad state and which hop contributes; separating network delay from server queueing or inference compute would require timestamps at those boundaries.
experiment: On a controlled remote-inference workload, record per-request network timings at each available hop and mark deadline misses. Fit the two-state transition model on one trace, then test its predicted probabilities of consecutive misses against held-out traces and injected bursty network conditions. Compare per-hop predictions with an end-to-end-only model.
evidence_quote: each untimely transmission on each interface of the UAVAP can be considered as a transition to a failed state for that link of the hop.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section III, “Burst Errors in UAVAP Systems.”
reported_gain: The paper reports that all UAVAP implementations outperform a direct-relaxed LTE link in burst-error performance; no numerical gain is available in the supplied context.
baseline: Direct-relaxed LTE link.
uncertainty: This is a burst-probability analysis, not an online diagnostic or a Root evaluation. Its combined-link analysis uses independently modeled interfaces and some scenarios are synthesized from separate measurement campaigns, so transfer to inference requires validating the model on per-request traces and separating network delays from compute and queueing.

title: The TSN Building Blocks in Linux
abstract: Various application areas e.g. industrial automation, professional audio-video, automotive in-vehicle, aerospace on-board, and mobile fronthaul networks require deterministic communication: loss-less forwarding with bounded maximum latency. There is a lot of ongoing standardization activity in different organizations to provide vendor-agnostic building blocks for Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN), what is aimed as the universal solution for deterministic forwarding in OSI Layer-2 networks. Furthermore, the implementation of those standards is also happening in Linux. Some of them require software changes only, but others have hardware support requirements. In this paper, we give an overview of the implementation of the main TSN standards in the mainline Linux kernel. Furthermore, we provide measurement results on key functionality in support of TSN, e.g., scheduled transmission and Linux bridging characteristics.
technical_mechanism: Use synchronized software and NIC hardware timestamps at transmit and receive: software TX, hardware TX, hardware RX, and software RX. Comparing adjacent timestamps separates host-side send/receive overhead from time on the wire and switching, making the network-delay component localizable.
why_it_works: NIC hardware timestamps bracket transmission across the link, while software timestamps mark the driver-side boundaries. With clocks synchronized, differences between these points can distinguish network or switching delay from sender-side scheduling and stack delay and receiver-side processing delay.
root_seam: Attach the four timestamp events to each Root request or packet, using request identity to correlate robot-side and server-side transport events. Compare hardware TX-to-RX time with the surrounding software-to-hardware intervals to determine whether a tail occurs on the network path or at an endpoint.
experiment: On a controlled robot-inference path, collect synchronized software and NIC hardware timestamps for each request packet while independently varying network conditions and server/GPU load. Check whether injected network delay appears in hardware TX-to-RX intervals while endpoint intervals remain stable; then assess whether naturally occurring tail requests localize the same way.
evidence_quote: It records 4 timestamps for each packet:
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, section “On scheduling precision”
reported_gain: With hardware-offloaded ETF scheduling, the average difference from the intended transmission time was 5 ns and the maximum observed difference was 11 ns.
baseline: Clock-nanosleep scheduled transmission; its maximum observed difference from intended timestamps was 3.5 µs in the reported sample.
uncertainty: The paper demonstrates timestamp-based timing characterization, not a controlled diagnosis of rare network tails. Its timestamp intervals can support network-versus-endpoint localization, but the context does not report a rare-delay injection experiment or a Root evaluation.

title: Measuring and Estimating Key Quality Indicators in Cloud Gaming services
abstract: User equipment is one of the main bottlenecks facing the gaming industry nowadays. The extremely realistic games which are currently available trigger high computational requirements of the user devices to run games. As a consequence, the game industry has proposed the concept of Cloud Gaming, a paradigm that improves gaming experience in reduced hardware devices. To this end, games are hosted on remote servers, relegating users' devices to play only the role of a peripheral for interacting with the game. However, this paradigm overloads the communication links connecting the users with the cloud. Therefore, service experience becomes highly dependent on network connectivity. To overcome this, Cloud Gaming will be boosted by the promised performance of 5G and future 6G networks, together with the flexibility provided by mobility in multi-RAT scenarios, such as WiFi. In this scope, the present work proposes a framework for measuring and estimating the main E2E metrics of the Cloud Gaming service, namely KQIs. In addition, different machine learning techniques are assessed for predicting KQIs related to Cloud Gaming user's experience. To this end, the main key quality indicators (KQIs) of the service such as input lag, freeze percent or perceived video frame rate are collected in a real environment. Based on these, results show that machine learning techniques provide a good estimation of these indicators solely from network-based metrics. This is considered a valuable asset to guide the delivery of Cloud Gaming services through cellular communications networks even without access to the user's device, as it is expected for telecom operators.
technical_mechanism: Timestamped action-to-visible-response measurement using frame-change detection: record each user action's timestamp, identify the first corresponding changed frame, and take the time difference as response latency. The framework also detects freezes from repeated frames, with capture-rate decimation to avoid false detections.
why_it_works: This is a concrete measurement operation, not just the paper's learned KQI estimator. It can expose a tail in user-visible end-to-end response times without needing application internals: per-action latency samples can be summarized by tail quantiles, while repeated displayed frames provide a separate freeze signal. It measures the combined path through network, server, and display, however, and does not by itself attribute delay to the network.
root_seam: At the robot/client observation point, pair action or request timestamps with timestamps for the first resulting visible state change, using request identity or controlled action intervals to associate them. Compare these end-to-end samples with robot/server transport timestamps, queueing, compute, and action-application events to determine whether a visible tail aligns with network delay or another stage. This offers Root an application-data-independent observable, but not network localization on its own.
experiment: In a controlled Root replay, record action timestamps and frame/state-change timestamps and compute per-action end-to-end latency and tail quantiles. Independently inject network delay, loss, or jitter while holding server load constant, then inject server queueing or compute delay while holding network conditions constant. Compare the visual-measurement tail and freeze signal with transport and server-stage timings; verify that capture-rate decimation avoids false freeze detections.
evidence_quote: For the latter one, it is taken the timestamp of those frames in which movement is detected.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section 4.1.3 (“Input Lag”); frame-based freeze measurement and decimation are described in Sections 4.1.1–4.1.2.
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The paper describes measurement of end-to-end response and freezes, not tail-specific evaluation or causal network localization. The transfer assumes Root can observe action timestamps and resulting visible state changes; a Root gain has not been measured.

title: Reliable and Distributed Network Monitoring via In-band Network Telemetry
abstract: Traditional network monitoring solutions usually lack of scalability due to their centralized nature collecting heartbeats from all network components via a single controller. As a solution, In-Band Network Telemetry (INT) framework has been recently proposed to collect network telemetry information more autonomously and distributedly by employing programmable switches. However, it imposes further challenges to (i) find suitable INT paths to optimize the control overhead and information freshness and (ii) ensure reliable delivery of control information over multi-hop INT paths. In this work, we propose a monitoring scheme, reliable Graph Partitioned INT (GPINT), by extending our previous work and integrating shared queue ring (SQR) as a reliability feature against potential failures in network telemetry collection due to network congestion and link degradation that may cause loss of the visibility of the network. We implement our proposal in a recent data plane programming language P4, and compare it with traditional Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) and also another state-of-the-art study employing Euler's method for INT path generation. Our analysis first shows the importance of having a data recovery mechanism against packet losses under different network conditions. Then, our emulation results indicate that GPINT with reliability extension performs much better than its opponent in terms of telemetry collection latency and overhead monitoring scheme even under a high amount of packet losses.
technical_mechanism: Piggyback per-switch queue depth and queuing latency onto an INT probe as it traverses a predetermined path; use the accumulated measurements to inspect queue buildup along the network path. The separate SQR recovery mechanism retains probes and uses next-hop feedback timeouts to flag a possibly unresponsive link, then probe completion can revise that status to congested.
why_it_works: Per-hop queue measurements provide direct evidence of where packets waited, helping distinguish network queue buildup from server queueing or GPU delay when correlated with inference-stage timestamps. SQR adds path-level loss or delay evidence, but its timeout alone cannot identify congestion as the cause.
root_seam: Correlate an inference request or transport flow with an INT probe traversing the robot-to-server path. Compare per-hop queue depth and queuing latency with robot/server transport timestamps, server queue time, GPU execution, and action-application time. Preserve SQR feedback timeout and eventual probe completion as separate link-status evidence.
experiment: In a controlled remote-inference setup, independently inject switch queue buildup, link loss/degradation, server queueing, and GPU delay. Correlate request or flow identity with per-hop INT queue measurements and SQR feedback/timeout/completion events. Measure whether queue measurements localize network waiting and distinguish it from non-network delay; report probe overhead. Do not infer a Root gain from the paper.
evidence_quote: each node through on the path extends this packet by appending its own measurements
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Introduction, INT description; the preceding sentence identifies queuing latency and queue depth as telemetry queried from P4-programmable switches.
reported_gain: The abstract reports better telemetry collection latency and monitoring overhead than its opponent under high packet loss; exact scalar gain is UNKNOWN.
baseline: SNMP and Pan et al.’s Euler-method INT path-based monitoring scheme
uncertainty: The paper supports per-hop queue telemetry as a diagnostic signal, but does not test request-level remote-inference correlation or a classifier separating network queue buildup from other inference-stage delays. Root integration and measured Root effects are UNKNOWN.

title: ChameleMon: Shifting Measurement Attention as Network State Changes
abstract: Flow-level network measurement is critical to many network applications. Among various measurement tasks, packet loss detection and heavy-hitter detection are two most important measurement tasks, which we call the two key tasks. In practice, the two key tasks are often required at the same time, but existing works seldom handle both tasks. In this paper, we design ChameleMon to support the two key tasks simultaneously. One key design/novelty of ChameleMon is to shift measurement attention as network state changes, through two dimensions of dynamics: 1) dynamically allocating memory between the two key tasks; 2) dynamically monitoring the flows of importance. To realize the key design, we propose a key technique, leveraging Fermat's little theorem to devise a flexible data structure, namely FermatSketch. FermatSketch is dividable, additive, and subtractive, supporting the two key tasks. We have fully implemented a ChameleMon prototype on a testbed with a Fat-tree topology. We conduct extensive experiments and the results show ChameleMon supports the two key tasks with low memory/bandwidth overhead, and more importantly, it can automatically shift measurement attention as network state changes.
technical_mechanism: ChameleMon uses compact, dividable FermatSketch structures to measure both per-flow packet loss and flow sizes, then reallocates sketch memory and monitoring attention as network state changes. In healthy states it emphasizes packet-accumulation measurements; when losses increase, it shifts resources toward detecting victim flows.
why_it_works: The shared sketch structure allows resources to move between loss detection and flow-size measurement instead of being fixed to separate measurement schemes. The resulting flow-level summaries can retain evidence of which flows experienced losses while using less memory than recording every flow or lost packet.
root_seam: Attach epoch-aligned ingress and egress packet counts or loss summaries to robot inference requests or flows. This could help distinguish transport loss from server queueing, GPU compute, or action-application delay, provided requests can be mapped to measured flows. The paper does not establish request-level latency diagnosis.
experiment: On a controlled robot-inference workload, compare ChameleMon-style compact per-flow loss and size sketches against full packet or per-request transport traces. Inject packet loss and congestion while holding server load and GPU work fixed, then measure tail-regression detection and flow localization accuracy, memory use, and monitoring overhead. Separately vary server queueing to test whether the summaries distinguish network delay from server delay.
evidence_quote: ChameleMon can monitor the network every 50ms and shift measurement attention within at most 3 epochs as network state changes.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, §7 Conclusion
reported_gain: The paper reports 50 ms network monitoring and attention shifts within at most 3 epochs; it also reports up to 15.9× and 23.2× memory savings over FlowRadar and LossRadar, respectively, for packet-loss detection.
baseline: FlowRadar and LossRadar are the stated memory-comparison baselines for the packet-loss results; no baseline is stated for the 50 ms monitoring interval or 3-epoch shift.
uncertainty: The evaluation concerns data-center flow measurement, not robot inference or request-level tail latency. The supplied text does not specify a complete state-change trigger rule or show how to associate sketch summaries with individual inference requests.

title: Accelerating Machine Learning Inference with GPUs in ProtoDUNE Data Processing
abstract: We study the performance of a cloud-based GPU-accelerated inference server to speed up event reconstruction in neutrino data batch jobs. Using detector data from the ProtoDUNE experiment and employing the standard DUNE grid job submission tools, we attempt to reprocess the data by running several thousand concurrent grid jobs, a rate we expect to be typical of current and future neutrino physics experiments. We process most of the dataset with the GPU version of our processing algorithm and the remainder with the CPU version for timing comparisons. We find that a 100-GPU cloud-based server is able to easily meet the processing demand, and that using the GPU version of the event processing algorithm is two times faster than processing these data with the CPU version when comparing to the newest CPUs in our sample. The amount of data transferred to the inference server during the GPU runs can overwhelm even the highest-bandwidth network switches, however, unless care is taken to observe network facility limits or otherwise distribute the jobs to multiple sites. We discuss the lessons learned from this processing campaign and several avenues for future improvements.
technical_mechanism: Estimate workload-specific network demand from the sub-saturation slope of switch traffic versus event-start rate, account for background traffic using the fitted intercept, and compare resulting demand with switch capacity. The authors use that capacity estimate to interpret the slowdown as outbound-link saturation and set a concurrency cap.
why_it_works: The fitted slope estimates outbound bits per event despite aggregate switch counters, while the intercept estimates traffic from other jobs. When aggregate traffic approaches the known link capacity and EmTrk wall time rises, this supports a network-contention diagnosis; the capacity calculation then yields an actionable concurrency limit. The paper reports the switch saturated while Google ingress was not. This identifies a site-side network bottleneck, but does not isolate per-request transport delay from queueing or compute.
root_seam: Join robot request-start rate or concurrency and request-stage timestamps with robot-side egress/NIC utilization or switch counters. Fit traffic against request rate below saturation to estimate per-request network demand and background load, then compare predicted demand with link capacity. This adds a way to infer workload-specific bandwidth demand from aggregate counters without requiring private infrastructure or per-packet traces.
experiment: Replay a fixed Root inference workload while varying request concurrency below and above the observed egress-capacity threshold. Record request start rate, aggregate egress traffic, per-request end-to-end and inference-stage latency, and server queue/GPU timings. Fit the below-saturation traffic-versus-rate slope and intercept, predict the saturation point, and check whether latency rises there and returns toward baseline when concurrency is capped. Treat the experiment as a network diagnosis test, not as evidence of a Root latency gain.
evidence_quote: The linear fit to the traffic below 80 Gb/s indicates that each event sends 4.2 ± 0.2 Gb of outbound traffic, on top of 44 ± 2 Gb/s of baseline traffic from non-ProtoDUNE sources.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section 4 Discussion and Figure 8 caption; the cap and recovery are described in Section 3.2.1, Outbound network saturation.
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The paper's evidence is from batch jobs and aggregate switch traffic, not robot action loops or per-request transport measurements. EmTrk wall time includes network latency but does not separate it from server queueing or compute. Traffic from other jobs contributes to the switch counters, and the authors report that they could not disambiguate its sources. The reported concurrency cap is an operational intervention, not a controlled Root experiment.

title: Generalizing Greenwald-Khanna Streaming Quantile Summaries for Weighted Inputs
abstract: Estimating quantiles, like the median or percentiles, is a fundamental task in data mining and data science. A (streaming) quantile summary is a data structure that can process a set S of n elements in a streaming fashion and at the end, for any phi in (0,1], return a phi-quantile of S up to an eps error, i.e., return a phi'-quantile with phi'=phi +- eps. We are particularly interested in comparison-based summaries that only compare elements of the universe under a total ordering and are otherwise completely oblivious of the universe. The best known deterministic quantile summary is the 20-year old Greenwald-Khanna (GK) summary that uses O((1/eps) log(eps n)) space [SIGMOD'01]. This bound was recently proved to be optimal for all deterministic comparison-based summaries by Cormode and Vesle'y [PODS'20]. In this paper, we study weighted quantiles, a generalization of the quantiles problem, where each element arrives with a positive integer weight which denotes the number of copies of that element being inserted. The only known method of handling weighted inputs via GK summaries is the naive approach of breaking each weighted element into multiple unweighted items and feeding them one by one to the summary, which results in a prohibitively large update time (proportional to the maximum weight of input elements). We give the first non-trivial extension of GK summaries for weighted inputs and show that it takes O((1/eps) log(eps n)) space and O(log(1/eps)+ log log(eps n)) update time per element to process a stream of length n (under some quite mild assumptions on the range of weights and eps). En route to this, we also simplify the original GK summaries for unweighted quantiles.
technical_mechanism: Maintain a deterministic weighted Greenwald–Khanna quantile summary: process each weighted observation as a single update, retain a compact subset with rank metadata, and delete entries only when the summary’s approximation invariant remains valid.
why_it_works: The maintained invariant bounds quantile error in rank, so the compact summary can estimate latency percentiles without storing every observation or expanding a weighted observation into many copies. This preserves distributional tail information, though it does not by itself identify the cause of a tail.
root_seam: Attach the summary to per-request network-delay measurements derived from robot/server transport timestamps, optionally maintaining separate summaries by request class or transport event. Root gains bounded-error latency quantiles with reduced storage and avoids retaining every measurement; causal localization still requires request identity or additional cross-layer signals.
experiment: Replay the same labeled Root request traces into the weighted summary and an exact per-request latency recorder. Compare estimated network-delay quantiles against exact quantiles at several ε settings, measure memory and update cost, and verify that injected network-delay tails remain visible separately from server queueing, GPU compute, and action-application delays.
evidence_quote: We give the first non-trivial extension of GK summaries for weighted inputs and show that it takes O((1/ε) log (εn)) space and O(log(1/ε) + log log(εn)) update time per element
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, abstract; also summarized in the supplied paper abstract.
reported_gain: Theoretical bounds: O((1/ε) log(εn)) space and O(log(1/ε) + log log(εn)) update time per element under stated assumptions.
baseline: Naively break each weighted element into multiple unweighted items and feed them to a GK summary; update time is proportional to the maximum input weight.
uncertainty: The paper concerns weighted quantile summaries, not network diagnosis. Its guarantees concern rank error, not latency-value error or causal attribution; the context reports no Root experiment or measured network-diagnostic gain.

title: Wi-Fi Multi-Link Operation: An Experimental Study of Latency and Throughput
abstract: In this article, we investigate the real-world capability of the multi-link operation (MLO) framework -- one of the key MAC-layer features included in the IEEE 802.11be amendment -- by using a large dataset containing 5 GHz spectrum occupancy measurements on multiple channels. Our results show that when both available links are often busy, as is the case in ultra-dense and crowded scenarios, MLO attains the highest throughput gains over single-link operation (SLO) since it is able to leverage multiple intermittent transmission opportunities. As for latency, if the two links exhibit statistically the same level of occupancy, MLO can outperform SLO by one order of magnitude. In contrast, in asymmetrically occupied links, MLO can sometimes be detrimental and even increase latency. We study this somewhat unexpected phenomenon, and find its origins to be packets suboptimally mapped to either link before carrying out the backoff, with the latter likely to be interrupted on the busier link. We cross validate our study with real-time traffic generated by a cloud gaming application and quantify MLO's benefits for latency-sensitive applications.
technical_mechanism: Decompose packet delay into queueing and link-access (contention/backoff) delay, then test deferred link allocation: run backoff on each interface and assign the head-of-queue packet to the interface whose backoff expires first, rather than assigning it before backoff.
why_it_works: The decomposition distinguishes waiting before interface assignment from delay after assignment. Deferring assignment uses more current link-state information and avoids committing a packet to a busy link just before occupancy pauses its backoff, exposing link contention as a source of tail delay rather than conflating it with queueing. Root could attach transport-path or interface identity and timestamps to requests, separate pre-send queue time from transport time, and test whether selecting among available paths later reduces the network tail.
root_seam: At the robot-side send/interface-selection boundary, retain request identity and timestamps for queue entry, path/interface assignment, backoff or send start, and transmission completion. Compare per-path access delay with queueing delay; where multiple paths exist, test deferred assignment against the current policy. The paper's mechanism is specifically Wi-Fi MAC contention and does not directly establish behavior for other transports.
experiment: Replay identical request arrivals and occupancy traces under immediate versus deferred interface assignment, comparing queueing delay, access delay, and 95th-percentile total delay; the paper also validates its trends with real cloud-gaming traffic.
evidence_quote: MLO-STR+ improves MLO-STR by delaying the link allocation of the packet at the head of the queue until one of the backoff counters expires, thereby leveraging up-to-date information on the link state
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, section on MLO-STR with Deferred Decision and its findings.
reported_gain: Up to 60% reduction in the 95th percentile of access delay and total delay for MLO-STR+ versus MLO-STR.
baseline: MLO-STR (for the reported up-to-60% reduction).
uncertainty: The study concerns Wi-Fi multi-link MAC access, not remote robot inference or general transport paths. Applying deferred path selection and the delay decomposition at Root would require suitable path/interface timestamps and, for the intervention, control over path selection.

title: Understanding the Benefits of Hardware-Accelerated Communication in Model-Serving Applications
abstract: It is commonly assumed that the end-to-end networking performance of edge offloading is purely dictated by that of the network connectivity between end devices and edge computing facilities, where ongoing innovation in 5G/6G networking can help. However, with the growing complexity of edge-offloaded computation and dynamic load balancing requirements, an offloaded task often goes through a multi-stage pipeline that spans across multiple compute nodes and proxies interconnected via a dedicated network fabric within a given edge computing facility. As the latest hardware-accelerated transport technologies such as RDMA and GPUDirect RDMA are adopted to build such network fabric, there is a need for good understanding of the full potential of these technologies in the context of computation offload and the effect of different factors such as GPU scheduling and characteristics of computation on the net performance gain achievable by these technologies. This paper unveils detailed insights into the latency overhead in typical machine learning (ML)-based computation pipelines and analyzes the potential benefits of adopting hardware-accelerated communication. To this end, we build a model-serving framework that supports various communication mechanisms. Using the framework, we identify performance bottlenecks in state-of-the-art model-serving pipelines and show how hardware-accelerated communication can alleviate them. For example, we show that GPUDirect RDMA can save 15--50% of model-serving latency, which amounts to 70--160 ms.
technical_mechanism: Fine-grained pipeline timing combined with controlled transport substitution: measure request/response transport intervals and GPU copy/inference stages separately, then compare TCP, RDMA, and GPUDirect RDMA to identify which stage accounts for latency differences.
why_it_works: Separating transport measurements from CUDA-event timing for GPU stages helps distinguish data-movement delay from copy and inference time. Substituting transports provides a controlled check on whether communication-path overhead is contributing to the observed latency.
root_seam: Attach request-correlated timestamps to robot/client send and receive events, server transport completion events, and GPU copy/inference spans. This could help Root distinguish transport delay from GPU work; the paper’s internal-fabric measurements do not by themselves characterize the robot-to-cloud access network.
experiment: On a fixed remote-inference workload, record per-request transport, copy, and inference spans while varying transport (TCP/RDMA/GDR) and input size or concurrency. Compare stage breakdowns and tail distributions; attribute only the measured spans, and retain a separate server-queue span if available.
evidence_quote: The client-perceived end-to-end model-serving latency is broken into two components: (i) transport latency and (ii) GPU latency.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section III.B, “Performance Metrics.”
reported_gain: 15–50% lower model-serving latency (70–160 ms) with GPUDirect RDMA compared to TCP-based transport.
baseline: TCP-based transport (ZeroMQ).
uncertainty: The context does not report tail percentiles or establish performance on the robot-to-cloud access path. TCP request timing is derived indirectly, and the described breakdown does not explicitly isolate server queueing.

title: Flock: Accurate network fault localization at scale
abstract: Inferring the root cause of failures among thousands of components in a data center network is challenging, especially for "gray" failures that are not reported directly by switches. Faults can be localized through end-to-end measurements, but past localization schemes are either too slow for large-scale networks or sacrifice accuracy. We describe Flock, a network fault localization algorithm and system that achieves both high accuracy and speed at datacenter scale. Flock uses a probabilistic graphical model (PGM) to achieve high accuracy, coupled with new techniques to dramatically accelerate inference in discrete-valued Bayesian PGMs. Large-scale simulations and experiments in a hardware testbed show Flock speeds up inference by >10000x compared to past PGM methods, and improves accuracy over the best previous datacenter fault localization approaches, reducing inference error by 1.19-11x on the same input telemetry, and by 1.2-55x after incorporating passive telemetry. We also prove Flock's inference is optimal in restricted settings
technical_mechanism: Use end-to-end flow measurements and network topology/routes as inputs to a Bayesian graphical model, then use maximum-likelihood inference to identify faulty links or devices. For latency, Flock converts each flow’s RTT into a binary bad/good observation using a threshold; its greedy search selects links that best explain the observations, with joint likelihood exploration updating shared flow contributions efficiently.
why_it_works: Flows traverse overlapping sets of candidate paths, so a link fault can explain correlated bad observations across flows without requiring full packet tracing or direct fault reports from switches. The probabilistic model accounts for uncertainty, including unknown ECMP paths. This offers a Root experiment using request-linked flow latency and candidate routes to test whether injected network faults can be localized. However, the method’s thresholded RTT signal does not by itself distinguish network delay from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application, nor does it specifically identify tail latency.
root_seam: Attach request identity and timestamps to flow-level RTT measurements, and provide topology plus candidate routes for those flows. Run controlled network-fault injections and compare inferred links with ground truth. Root would gain component-level attribution from sparse end-to-end signals; further signals or controls would be needed to separate network delay from server-side stages.
experiment: Replay or collect request-linked flow RTTs and route candidates under controlled link-delay or packet-loss injections, with matched healthy runs. Apply Flock-style thresholding and link inference, then measure localization precision and recall and compare against timing-only alerts. Record server queue, GPU, and action-application timings separately to test whether apparent network diagnoses are actually server-side delays.
evidence_quote: To capture symptoms of high latency, we use a “per-flow” analysis which is in effect a special case of the per-packet model where the number of packets sent is 1, and the number of bad packets is set to 1 if the flow’s RTT is above a threshold and 0 otherwise.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, model conversion bullets under per-flow analysis; the input telemetry and topology description appears earlier in the selected PDF text.
reported_gain: Inference error reduced by 1.19–11x versus the best previous datacenter fault-localization approaches on the same input telemetry; greater reductions are reported after incorporating passive telemetry.
baseline: Best previous datacenter fault-localization approaches, using the same input telemetry.
uncertainty: The context supports network-component fault localization from end-to-end flow measurements, but does not establish that the method diagnoses tail latency specifically or separates network delay from server queueing, GPU compute, and action application. Root-specific performance is unmeasured.

title: Retroactive Parametrized Monitoring
abstract: In online monitoring, we first synthesize a monitor from a formal specification, which later runs in tandem with the system under study, incrementally receiving its progress and evolving with the system. In offline monitoring the trace is logged as the system progresses to later do post-mortem analysis after the system has finished executing. In this paper we propose retroactive dynamic parametrization, a technique that allows a monitor to revisit the past log as it progresses, while still executing in an online manner. This feature allows new monitors to be incorporated into a running system and to revisit the past for particular behaviors based on new information discovered. Retroactive parametrization also allows a monitor to lazily ignore events and revisit and process them later, when it discovers that it should have followed those events. We showcase the use of retroactive dynamic parametrization to monitor denial of service attacks on a network using network logs.
technical_mechanism: Threshold-triggered retroactive monitoring: monitor a cheap summary of incoming events, and when a condition is met, retrieve relevant earlier events from a log and run a finer-grained monitor over them, then continue monitoring live events.
why_it_works: It avoids continuously maintaining expensive detailed state. A later signal can trigger recovery and analysis of the relevant past, providing context that was not retained in the live monitor. For Root, this could support a low-overhead first pass with selective retrieval of request-correlated transport events around a suspected latency tail; it would supply temporal context, not by itself distinguish network delay from server or GPU delay.
root_seam: At the robot/server request-identity and timestamp boundary, retain or index transport-event logs and use a latency or queue threshold to trigger retrieval of the affected request's preceding packet, ACK, loss, or queue events. Compare this selective-retroactive collection against always-on detailed tracing for tail localization and collection overhead.
experiment: The paper evaluates DDoS monitors on network-flow batches. Its retroactive monitor defers entropy calculation until traffic volume crosses a threshold, then retrieves and processes relevant past flows. It compares brute-force, retroactive, and aggregated implementations on known attack/no-attack datasets and reports runtime and memory behavior.
evidence_quote: The monitor only calculates the entropy, using RP, when the volume of traffic for an address surpasses the threshold.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section 5, empirical evaluation, description of implementation S2 (Retroactive).
reported_gain: Qualitatively, the aggregated implementation is described as extremely fast compared with the brute-force and retroactive implementations; retroactive memory use remains close to constant, with a rise when past flows are retrieved and processed. No numeric gain is available in the supplied context.
baseline: Brute-force dynamic parametrization (S1) and retroactive implementation (S2); the aggregated implementation (S3) is also compared in the multi-batch experiment.
uncertainty: The study detects DDoS from sampled, batched flow records, not inference latency tails. It does not establish request-level packet/ACK timing or distinguish network delay from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application. Transfer to Root is a proposed use of the selective retroactive retrieval mechanism, not a demonstrated result.

title: Data-Driven Latency Probability Prediction for Wireless Networks: Focusing on Tail Probabilities
abstract: With the emergence of new application areas, such as cyber-physical systems and human-in-the-loop applications, there is a need to guarantee a certain level of end-to-end network latency with extremely high reliability, e.g., 99.999%. While mechanisms specified under IEEE 802.1as time-sensitive networking (TSN) can be used to achieve these requirements for switched Ethernet networks, implementing TSN mechanisms in wireless networks is challenging due to their stochastic nature. To conform the wireless link to a reliability level of 99.999%, the behavior of extremely rare outliers in the latency probability distribution, or the tail of the distribution, must be analyzed and controlled. This work proposes predicting the tail of the latency distribution using state-of-the-art data-driven approaches, such as mixture density networks (MDN) and extreme value mixture models, to estimate the likelihood of rare latencies conditioned on the network parameters, which can be used to make more informed decisions in wireless transmission. Actual latency measurements of IEEE 802.11g (WiFi), commercial private and a software-defined 5G network are used to benchmark the proposed approaches and evaluate their sensitivities concerning the tail probabilities.
technical_mechanism: Fit a conditional latency-density model from measured packet delays and network conditions; use an extreme-value mixture model that combines a Gaussian-mixture bulk with a generalized Pareto tail, with neural-network-predicted parameters, to estimate rare-delay probabilities.
why_it_works: Modeling the tail explicitly avoids relying on a Gaussian mixture whose tail can diverge from empirical rare-delay behavior. Conditioning on transmission state, such as MCS, relates tail risk to wireless conditions. Applied in Root, timestamped transport measurements plus available network-state signals could estimate whether a request's network delay is unusually likely under comparable conditions.
root_seam: Attach to timestamped robot-to-server and server-to-robot transport events, joined by request identity, and condition the predictor on available link-state signals. Compare predicted network-delay tails against measured link delay separately from server queueing, GPU computation, and action application. The paper does not identify off-path flows or shared-resource causes, so it does not support n02.
experiment: On a robot-cloud loop, collect timestamped request/response packet delays and available wireless conditions across repeated runs. Train and evaluate the tail predictor against held-out measurements and a Gaussian-mixture baseline; compare calibration and detection of rare network-delay events, while separately measuring server and action-application time.
evidence_quote: In this extreme value MDN scheme, tail parameters of the distribution (threshold, tail index, and scale) are being estimated by the neural network in addition to the bulk distribution parameters.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section III, Approach.
reported_gain: The paper reports that the GMEVM predictor closely follows the empirical tail where the GMM predictor diverges; it also reports that 1 ms Gaussian-noise regularization improves GMEVM performance for non-smooth conditional tails. No numerical gain is available in the supplied text.
baseline: Gaussian-mixture model (GMM) / mixture density network without the generalized Pareto tail component.
uncertainty: The method predicts conditional wireless-link latency distributions; the supplied text does not establish attribution to off-path flows or shared resources, or validate the predictor on robot-cloud action loops. It also does not fully establish separation of network delay from other end-to-end latency components.

title: EdgeP4: A P4-Programmable Edge Intelligent Ethernet Switch for Tactile Cyber-Physical Systems
abstract: Tactile Internet based operations, e.g., telesurgery, rely on end-to-end closed loop control for accuracy and corrections. The feedback and control are subject to network latency and loss. We design two edge intelligence algorithms hosted at P4 programmable end switches. These algorithms locally compute and command corrective signals, thereby dispense the feedback signals from traversing the network to the other ends and save on control loop latency and network load. We implement these algorithms entirely on data plane on Netronome Agilio SmartNICs using P4. Our first algorithm, pose correction, is placed at the edge switch connected to an industrial robot gripping a tool. The round trip between transmitting force sensor array readings to the edge switch and receiving correct tip coordinates at the robot is shown to be less than 100 μ s. The second algorithm, tremor suppression, is placed at the edge switch connected to the human operator. It suppresses physiological tremors of amplitudes smaller than 100 μ m which not only improves the application's performance but also reduces the network load up to 99.9%. Our solution allows edge intelligence modules to seamlessly switch between the algorithms based on the tasks being executed at the end hosts.
technical_mechanism: Per-packet switch-residence measurement: add ingress and egress timestamps to a telemetry header, then subtract them to measure time inside the switch. The packet also carries a sequence ID, supporting correlation with the corresponding request or response.
why_it_works: This goes beyond bypassing the network for pose correction: it supplies a concrete timing signal that can isolate delay within an instrumented switch from delay elsewhere in the action loop. Correlated with robot- and server-side timestamps, it could expose whether a tail coincides with switch residence or lies outside that measured segment. It does not, by itself, measure every network link or distinguish link delay from server queueing.
root_seam: Instrument a robot-adjacent programmable switch or SmartNIC to attach per-packet ingress/egress times and port metadata, retaining the sequence/request identity. Correlate those records with Root's robot-side send/receive and server-side queue and inference timestamps; no access to Reflex's private infrastructure is assumed.
experiment: Replay matched action-loop traffic while independently injecting switch contention and server queueing. Collect endpoint timestamps, packet identities, and switch ingress/egress timestamps; compare tail requests across conditions. Test whether switch-residence measurements rise under switch contention but remain stable under server-only queueing, and whether endpoint delay not explained by switch residence remains separately attributable. Treat any result as a Root experiment, not a reported paper gain.
evidence_quote: We include the ingress and egress timestamps of packets into the telemetry header. The difference between the two is used to measure the time a packet spends inside the switch.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, section 4.1.1, Experimental Results and Discussion; packet fields and sequence ID described in the implementation text preceding section 4.
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The paper measures switch residence, not end-to-end network delay or tail distributions, and does not demonstrate localization of delay outside that switch. Root would need endpoint and server-stage timestamps to distinguish unmeasured network delay from server queueing, compute, or action application.

title: AdapINT: A Flexible and Adaptive In-Band Network Telemetry System Based on Deep Reinforcement Learning
abstract: In-band Network Telemetry (INT) has emerged as a promising network measurement technology. However, existing network telemetry systems lack the flexibility to meet diverse telemetry requirements and are also difficult to adapt to dynamic network environments. In this paper, we propose AdapINT, a versatile and adaptive in-band network telemetry framework assisted by dual-timescale probes, including long-period auxiliary probes (APs) and short-period dynamic probes (DPs). Technically, the APs collect basic network status information, which is used for the path planning of DPs. To achieve full network coverage, we propose an auxiliary probes path deployment (APPD) algorithm based on the Depth-First-Search (DFS). The DPs collect specific network information for telemetry tasks. To ensure that the DPs can meet diverse telemetry requirements and adapt to dynamic network environments, we apply the deep reinforcement learning (DRL) technique and transfer learning method to design the dynamic probes path deployment (DPPD) algorithm. The evaluation results show that AdapINT can redesign the telemetry system according to telemetry requirements and network environments. AdapINT can reduce telemetry latency by 75% in online games and video conferencing scenarios. For overhead-aware networks, AdapINT can reduce control overheads by 34% in cloud computing services.
technical_mechanism: Use low-frequency auxiliary probes on non-overlapping paths to collect link latency and network status; use missing probes to narrow a fault to links on their paths. Use the resulting status to plan higher-frequency, task-specific probes.
why_it_works: Link-level measurements provide a concrete network-delay signal, while non-overlapping probe paths make a missing probe informative about which links may have failed. This could help Root distinguish network delay or failure from server-side and inference delays.
root_seam: Attach probe measurements to the robot request’s time window and path, and compare per-link latency or probe loss with the request’s end-to-end latency. This supplies network-path evidence without requiring full application tracing.
experiment: In a controlled Root test, inject delay or loss on one network link while holding server queueing and inference compute constant. Compare localization using end-to-end latency alone against latency plus per-link auxiliary-probe results; measure localization accuracy and telemetry overhead.
evidence_quote: After obtaining the link latency, users can quickly know the location of the network fault by determining whether the latency is abnormal or not.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Telemetry Results Analysis section.
reported_gain: 75% reduction in telemetry latency in online games and video conferencing scenarios.
baseline: Traditional network telemetry systems.
uncertainty: The reported evaluations are simulations, and the context does not establish performance on robot inference workloads or quantify Root-specific localization accuracy.

title: Compact Data Structures for Network Telemetry
abstract: Collecting and analyzing of network traffic data (network telemetry) plays a critical role in managing modern networks. Network administrators analyze their traffic to troubleshoot performance and reliability problems, and to detect and block cyberattacks. However, conventional traffic-measurement techniques offer limited visibility into network conditions and rely on offline analysis. Fortunately, network devices -- such as switches and network interface cards -- are increasingly programmable at the packet level, enabling flexible analysis of the traffic in place, as the packets fly by. However, to operate at high speed, these devices have limited memory and computational resources, leading to trade-offs between accuracy and overhead. In response, an exciting research area emerged, bringing ideas from compact data structures and streaming algorithms to bear on important networking telemetry applications and the unique characteristics of high-speed network devices. In this paper, we review the research on compact data structures for network telemetry and discuss promising directions for future research.
technical_mechanism: Accumulate per-hop queue residence time in packet-carried path telemetry, then aggregate delayed packets or flows with an in-network heavy-hitter structure. Queue residence is measured as the time a packet exits the queue minus the time it entered.
why_it_works: The per-hop queue signal directly measures network queueing rather than inferring it from end-to-end latency, which can also include server queueing, GPU compute, or action application. Accumulating it across a packet's path exposes total network queue delay; heavy-hitter aggregation can identify flows or paths experiencing unusually high delay without retaining a full packet trace. This is a concrete diagnostic operation, though the paper is a survey rather than an evaluation of one implementation.
root_seam: Where programmable switches or SmartNICs are available, associate packet or flow identity with robot-side and server-side request timestamps, collect queue-entry and queue-exit timestamps per hop, and accumulate queue delay along the path. Compare that network component with server queue, GPU, and action-application timings. An in-network heavy-hitter summary could retain delayed flows while avoiding full packet-level trace export.
experiment: Replay identical inference-request traffic while independently inducing network queueing, server queueing, GPU delay, and action-application delay. Compare end-to-end timestamps alone against per-hop queue-delay accumulation and delayed-flow aggregation. Measure attribution and localization accuracy, false network attribution under non-network delays, and telemetry overhead against packet-level tracing.
evidence_quote: For example, as a packet goes through a switch, it can detect the delay it experienced in the queue by computing the difference between the time it entered the queue and the time it left the queue. As the packet traverses the network, it can aggregate the queuing delay it experienced across the entire path.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section 7.1, “Network-wide Measurements”
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The survey describes a transferable queue-delay accumulation operation and a possible heavy-hitter use, but does not evaluate a complete method or establish its accuracy, implementation requirements, or Root-specific benefit. The compact-sketch discussion does not provide enough evidence here to promote n09, and no fewer-measurements comparison is established for n10.

title: Causality Diagrams using Hybrid Vector Clocks
abstract: Causality in distributed systems is a concept that has long been explored and numerous approaches have been made to use causality as a way to trace distributed system execution. Traditional approaches usually used system profiling and newer approaches profiled clocks of systems to detect failures and construct timelines that caused those failures. Since the advent of logical clocks, these profiles have become more and more accurate with ways to characterize concurrency and distributions, with accurate diagrams for message passing. Vector clocks addressed the shortcomings of using traditional logical clocks, by storing information about other processes in the system as well. Hybrid vector clocks are a novel approach to this concept where clocks need not store all the process information. Rather, we store information of processes within an acceptable skew of the focused process. This gives us an efficient way of profiling with substantially reduced costs to the system. Building on this idea, we propose the idea of building causal traces using information generated from the hybrid vector clock. The hybrid vector clock would provide us with a strong sense of concurrency and distribution, and we theorize that all the information generated from the clock is sufficient to develop a causal trace for debugging. We post-process and parse the clocks generated from an execution trace to develop a swimlane on a web interface, that traces the points of failure of a distributed system. We also provide an API to reuse this concept for any generic distributed system framework.
technical_mechanism: Hybrid-vector-clock causal ordering of logged message events, combined with explicit failure flags and missed-poll detection, to isolate a failed message or process in physical-time swimlanes.
