why_it_works: Each process updates its clock on local/send events and merges the incoming clock on receive, preserving partial causal order while tracking physical-time epochs and bounded clock offsets. The parser orders send and receive times and the interface can isolate a subset of messages, including failures. This provides a concrete cross-layer diagnostic operation with less clock state than a full vector clock. With matched robot/server transport events, delayed intervals could be placed in causal context; explicit send/receive timestamps would still be needed to distinguish network delay from server queueing or computation.
root_seam: Attach HVC metadata and explicit timestamps to matched robot send, server receive, server completion, and robot receive events; record transport failure/loss indicators and process polls. The resulting causal swimlane could expose which event boundary contains a tail and which downstream events depend on it, without requiring full vector-clock state. The paper does not establish that HVC alone measures network delay.
experiment: In a controlled Root run, emit matched HVC-tagged boundary events and explicit timestamps. Inject transport delay or loss independently from server queueing and compute delay. Check whether the causal swimlane isolates the affected message/process and whether the explicit boundary times distinguish the injected network interval from server-side intervals; compare clock metadata overhead with full vector clocks.
evidence_quote: The API was capable of isolating a particular message and zooming in on a visualization of a snapshot that isolated a subset of messages from a trace.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, IV.C, “Designing the Web interface,” item 1
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The paper demonstrates failure-oriented trace isolation and describes HVC ordering, but does not evaluate network tail-latency localization, transport delay separation, or a Root system. The proposed Root experiment must supply explicit send/receive and processing boundary timestamps.

title: Characterizing TCP's Performance for Low-Priority Flows Inside a Cloud
abstract: Many cloud systems utilize low-priority flows to achieve various performance objectives (e.g., low latency, high utilization), relying on TCP as their preferred transport protocol. However, the suitability of TCP for such low-priority flows is relatively unexplored. Specifically, how prioritization-induced delays in packet transmission can cause spurious timeouts and low utilization. In this paper, we conduct an empirical study to investigate the performance of TCP for low-priority flows under a wide range of realistic scenarios: use-cases (with accompanying workloads) where the performance of low-priority flows is crucial to the functioning of the overall system as well as various network loads and other network parameters. Our findings yield two key insights: 1) for several popular use-cases (e.g., network scheduling), TCP's performance for low-priority flows is within 2x of a near-optimal scheme, 2) for emerging workloads that exhibit an on-off behavior in the high priority queue (e.g., distributed ML model training), TCP's performance for low-priority flows is poor. Finally, we discuss and conduct preliminary evaluation to show that two simple strategies -- weighted fair queuing (WFQ) and cross-queue congestion notification -- can substantially improve TCP's performance for low-priority flows.
technical_mechanism: Cross-Queue Congestion Notification uses low-overhead, high-priority probe packets to create a secondary feedback loop. Switches ECN-mark probes when the high-priority queue exceeds a threshold; the sender uses those marks to identify priority-induced congestion and pause low-priority TCP transmissions.
why_it_works: Ordinary low-priority TCP feedback can stall behind high-priority traffic, obscuring why packets are delayed. The non-blocking probe loop reports high-priority queue congestion independently, helping separate priority-induced network delay from other causes and avoiding excess low-priority queue buildup, packet loss, and spurious backoffs.
root_seam: Attach probe/ECN feedback to request or flow identity and correlate it with robot-side send/receive timestamps. A mark indicates high-priority queue congestion during the request; its absence would not rule out low-priority queueing, server queueing, GPU compute, or action-application delay. This could give Root a cross-queue network signal without assuming access to Reflex's private infrastructure.
experiment: In the workload-co-location experiment with 12MB gradient updates, compare TCP+ (cross-queue notification) against TCP and measure low-priority flow completion times, including p99. A Root experiment could similarly correlate request-level probe marks with end-to-end tail latency and other pipeline timestamps.
evidence_quote: probe packets get marked if the length of the high priority queue exceeds a certain threshold
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Cross-Queue Congestion Notification (CQCN) section.
reported_gain: Up to 6× decrease in FCTs for medium flows at p99 in the preliminary evaluation.
baseline: TCP without cross-queue congestion notification.
uncertainty: This is a cloud transport study, not a robot-inference evaluation. The paper notes that probe thresholds require tuning and probing can interfere with high-priority traffic; no Root gain is reported.

title: COREC: Concurrent Non-Blocking Single-Queue Receive Driver for Low Latency Networking
abstract: Existing network stacks tackle performance and scalability aspects by relying on multiple receive queues. However, at software level, each queue is processed by a single thread, which prevents simultaneous work on the same queue and limits performance in terms of tail latency. To overcome this limitation, we introduce COREC, the first software implementation of a concurrent non-blocking single-queue receive driver. By sharing a single queue among multiple threads, workload distribution is improved, leading to a work-conserving policy for network stacks. On the technical side, instead of relying on traditional critical sections - which would sequentialize the operations by threads - COREC coordinates the threads that concurrently access the same receive queue in non-blocking manner via atomic machine instructions from the Read-Modify-Write (RMW) class. These instructions allow threads to access and update memory locations atomically, based on specific conditions, such as the matching of a target value selected by the thread. Also, they enable making any update globally visible in the memory hierarchy, bypassing interference on memory consistency caused by the CPU store buffers. Extensive evaluation results demonstrate that the possible additional reordering, which our approach may occasionally cause, is non-critical and has minimal impact on performance, even in the worst-case scenario of a single large TCP flow, with performance impairments accounting to at most 2-3 percent. Conversely, substantial latency gains are achieved when handling UDP traffic, real-world traffic mix, and multiple shorter TCP flows.
technical_mechanism: Share one NIC receive queue among multiple worker threads; use atomic read-modify-write coordination to claim and process descriptor batches without locking, making packet processing work-conserving.
why_it_works: A single-thread-per-queue receive path can serialize packet processing and leave work waiting even when other cores are available. Concurrent workers can drain that queue in parallel, potentially reducing receiver-side queueing and tail latency. This is an intervention on receive processing, not a mechanism that directly reconstructs or attributes a particular request's network delay.
root_seam: At the server-side NIC receive path, compare a shared-queue concurrent receiver with the ordinary per-queue single-thread configuration while recording request-correlated receive and inference timestamps. A tail reduction would support receive-queue service contention as a contributor; packet arrival and processing timestamps would still be needed to separate network transit from receiver queueing, server scheduling, GPU compute, and action application.
experiment: Replay the same remote-inference request traffic under the standard receiver and a COREC-like shared-queue receiver. Capture packet arrival, dequeue, and request completion timestamps, and compare tail latency and queue-wait intervals under matched offered load.
evidence_quote: By sharing a single queue among multiple threads, workload distribution is improved, leading to a work-conserving policy for network stacks.
evidence_location: Abstract; also selected PDF text, Section 3 contribution summary.
reported_gain: The abstract reports substantial latency gains for UDP traffic, real-world traffic mixes, and multiple shorter TCP flows; no exact latency improvement is provided in the supplied context. It also reports at most 2–3% performance impairment for a single large TCP flow.
baseline: Standard DPDK scale-out policy (v21.11), with each receive queue managed by an individual thread.
uncertainty: The paper measures driver and forwarding latency, not remote-robot inference requests or request-to-packet causality. The supplied text does not establish that a Root tail is caused by receive-queue buildup. Thus n01 and n02 lack the requested reconstruction or off-path/shared-resource identification operation; n06 remains unresolved because the method mitigates a possible per-queue processing bottleneck but does not distinguish queue buildup from other tail causes.

title: Experimental Evaluation of Interactive Edge/Cloud Virtual Reality Gaming over Wi-Fi using Unity Render Streaming
abstract: Virtual Reality (VR) streaming enables end-users to seamlessly immerse themselves in interactive virtual environments using even low-end devices. However, the quality of the VR experience heavily relies on Wireless Fidelity (Wi-Fi) performance, since it serves as the last hop in the network chain. Our study delves into the intricate interplay between Wi-Fi and VR traffic, drawing upon empirical data and leveraging a Wi-Fi simulator. In this work, we further evaluate Wi-Fi's suitability for VR streaming in terms of the Quality of Service (QoS) it provides. In particular, we employ Unity Render Streaming to remotely stream real-time VR gaming content over Wi-Fi 6 using Web Real-Time Communication (WebRTC), considering a server physically located at the network's edge, near the end user. Our findings demonstrate the system's sustained network performance, showcasing minimal round-trip time (RTT) and jitter at 60 and 90 frames per second (fps). In addition, we uncover the characteristics and patterns of the generated traffic streams, unveiling a distinctive video transmission approach inherent to WebRTC-based services: the systematic packetization of video frames (VFs) and their transmission in discrete batches at regular intervals, regardless of the targeted frame rate. This interval-based transmission strategy maintains consistent video packet delays across video frame rates but leads to increased Wi-Fi airtime consumption. Our results demonstrate that shortening the interval between batches is advantageous, as it enhances Wi-Fi efficiency and reduces delays in delivering complete frames.
technical_mechanism: Analyze endpoint packet traces to identify video-frame packets released in regularly spaced batches; compare packet delay with complete-frame assembly delay, then vary the inter-batch interval in a Wi-Fi simulator to measure its effects on delay and airtime.
why_it_works: The packet-batch pattern exposes sender pacing as a source of delay distinct from Wi-Fi packet queuing: packet delays can remain similar while waiting between batches increases complete-frame delivery time. Endpoint traces and simulator interventions help separate these effects.
root_seam: Attach timestamps and request/frame identity to robot-side and server-side transport events, group packets by frame and batch, and compare packet-level network delay with frame completion time. A controlled pacing-interval change could test whether a regression comes from sender batching rather than network queueing, server compute, or action application.
experiment: On a controlled remote-inference workload, capture endpoint packet timestamps and frame/request identities, then vary the inter-batch interval while holding network conditions and compute constant. Compare packet-delay and frame-completion distributions, including tail percentiles; separately vary network load to identify queueing effects.
evidence_quote: longer inter-batch times lead to prolonged VF delays. In particular, the average delays are 3.10, 3.52, 4.45, 6.40, and 8.18 ms for inter-batch times of 0.01, 1, 2, 4, and 5.56 ms, respectively.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section 8.2.2, “Using distinct inter-batch times”
reported_gain: At 60 fps in simulation, average video-frame delay was 3.10 ms with a 0.01 ms inter-batch interval versus 8.18 ms with a 5.56 ms interval.
baseline: 5.56 ms inter-batch interval
uncertainty: This is controlled VR traffic characterization and simulation, not an online tail-latency detector. The context does not establish how reliably the method localizes tails in remote robot inference or under variable network conditions.

title: Approaching 100% Confidence in Stream Summary through ReliableSketch
abstract: To approximate sums of values in key-value data streams, sketches are widely used in databases and networking systems. They offer high-confidence approximations for any given key while ensuring low time and space overhead. While existing sketches are proficient in estimating individual keys, they struggle to maintain this high confidence across all keys collectively, an objective that is critically important in both algorithm theory and its practical applications. We propose ReliableSketch, the first to control the error of all keys to less than Λ with a small failure probability Δ, requiring only O(1 + Δ(NΛ)) amortized time and O(NΛ + (1Δ)) space. Furthermore, its simplicity makes it hardware-friendly, and we implement it on CPU servers, FPGAs, and programmable switches. Our experiments show that under the same small space, ReliableSketch not only keeps all keys' errors below Λ but also achieves near-optimal throughput, outperforming competitors with thousands of uncontrolled estimations. We have made our source code publicly available.
technical_mechanism: Use ReliableSketch as a bounded-error, all-keys stream summary: Error-Sensible buckets sense per-key estimation error during updates, and Double Exponential Control suppresses keys with larger errors across layers.
why_it_works: Unlike ordinary counter sketches that mix colliding keys without observing each key’s error, this method aims to keep every queried key’s sum error below a configured bound with high overall confidence. Root could encode network-tail evidence as keyed indicator counts—for example, threshold exceedances by transport event type or request class—and retain estimates for many keys under a memory budget. Keys whose estimated counts are sufficiently beyond the error bound remain distinguishable from noise. The paper does not establish that this preserves latency quantiles or causal attribution, so promotion is for the sketch’s transferable all-key summary operation, not a claim that it diagnoses tails by itself.
root_seam: At Root’s sparse retained-trace or telemetry aggregation stage, feed keyed indicators derived from timestamped transport and server events into the sketch. Keying by event layer and request class could preserve compact, bounded-error summaries of tail-threshold exceedances without retaining every record. The sketch does not itself separate network delay from queueing, GPU compute, or action application; Root must provide those distinctions in the keys or measurements.
experiment: Replay the same timestamped Root request and transport-event traces through ReliableSketch and a full-recording reference under matched memory budgets. Encode threshold exceedances as keyed indicators, varying keys across event layer and request class. Compare per-key exceedance-count errors and whether injected network-tail regressions remain detectable, while separately checking attribution against full records. Include collision-heavy traces and thresholds near the configured error bound.
evidence_quote: Our main strategy is to sense errors in all keys in real-time, controlling those with larger errors to prevent any from becoming outliers.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Introduction, compatibility discussion and description of the two key techniques
reported_gain: The paper reports keeping all keys’ errors below Λ with high overall confidence and near-optimal throughput under the same small space; quantitative gain: UNKNOWN.
baseline: Counter-based and heap-based sketches; specific comparison configuration: UNKNOWN.
uncertainty: The paper summarizes keyed sums, not latency quantiles or causal network delays. Whether threshold-indicator summaries preserve Root’s diagnostic power—especially for rare events and counts near the error bound—requires the proposed controlled replay experiment.

title: Early Detection of Network Service Degradation: An Intra-Flow Approach
abstract: This research presents a novel method for predicting service degradation (SD) in computer networks by leveraging early flow features. Our approach focuses on the observable (O) segments of network flows, particularly analyzing Packet Inter-Arrival Time (PIAT) values and other derived metrics, to infer the behavior of non-observable (NO) segments. Through a comprehensive evaluation, we identify an optimal O/NO split threshold of 10 observed delay samples, balancing prediction accuracy and resource utilization. Evaluating models including Logistic Regression, XGBoost, and Multi-Layer Perceptron, we find XGBoost outperforms others, achieving an F1-score of 0.74, balanced accuracy of 0.84, and AUROC of 0.97. Our findings highlight the effectiveness of incorporating comprehensive early flow features and the potential of our method to offer a practical solution for monitoring network traffic in resource-constrained environments. This approach ensures enhanced user experience and network performance by preemptively addressing potential SD, providing the basis for a robust framework for maintaining high-quality network services.
technical_mechanism: Use the first 10 observed LAN-delay samples from a flow to compute early-flow features—including delay and jitter statistics, individual values, and SD-event attributes—and classify whether service degradation will occur in the unobserved remainder.
why_it_works: Early packet inter-arrival patterns can signal later degradation, allowing prediction from a flow segment that remains visible before hardware offload rather than requiring continuous packet-level observation. In Root, similar early transport signals or retained summaries could flag a request for a network tail before its full execution completes.
root_seam: Attach flow or request identity to robot/server transport timestamps and early packet inter-arrival measurements. Use the early-flow prediction to distinguish likely network degradation from server queueing, GPU compute, or action-application delay; the paper itself does not establish that its LAN-delay classifier separates those Root causes.
experiment: On replayed or controlled remote-inference requests, compute the proposed early-flow features from the first 10 observed LAN-delay samples and predict a later network-tail event. Compare against full-flow diagnosis and simple thresholds, measure detection lead time, false alarms, and retained telemetry cost, and separately record server queue, GPU, and action-application timings. For the profiling-trigger lane, test whether predictions selectively trigger detailed profiling and quantify missed tails and profiling overhead.
evidence_quote: uses early flow features from the O part to predict SD events in the NO part
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section II.F, “Intra-Flow Service Degradation Detection”
reported_gain: At an O/NO split threshold of 10 observed delays, XGBoost achieved F1-score 0.74, balanced accuracy 0.84, and AUROC 0.97.
baseline: Compared Logistic Regression, XGBoost, and MLP with null, all-true, random, and heuristic predictors; the reported results state that trained models outperformed the simple baseline predictors.
uncertainty: The evaluation uses TCP flows from one university dormitory network, and the authors note that validation across diverse environments is future work. It predicts service degradation in the unobserved flow remainder, not specifically remote-robot inference tail latency. The paper does not evaluate using predictions to trigger expensive profiling.

title: Strategies for Tracking Individual IP Packets Towards DDoS
abstract: The identification of the exact path that packets are routed in the network is quite a challenge. This paper presents a novel, efficient traceback strategy in combination with a defence system against distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks named Tracemax. A single packets can be directly traced over many more hops than the current existing techniques allow. It let good connections pass while bad ones get thwarted. Initiated by the victim the routers in the network cooperate in tracing and become automatically self-organised and self-managed. The novel concept support analyses of packet flows and transmission paths in a network infrastructure. It can effectively reduce the effect of common bandwidth and resource consumption attacks and foster in addition early warning and prevention.
technical_mechanism: Selective per-packet path stamping and reconstruction: participating routers append compact IDs for their outgoing physical ports to a packet; the receiver matches the ordered IDs against configured topology to recover that packet’s route.
why_it_works: Unlike aggregate route logs, the stamp records the route actually taken by an individual packet, so packets from the same request can be compared even when routing varies or packets are reordered. Correlating selected inference packets with request identity and endpoint timestamps could expose a route change associated with a tail request. The labels identify path, not per-hop delay, so they cannot alone identify a slow link or separate network delay from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application.
root_seam: At a controlled Root testbed, associate selected robot/server transport packets with request IDs and endpoint timestamps, and enable port-ID marking only on cooperating test routers. Reconstruct each marked packet’s path from the known topology. This adds packet-specific route evidence; it does not require assuming access to Reflex infrastructure.
experiment: Send matched inference requests over a controlled topology with known stable and rerouted paths. Mark selected packets, correlate their reconstructed paths with request IDs and endpoint timing, and test whether tail requests coincide with route changes or particular paths. Validate reconstructed paths against known routes, measure marking overhead, and use transport timestamps to distinguish network time from server processing and action application.
evidence_quote: Every router writes the assigned and predefined ID of the physical port into the packets Option Field at the outgoing interface.
evidence_location: Section 5.1, “Marking scheme”; reconstruction from the ordered IDs is described in Sections 5.2–5.3.
reported_gain: The paper reports tracing more than 50 hops for a single packet; no Root-measured gain is reported.
baseline: Table 1 compares Tracemax with existing traceback strategies, including a listed 9-hop limit for RS-DRS. No controlled Root baseline is reported.
uncertainty: The paper demonstrates path labeling and reconstruction, not request-level correlation or latency measurement. Its prototype uses virtual machines and manual reconstruction; routers must cooperate and be configured. The experiment must establish request-to-packet association and whether path evidence helps explain Root tail requests.

title: Programmable Cycle-Specified Queue for Long-Distance Industrial Deterministic Packet Scheduling
abstract: The time-critical industrial applications pose intense demands for enabling long-distance deterministic networks. However, previous priority-based and weight-based scheduling methods focus on probabilistically reducing average delay, which ignores strictly guaranteeing task-oriented on-time packet delivery with bounded worst-case delay and jitter. This paper proposes a new Programmable Cycle-Specified Queue (PCSQ) for long-distance industrial deterministic packet scheduling. By implementing the first high-precision rotation dequeuing, PCSQ enables microsecond-level time slot resource reservation (noted as T) and especially jitter control of up to 2T. Then, we propose the cycle tags computation to approximate cyclic scheduling algorithms, which allows packets to actively pick and lock their favorite queue in a sequence of nodes. Accordingly, PCSQ can precisely defer packets to any desired time. Further, the queue coordination and cycle mapping mechanisms are delicately designed to solve the cycle-queue mismatch problem. Evaluation results show that PCSQ can schedule tens of thousands of time-sensitive flows and strictly guarantee ms-level delay and us-level jitter.
technical_mechanism: Programmable cycle-specified queueing: map packets to cycle-indexed queues using packet cycle tags, then rotate and drain each queue in scheduled time slots; queue coordination handles slot-boundary mismatch and permits at most a one-queue shift when the mapped queue is full.
why_it_works: Cycle-based pacing smooths bursts and discretizes queue waiting time, while draining the current queue within its slot bounds queue buildup and limits scheduling jitter. This is a traffic-control mechanism rather than a direct tail-cause classifier, so its queue bounds could support a controlled test of whether a tail responds to queue scheduling.
root_seam: At the robot-side egress or network-switch egress, correlate request timestamps with per-port queue occupancy, cycle/queue assignment, and dequeue time. A controlled PCSQ-versus-existing-scheduler comparison could test whether tail delay changes with queue buildup; separate transport and endpoint timestamps would still be needed to distinguish network delay from server queueing, compute, or action application.
experiment: Replay the same remote-control request traffic and background load under the existing scheduler and PCSQ. Record per-request send/arrival times, per-hop queue occupancy and queue/cycle assignment, and tail latency and jitter. Check whether high-delay requests coincide with queue buildup and whether bounded cycle queues reduce those tails without changing server-side processing.
evidence_quote: The cyclic scheduling can strictly bound the queuing delay by smoothing the bursts and discretizing the queue waiting time.
evidence_location: selected_pdf_text, discussion of cyclic scheduling and bounded queuing delay; PCSQ enqueue/dequeue and rotation descriptions.
reported_gain: Up to 98.6% jitter reduction compared with strict-priority scheduling.
baseline: Strict-priority (SP) scheduling for the reported jitter comparison.
uncertainty: The paper evaluates a scheduling intervention, not a diagnostic classifier for queue buildup versus other tail causes. Its reported gains are not Root results, and the supplied text does not provide a direct event-sequence method for separating jitter, retransmission, and endpoint stalls.

title: FogROS2-PLR: Probabilistic Latency-Reliability For Cloud Robotics
abstract: Cloud robotics enables robots to offload computationally intensive tasks to cloud servers for performance, cost, and ease of management. However, the network and cloud computing infrastructure are not designed for reliable timing guarantees, due to fluctuating Quality-of-Service (QoS). In this work, we formulate an impossibility triangle theorem for: Latency reliability, Singleton server, and Commodity hardware. The LSC theorem suggests that providing replicated servers with uncorrelated failures can exponentially reduce the probability of missing a deadline. We present FogROS2-Probabilistic Latency Reliability (PLR) that uses multiple independent network interfaces to send requests to replicated cloud servers and uses the first response back. We design routing mechanisms to discover, connect, and route through non-default network interfaces on robots. FogROS2-PLR optimizes the selection of interfaces to servers to minimize the probability of missing a deadline. We conduct a cloud-connected driving experiment with two 5G service providers, demonstrating FogROS2-PLR effectively provides smooth service quality even if one of the service providers experiences low coverage and base station handover. We use 99 Percentile (P99) latency to evaluate anomalous long-tail latency behavior. In one experiment, FogROS2-PLR improves P99 latency by up to 3.7x compared to using one service provider. We deploy FogROS2-PLR on a physical Stretch 3 robot performing an indoor human-tracking task. Even in a fully covered Wi-Fi and 5G environment, FogROS2-PLR improves the responsiveness of the robot reducing mean latency by 36% and P99 latency by 33%.
technical_mechanism: Replicate each robot request across independently connected network interfaces and cloud servers, then return the first response and discard later duplicates. A deadline-aware matcher assigns interfaces to servers to minimize deadline-miss probability.
why_it_works: Independent paths and replicas can experience uncorrelated delays or failures; racing responses lets a timely path avoid waiting for a slow one. The paper evaluates tail latency, including during cellular coverage and handover changes, and also deploys the method on a physical robot.
root_seam: At the robot-side request proxy, attach a request ID and timestamps to each interface-specific send and response. Root could compare per-path completion times and identify whether a slow request was rescued by another path. This is a mitigation and comparative signal, not a method for distinguishing network delay from server queueing or compute time.
experiment: On a remote robot-inference loop, compare a single path with replicated requests over two independent interfaces and first-response selection. Inject controlled delay, loss, or handover on one interface while holding the inference service constant; record per-path request/response timing, end-to-end P99, and deadline misses.
evidence_quote: FogROS2-PLR replicates requests over multiple independent network interfaces to cloud servers at different regions and routes the first response back to the robot.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section IV, FogROS2-PLR System Design.
reported_gain: P99 latency improved by up to 3.7x in the driving experiment; on the physical Stretch 3 robot, P99 improved by 33%.
baseline: Single service provider in the driving experiment; single-network option for the Stretch 3 comparison.
uncertainty: The reported gains are for the paper's cloud robotics workloads, not Root. The mechanism masks tails rather than diagnosing their cause, and the supplied text does not establish per-path measurements that separate network delay from server queueing or compute.

title: SwiftQueue: Optimizing Low-Latency Applications with Swift Packet Queuing
abstract: Low Latency, Low Loss, and Scalable Throughput (L4S), as an emerging router-queue management technique, has seen steady deployment in the industry. An L4S-enabled router assigns each packet to the queue based on the packet header marking. Currently, L4S employs per-flow queue selection, i.e. all packets of a flow are marked the same way and thus use the same queues, even though each packet is marked separately. However, this may hurt tail latency and latency-sensitive applications because transient congestion and queue buildups may only affect a fraction of packets in a flow. We present SwiftQueue, a new L4S queue-selection strategy in which a sender uses a novel per-packet latency predictor to pinpoint which packets likely have latency spikes or drops. The insight is that many packet-level latency variations result from complex interactions among recent packets at shared router queues. Yet, these intricate packet-level latency patterns are hard to learn efficiently by traditional models. Instead, SwiftQueue uses a custom Transformer, which is well-studied for its expressiveness on sequential patterns, to predict the next packet's latency based on the latencies of recently received ACKs. Based on the predicted latency of each outgoing packet, SwiftQueue's sender dynamically marks the L4S packet header to assign packets to potentially different queues, even within the same flow. Using real network traces, we show that SwiftQueue is 45-65% more accurate in predicting latency and its variations than state-of-art methods. Based on its latency prediction, SwiftQueue reduces the tail latency for L4S-enabled flows by 36-45%, compared with the existing L4S queue-selection method.
technical_mechanism: A sender-side Transformer uses recent ACK latencies and packet context to predict per-packet latency spikes; it then changes the packet's ECN marking so L4S routers place predicted high-latency packets on an alternative queue.
why_it_works: Recent ACK latency reflects queuing and propagation effects, while packet timestamps, sizes, and flow IDs provide context for packet and cross-flow interactions. Attention over this history can predict sharp latency changes; per-packet queue selection can then steer packets away from a less favorable queue. This is a predictive control mechanism, not a method for identifying the specific cause of a delay.
root_seam: A possible Root attachment is the sender's per-request or per-packet ACK-latency sequence, joined by request identity and timestamps. It could provide an early signal of network-path latency changes, but the paper does not separate network queuing from propagation delay, server queueing, GPU compute, or action application. Its queue-marking intervention also requires L4S-capable routers and is not directly available to Root by assumption.
experiment: On a controlled remote-inference path with packet/ACK timestamps and request IDs, replay or induce transient network congestion and test whether a predictor using recent ACK latencies flags request-tail episodes before completion. Compare against ordinary per-flow latency measurement and separately record server queueing, GPU, and action-application time. Treat the paper's queue-marking control as an optional intervention only where L4S is available.
evidence_quote: a Transformer that predicts next outgoing packet’s latency based on information (latencies and queue selections) of recent packets from the same sender
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, SwiftQueue overview; also supported by the abstract.
reported_gain: 45–65% greater accuracy in predicting latency and its variations; 36–45% reduction in tail latency for L4S-enabled flows.
baseline: State-of-the-art prediction methods for prediction accuracy; default L4S queue-selection logic for the reported tail-latency reduction.
uncertainty: The paper predicts end-to-end packet latency, which includes queuing and propagation delay, but does not isolate queue buildup from other causes. Its usefulness for diagnosing remote robot inference tails is therefore unresolved; the reported gains are not Root measurements.

title: ZipCache: A DRAM/SSD Cache with Built-in Transparent Compression
abstract: As a core component in modern data centers, key-value cache provides high-throughput and low-latency services for high-speed data processing. The effectiveness of a key-value cache relies on its ability of accommodating the needed data. However, expanding the cache capacity is often more difficult than commonly expected because of many practical constraints, such as server costs, cooling issues, rack space, and even human resource expenses. A potential solution is compression, which virtually extends the cache capacity by condensing data in cache. In practice, this seemingly simple idea has not gained much traction in key-value cache system design, due to several critical issues: the compression-unfriendly index structure, severe read/write amplification, wasteful decompression operations, and heavy computing cost. This paper presents a hybrid DRAM-SSD cache design to realize a systematic integration of data compression in key-value cache. By treating compression as an essential component, we have redesigned the indexing structure, data management, and leveraged the emerging computational SSD hardware for collaborative optimizations. We have developed a prototype, called ZipCache. Our experimental results show that ZipCache can achieve up to 72.4% higher throughput and 42.4% lower latency, while reducing the write amplification by up to 26.2 times.
technical_mechanism: Hash-assisted targeted decompression: the B+ tree leaf page is partitioned into sub-pages, and hashing the requested key identifies its sub-page so decompression can stop once that target is reconstructed.
why_it_works: The operation avoids decompressing the rest of the page for a cache read. This is a concrete retrieval-acceleration mechanism relevant to n12's comparable-baseline retrieval question, but it does not detect or localize network delay.
root_seam: At a comparable-baseline retrieval service, attach the request key and identity to retrieval timestamps and compare targeted-retrieval time against the existing lookup time. Keep those measurements separate from transport, server queueing, GPU compute, and action-application time; this paper supplies no network-tail signal.
experiment: In a controlled Root replay, compare the existing baseline lookup with hash-assisted targeted retrieval for the same requests and cached objects. Record retrieval latency and end-to-end latency separately, along with robot/server transport, queueing, GPU, and action-application timestamps. Treat any retrieval improvement as a Root measurement, not as a result established by this paper.
evidence_quote: To fetch a cache object from a B+ tree leaf page, we can determine its associated sub-page through a simple hashing and hence accordingly configure the decompression early termination.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section 3.2, DRAM Cache Tier
reported_gain: Up to 42.4% lower 90-percentile read latency.
baseline: CacheLib, Kangaroo, and xcache.
uncertainty: The reported latency gain is for the paper's cache workloads, not Root. The text does not establish that Root has a comparable-baseline retrieval service or that this operation helps diagnose network tails.

title: Mint: Cost-Efficient Tracing with All Requests Collection via Commonality and Variability Analysis
abstract: Distributed traces contain valuable information but are often massive in volume, posing a core challenge in tracing framework design: balancing the tradeoff between preserving essential trace information and reducing trace volume. To address this tradeoff, previous approaches typically used a '1 or 0' sampling strategy: retaining sampled traces while completely discarding unsampled ones. However, based on an empirical study on real-world production traces, we discover that the '1 or 0' strategy actually fails to effectively balance this tradeoff. To achieve a more balanced outcome, we shift the strategy from the '1 or 0' paradigm to the 'commonality + variability' paradigm. The core of 'commonality + variability' paradigm is to first parse traces into common patterns and variable parameters, then aggregate the patterns and filter the parameters. We propose a cost-efficient tracing framework, Mint, which implements the 'commonality + variability' paradigm on the agent side to enable all requests capturing. Our experiments show that Mint can capture all traces and retain more trace information while optimizing trace storage (reduced to an average of 2.7%) and network overhead (reduced to an average of 4.2%). Moreover, experiments also demonstrate that Mint is lightweight enough for production use.
technical_mechanism: On agents, Mint parses spans and sub-traces into recurring patterns and variable parameters. It retains compact pattern and trace metadata for every request, using Bloom Filters to associate trace IDs with patterns; symptom and edge-case samplers select abnormal/outlier traces or rare paths whose parameters are then uploaded for fuller reconstruction. Other traces remain available as approximate traces.
why_it_works: The retained common structure preserves request paths and topology even when detailed parameters are omitted, while abnormal values and rare execution paths can trigger retention of those details. This can expose candidate slow requests and preserve context for analysis, but it does not reconstruct packet/ACK events or establish whether delay arose on the network rather than in queues or compute.
root_seam: A transferable attachment point is the request/trace ID and its retained approximate execution path, topology, and duration attributes. Root could test whether symptom-triggered retention captures slow robot inference requests while reducing trace traffic. Mint does not provide packet-level causal reconstruction or network-versus-server delay attribution, so Root would need transport timestamps or packet/ACK/loss telemetry for that distinction.
experiment: Replay identical remote-inference requests with Mint-style pattern/parameter parsing and symptom-triggered retention enabled versus full tracing and ordinary sampling. Inject network delay/loss separately from server queueing and GPU delay; measure tail-request capture, retained diagnostic detail, network overhead, and whether transport events can be distinguished from server-side delays.
evidence_quote: the Symptom Sampler monitors the Params Buffer, marking traces with abnormal values (e.g., status code 502) or outliers (e.g., unusually large duration values) as sampled traces; the Edge-Case Sampler monitors the Pattern Library, marking traces with rare execution paths as sampled traces.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Mint workflow and key-trace sampling description.
reported_gain: Average trace storage overhead reduced to 2.7% and network overhead to 4.2%; the paper also reports retaining all requests.
baseline: Compared with tracing approaches including OpenTelemetry head sampling, OpenTelemetry tail sampling, Hindsight, and Sieve; the reported average reductions are stated for Mint, but the excerpt does not specify a single baseline for those averages. UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The paper evaluates distributed-service tracing, not remote robot inference. Its measured overhead reductions and retention results do not establish network-tail localization. It uses outlier duration as a retention trigger, but the supplied context does not show that this trigger activates an expensive profiler, leaving that transfer unresolved.

title: Do Data Center Network Metrics Predict Application-Facing Performance?
abstract: Applications that run in large-scale data center networks (DCNs) rely on the DCN's ability to deliver application requests in a performant manner. DCNs expose a complex design and operational space, and network designers and operators care how different options along this space affect application performance. One might run controlled experiments and measure the corresponding application-facing performance, but such experiments become progressively infeasible at a large scale, and simulations risk yielding inaccurate or incomplete results. Instead, we show that we can predict application-facing performance through more easily measured network metrics. For example, network telemetry metrics (e.g., link utilization) can predict application-facing metrics (e.g., transfer latency). Through large-scale measurements of production networks, we study the correlation between the two types of metrics, and construct predictive, interpretable models that serve as a suggestive guideline to network designers and operators. We show that no single network metric is universally the best predictor (even though some prior work has focused on a single predictor). We found that simple linear models often have the lowest error, while queueing-based models are better in a few cases.
technical_mechanism: Compress per-RPC measurements into mergeable t-digests, retaining approximate distribution quantiles; use the summarized tail AFMs alongside network-level metrics to fit predictive models and identify congestion knees.
why_it_works: T-digests retain distributional information with high approximation accuracy, especially in the tail, while reducing the storage and computation required for billions of RPCs. Their mergeability supports aggregation, allowing tail latency summaries to be compared with network metrics without retaining every raw RPC measurement.
root_seam: Attach a t-digest to robot request or inference-stage latency measurements, keyed by an appropriate time window and request class, and compare its tail quantiles with transport events or network telemetry. This could make tail summaries practical to retain, but the paper’s five-minute aggregation does not establish request-level network attribution or separate network delay from server and application delay.
experiment: On a controlled remote-inference workload, compare raw per-request traces with t-digest summaries at matched storage budgets. Measure tail-quantile estimation error and whether models using summarized AFMs and network metrics identify injected network-delay or congestion periods. Keep request classes and time windows aligned, and separately record server queueing and compute time.
evidence_quote: T-digests preserve the original distribution of the data through approximated quantiles. Compared to other compression methods, such as binning with histograms, the t-digest data structure has high approximation accuracy, especially at the tail, and can be merged with other independent t-digests
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, §4.3, “RPC instrumentation”
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The paper reports tail-preserving summaries and network-metric-to-AFM prediction in datacenter RPCs, not a Root or robot-inference evaluation. Its AFM summaries are aggregated over five-minute intervals, so their suitability for localizing short-lived network tails is unestablished.

title: Guiding Retrieval using LLM-based Listwise Rankers
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong promise as rerankers, especially in ``listwise'' settings where an LLM is prompted to rerank several search results at once. However, this ``cascading'' retrieve-and-rerank approach is limited by the bounded recall problem: relevant documents not retrieved initially are permanently excluded from the final ranking. Adaptive retrieval techniques address this problem, but do not work with listwise rerankers because they assume a document's score is computed independently from other documents. In this paper, we propose an adaptation of an existing adaptive retrieval method that supports the listwise setting and helps guide the retrieval process itself (thereby overcoming the bounded recall problem for LLM rerankers). Specifically, our proposed algorithm merges results both from the initial ranking and feedback documents provided by the most relevant documents seen up to that point. Through extensive experiments across diverse LLM rerankers, first stage retrievers, and feedback sources, we demonstrate that our method can improve nDCG@10 by up to 13.23% and recall by 28.02%--all while keeping the total number of LLM inferences constant and overheads due to the adaptive process minimal. The work opens the door to leveraging LLM-based search in settings where the initial pool of results is limited, e.g., by legacy systems, or by the cost of deploying a semantic first-stage.
technical_mechanism: SlideGar uses a precomputed corpus similarity graph to retrieve neighbors of highly ranked documents, then merges those feedback documents with the initial retrieval results in successive listwise-ranking windows.
why_it_works: The precomputed graph reuses document-to-document similarity relationships, so the system can expand the candidate set with likely relevant documents without re-querying the index; the context describes graph lookups as constant-time and the added latency as negligible.
root_seam: A possible retrieval-side transfer is an offline index of comparable requests or tasks, reused to obtain candidate references without repeatedly searching a large corpus. This would not expose or localize a network tail: the method observes ranking relevance, not transport events, queues, or network timing.
experiment: The paper evaluates SlideGar across retrievers and listwise rankers against non-adaptive LLM reranking, measuring ranking quality, recall, and latency. A Root transfer could compare ordinary retrieval with graph-neighbor reuse for identical request sets, measuring retrieval latency and candidate quality separately from network, server-queue, GPU, and action-application time.
evidence_quote: By using a document-to-document similarity graph (“corpus graph”, akin to HNSW [16]), this process can be accomplished with minimal overheads.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section 2.2, “Adaptive Retrieval”
reported_gain: Up to 13.23% improvement in nDCG@10 and 28.02% in recall; the SlideGar component adds about 2.6 ms, reported as 0.02% of ranker latency.
baseline: Standard non-adaptive LLM reranking; the paper also compares an RM3-based adaptive variant.
uncertainty: The reported results concern information retrieval, not remote robot inference or network-tail diagnosis. No Root experiment or network-specific measurement is reported.

title: RTAMT -- Runtime Robustness Monitors with Application to CPS and Robotics
abstract: In this paper, we present Real-Time Analog Monitoring Tool (RTAMT), a tool for quantitative monitoring of Signal Temporal Logic (STL) specifications. The library implements a flexible architecture that supports: (1) various environments connected by an Application Programming Interface (API) in Python, (2) various flavors of temporal logic specification and robustness notion such as STL, including an interface-aware variant that distinguishes between input and output variables, and (3) discrete-time and dense-time interpretation of STL with generation of online and offline monitors. We specifically focus on robotics and Cyber-Physical Systems (CPSs) applications, showing how to integrate RTAMT with (1) the Robot Operating System (ROS) and (2) MATLAB/Simulink environments. We evaluate the tool by demonstrating several use scenarios involving service robotic and avionic applications.
technical_mechanism: Assumption-based STL fault localization: monitor a system-level temporal property and subsystem-level assumptions, then use which subsystem specification is violated to identify a likely source of system failure.
why_it_works: This adds diagnostic attribution beyond simply reporting a temporal-property violation. For a robot-to-cloud loop, separately specifying the request-to-transport, transport-to-server, and server-to-action intervals could let a failed end-to-end deadline be associated with the stage whose monitored property fails. The paper demonstrates this style of subsystem localization for a planner malfunction, but does not itself test network signals or network-delay attribution.
root_seam: Attach request IDs and timestamps at robot send, server receive, server reply, and robot action receipt/application. Feed these stage events and the end-to-end deadline into an online STL monitor, with subsystem assumptions for each interval. This would provide stage-level evidence Root does not get from an end-to-end timeout alone; transport packet or ACK/loss data would still be needed to distinguish network delay from other delay within a stage.
experiment: In a controlled Root test, establish healthy timing distributions and monitor a bounded end-to-end response property plus separate stage-bound properties using timestamped request IDs. Inject network delay/loss, server queueing, GPU slowdown, and delayed action application separately. Check whether the failed subsystem property identifies the injected stage and whether robustness trends distinguish near-deadline behavior from larger violations. The paper reports only a simulated planner-malfunction localization experiment, not this Root experiment.
evidence_quote: This STL assumption-based fault localization approach can also find a system issue caused by perception or controller failure
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section 6.2, HSR fault-localization experiment.
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The paper supports subsystem-level fault localization for a planner malfunction, but does not demonstrate that its assumptions can isolate network delay from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application. Network-stage specifications and transport-event inputs would need to be designed and tested in Root.

title: Tracezip: Efficient Distributed Tracing via Trace Compression
abstract: Distributed tracing serves as a fundamental building block in the monitoring and testing of cloud service systems. To reduce computational and storage overheads, the de facto practice is to capture fewer traces via sampling. However, existing work faces a trade-off between the completeness of tracing and system overhead. On one hand, head-based sampling indiscriminately selects requests to trace when they enter the system, which may miss critical events. On the other hand, tail-based sampling first captures all requests and then selectively persists the edge-case traces, which entails the overheads related to trace collection and ingestion. Taking a different path, we propose Tracezip in this paper to enhance the efficiency of distributed tracing via trace compression. Our key insight is that there exists significant redundancy among traces, which results in repetitive transmission of identical data between services and the backend. We design a new data structure named Span Retrieval Tree (SRT) that continuously encapsulates such redundancy at the service side and transforms trace spans into a lightweight form. At the backend, the complete traces can be seamlessly reconstructed by retrieving the common data that are already delivered by previous spans. Tracezip includes a series of strategies to optimize the structure of SRT and a differential update mechanism to efficiently synchronize SRT between services and the backend. Our evaluation on microservices benchmarks, popular cloud service systems, and production trace data demonstrates that Tracezip can achieve substantial performance gains in trace collection with negligible overhead. We have implemented Tracezip inside the OpenTelemetry Collector, making it compatible with existing tracing APIs.
technical_mechanism: Online, lossless span compression using a service-side Span Retrieval Tree (SRT): spans are encoded as a path identifier plus their unique values, while differential updates synchronize changed SRT data with the receiver. The receiver reconstructs complete spans from its synchronized data.
why_it_works: Repeated span fields are transmitted once and retrieved for later spans, reducing the telemetry volume while preserving trace contents. For streaming diagnosis, this could make it practical to retain more requests—including outliers that sampling might miss—and inspect their traces. It can expose end-to-end span timing and service relationships, but the paper does not establish that it identifies network delay separately from server queueing, compute, or action application.
root_seam: Attach at Root's OpenTelemetry span-export boundary, preserving request identity and existing span timing while compressing repeated fields and synchronizing dictionary updates. Root could retain more request traces under a telemetry budget; this adds trace coverage, not packet-, ACK-, or loss-level evidence for localizing transport delay.
experiment: Under the same remote-inference workload, compare ordinary export with SRT-compressed export at a fixed telemetry bandwidth or storage budget. Measure retained request coverage, outlier-trace completeness and reconstruction correctness, export/backend overhead, and inference tail latency. Independently record transport, server-queue, GPU, and action-application timings to test whether newly retained traces help identify which stage coincides with a tail. Treat this as a proposed Root experiment, not a paper result.
evidence_quote: Tracezip transforms spans into a concise representation upon their generation at the service side, which can be seamlessly decompressed at the backend side. This strategy significantly reduces the volume of data that needs to be transmitted.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Introduction; SRT encoding details in Section 3 and differential synchronization in Section 4.2.
reported_gain: The paper reports around 10%–45% performance improvement in trace collection; the supplied excerpt does not specify the metric and comparison for that range. On Alibaba production traces, it reports Tracezip improved compression performance by 35.1%, 43.6%, and 37.8% versus gzip, bzip2, and lzma, respectively.
baseline: For the reported Alibaba comparison: gzip, bzip2, and lzma. The comparison baseline associated with the general 10%–45% claim is UNKNOWN.
uncertainty: The operation and its trace-volume effect are supported, and its online lossless compression is a plausible transfer for streaming diagnosis. The paper evaluates trace compression, not remote-robot inference diagnosis; it does not show improved network-tail localization or distinguish transport delay from compute and queueing.

title: LA-IMR: Latency-Aware, Predictive In-Memory Routing and Proactive Autoscaling for Tail-Latency-Sensitive Cloud Robotics
abstract: Hybrid cloud-edge infrastructures now support latency-critical workloads ranging from autonomous vehicles and surgical robotics to immersive AR/VR. However, they continue to experience crippling long-tail latency spikes whenever bursty request streams exceed the capacity of heterogeneous edge and cloud tiers. To address these long-tail latency issues, we present Latency-Aware, Predictive In-Memory Routing and Proactive Autoscaling (LA-IMR). This control layer integrates a closed-form, utilization-driven latency model with event-driven scheduling, replica autoscaling, and edge-to-cloud offloading to mitigate 99th-percentile (P99) delays. Our analytic model decomposes end-to-end latency into processing, network, and queuing components, expressing inference latency as an affine power-law function of instance utilization. Once calibrated, it produces two complementary functions that drive: (i) millisecond-scale routing decisions for traffic offloading, and (ii) capacity planning that jointly determines replica pool sizes. LA-IMR enacts these decisions through a quality-differentiated, multi-queue scheduler and a custom-metric Kubernetes autoscaler that scales replicas proactively -- before queues build up -- rather than reactively based on lagging CPU metrics. Across representative vision workloads (YOLOv5m and EfficientDet) and bursty arrival traces, LA-IMR reduces P99 latency by up to 20.7 percent compared to traditional latency-only autoscaling, laying a principled foundation for next-generation, tail-tolerant cloud-edge inference services.
technical_mechanism: LA-IMR uses a calibrated closed-form latency model that separates inference processing, task-agnostic network RTT, and queueing delay. On each request, it estimates arrival rate and predicts per-replica latency; if the predicted latency breaches the SLO, it routes or offloads the request, while sustained predicted load drives replica autoscaling before queues build.
why_it_works: The model predicts superlinear latency growth under rising utilization and estimates queueing pressure, allowing the controller to add capacity or redirect requests before overload produces long waits. Its network term is represented as RTT, but the method does not diagnose packet-level causes or distinguish an observed network tail from other sources of delay.
root_seam: A Root experiment could attach request timestamps and identity to the robot-to-server round trip, record the model's predicted processing/network/queue components alongside observed latency, and compare predictions with measured outcomes. The RTT term could provide a coarse network-delay baseline, but the paper does not offer packet, ACK, loss, or per-request network attribution; those signals would still need to be collected separately to localize a network tail.
experiment: Replay bursty robot inference requests with controlled network RTT and server load independently varied. Compare predicted component delays and SLO-triggered routing/scaling decisions against measured request-level end-to-end, network, processing, and queue delays. Test whether the RTT term helps separate network-induced tails from server-side queueing or compute.
evidence_quote: The model decomposes latency into three components: (i) an inference-processing term that scales with instance utilization according to an affine power law, (ii) a task-agnostic network round-trip time (RTT), and (iii) an analytically derived M/M/c queuing delay.
evidence_location: selected_pdf_text, Introduction; latency model description
reported_gain: Up to 20.7% lower P99 latency under bursty workloads; at arrival rate 6 req/s, P99 is reported as 5.4 s or less versus 6.8 s for the baseline.
baseline: A conventional latency-focused/reactive autoscaling strategy using Prometheus-measured latency.
uncertainty: The paper reports a modeled network RTT component, not a method for diagnosing packet-level network tails. The supplied context does not establish per-request component measurement accuracy under independently controlled network and server delays. The robotics evaluation uses bursty arrival-rate variation, but does not report a controlled experiment isolating rare network delays.

title: QUIC Steps: Evaluating Pacing Strategies in QUIC Implementations
abstract: Pacing is a key mechanism in modern transport protocols, used to regulate packet transmission timing to minimize traffic burstiness, lower latency, and reduce packet loss. Standardized in 2021, QUIC is a UDP-based protocol designed to improve upon the TCP / TLS stack. While the QUIC protocol recommends pacing, and congestion control algorithms like BBR rely on it, the user-space nature of QUIC introduces unique challenges. These challenges include coarse-grained timers, system call overhead, and OS scheduling delays, all of which complicate precise packet pacing. This paper investigates how pacing is implemented differently across QUIC stacks, including quiche, picoquic, and ngtcp2, and evaluates the impact of system-level features like GSO and Linux qdiscs on pacing. Using a custom measurement framework and a passive optical fiber tap, we establish a baseline with default settings and systematically explore the effects of qdiscs, hardware offloading using the ETF qdisc, and GSO on pacing precision and network performance. We also extend and evaluate a kernel patch to enable pacing of individual packets within GSO buffers, combining batching efficiency with precise pacing. Kernel-assisted and purely user-space pacing approaches are compared. We show that pacing with only user-space timers can work well, as demonstrated by picoquic with BBR. With quiche, we identify FQ as a qdisc well-suited for pacing QUIC traffic, as it is relatively easy to use and offers precise pacing based on packet timestamps. Our findings provide new insights into the trade-offs involved in implementing pacing in QUIC and highlight potential optimizations for real-world applications like video streaming and video calls.
technical_mechanism: Measure on-wire packet inter-packet gaps and packet-train lengths, then compare timestamp-based pacing configurations (such as FQ) against default pacing under a controlled bottleneck. Packet bursts and their timing expose sender-side pacing problems that can contribute to queue buildup; congestion-window and loss-event analysis can reveal when transport behavior complicates that diagnosis.
why_it_works: A passive packet capture provides actual transmission timing rather than relying only on application-level latency. A controlled bottleneck and pacing interventions let the experiment test whether bursty sending coincides with queue-related loss or delay. The paper also shows that congestion-control behavior can confound interpretation, so packet timing should be considered alongside loss and congestion-window events.
root_seam: Attach packet/request identity and send/ACK timestamps at the robot and inference server transport boundaries; retain packet-gap or burst summaries and, where available, queue and loss signals. This would help distinguish sender bursts and transport queueing from server queueing, GPU compute, and action application. The paper does not establish access to Root's private infrastructure.
experiment: In a repeatable remote-inference workload, compare default transport pacing with timestamp-based pacing while holding model, request rate, and compute constant. Capture packet send/ACK timing and queue/loss signals, and correlate them with end-to-end tail latency and server/GPU timings. Test whether pacing changes network-tail episodes without changing compute or action-application time.
evidence_quote: The precision of FQ is 0.12 ms, which is better than the ETF implementations. The baseline measurements without any qdisc show the worst precision with 0.94 ms.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, ETF/LaunchTime evaluation paragraph
reported_gain: FQ pacing precision: 0.12 ms versus 0.94 ms in the no-qdisc baseline. This is a paper result, not a Root gain.
baseline: Default configuration without a qdisc for the pacing-precision comparison.
uncertainty: The evaluation uses a controlled 40 Mbit/s, 40 ms RTT setup and a bulk file transfer, not remote robot inference or rare control-loop tails. Packet burstiness is a diagnostic signal, not direct proof that a particular Root latency episode was caused by queue buildup.

title: MM-INT: Telemetry in Programmable Switches with Multiple Queues using Source-based Multipath Routing
abstract: This article emphasizes the importance of queues associated with the ports of switches in network monitoring. Traditionally, data collection about these queues is done using programmable data planes and telemetry based on INT (In-band Network Telemetry) probes, assuming there is only a single queue per output port. The MM-INT (Multiqueue Multicast - INT) is a solution that utilizes registers to store data from all queues and ports, enabling the efficient collection of monitoring information. The MM-INT avoids probe overload and employs the origin-based routing mechanism and multicast trees for the probes. The results demonstrate significant reductions in the number of probes sent compared to other traditional solutions found in the literature.
technical_mechanism: In the switch egress pipeline, update a dedicated register with queue telemetry as each data packet passes through its logical queue; an INT probe reads the registers to collect telemetry for all queues and ports on that switch.
why_it_works: Per-queue occupancy reveals which queue is building up instead of reporting only the queue traversed by a probe. Comparing queue occupancy with a request's network timing could help identify a congestion-related tail, while avoiding a separate probe for each queue.
root_seam: Attach switch queue telemetry to the relevant request or time window using INT probes, and compare occupancy by port and logical queue with robot/server transport timestamps. This adds queue-level evidence for separating network queue buildup from server queueing or compute delay; the paper does not itself provide request-level correlation.
experiment: In a controlled Root replay or testbed, vary load on one switch queue while holding server/GPU work and other network conditions steady. Collect MM-INT per-queue occupancy alongside request transport timestamps and tail latency; test whether the affected queue's occupancy tracks the network tail and distinguishes it from server-side delay. Compare telemetry coverage and probe overhead with per-queue probing.
evidence_quote: each data packet, before being removed from the queue to be transmitted to the outgoing link, invokes the calls to obtain the INT telemetry
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, MM-INT mechanism description (egress pipeline); the following passage says returned telemetry is stored in per-queue registers and the probe reads those registers.
reported_gain: 4x fewer probes and approximately 2.8x fewer bytes for telemetry collection in the evaluated topology.
baseline: Traditional INT solutions evaluated in the paper (Solutions S1 and S2); the text also describes comparison with traditional solutions from the literature.
uncertainty: The evaluation is a Mininet/BMv2 demonstration with heavy traffic and queue-occupancy reporting, not a Root inference-tail study. The supplied text does not establish telemetry freshness, request-level attribution, or how accurately occupancy predicts latency.

title: Measuring Round-Trip Response Latencies Under Asymmetric Routing
abstract: Latency is a key indicator of Internet service performance. Continuously tracking the latency of client requests enables service operators to quickly identify bottlenecks, perform adaptive resource allocation or routing, and mitigate attacks. Passively measuring the response latency at intermediate vantage points is attractive since it provides insight into the experience of real clients without requiring client instrumentation or incurring probing overheads. This paper presents PIRATE, a passive approach to measure response latencies when only the client-to-server traffic is visible, even when transport headers are encrypted. PIRATE estimates the time gap between causal pairs - two requests such that the response to the first triggered the second - as a proxy for the client-side response latency. Our experiments with a realistic web application show that PIRATE can estimate the response latencies measured at the client application layer to within 1 percent. A PIRATE-enhanced layer-4 load balancer (with DSR) cuts tail latencies by 37 percent.
technical_mechanism: At an intermediate vantage point observing only client-to-server traffic, PIRATE detects prominent inter-packet gaps that separate request bursts and treats the first packet after a gap as a causally triggered request. It estimates client-visible response latency from the interval between successive such requests; an IPG-distribution method can estimate average latency from the prominent inter-batch gap and the smaller packet-gap modes.
why_it_works: For closed-loop applications, the client may send a follow-up request only after receiving and processing a response. The request-to-follow-up interval therefore reflects response latency plus client think time, without needing reverse-path visibility or clear transport headers. This could give Root passive, client-visible end-to-end timing from robot-to-server request traffic, but does not by itself separate network delay from server processing or client think time. Applying burst-gap identification also depends on the paper’s prominent-gap assumption, which may not hold for paced traffic.
root_seam: Attach at a robot-to-cloud traffic observation point and associate successive requests on a connection using packet-arrival timestamps. Compare the resulting closed-loop intervals with robot-side application/request timestamps and server-side receive, queue, and completion timestamps to distinguish network transit from server queueing, compute, and client processing. A differential tail-versus-healthy-request use is plausible, but the supplied context does not demonstrate that comparison.
experiment: Replay robot-to-cloud action-loop request traffic with controlled network delay, loss, and server queue/compute delays. Compare PIRATE-style burst-gap interval estimates against robot application-layer response timings and server timestamps for tail and healthy requests; test both bursty and paced traffic, and quantify errors and whether network-originated tails can be distinguished from server-side delay.
evidence_quote: The time interval between consecutive causally-triggered requests provides an estimate of the response latency.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, §3 PIRATE, paragraph beginning “Our second key idea is to leverage the timings of packet arrivals”.
reported_gain: Within 1 percent accuracy against client application-layer response latency in a realistic web application; the PIRATE-enhanced load balancer reduced 99th-percentile tail response latency by an average of 37% across loads.
baseline: Client application-layer response latency for the accuracy comparison; vanilla layer-4 load balancer for the tail-latency comparison.
uncertainty: The evidence concerns web workloads, not robot inference. Causal-pair timing includes client think time and server processing as well as network effects, and the prominent packet-gap assumption can fail under pacing. The context does not establish differential tail-versus-healthy diagnosis or a cheap trigger for profiling.

title: E²GraphRAG: Streamlining Graph-based RAG for High Efficiency and Effectiveness
abstract: Graph-based RAG methods like GraphRAG have shown promising global understanding of the knowledge base by constructing hierarchical entity graphs. However, they often suffer from inefficiency and rely on manually pre-defined query modes, limiting practical use. In this paper, we propose E²GraphRAG, a streamlined graph-based RAG framework that improves both Efficiency and Effectiveness. During the indexing stage, E²GraphRAG constructs a summary tree with large language models and an entity graph with SpaCy based on document chunks. We then construct bidirectional indexes between entities and chunks to capture their many-to-many relationships, enabling fast lookup during both local and global retrieval. For the retrieval stage, we design an adaptive retrieval strategy that leverages the graph structure to retrieve and select between local and global modes. Experiments show that E²GraphRAG achieves up to 10 times faster indexing than GraphRAG and 100 times speedup over LightRAG in retrieval while maintaining competitive QA performance.
technical_mechanism: Build bidirectional entity-to-chunk and chunk-to-entity indexes over a SpaCy-extracted entity graph and document chunks, then use those mappings to retrieve relevant chunks directly rather than repeatedly searching or reconstructing graph-to-chunk associations.
why_it_works: The indexes precompute the many-to-many mapping between entities and chunks, so retrieval can look up chunks associated with query entities (and entities associated with candidate chunks) efficiently. This is a concrete indexing-and-reuse mechanism for faster comparable baseline retrieval, though it concerns document retrieval rather than network-tail diagnosis.
root_seam: Potentially transferable only as a lookup/reuse pattern for repeated Root comparisons: pre-index request identities or transport events to retrieve comparable healthy requests or retained traces. The paper provides no network signals, transport events, or tail-localization method, so this is an adjacent transfer rather than a direct diagnostic technique.
experiment: On a fixed corpus of requests and retained traces, compare indexed lookup of comparable healthy requests against a scan-based baseline. Measure lookup latency and whether the selected comparisons help distinguish transport delay from server queueing or compute; this would test transfer to Root, not reproduce the paper's QA experiment.
evidence_quote: we build two one-to-many indexes to link entities and chunks and reflect the many-to-many relations between them.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, entity graph extraction and indexing description.
reported_gain: Up to 100× retrieval speedup over LightRAG; also up to 10× faster indexing than GraphRAG.
baseline: LightRAG for the reported retrieval speedup; GraphRAG for the reported indexing speedup.
uncertainty: The paper supports faster indexed retrieval in its RAG setting, but does not test comparable-request retrieval, network telemetry, or Root. The degree to which this indexing pattern would improve Root diagnostics is unmeasured.

title: S"oze: One Network Telemetry Is All You Need for Per-flow Weighted Bandwidth Allocation at Scale
abstract: Weighted bandwidth allocation is a powerful abstraction that has a wide range of use cases in modern data center networks. However, realizing highly agile and precise weighted bandwidth allocation for large-scale cloud environments is fundamentally challenging. In this paper, we propose S"oze, a lightweight decentralized weighted bandwidth allocation system that leverages simple network telemetry features of commodity Ethernet switches. Given the flow weights, S"oze can effectively use the telemetry information to compute and enforce the weighted bandwidth allocations without per-flow, topology, or routing knowledge. We demonstrate the effectiveness of S"oze through simulations and testbed experiments, improving TPC-H jobs completion time by up to 0.59× and 0.79× on average.
technical_mechanism: Switches measure per-hop queueing delay and retain the maximum queueing-delay value (maxQD) in each data packet; the receiver reflects it in ACKs. The sender uses that signal in an adaptive rate-update algorithm, with queueing delay mapped to weighted fair share. The maximum per-hop value is used to identify the flow’s bottleneck hop without knowing which hop produced it.
why_it_works: Queueing delay is a direct signal of network queueing, and its dynamics reflect the difference between link arrival rate and bandwidth. Across hops, the maximum queueing delay is argued to correspond to the flow’s bottleneck. For Root, a compact packet/ACK-carried signal could expose network queue buildup and point to a congested hop without requiring full packet-path tracing. It would not, on its own, explain server queueing, GPU compute, or action-application delay.
root_seam: Attach request identity and timestamps to robot-side send/receive events and server-side packet/ACK events; retain per-hop queueing delay or maxQD where available. Compare the signal with end-to-end inference latency and server/GPU timings to test whether network queueing explains a tail.
experiment: Replay remote inference traffic in a controlled Root setup while injecting queue buildup at a known network hop, then compare request tail latency and per-request maxQD against an otherwise identical no-injected-queue run. Check whether maxQD rises and identifies the injected bottleneck while server queue, GPU, and action-application timings remain unchanged.
