evidence_quote: When the data packet travels the forwarding path, it compares and keeps the highest per-hop queueing delay on each hop.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, §3.2.3, “Collect maxQD in data packet and reflect in ACK packet.”
reported_gain: TPC-H job completion time improved by up to 0.59× and 0.79× on average, as stated in the abstract; the context does not clarify the interpretation of these ratios.
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: This is a bandwidth-allocation and congestion-control mechanism, not a request-to-packet causal reconstruction method, so it does not support n01. Its bottleneck claim concerns queueing delay across network hops; applying it to Root depends on access to comparable transport telemetry and request correlation. The reported TPC-H gain is not a Root diagnostic gain.

title: Understanding and Mitigating Network Latency Effect on Teleoperated-Robot with Extended Reality
abstract: Robot teleoperation with extended reality (XR teleoperation) enables intuitive interaction by allowing remote robots to mimic user motions with real-time 3D feedback. However, existing systems face significant motion-to-motion (M2M) latency--the delay between the user's latest motion and the corresponding robot feedback--leading to high teleoperation error and mission completion time. This issue stems from the system's exclusive reliance on network communication, making it highly vulnerable to network degradation. To address these challenges, we introduce TeleXR, the first end-to-end, fully open-sourced XR teleoperation framework that decouples robot control and XR visualization from network dependencies. TeleXR leverages local sensing data to reconstruct delayed or missing information of the counterpart, thereby significantly reducing network-induced issues. This approach allows both the XR and robot to run concurrently with network transmission while maintaining high robot planning accuracy. TeleXR also features contention-aware scheduling to mitigate GPU contention and bandwidth-adaptive point cloud scaling to cope with limited bandwidth.
technical_mechanism: Dual reconstruction: the robot uses an online trajectory planner to fill in delayed or missing user-pose waypoints from its current pose, speed, and direction; the XR side extrapolates robot pose from the latest received state and current local user pose, then updates its estimate when new robot data arrives. A robot-side target queue orders waypoints by timestamp.
why_it_works: Local sensing and state let the control and visualization pipelines keep running instead of waiting for every network update. The robot plans through missing or delayed commands, while the XR side estimates current robot state and corrects that estimate on receipt of newer data. Timestamp ordering also prevents out-of-order arrivals from being executed as if they were current.
root_seam: Attach request identity and timestamps at the robot command and feedback boundaries, and compare those with robot-side and server-side transport events and per-stage timings. This method itself mitigates the effects of delay rather than diagnosing its cause; Root could use the timing boundaries to distinguish network waiting from control, visualization, or compute time, and could test reconstruction as a separate mitigation.
experiment: Replay identical robot action loops under controlled added delay, jitter, packet loss, and reordering, with and without dual reconstruction. Record command-to-actuation and actuation-to-feedback timestamps alongside transport and per-stage timings; compare tail latency, trajectory error, and waiting time, while separately varying server/GPU load.
evidence_quote: Consequently, all the delayed and missing hand poses are compensated by the generated waypoints, so the original user motion is reconstructed even under network degradation.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, §III-B, Robot Control
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: Systems that wait for delayed network responses; no quantitative gain for dual reconstruction is provided in the supplied context.
uncertainty: The supplied text describes the reconstruction and timing decomposition, but provides no quantitative result for the network-mitigation mechanism. It does not establish a diagnostic comparison of healthy and tail requests or a network-specific Root gain.

title: Dynamic Pacing for Real-time Satellite Traffic
abstract: Google's congestion control (GCC) has become a cornerstone for real-time video and audio communication, yet its performance remains fragile in emerging Low Earth Orbit (LEO) networks. In this paper, we study the behavior of videoconferencing systems in LEO constellations. We observe that video quality degrades due to inherent delays and network instability introduced by the high altitude and rapid movement of LEO satellites, with these effects exacerbated by WebRTC's conventional "one-size-fits-all" sender-side pacing queue management. To address these challenges, we introduce a data-driven queue management mechanism that tunes the maximum pacing queue capacity based on predicted handover activity, minimizing latency during no-handover periods and prioritizing stability when entering periods of increased handover activity. Our method yields up to 3x improvements in video bitrate and reduces freeze rate by 62% in emulation, while delivering up to a 41% reduction in freeze rate and 40% decrease in mean packet loss on real Starlink constellations compared to WebRTC's default pacing queue policy.
technical_mechanism: Sender-side pacing-queue delay attribution via queue-limit intervention: compare queued-packet waiting with end-to-end delay and transport outcomes while capping the pacer queue according to predicted handover activity.
why_it_works: The paper distinguishes a sender queue tail from network instability by changing the queue limit and observing the resulting delay, packet loss, and bitrate: excessive buffering during stable periods creates sender-side delay spikes, while larger queues during handovers absorb link disruptions. This provides an intervention-based diagnostic for queue buildup, though it does not offer per-request attribution or isolate all other tail causes. Root can test whether a tail shrinks when sender queue waiting is reduced, while separately recording network transport, server queue, GPU, and action-application time.
root_seam: At the robot-side sender pacer, record request/frame identity and enqueue/dequeue timestamps, queue occupancy, and transport timestamps; run a controlled queue-cap change keyed to predicted or observed network instability. Compare sender queue wait against post-dequeue network delay and downstream server/GPU/action timings.
experiment: Replay the same controlled remote-inference workload across fixed and reduced sender-pacer queue limits during stable-link runs, then repeat with induced handover-like loss or outage periods and a handover-aware limit. Measure per-request pacer wait, transport delay/loss, server queueing, GPU time, and action-application delay; test whether the intervention moves tails specifically in the sender-queue component or during unstable transport.
evidence_quote: This excessive buffering causes bloated sender-side queues; draining them introduces delay spikes and burst traffic that leads GCC to conservatively lower its target bitrate.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section IV-C, Sparse Satellite Constellations; queue-limit adaptation and network-delay context also in Sections I and III-D.
reported_gain: Up to 3x video bitrate improvement and 62% lower freeze rate in emulation; up to 41% lower freeze rate and 40% lower mean packet loss on live Starlink versus WebRTC default pacing queue policy. No Root-measured gain reported.
baseline: WebRTC default pacing queue policy; live Starlink experiments also compare random queue-size and rule-based handover policies.
uncertainty: The paper supports diagnosing sender-side queue buildup through queue-limit intervention and delay/outcome changes, but does not report per-request queue occupancy or a full delay decomposition. Its live handover predictor also extrapolates from the previous interval. Root transfer remains a proposed controlled experiment, not a demonstrated Root result.

title: CrossTrace: Efficient Cross-Thread and Cross-Service Span Correlation in Distributed Tracing for Microservices
abstract: Distributed tracing has become an essential technique for debugging and troubleshooting modern microservice-based applications, enabling software engineers to detect performance bottlenecks, identify failures, and gain insights into system behavior. However, implementing distributed tracing in large-scale applications remains challenging due to the need for extensive instrumentation. To reduce this burden, zero-code instrumentation solutions, such as those based on eBPF, have emerged, allowing span data to be collected without modifying application code. Despite this promise, span correlation, the process of establishing causal relationships between spans, remains a critical challenge in zero-code approaches. Existing solutions often rely on thread affinity, compromise system security by requiring the kernel integrity mode to be disabled, or incur significant computational overhead due to complex inference algorithms. This paper presents CrossTrace, a practical and efficient distributed tracing solution designed to support the debugging of microservice applications without requiring source code modifications. CrossTrace employs a greedy algorithm to infer intra-service span relationships from delay patterns, eliminating reliance on thread identifiers. For inter-service correlation, CrossTrace embeds span identifiers into TCP packet headers via eBPF, enabling secure and efficient correlation compromising system security policies. Evaluation results show that CrossTrace can correlate thousands of spans within seconds with over 90% accuracy, making it suitable for production deployment and valuable for microservice observability and diagnosis.
technical_mechanism: CrossTrace uses eBPF to propagate span IDs in TCP header options between services, linking network communication to parent and child spans without application changes. Within a service, it infers ingress-to-egress span relationships by scoring candidate delay patterns and greedily assigning the most likely correlations.
why_it_works: Propagated span IDs provide an explicit causal link across services, while kernel-level event capture supplies timestamps for request and response spans. The resulting request-linked timeline could help Root associate transport events with the relevant inference request. It does not, by itself, separate network delay from server queueing, compute, or action application.
root_seam: Attach span or request identity to robot-side and server-side transport events, then compare linked send/receive timestamps with inference-stage timestamps. This could expose which service or communication interval accounts for a tail, but packet-level attribution and separation from compute would need to be validated in Root.
experiment: On controlled Root requests with known injected network delay and known server-side queue or compute delay, compare linked eBPF transport/span timelines against ground truth and existing tracing. Measure whether the mechanism identifies the delayed interval and request correctly, along with collection overhead.
evidence_quote: When the request reaches the socket layer, the eBPF program retrieves the data from the shared map and embeds the span ID in the TCP header.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section III.C, “Cross-service Span Correlation”
reported_gain: CrossTrace reports over 90% intra-service correlation accuracy under high concurrency; its TCP-header span propagation overhead was reported as typically under 50 ns to reserve header space, under 300 ns to write, and over 600 ns to read.
baseline: Intra-service correlation is compared with TraceWeaver; TCP-header propagation overhead is measured across 50,000 requests. A comparative baseline for the reported per-operation overhead values is UNKNOWN.
uncertainty: The paper establishes cross-service span correlation, not a tested method for localizing network tails in remote robot inference. Its traces may help distinguish intervals, but the supplied evidence does not show separation of transport delay from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application. The abnormal-request option for returning multiple correlations is described, but measured overhead savings from triggered retention are not reported.

title: Towards Timing Isolation for Mixed-Criticality Communication in Software-Defined Vehicles
abstract: As the automotive industry transitions toward centralized Linux-based architectures, ensuring the predictable execution of mixed-criticality applications becomes essential. However, concurrent use of the Linux network stack introduces interference, resulting in unpredictable latency and jitter. To address this challenge, we present a layered software architecture that enforces timing isolation for Ethernet-based data exchange between mixed-criticality applications on Linux-based automotive control units. Our approach integrates traffic prioritization strategies at the middleware layer, the network stack layer, and the hardware layer to achieve isolation across the full software stack. At the middleware layer, we implement a fixed-priority, non-preemptive scheduler to manage publishers of varying criticality. At the network layer, we leverage the express data path (XDP) to route high-priority data directly from the network interface driver into critical application memory, bypassing the standard Linux network stack. At the hardware layer, we dedicate a network interface card (NIC) queue exclusively to real-time traffic. We demonstrate how our architecture performs in a Data Distribution Service (DDS)-based system. Our evaluation shows that the approach leads to consistent and predictable latencies for real-time traffic, even under heavy interference from best-effort applications.
technical_mechanism: Isolate real-time DDS traffic across middleware, network stack, and NIC: schedule middleware operations with a non-preemptive fixed-priority executor; use AF_XDP/eBPF to redirect matching RTPS packets directly to userspace; and steer real-time traffic to dedicated high-priority NIC queues while best-effort traffic uses other queues.
why_it_works: Priority scheduling bounds interference from lower-priority middleware work. AF_XDP bypasses much of the shared Linux networking stack and avoids packet-copying overhead, while dedicated NIC queues prevent best-effort packets from delaying real-time packets in shared queues. Under controlled best-effort load, comparing this configuration with the conventional stack can test whether host-stack and NIC contention contribute to latency tails.
root_seam: At the robot and inference-server transport boundary, classify packets by request identity or traffic marking, steer selected traffic through an AF_XDP path and dedicated NIC queues, and compare tail latency with the ordinary path under matched load. This is an intervention that can implicate host-stack or NIC queue contention; it does not by itself separate those effects from wire delay, server queueing, GPU compute, or action application.
experiment: On a remote-inference request stream, compare ordinary networking with AF_XDP redirection and dedicated real-time NIC queues while holding request rate and payload constant. Add controlled best-effort traffic up to line rate; capture synchronized send/receive timestamps and report tail latency and jitter per configuration. The paper evaluates RTT and one-way delay with and without line-rate interference, but does not test a robot inference loop.
evidence_quote: We use the latter mechanism to redirect incoming traffic right into our middleware layer in a zero-copy fashion.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section III-B, Network Stack; NIC queue isolation is described in Section III-C.
reported_gain: The paper reports that baseline maximum RTT increased up to a factor of 7 under interference, while its combined approach kept maximum RTT values under 500 µs in congestion tests. It also reports lower variance with the approach; the reported gains are not Root measurements.
baseline: A configuration using conventional socket programming and the default Linux networking stack and configuration, without AF_XDP or NIC queue separation; the middleware configuration is the same.
uncertainty: The evaluation enables all mitigation strategies together, and the authors state that individual strategy effects remain future work. The experiment is a two-host DDS testbed, not remote robot inference, and the architecture mitigates interference rather than directly identifying the source of an individual rare tail.

title: A Hybrid TDMA/CSMA Protocol for Time-Sensitive Traffic in Robot Applications
abstract: Recent progress in robotics has underscored the demand for real-time control in applications such as manufacturing, healthcare, and autonomous systems, where the timely delivery of mission-critical commands under heterogeneous robotic traffic is paramount for operational efficacy and safety. In these scenarios, mission-critical traffic follows a strict deadline-constrained communication pattern: commands must arrive within defined QoS deadlines, otherwise late arrivals can degrade performance or destabilize control loops.In this work, we demonstrate on a real-time SDR platform that CSMA, widely adopted in robotic communications,suffers severe degradation under high robot traffic loads, with contention-induced collisions and delays disrupting the on-time arrival of mission-critical packets. To address this problem, we propose an IEEE 802.11-compatible hybrid TDMA/CSMA protocol that combines TDMA's deterministic slot scheduling with CSMA's adaptability for heterogeneous robot traffic.The protocol achieves collision-free, low-latency mission-critical command delivery and IEEE 802.11 compatibility through the synergistic integration of sub-microsecond PTP-based slot synchronization-essential for establishing precise timing for TDMA, a three-session superframe with dynamic TDMA allocation for structured and adaptable traffic management,and beacon-NAV protection to preemptively secure these critical communication sessions from interference. Emulation experiments on real-time SDR testbed and Robot Operating System (ROS) simulation show that the proposed protocol reduces missed-deadline errors by 93% compared to the CSMA baseline. In high-speed robot path-tracking ROS simulations, the protocol lowers Root Mean Square (RMS) trajectory error by up to 90% compared with a CSMA baseline, all while maintaining throughput for non-critical traffic within +-2%.
technical_mechanism: Protect deadline-critical robot commands from competing traffic by synchronizing nodes with sub-microsecond PTP, assigning commands dynamic TDMA slots in a three-section superframe, and using beacon NAV reservations to prevent CSMA transmissions from overlapping those slots.
why_it_works: Scheduled, protected transmission slots reduce contention, collisions, and backoff delays for critical commands while leaving residual channel time for non-critical CSMA traffic. Comparing delivery outcomes under CSMA and the hybrid protocol tests whether shared-medium contention contributes to deadline misses.
root_seam: At the robot-side wireless transport, attach request or command identity and send/receive timestamps, then compare deadline misses and delivery timing under ordinary access versus protected slots. This can expose contention-related delay in the wireless hop, but does not by itself separate that delay from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application.
experiment: Replay identical robot command and background-traffic workloads under CSMA and the hybrid TDMA/CSMA scheme. Record per-command send and receive times, deadline misses, packet loss, and non-critical throughput; compare tail delivery latency and failures while keeping traffic and network conditions fixed.
evidence_quote: With the hybrid TDMA/CSMA protocol, the missed deadline error rate is reduced by 93% compared to the conventional CSMA baseline.
evidence_location: selected_pdf_text, Section III experimental results (hybrid protocol delivery status); protocol components are described in Section III, Design Principles.
reported_gain: 93% reduction in missed-deadline error rate versus CSMA; ROS path-tracking RMS trajectory error reduced by up to 90%.
baseline: Conventional CSMA
uncertainty: The demonstrated mechanism is for a shared wireless robot network, not a robot-to-cloud inference path. The context does not establish that it can be deployed on Root's transport or diagnose tails caused by server-side queueing, GPU compute, or action application.

title: Empirical Evaluation of a 5G Transparent Clock for Time Synchronization in a TSN-5G Network
abstract: Time synchronization is essential for industrial IoT and Industry 4.0/5.0 applications, but achieving high synchronization accuracy in Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN)-5G networks is challenging due to jitter and asymmetric delays. 3GPP TS 23.501 defines three 5G synchronization modes: time-aware system, boundary clock (BC), and transparent clock (TC), where TC offers a promising solution. However, to the best of our knowledge, there is no empirical evaluation of TC in a TSN-5G network. This paper empirically evaluates an 5G end-to-end TC in a TSN-5G network, implemented on commercial TSN switches with a single clock. For TC development, we compute the residence time in 5G and recover the clock domain at the slave node. We deploy a TSN-5G testbed with commercial equipment for synchronization evaluation by modifying the Precision Timing Protocol (PTP) message transmission rates. Experimental results show a peak-to-peak synchronization of 500 ns, meeting the industrial requirement of < 1 us, with minimal synchronization offsets for specific PTP message transmission rates.
technical_mechanism: Measure network residence time with ingress and egress timestamps from a shared clock, then add that duration to PTP correction fields so the receiver can compensate for variable network delay.
why_it_works: The paired timestamps directly quantify time spent traversing the 5G segment, including its variable delay, rather than conflating that residence time with the rest of the synchronization path. The paper also measures uplink and downlink residence times separately to account for asymmetry. For Root, the transferable operation is to timestamp transport-boundary events and compare their duration with server-side queueing and GPU-compute intervals; this paper itself does not measure inference server or GPU time.
root_seam: Attach synchronized timestamps or a common request identity at the robot-side and server-side transport boundaries, and retain the corresponding ingress/egress events. Compare the measured network interval against separately measured server-queue and GPU-compute intervals to localize a tail. The paper's measurement requires a shared time reference across timestamping points; it does not establish that Root has such clock synchronization.
experiment: On controlled remote-inference requests, vary network conditions while holding server and GPU load steady, then vary server/GPU load while holding network conditions steady. Compare transport-boundary residence-time estimates with end-to-end latency and server queue/compute measurements; test whether the timestamps localize network-induced tails, including uplink/downlink asymmetry.
evidence_quote: NW-TT and DS-TT assign timestamps to the “Sync” packets at the ingress (*t₁′*) and egress (*t₂′*) of the 5GS, respectively.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section IV, “Transparent Clock Design,” subsection “Calculation of the 5GS residence time.”
reported_gain: 500 ns peak-to-peak synchronization accuracy; this is a synchronization result, not a measured Root or inference-latency gain.
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The paper evaluates PTP synchronization, not remote inference, and does not measure server queueing or GPU compute. Its demonstrated residence-time measurement depends on synchronized timestamping points; transfer to Root would require suitable timestamping and request correlation.

title: CALL: Context-Aware Low-Latency Retrieval in Disk-Based Vector Databases
abstract: Embedding models capture both semantic and syntactic structures of queries, often mapping different queries to similar regions in vector space. This results in non-uniform cluster access patterns in modern disk-based vector databases. While existing approaches optimize individual queries, they overlook the impact of cluster access patterns, failing to account for the locality effects of queries that access similar clusters. This oversight increases cache miss penalty. To minimize the cache miss penalty, we propose CALL, a context-aware query grouping mechanism that organizes queries based on shared cluster access patterns. Additionally, CALL incorporates a group-aware prefetching method to minimize cache misses during transitions between query groups and latency-aware cluster loading. Experimental results show that CALL reduces the 99th percentile tail latency by up to 33% while consistently maintaining a higher cache hit ratio, substantially reducing search latency.
technical_mechanism: Group batched queries by overlap in their required cluster IDs, reorder queries to reuse cached clusters, and prefetch clusters needed by the next group at group transitions. A load-weighted greedy packing step balances large cluster reads across worker threads.
why_it_works: Queries that need similar clusters run near one another, increasing cache hits and reducing repeated disk reads. Group-boundary metadata lets the system prefetch upcoming clusters before they are needed; size-aware packing reduces straggler load times. This is a concrete reuse mechanism for comparable retrieval requests, but it reduces storage I/O rather than identifying network delay.
root_seam: A possible Root experiment is to group comparable inference requests by shared required data or model artifacts and measure whether reuse reduces fetches. The paper provides no robot/server transport events, packet or ACK signals, or method for separating network delay from server queueing and compute, so it does not directly diagnose a network tail.
experiment: Implemented in FAISS and evaluated on disk-based IVF vector search with bursty query workloads. Compared against CLRU, WLRU, and FIFO cache policies; measured cache-hit ratio, search latency, grouping time, and cluster-loading latency.
evidence_quote: Instead, our approach shifts caching granularity from individual queries to groups of queries sharing similar cluster access patterns.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Introduction, “Our Approach.”
reported_gain: Up to 33% reduction in 99th-percentile latency versus WLRU on the fever dataset; up to 84% improvement in end-to-end search latency is also reported.
baseline: WLRU, FIFO, and CLRU cache policies; the 33% tail-latency comparison is against WLRU.
uncertainty: The context supports the retrieval-reuse operation and its measured effect, but gives no evidence that the mechanism applies to remote robot inference or exposes network-tail causes.

title: Toward Co-adapting Machine Learning Job Shape and Cluster Topology
abstract: Allocating resources to distributed machine learning jobs in multi-tenant torus-topology clusters must meet each job's specific placement and communication requirements, which are typically described using shapes. There is an inherent tension between minimizing network contention and maximizing cluster utilization when placing various-shaped jobs. While existing schedulers typically optimize for one objective at the expense of the other, we demonstrate that both can be achieved simultaneously. Our proposed approach, RFold, adapts both job shapes and the underlying cluster topology at runtime. This is accomplished by combining two techniques: (1) identifying homomorphic job shapes that support the jobs communication needs, and (2) reconfiguring the optical circuit switch-enabled topology to support more diverse job shapes. Preliminary evaluation performed on a 4096-node torus cluster simulator indicates that RFold can improve absolute cluster utilization by 57% and reduce job completion time by up to 11x relative to existing methods
technical_mechanism: Controlled link-contention perturbation: measure a job’s communication time at a fixed placement, then add a co-runner using the shared link and increase its communication load; the target’s latency response acts as a causal signal of network contention.
why_it_works: Unlike passive timing alone, the intervention changes shared-link load while measuring communication time. The paper reports increasing slowdown as the competing job’s load rises, supporting contention as a cause of delay. This could distinguish a network-contention tail from queue wait when request admission/start and communication intervals are separately measured.
root_seam: At the transport or communication layer, correlate request/job identity with enqueue, start, and communication timestamps. For a reproducible test, hold placement and compute workload fixed while varying competing traffic on a shared link; measure the target’s communication latency separately from queueing, GPU compute, and action application. Root need not access the paper’s private infrastructure.
experiment: Replay matched Root inference requests with fixed placement and compute. Compare an uncontended run with controlled co-runner traffic on the suspected shared path, increasing the co-runner load across trials. Record enqueue-to-start, communication, server queue, GPU, and action-application intervals separately. Test whether the target’s communication tail tracks the induced link load while queue wait remains unchanged.
evidence_quote: When the one job’s communication load was doubled (or tripled), the other measured job’s communication time escalated by 95% (and 186%), respectively.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, TPU v2 placement and shared-link contention experiment, immediately before the RFold section.
reported_gain: Up to 11× lower job completion time versus the reconfiguration-only policy; the paper also reports 57% higher absolute cluster utilization. These are scheduling results, not Root-measured gains.
baseline: Reconfiguration-only policy for the reported job-completion-time comparison; UNKNOWN for the utilization comparison.
uncertainty: The controlled contention experiment supports a transferable causal diagnostic, but the paper does not evaluate Root or decompose end-to-end tails into queueing and network delay. The diagnostic requires identifiable communication intervals and a controllable or reproducible competing-load condition.

title: TWIN: Two window inspection for online change point detection
abstract: We propose a new class of sequential change point tests, both for changes in the mean parameter and in the overall distribution function. The methodology builds on a two-window inspection scheme (TWIN), which aggregates data into symmetric samples and applies strong weighting to enhance statistical performance. The detector yields logarithmic rather than polynomial detection delays, representing a substantial reduction compared to state-of-the-art alternatives. Delays remain short, even for late changes, where existing methods perform worst. Moreover, the new procedure also attains higher power than current methods across broad classes of local alternatives. For mean changes, we further introduce a self-normalized version of the detector that automatically cancels out temporal dependence, eliminating the need to estimate nuisance parameters. The advantages of our approach are supported by asymptotic theory, simulations and an application to monitoring COVID19 data. Here, structural breaks associated with new virus variants are detected almost immediately by our new procedures. This indicates potential value for the real-time monitoring of future epidemics. Mathematically, our approach is underpinned by new exponential moment bounds for the global modulus of continuity of the partial sum process, which may be of independent interest beyond change point testing.
technical_mechanism: Use a sequential two-window inspection (TWIN) change-point detector: aggregate symmetric samples from the monitored time series and apply strong weighting to detect a change in its mean or distribution. Use its alarm as a trigger to start expensive profiling, rather than profiling continuously.
why_it_works: The weighting is designed for short detection delays, including for late changes, while the sequential test controls a specified false-positive level. On Root, the detector could monitor request latency or transport-event metrics and trigger profiling when those metrics shift. It detects a change, not its cause, so network delay would still need to be distinguished from server queueing, GPU compute, and action application using the triggered profile.
root_seam: Attach the detector to a timestamped per-request latency series, or a transport-specific metric if available, and use its alarm to initiate richer tracing for subsequent requests. This offers a candidate low-cost trigger for profiling, but the paper does not establish how to separate network regressions from other latency sources.
experiment: Replay healthy Root request traces, then inject controlled network-delay regressions at varied onset times and magnitudes. Compare TWIN-triggered profiling with continuous profiling and a fixed-threshold trigger, measuring detection delay, false alarms, and profiling overhead; separately label network, queueing, compute, and action-application delays to assess localization.
evidence_quote: The methodology builds on a two-window inspection scheme (TWIN), which aggregates data into symmetric samples and applies strong weighting to enhance statistical performance.
evidence_location: Abstract; also repeated in selected PDF text near the beginning.
reported_gain: The abstract reports logarithmic rather than polynomial detection delays versus state-of-the-art alternatives, but provides no Root-specific gain.
baseline: State-of-the-art alternative sequential change-point methods; the supplied text does not identify a single baseline for the abstract’s gain claim.
uncertainty: No Root or network-latency evaluation is supplied. The detector signals a statistical change but does not identify whether the cause is network delay, server queueing, GPU compute, or action application; trigger overhead and false-alarm behavior on Root metrics are untested.

title: Host-Side Telemetry for Performance Diagnosis in Cloud and HPC GPU Infrastructure
abstract: Diagnosing GPU tail latency spikes in cloud and HPC infrastructure is critical for maintaining performance predictability and resource utilization, yet existing monitoring tools lack the granularity for root cause analysis in shared computing environments. We introduce an eBPF-based telemetry system that provides unified host-side monitoring of GPU workloads, correlating eBPF-derived host metrics with GPU-internal events for holistic system observability. The system achieves 81--88% diagnostic accuracy, detects spikes within 5 seconds, and completes root cause analysis in 6--8 seconds, operating with 1.21% CPU overhead at 100Hz sampling. Evaluated on distributed learning workloads, the system identifies root causes including NIC contention, PCIe pressure, and CPU interference, enabling operational debugging for multi-tenant GPU infrastructure without requiring cluster-wide instrumentation.
technical_mechanism: Synchronize host and GPU telemetry, detect a latency spike at a 3σ threshold, then rank host-side candidate causes by combining each metric's deviation from baseline with its maximum lagged cross-correlation to GPU latency. Signals include NET_RX softirqs and NIC queue lengths, scheduler and block-I/O events, NVML and PCIe metrics, and NCCL phase timestamps.
why_it_works: Temporal correlation between a latency spike and host signals can surface interference coincident with the regression, while the multi-source metric set helps distinguish NIC contention from CPU, I/O, PCIe, or GPU causes. The injected NIC-burst experiment supports diagnosis of NIC-related interference, but the correlation is evidence of temporal association rather than request-to-packet causality.
root_seam: Attach host-side eBPF probes for NET_RX softirqs and NIC queue lengths, and correlate their timestamped signals with robot request latency and server-side inference-stage timestamps. This could indicate whether a tail coincides with NIC activity rather than compute, but would not by itself reconstruct a request's packets or prove causation.
experiment: On a controlled robot-to-server inference workload, inject NIC contention and separately inject server/GPU compute delay while recording request latency, server-stage timestamps, NET_RX activity, and NIC queue lengths. Test whether the correlation ranking identifies the injected network cause and separates it from compute delay; compare against latency-only diagnosis.
evidence_quote: When a spike is detected, it calculates a "spike score" for each metric indicating deviation from baseline, then computes lagged cross-correlation between GPU latency and host metrics to identify temporally related signals.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, §2.2 Diagnosis and Correlation
reported_gain: 84.7% mean diagnostic accuracy with 1.21% CPU overhead; NIC-burst accuracy 88.1%.
baseline: Compared with GPU-centric monitoring (62.8% accuracy), cluster-level analysis (68.3%), and deep profiling (82.1%); the paper reports 30–50 seconds to RCA for offline cluster analysis versus 6–8 seconds for its system.
uncertainty: The evaluation uses controlled, single-node GPU experiments and NCCL workloads, not robot inference. The context does not establish request-level network attribution, causal identification of off-path flows, or direct separation of network transit delay from server queueing and GPU compute.

title: Distributed Incast Detection in Data Center Networks
abstract: Incast traffic in data centers can lead to severe performance degradation, such as packet loss and increased latency. Effectively addressing incast requires prompt and accurate detection. Existing solutions, including MA-ECN, BurstRadar and Pulser, typically rely on fixed thresholds of switch port egress queue lengths or their gradients to identify microburst caused by incast flows. However, these queue length related methods often suffer from delayed detection and high error rates. In this study, we propose a distributed incast detection method for data center networks at the switch-level, leveraging a probabilistic hypothesis test with an optimal detection threshold. By analyzing the arrival intervals of new flows, our algorithm can immediately determine if a flow is part of an incast traffic from its initial packet. The experimental results demonstrate that our method offers significant improvements over existing approaches in both detection speed and inference accuracy.
technical_mechanism: DIDIE detects a specific network-congestion pattern from flow-arrival timing and destination identity: at a switch, it compares the interval between consecutive flows with a threshold and checks whether their destination IPs match, using a probabilistic hypothesis test with a threshold selected from an ROC-based cost function. It can flag an incast flow from its first packet and retroactively reclassify the leading flow when a subsequent flow confirms the pattern. This is early incast diagnosis, not a general detector of queue buildup or network latency.
why_it_works: Closely timed flows sharing a destination are evidence of many-to-one incast. Unlike queue-length thresholds, which wait for traffic to accumulate and can be affected by background traffic, this signal can identify the incast pattern before queue buildup is the detection input. For Root, that offers a way to test whether a network-side tail coincides with a specific fan-in traffic pattern; it does not by itself establish that a request’s delay was network rather than server queueing, compute, or action application.
root_seam: At a server-side switch or packet-capture point, associate request identities with flow first-packet arrival timestamps and destination IPs. Compare DIDIE flags against request latency and independently measured transport, server-queue, compute, and action-application intervals. This would add an early, interpretable incast signal without requiring queue-length telemetry, but requires suitable packet-event visibility.
experiment: Replay or shape controlled many-to-one traffic toward the inference server, varying fan-in and arrival offsets, alongside regular background traffic. In separate trials, introduce server-queue and GPU-compute delays without incast. Measure DIDIE flag timing and false positives against request-level tail events and independently timed network and server stages; compare with queue-length and queue-gradient thresholds where available. Treat this as a Root experiment, not a gain reported by the paper.
evidence_quote: By analyzing the arrival intervals of new flows, our algorithm can immediately determine if a flow is part of an incast traffic from its initial packet.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Abstract; the arrival-interval and same-destination rule is in Section III, Problem Formulation, and the probabilistic test and threshold selection are in Section IV, Proposed Method.
reported_gain: Paper-reported simulation result: in the mixed FB_Hadoop traffic experiment, DIDIE reports average detection times of 1.2 ns at 60% sender load and 2.7 ns at 30% sender load, with 0% FPR in both cases. These are incast-detection results, not Root gains.
baseline: Queue-length threshold and queue-length-gradient threshold methods. In the mixed-traffic experiment at 60% sender load, the paper reports 31,766 ns average detection time and 14.3% FPR for a 10 KB queue-length threshold, and 14,169 ns and 25.0% FPR for a 3 GB/s queue-gradient threshold.
uncertainty: The detector targets many-to-one incast under the paper’s traffic assumptions; it does not diagnose general network tails or directly measure per-request network delay. Root transfer depends on access to suitable switch-side or packet-event timing and destination information. The reported evaluation is in NS-3, not a remote-robot inference system.

title: P4-TAS: P4-Based Time-Aware Shaper for Time-Sensitive Networking
abstract: Time-sensitive networking (TSN) is a set of IEEE standards that extends Ethernet with real-time capabilities. Among its mechanisms, the time-aware shaper (TAS) periodically opens and closes egress queues to protect scheduled traffic from lower-priority flows, ensuring low latency and bounded delay. Deterministic networking (DetNet), standardized by the IETF, provides similar guarantees at Layer 3 and can leverage TSN mechanisms such as the TAS. Commercially available TSN-capable switches implement TAS in hardware but rarely disclose internal delays in the TAS mechanism itself. Such delays directly affect scheduling precision, yet information about them is largely unavailable to system designers. In this work, we present P4-TAS, a P4-based implementation of the TAS on the Intel Tofino 2 switching ASIC that additionally supports per-stream filtering and policing (PSFP) and PTP time synchronization. First, we design a novel mechanism for periodic queue control that uses a continuous stream of internally generated control frames for time-triggered queue state updates. To the best of our knowledge, this enables TAS on a P4-programmable ASIC for the first time. P4-TAS additionally provides an MPLS/TSN translation layer that enables TSN time-based shaping to be applied at the boundary between TSN and DetNet domains, supporting line rates up to 400 Gb/s per port. Second, we identify and quantify three sources of internal delay that affect the precision of TAS gate transitions, providing transparency that enables more accurate TAS configuration. Our evaluation demonstrates a worst-case accumulated internal delay of 86 ns between time slices, which is well below values reported for commercial switches. Third, we propose a measurement methodology to externally measure TAS time slice accuracy, and introduce gate switching intervals (GSIs) to mitigate overlap between consecutive time slices.
technical_mechanism: Infer actual time-aware-shaper (TAS) time-slice boundaries and durations by detecting priority transitions in shaped output traffic on a dedicated measurement switch, then compare those observed intervals with configured intervals. This is black-box measurement of network gate timing, not ordinary request tracing or latency thresholding.
why_it_works: The output traffic exposes when scheduled queue gates actually take effect. Comparing observed transitions with configured boundaries reveals gate-transition timing error and overlap, providing a concrete way to detect network scheduling delay without switch-internal telemetry. It isolates a network-side timing contribution, but does not itself attribute an inference request’s end-to-end tail or distinguish server queueing and GPU compute.
root_seam: Attach synchronized timestamps and request or flow identity at robot-side and server-side packet observation points. On a TAS-shaped path, record packet priorities or equivalent observable traffic classes at egress and compare inferred gate intervals with the schedule; correlate interval deviations with request tails and server/GPU timings. This can localize scheduling delay without assuming access to Reflex’s private switch infrastructure.
experiment: In a controlled Root test, send timestamped inference-like traffic through a TAS-shaped path while varying configured slice boundaries and contention. Detect output priority transitions with an independent measurement point, compare inferred and configured intervals, and correlate discrepancies with request-level tail latency while separately recording server queueing, GPU compute, and action-application time. Include a no-TAS or unchanged-schedule condition as a control.
evidence_quote: The methodology uses a dedicated measurement switch that detects time slice boundaries in the shaped output traffic to determine the actual duration of individual time slices.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Introduction, contribution describing the external measurement methodology; corroborated in Evaluation of P4-TAS, subsection “Measurement Results.”
reported_gain: Worst-case accumulated internal delay of about 86 ns between tGCL entries; with gate switching intervals, mean externally measured slice-duration deviation was −18 ns.
baseline: No controlled quantitative baseline comparison is provided; the paper cites microsecond-scale gate-transition delays reported for some commercial TSN switches.
uncertainty: The measurement diagnoses TAS gate timing, not arbitrary network tails or request-level causality. Root would need observable traffic classes and synchronized measurement points, and the inferred network timing must be correlated with request identity and separated from server and GPU timing.

title: PLATONT: Learning a Platonic Representation for Unified Network Tomography
abstract: Network tomography aims to infer hidden network states, such as link performance, traffic load, and topology, from external observations. Most existing methods solve these problems separately and depend on limited task-specific signals, which limits generalization and interpretability. We present PLATONT, a unified framework that models different network indicators (e.g., delay, loss, bandwidth) as projections of a shared latent network state. Guided by the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, PLATONT learns this latent state through multimodal alignment and contrastive learning. By training multiple tomography tasks within a shared latent space, it builds compact and structured representations that improve cross-task generalization. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that PLATONT consistently outperforms existing methods in link estimation, topology inference, and traffic prediction, achieving higher accuracy and stronger robustness under varying network conditions.
technical_mechanism: Multi-indicator network tomography: encode path delay, loss, and bandwidth as aligned views of a shared network state, then use tomography tasks to infer per-link performance and identify congested links from path-level observations.
why_it_works: A request tail can reflect congestion on an internal link shared with other flows, even when Root cannot directly observe that link. Combining correlated path indicators and inferring per-link congestion can expose a candidate shared bottleneck rather than merely reporting that end-to-end latency was high. The paper specifically evaluates congested-link diagnosis, making this more than a general representation-learning proposal.
root_seam: Attach timestamped request and transport measurements to the robot-to-server path; collect path delay, loss, and bandwidth observations, plus a path-to-link mapping or candidate topology. Use inferred congested links to identify shared-resource candidates. Keep server queueing, GPU time, and action-application time separately timestamped so they are not attributed to network delay.
experiment: In a controlled Root setup with a known path topology, vary competing traffic on selected shared links and issue timestamped inference requests. Feed path delay, loss, and bandwidth observations to the multi-indicator tomography model; test whether it identifies the deliberately congested link for tail requests. Compare against single-indicator tomography and no-tomography baselines, and independently measure server queueing, GPU compute, and action application. This tests diagnostic localization, not a Root latency improvement.
evidence_quote: We select congested link identification as a representative evaluation metric, as it is a classical and widely-studied problem in network tomography that directly impacts network management decisions.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Experiment Results, subsection D, “Link Performance Estimation.”
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: Range tomography is named as the link-performance inference baseline; the supplied text gives no numerical comparison against it.
uncertainty: The paper supports inferring congested links from network measurements, but does not establish attribution of an individual inference request's tail to a link or distinguish network delay from server-side delay. Root would need suitable path measurements and topology or path-to-link information; results on the paper's datasets do not establish a Root-measured gain.

title: Causal Intervention Sequence Analysis for Fault Tracking in Radio Access Networks
abstract: To keep modern Radio Access Networks (RAN) running smoothly, operators need to spot the real-world triggers behind Service-Level Agreement (SLA) breaches well before customers feel them. We introduce an AI/ML pipeline that does two things most tools miss: (1) finds the likely root-cause indicators and (2) reveals the exact order in which those events unfold. We start by labeling network data: records linked to past SLA breaches are marked `abnormal', and everything else `normal'. Our model then learns the causal chain that turns normal behavior into a fault. In Monte Carlo tests the approach pinpoints the correct trigger sequence with high precision and scales to millions of data points without loss of speed. These results show that high-resolution, causally ordered insights can move fault management from reactive troubleshooting to proactive prevention.
technical_mechanism: Select candidate indicators linked to the SLA condition using root-cause discovery, build a causal subgraph for those indicators from normal behavior, then compare normal and abnormal time-series distributions and order detected deviation onsets using K-S tests and Z-scores. The earliest detected deviation is treated as the likely root cause.
why_it_works: This is more than anomaly logging: causal selection narrows the indicators to inspect, while distributional deviation tests identify which selected indicators changed and when their anomalies began. That gives a concrete differential/first-divergence operation that could be tested on matched healthy and tail inference requests. The paper demonstrates the operation on RAN indicators, but not on individual requests.
root_seam: Attach request identities and synchronized timestamps to robot/server transport events and inference-stage events. Use healthy requests as the normal reference and tail requests as abnormal, applying causal candidate selection and onset ordering to distinguish transport divergence from queueing, GPU compute, and action application.
experiment: On a fixed inference workload, collect request-identified healthy and tail samples with timestamped transport, queue, GPU, and action-application events. Apply the paper’s candidate-selection, normal-state subgraph, and K-S/Z-score onset-ordering procedure. Check whether the earliest deviation localizes to network transport, and compare localization with ordinary latency tracing and PCMCI-style normal-versus-abnormal graph comparison.
evidence_quote: The third component applies univariate deviation detection on the time series data of the selected intervention variables, identified as root cause candidates in the second component to capture the temporal anomaly events comprising the sequence of the intervention incidents that led to the SLA violation and identify the earliest event as the most likely root cause
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section III.A, Summary
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: PCMCI applied separately to normal and abnormal data; the paper reports qualitatively that PCMCI-only results were much worse than the proposed RCD plus Z-score and K-S approach.
uncertainty: The paper uses RAN KPI time series aggregated at 15-second granularity, not per-request remote-inference traces. It does not establish request-level attribution or demonstrate separation of network delay from server queueing and compute. Root-specific effectiveness remains to be tested.

title: A Simple and Effective Framework for Symmetric Consistent Indexing in Large-Scale Dense Retrieval
abstract: Dense retrieval has become the industry standard in large-scale information retrieval systems due to its high efficiency and competitive accuracy. Its core relies on a coarse-to-fine hierarchical architecture that enables rapid candidate selection and precise semantic matching, achieving millisecond-level response over billion-scale corpora. This capability makes it essential not only in traditional search and recommendation scenarios but also in the emerging paradigm of generative recommendation driven by large language models, where semantic IDs-themselves a form of coarse-to-fine representation-play a foundational role. However, the widely adopted dual-tower encoding architecture introduces inherent challenges, primarily representational space misalignment and retrieval index inconsistency, which degrade matching accuracy, retrieval stability, and performance on long-tail queries. These issues are further magnified in semantic ID generation, ultimately limiting the performance ceiling of downstream generative models. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a simple and effective framework named SCI comprising two synergistic modules: a symmetric representation alignment module that employs an innovative input-swapping mechanism to unify the dual-tower representation space without adding parameters, and an consistent indexing with dual-tower synergy module that redesigns retrieval paths using a dual-view indexing strategy to maintain consistency from training to inference. The framework is systematic, lightweight, and engineering-friendly, requiring minimal overhead while fully supporting billion-scale deployment. We provide theoretical guarantees for our approach, with its effectiveness validated by results across public datasets and real-world e-commerce datasets.
technical_mechanism: Consistent dual-view ANN indexing: cluster items using query-tower embeddings, then use item-tower embeddings for within-cluster residual quantization. This aligns coarse lookup with the query representation while retaining item representations for fine retrieval.
why_it_works: Queries and coarse cluster centers occupy the same representation space, making relevant clusters more likely to be searched. This can preserve retrieval quality with a smaller search scope, enabling a faster comparable retrieval baseline.
root_seam: Could be adapted where Root needs a fast comparable retrieval baseline: build or configure the ANN index with query-aligned coarse clusters and measure retrieval quality and cost at matched search scopes. It does not directly identify or localize network delay.
experiment: Compare standard Bert2Tower IVF-PQ against the dual-view index on the same workload. Sweep nprobe and measure Recall/MRR and search cost or latency, checking whether the SCI index reaches comparable ranking quality at a smaller search scope.
evidence_quote: CI at nprobe=8 achieves an MRR@100 of 0.3613, a value comparable to the baseline which requires a larger search scope of nprobe=16 to reach a similar score of 0.3829.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, IVF-PQ results following Section 4.4.
reported_gain: At nprobe=1, Recall@10 improves by 18% relative to the traditional index; at nprobe=8, the reported MRR@100 is comparable to the baseline at nprobe=16, indicating approximately half the search scope for similar ranking quality.
baseline: Bert2Tower with a traditional IVF-PQ index.
uncertainty: The reported efficiency comparison is based on search scope, not a direct wall-clock latency measurement. Transfer to Root is limited to faster comparable retrieval; the paper does not diagnose network tails.

title: Long-term Monitoring of Kernel and Hardware Events to Understand Latency Variance
abstract: This paper presents our experience to understand latency variance caused by kernel and hardware events, which are often invisible at the application level. For this purpose, we have built VarMRI, a tool chain to monitor and analyze those events in the long term. To mitigate the "big data" problem caused by long-term monitoring, VarMRI selectively records a subset of events following two principles: it only records events that are affecting the requests recorded by the application; it records coarse-grained information first and records additional information only when necessary. Furthermore, VarMRI introduces an analysis method that is efficient on large amount of data, robust on different data set and against missing data, and informative to the user. VarMRI has helped us to carry out a 3,000-hour study of six applications and benchmarks on CloudLab. It reveals a wide variety of events causing latency variance, including interrupt preemption, Java GC, pipeline stall, NUMA balancing etc.; simple optimization or tuning can reduce tail latencies by up to 31%. Furthermore, the impacts of some of these events vary significantly across different experiments, which confirms the necessity of long-term monitoring.
technical_mechanism: VarMRI records kernel and hardware events only for application-selected requests, at thread granularity, starting with low-overhead cumulative event counts and lengths. Its impact analysis compares request latency variance with and without high event values, then applies event-type rules to adjust for correlated causes. More detailed timing or call-stack data is collected when needed. For network-related diagnosis, this can expose NIC interrupt lengths and sendmsg-related kernel instructions associated with request tails.
why_it_works: Request-scoped recording connects kernel and hardware activity to application work while avoiding machine-wide event traces. Coarse cumulative measurements reduce recording cost; comparing latency for requests with and without high event values helps prioritize candidate causes, and further detail can narrow an investigation. The reported Memcached results associate high p99 latency with high p99 interrupt lengths and suggest burstier interrupts affect a small number of requests. This can reveal server-side network-stack interference, but does not identify packet-level delay or establish whether network behavior caused the interrupt burstiness.
root_seam: Attach request identity and start/stop recording to the robot inference request's server-side worker thread. Retain coarse event counts and lengths alongside request latency, including NIC interrupt activity; collect timing or call stacks for selected tail requests when coarse data flags a candidate. This could distinguish server-side interrupt/preemption or sendmsg overhead from other request processing, but Root would still need transport timestamps or packet/ACK/loss evidence to separate network transit delay from server-side delay.
experiment: Replay robot inference requests with request-level tail selection. Compare VarMRI-style thread-scoped cumulative event recording against a no-recording run for trace volume, throughput, and p99 latency; then compare tail and non-tail requests for NIC interrupt lengths and sendmsg-related kernel activity. For requests flagged by coarse data, collect detailed event timing or call stacks and compare against transport-side timestamps to test whether the delay is server-side or in network transit.
evidence_quote: VarMRI records cumulative values of kernel and hardware events first, and then records their exact timing or call stacks only when necessary.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, section 4.1, “VarMRI’s approaches”; network example in section 6.3, “Memcached.”
reported_gain: Up to 31% tail-latency reduction from simple optimizations or tuning across the study. Separately, recording events for 1% of Memcached requests generated 1MB of trace per second and reduced maximal throughput by 0.49%, with no observable p99 impact. These are paper-reported results, not Root measurements.
baseline: For the up-to-31% result, the abstract does not specify a single comparison baseline. For the recording-overhead result, the throughput comparison baseline is not specified; the paper reports no observable p99 impact.
uncertainty: The method diagnoses kernel and hardware events, not packet sequences or end-to-end transport delay. The paper says interrupt burstiness may be affected by network behavior but that this is beyond its scope. The request-level selection trigger and the detailed conditions for escalating to timing or call-stack recording are not fully specified in the supplied text.

title: A Survey of Real-Time Support, Analysis, and Advancements in ROS 2
abstract: The Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2) has emerged as a relevant middleware framework for robotic applications, offering modularity, distributed execution, and communication. In the last six years, ROS 2 has drawn increasing attention from the real-time systems community and industry. This survey presents a comprehensive overview of research efforts that analyze, enhance, and extend ROS 2 to support real-time execution. We first provide a detailed description of the internal scheduling mechanisms of ROS 2 and its layered architecture, including the interaction with DDS-based communication and other communication middleware. We then review key contributions from the literature, covering timing analysis for both single- and multi-threaded executors, metrics such as response time, reaction time, and data age, and different communication modes. The survey also discusses community-driven enhancements to the ROS 2 runtime, including new executor algorithm designs, real-time GPU management, and microcontroller support via micro-ROS. Furthermore, we summarize techniques for bounding DDS communication delays, message filters, and profiling tools that have been developed to support analysis and experimentation. To help systematize this growing body of work, we introduce taxonomies that classify the surveyed contributions based on different criteria. This survey aims to guide both researchers and practitioners in understanding and improving the real-time capabilities of ROS 2.
technical_mechanism: Correlate distributed ROS 2 publication, reception, and callback trace events into message-flow causal links, then use their timestamps to inspect end-to-end and communication intervals.
why_it_works: Causal links and event timing let Root locate where a request's latency accumulates across a distributed ROS 2 pipeline, rather than treating end-to-end delay as one opaque measurement. Transport-related intervals can be compared with callback execution intervals, though the survey does not establish that all network delay can be separated from DDS or host-side delay.
root_seam: Attach tracing at robot-side publish and server-side receive events, keyed by message identity, and correlate them with callback execution timestamps. This could localize delay to a communication interval versus application processing without assuming access to private infrastructure.
experiment: Replay a robot-to-server ROS 2 inference request stream while injecting controlled network delay, jitter, and loss. Compare traced publication-to-reception intervals and callback intervals against packet-level timestamps and ground truth; test whether injected tail events are localized to communication rather than compute or queueing.
evidence_quote: The extended tool can automatically detect one-to-one and one-to-many causal links between received and published messages for direct links
evidence_location: selected_pdf_text, paragraph beginning “Bédard et al. [11] developed ros2_tracing”
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: This is a survey summarizing tracing approaches, not a paper presenting one evaluated tail-diagnosis method. The context does not report rare-network-delay detection or localization accuracy; n13 also lacks a robot-to-cloud-specific evaluation.

title: ProfInfer: An eBPF-based Fine-Grained LLM Inference Profiler
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) move from research to production, understanding how inference engines behave in real time has become both essential and elusive. Unlike general-purpose engines such as ONNX Runtime, today's LLM inference systems offer little operator-level visibility, leaving developers blind to where time and resources go. Even basic questions -- is this workload memory-bound or compute-bound? -- often remain unanswered. To close this gap, we develop a fine-grained, non-intrusive profiling framework for modern LLM inference engines, exemplified by llama-cpp but applicable to similar runtime architectures. Built on extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) technology, our system dynamically attaches probes to runtime functions across multiple layers -- without modifying or recompiling the source. It transforms collected traces into rich visualizations of operators, graphs, timelines, and hardware counter trends, exposing how dense inference, Mixture-of-Experts routing, and operator offloading behave in practice. With less than 4% runtime overhead and high profiling fidelity, our framework makes LLM inference both transparent and diagnosable, turning performance profiling into a practical tool for optimization, scheduling, and resource-aware deployment.
technical_mechanism: Correlate inference-thread scheduler state with runtime timings: eBPF scheduler tracepoints identify when an inference thread is runnable versus running, while function-entry/return probes time inference work. At Root, pairing server-side scheduling and compute intervals with robot/server request-boundary timestamps could separate server scheduling or compute delay from the remaining transport delay.
why_it_works: A slow request alone does not reveal whether time was spent waiting for server CPU, executing inference, or in transport. Scheduler-state events can expose runnable-but-not-running intervals, and runtime probes can measure instrumented inference intervals. With request-boundary timestamps, Root could compare those server-side intervals against end-to-end time and test whether the residual tracks injected network delay. The paper does not itself measure transport or establish request-to-packet causality.
root_seam: On the server, attach filtered scheduler tracepoints to inference-thread identities and timestamp inference/runtime boundaries; associate those events with request IDs and robot send/receive plus server receive/respond timestamps. This adds server scheduling-state evidence and avoids treating all latency outside measured compute as network without checking the boundaries.
experiment: Replay controlled requests while independently injecting network delay, server CPU contention that leaves inference threads runnable, and inference compute slowdown. Compare boundary timestamps and scheduler/runtime intervals against ground truth. Check whether network delay increases the unaccounted transport interval, contention increases runnable-but-not-running time, and compute slowdown increases measured execution time; measure tracing overhead.
evidence_quote: The handlers of these tracepoints can read the state of a thread, i.e., running, runnable, or idle.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, §3.3.4, “Scheduler tracing.”
reported_gain: ProfInfer reports less than 4% runtime overhead in the abstract; this is not a Root gain.
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The paper traces scheduler events for inference threads and measures runtime intervals, but does not instrument network events, correlate traces to remote request identities, or demonstrate network-versus-server decomposition. Root would need endpoint timestamps and request association; the proposed experiment tests whether those additions make the separation reliable.

title: Camel: Frame-Level Bandwidth Estimation for Low-Latency Live Streaming under Video Bitrate Undershooting
abstract: Low-latency live streaming (LLS) has emerged as a popular web application, with many platforms adopting real-time protocols such as WebRTC to minimize end-to-end latency. However, we observe a counter-intuitive phenomenon: even when the actual encoded bitrate does not fully utilize the available bandwidth, stalling events remain frequent. This insufficient bandwidth utilization arises from the intrinsic temporal variations of real-time video encoding, which cause conventional packet-level congestion control algorithms to misestimate available bandwidth. When a high-bitrate frame is suddenly produced, sending at the wrong rate can either trigger packet loss or increase queueing delay, resulting in playback stalls. To address these issues, we present Camel, a novel frame-level congestion control algorithm (CCA) tailored for LLS. Our insight is to use frame-level network feedback to capture the true network capacity, immune to the irregular sending pattern caused by encoding. Camel comprises three key modules: the Bandwidth and Delay Estimator and the Congestion Detector, which jointly determine the average sending rate, and the Bursting Length Controller, which governs the emission pattern to prevent packet loss. We evaluate Camel on both large-scale real-world deployments and controlled simulations. In the real-world platform with 250M users and 2B sessions across 150+ countries, Camel achieves up to a 70.8% increase in 1080P resolution ratio, a 14.4% increase in media bitrate, and up to a 14.1% reduction in stalling ratio. In simulations under undershooting, shallow buffers, and network jitter, Camel outperforms existing congestion control algorithms, with up to 19.8% higher bitrate, 93.0% lower stalling ratio, and 23.9% improvement in bandwidth estimation accuracy.
technical_mechanism: Frame-level transport congestion detection: aggregate feedback by frame, use the first packet's RTT as a less burst-distorted delay signal, and infer congestion from the gradient of frame-level delay against bytes in flight. The bandwidth estimator and burst-length controller prepare and use these signals, but the detector is the diagnostic operation.
why_it_works: The first packet's RTT is less affected by queueing induced by later packets in its burst. Measuring delay change against in-flight bytes, rather than packet time order, provides a signal for queue buildup while reducing interference from adjacent frames and encoder-driven idle gaps. This can expose network congestion associated with increased in-flight data, rather than merely logging end-to-end latency.
root_seam: At the robot or server transport endpoint, associate request/frame identity with RTCP-like feedback or packet/ACK timestamps, RTT, and bytes in flight. Root could test whether the delay-versus-inflight signal flags network queueing on tail requests; compare it with server queue time, GPU time, and action-application time to avoid attributing those delays to the network. The paper does not require access to Reflex's private infrastructure.
experiment: Replay comparable inference requests in a controlled Root test with induced jitter, bandwidth changes, and shallow buffers, alongside conditions that increase server queueing or compute time without changing the network. Record per-request transport feedback, first-packet RTT, bytes in flight, and end-to-end latency. Evaluate whether the frame/request-level delay gradient identifies network-delayed tails and reduces false attribution compared with packet-level estimates and end-to-end latency alone.
evidence_quote: we compute the gradient of frame-level delay with respect to the number of bytes in flight. If this gradient exceeds a predefined threshold, congestion is inferred
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, §4.2, Congestion Detector
reported_gain: In simulations, up to 23.9% improvement in bandwidth-estimation accuracy and 93.0% lower stalling ratio; these are paper-reported streaming results, not Root gains.
baseline: Simulation comparisons included GCC, BBR, Copa, Pudica, SQP, and Salsify; real-world A/B testing compared Camel with the platform's BBR-based variant.
uncertainty: The paper supports frame-level congestion inference and evaluates network jitter, but does not evaluate remote inference request tails or prove localization against server queueing and compute. The congestion gradient is a thresholded signal, not a complete causal diagnosis.

title: Asynchronous Verified Semantic Caching for Tiered LLM Architectures
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) now sit in the critical path of search, assistance, and agentic workflows, making semantic caching essential for reducing inference cost and latency. Production deployments typically use a tiered static-dynamic design: a static cache of curated, offline vetted responses mined from logs, backed by a dynamic cache populated online. In practice, both tiers are commonly governed by a single embedding similarity threshold, which induces a hard tradeoff: conservative thresholds miss safe reuse opportunities, while aggressive thresholds risk serving semantically incorrect responses. We introduce Krites, an asynchronous, LLM-judged caching policy that expands static coverage without changing serving decisions. On the critical path, Krites behaves exactly like a standard static threshold policy. When the nearest static neighbor of the prompt falls just below the static threshold, Krites asynchronously invokes an LLM judge to verify whether the static response is acceptable for the new prompt. Approved matches are promoted into the dynamic cache, allowing future repeats and paraphrases to reuse curated static answers and expanding static reach over time. In trace-driven simulations on conversational and search workloads, Krites increases the fraction of requests served with curated static answers (direct static hits plus verified promotions) by up to3.9 times for conversational traffic and search-style queries relative to tuned baselines, with unchanged critical path latency.
technical_mechanism: On a static-cache miss whose nearest embedding neighbor falls in a similarity grey zone, asynchronously ask an LLM judge whether the curated answer is acceptable. If approved, promote that answer into the dynamic cache under the new prompt key so future repeats or paraphrases can reuse it without changing the triggering request's serving path.
why_it_works: The judge recovers safe reuse opportunities that a conservative similarity threshold would reject. Promotion makes the approved answer available through the dynamic cache on later requests, avoiding backend inference for those requests while keeping verification off the critical path.
root_seam: For remote robot inference, a request identity and prompt could anchor a semantic cache lookup and verified promotion, potentially avoiding a remote inference call for repeated or equivalent requests. This could reduce exposure to network delay, but it does not diagnose or localize a network tail; Root would need separate transport and server timing to distinguish avoided network time from queueing or compute.
experiment: Trace-driven simulations on conversational and search workloads compared Krites with tuned static-threshold baselines using the same embeddings, thresholds, and request order. The simulations used benchmark equivalence classes as an oracle judge. A separate 100-pair human-audited sample assessed a concrete LLM judge.
evidence_quote: When the nearest static neighbor of the prompt falls just below the static threshold, Krites asynchronously invokes an LLM judge to verify whether the static response is acceptable for the new prompt. Approved matches are promoted into the dynamic cache
evidence_location: Abstract; selected PDF text, Sections 3.1 and 3.3 describe the grey-zone trigger and auxiliary overwrite.
reported_gain: Static-origin serves increased from 8.2% to 19.4% (+136.5%) on SemCacheLMArena and from 2.2% to 8.6% (+290.3%) on SemCacheSearchQueries; unchanged critical-path latency is reported.
baseline: Tuned GPTCache-style static-threshold policy, using the same embeddings, ground-truth labels, and thresholds.
uncertainty: Headline simulations use an oracle judge derived from benchmark equivalence classes, not an LLM judge in the simulation loop. The 99/100 agreement result comes from a small human-audited sample. The work evaluates cache reuse, not network-tail diagnosis.

title: High-Fidelity Network Management for Federated AI-as-a-Service: Cross-Domain Orchestration
abstract: To support the emergence of AI-as-a-Service (AIaaS), communication service providers (CSPs) are on the verge of a radical transformation-from pure connectivity providers to AIaaS a managed network service (control-and-orchestration plane that exposes AI models). In this model, the CSP is responsible not only for transport/communications, but also for intent-to-model resolution and joint network-compute orchestration, i.e., reliable and timely end-to-end delivery. The resulting end-to-end AIaaS service thus becomes governed by communications impairments (delay, loss) and inference impairments (latency, error).
