A central open problem is an operational AIaaS control-and-orchestration framework that enforces high fidelity, particularly under multi-domain federation. This paper introduces an assurance-oriented AIaaS management plane based on Tail-Risk Envelopes (TREs): signed, composable per-domain descriptors that combine deterministic guardrails with stochastic rate-latency-impairment models. Using stochastic network calculus, we derive bounds on end-to-end delay violation probabilities across tandem domains and obtain an optimization-ready risk-budget decomposition. We show that tenant-level reservations prevent bursty traffic from inflating tail latency under TRE contracts. An auditing layer then uses runtime telemetry to estimate extreme-percentile performance, quantify uncertainty, and attribute tail-risk to each domain for accountability. Packet-level Monte-Carlo simulations demonstrate improved p99.9 compliance under overload via admission control and robust tenant isolation under correlated burstiness.
technical_mechanism: Controlled domain degradation with marginal tail attribution: scale domain service rates, measure the resulting change in end-to-end p99.9 delay, and attribute tail growth to the domains with the largest marginal contribution.
why_it_works: This goes beyond observing that the end-to-end tail worsened: a controlled change to domain capacity tests which domain’s degradation most affects the tail. That makes a useful, coarse causal diagnostic for rare-delay investigations. The paper supports the mechanism in simulation, though it does not isolate network delay from compute delay or establish packet-level diagnosis.
root_seam: Attach at Root’s request-level end-to-end latency measurement and the robot/server transport or service-domain boundary. During a controlled test, perturb network capacity or impairment in one domain at a time and compare the resulting p99.9 tail change with the unperturbed path. This could identify which segment drives tail growth without full internal tracing; separate measurements are still needed to distinguish transport from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application.
experiment: Replay a representative remote-inference workload and inject controlled delay, loss, or capacity degradation into one transport segment at a time, plus separate server-side queue or compute perturbations. Measure end-to-end p99.9 and per-stage timings against an unperturbed control, then test whether marginal tail changes correctly identify the perturbed segment. Do not treat the paper’s simulation result as a Root gain.
evidence_quote: The marginal decomposition further shows that not all domains contribute equally to the tail increase: the most capacity-critical domain(s) account for a disproportionate share of ∆Q0.999(D)
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section V, Simulation Results, Results discussion of controlled domain degradation.
reported_gain: Qualitatively, controlled domain degradation increases p99.9 delay and marginal attribution identifies disproportionate contributions from capacity-critical domains; no numeric attribution gain is provided.
baseline: Nominal service rates (s = 1) for the domain-degradation comparison.
uncertainty: The paper does not specify the marginal attribution formula in the supplied text, and its impairment model covers both network and compute. The simulation varies domain service rates, not packet loss or transport events; Root would need controlled interventions and stage-specific measurements to establish network-specific localization. No Root-measured gain is available.

title: Spritz: Path-Aware Load Balancing in Low-Diameter Networks
abstract: Low-diameter topologies such as Dragonfly and Slim Fly are increasingly adopted in HPC and datacenter networks, yet existing load balancing techniques either rely on proprietary in-network mechanisms or fail to utilize the full path diversity of these topologies. We introduce Spritz, a flexible sender-based load balancing framework that shifts adaptive topology-aware routing to the endpoints using only standard Ethernet features. We propose two algorithms, Spritz-Scout and Spritz-Spray that, respectively, explore and adaptively cache efficient paths using ECN, packet trimming, and timeout feedback. Through simulation on Dragonfly and Slim Fly topologies with over 1000 endpoints, Spritz outperforms ECMP, UGAL-L, and prior sender-based approaches by up to 1.8x in flow completion time under AI training and datacenter workloads, while offering robust failover with performance improvements of up to 25.4x under link failures, all without additional hardware support. Spritz enables datacenter-scale, commodity Ethernet networks to efficiently leverage low-diameter topologies, offering unified routing and load balancing for the Ultra Ethernet era.
technical_mechanism: Per-path ACK/ECN and loss-feedback filtering: associate transport feedback with the sender-selected path, retain paths receiving clean ACKs, count ECN marks, and remove paths on sustained ECN, NACK, or timeout; a timeout also temporarily blocks that path.
why_it_works: The feedback is tied to a specific path, so worsening ECN or loss signals can implicate a transport route without collecting a full trace. This is a network-condition signal, not a direct measurement of end-to-end delay: it cannot by itself separate network delay from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application. A controlled Root experiment can join path-tagged feedback to request IDs and compare affected and healthy requests while measuring those other stages separately.
root_seam: At the transport sender, record request or flow identity alongside selected path entropy and per-path ACK/ECN, trim/NACK, and timeout events. This could show whether tail requests share a path with rising congestion or loss, avoiding full packet-trace collection. It requires transport/path visibility and a reliable mapping from inference requests to flows; the paper does not demonstrate request-level localization.
experiment: Replay matched inference requests through controllable alternate paths with induced congestion and loss. Join request IDs to selected paths and feedback, then assess whether path feedback identifies network-impaired requests against ordinary request logging. Independently measure transport time, server queueing, GPU compute, and action-application time; compare localization accuracy and trace-collection volume. The paper reports no Root measurements.
evidence_quote: Each sent packet may result in one of the following outcomes: • ACK (no ECN mark): Good path. • ACK (ECN mark): Congestion is building up.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section IV-A, “Spritz-Scout,” Feedback Logic description; Algorithm 2 and its accompanying explanation.
reported_gain: Up to 1.8x flow completion time improvement; up to 25.4x under link failures (paper-reported load-balancing results, not diagnostic gains).
baseline: ECMP, UGAL-L, and prior sender-based approaches for general comparisons; Valiant and uniform/weighted OPS for failure comparisons.
uncertainty: The method is evaluated in simulation on Dragonfly and Slim Fly networks. It supplies path-specific congestion and failure clues, but does not establish request-level tail localization or distinguish network delay from server-side and robot-side delay.

title: Adaptive Prefiltering for High-Dimensional Similarity Search: A Frequency-Aware Approach
abstract: High-dimensional similarity search underpins modern retrieval systems, yet uniform search strategies fail to exploit the heterogeneous nature of real-world query distributions. We present an adaptive prefiltering framework that leverages query frequency patterns and cluster coherence metrics to dynamically allocate computational budgets. Our approach partitions the query space into frequency tiers following Zipfian distributions and assigns differentiated search policies based on historical access patterns and local density characteristics. Experiments on ImageNet-1k using CLIP embeddings demonstrate that frequency-aware budget allocation achieves equivalent recall with 20.4% fewer distance computations compared to static nprobe selection, while maintaining sub-millisecond latency on GPU-accelerated FAISS indices. The framework introduces minimal overhead through lightweight frequency tracking and provides graceful degradation for unseen queries through coherence-based fallback policies.
technical_mechanism: Adaptive IVF probing: assign each cluster a search budget based on frequency tiers and coherence, using deeper search for rare, diffuse clusters and shallower search for frequent, coherent clusters.
why_it_works: Uniform probing spends the same effort on clusters of different difficulty. Budgeting by cluster statistics reduces vector comparisons on common, coherent queries while retaining extra search effort for difficult clusters. In Root, this could provide a faster, matched retrieval path whose server-side time can be measured separately from network delay.
root_seam: Attach the policy to the server-side retrieval stage and correlate each request ID with its IVF search duration and vectors examined. Compare adaptive and uniform probing for matched queries; keep transport timings separate so retrieval savings are not mistaken for network improvements.
experiment: Replay the same representative query set against uniform and adaptive IVF policies at matched recall targets. Record per-request retrieval latency and work, alongside transport timing, and compare tail behavior and recall. The paper's experiment provides a concrete uniform-probing baseline and recall-controlled comparison.
evidence_quote: The policy assigns budget multipliers based on the relative frequency and coherence of the assigned cluster.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section 4.1, Policy Construction
reported_gain: 20.44% fewer vectors examined at 95% recall and 14.98% fewer at 98% recall versus uniform probing.
baseline: Uniform IVF probing (static probe count), evaluated at matched recall targets.
uncertainty: The paper evaluates similarity-search compute, not network tail latency or robot inference. Transfer to Root is as a server-retrieval control for separating search cost from transport delay; no Root gain is reported.

title: Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search for Modern AI: A Projection-Augmented Graph Approach
abstract: Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search (ANNS) is fundamental to modern AI applications. Most existing solutions optimize query efficiency but fail to align with the practical requirements of modern workloads. In this paper, we outline six critical demands of modern AI applications: high query efficiency, fast indexing, low memory footprint, scalability to high dimensionality, robustness across varying retrieval sizes, and support for online insertions. To satisfy all these demands, we introduce Projection-Augmented Graph (PAG), a new ANNS framework that integrates projection techniques into a graph index. PAG reduces unnecessary exact distance computations through asymmetric comparisons between exact and approximate distances as guided by projection-based statistical tests. Three key components are designed and integrated into the graph index to optimize indexing and searching. Experiments on six modern datasets demonstrate that PAG consistently achieves superior queries per second (QPS)-recall performance -- up to 5x faster than HNSW -- while offering fast indexing speed and moderate memory footprint. PAG remains robust as dimensionality and retrieval size increase and naturally supports online insertions.
technical_mechanism: Projection-augmented graph retrieval uses probabilistic projection tests to skip unnecessary exact distance computations; a Test Feedback Buffer retains false positives so they can be reused in later search steps.
why_it_works: Projection tests screen graph candidates before expensive exact distance calculations. Retaining likely-useful false positives lets later steps reuse computed distances rather than repeat work, accelerating retrieval of comparable items.
root_seam: Attach an approximate-nearest-neighbor index to Root's store of completed requests, using request embeddings to retrieve comparable healthy cases. This could speed baseline lookup, but would not itself identify whether a tail came from network delay rather than server or GPU time.
experiment: Build an index over completed Root requests and compare PAG with HNSW on the same request embeddings and corpus. Measure lookup latency and recall for comparable-case retrieval, then test whether retrieved cases help classify injected network-delay tails separately from server queueing and GPU compute.
evidence_quote: PAG reduces unnecessary exact distance computations through asymmetric comparisons between exact and approximate distances as guided by projection-based statistical tests.
evidence_location: Abstract; also selected PDF text, discussion of PRT and Test Feedback Buffer in the contributions.
reported_gain: Up to 5x faster QPS-recall performance than HNSW on the paper's datasets.
baseline: HNSW
uncertainty: The paper evaluates approximate vector retrieval, not Root requests or network-tail diagnosis. TFB reuses false positives within search; the context does not establish reuse of prior request results across searches.

title: Measurement-Driven O-RAN Diagnostics with Tail Latency and Scheduler Indicators
abstract: We investigate cross-layer performance diagnostics for an O-RAN instance by jointly analyzing application-level latency and radio-layer behavior from a real measurement campaign. Measurements were conducted at multiple link distances (2, 6 and 11 meters) using two representative UE configurations (a commercial smartphone and a modem-based device), under both static conditions and a controlled dynamic obstruction scenario. Rather than relying on averages, the study adopts tail-focused latency characterization (e.g., 95th percentile and exceedance probabilities) and connects it to scheduler- and link-adaptation indicators (e.g., block error behavior, modulation/coding selection and signal quality). The results reveal (i) UE-dependent differences that primarily manifest in the latency tail, (ii) systematic scaling of tail latency with distance and payload and (iii) cases where radio-layer dynamics are detectable even when end-to-end latency appears stable, motivating the need for cross-layer evidence. Distinct from much of the existing literature (often centered on throughput, simulated setups, or single-layer KPIs) this work contributes a measurement-driven methodology for interpretable O-RAN diagnostics and proposes lightweight, window-based "degradation flags" that combine tail latency and radio indicators to support practical monitoring and troubleshooting.
technical_mechanism: Aggregate ICMP latency into overlapping 10-second windows, join each with gNB scheduler indicators, and flag windows where the latency tail exceeds a threshold while a scheduler-side excursion (such as elevated BLER) is present.
why_it_works: A coincident latency tail and radio-reliability/adaptation excursion provides evidence consistent with a radio-driven delay; scheduler excursions can also reveal radio stress when ping latency remains stable. This is cross-layer correlation, not packet-level causal reconstruction or proof of cause.
root_seam: Attach request or probe timestamps to transport observations and, where applicable, wireless link indicators; align those with server queue and GPU timings. The windowed comparison could help identify radio-path contributions, but the paper does not provide a mechanism for attributing individual robot requests or separating all stages of the path.
experiment: For matched robot inference requests, collect request timestamps, network RTT or transport events, server queue/GPU timings, and available radio indicators. Apply the paper's overlapping-window join and joint tail-plus-radio flag; compare flagged windows against unflagged windows and independently verified network-tail episodes. Measure attribution accuracy and alert overhead.
evidence_quote: we define a lightweight “degradation flag” per window that triggers when both (i) the latency tail exceeds a threshold and (ii) a scheduler-side excursion is present (e.g., elevated BLER).
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section V.F, “Windowed cross-layer coupling and lightweight diagnostics”
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: The paper reports comparison across baseline, dynamic-obstruction, and static measurement scenarios; it does not report a controlled gain against a diagnostic baseline.
uncertainty: The windowed joint flag is concrete and experimentally testable, but the reported example has only 13 joined windows and does not establish causal attribution. It does not analyze off-path flows, queue buildup, packet-level divergence, robot action loops, streaming, or server/GPU timing. Differential diagnosis, expensive profiling triggers, and full network-versus-compute separation therefore remain unresolved.

title: BLADE: Adaptive Wi-Fi Contention Control for Next-Generation Real-Time Communication
abstract: Next-generation real-time communication (NGRTC) applications, such as cloud gaming and XR, demand consistently ultra-low latency. However, through our first large-scale measurement, we find that despite the deployment of edge servers, dedicated congestion control, and loss recovery mechanisms, cloud gaming users still experience long-tail latency in Wi-Fi networks. We further identify that Wi-Fi last-mile access points (APs) serve as the primary latency bottleneck. Specifically, short-term packet delivery droughts, caused by fundamental limitations in Wi-Fi contention control standards, are the root cause. To address this issue, we propose BLADE, an adaptive contention control algorithm that dynamically adjusts the contention windows (CW) of all Wi-Fi transmitters based on the channel contention level in a fully distributed manner. Our NS3 simulations and real-world evaluations with commercial Wi-Fi APs demonstrate that, compared to standard contention control, BLADE reduces Wi-Fi packet transmission tail latency by over 5X under heavy channel contention and significantly stabilizes MAC throughput while ensuring fast and fair convergence. Consequently, BLADE reduces the video stall rate in cloud gaming by over 90%.
technical_mechanism: Cross-layer tail attribution using aligned server-to-AP RTT, end-to-end frame latency, and AP packet-delivery counts in 200 ms intervals: identify high-latency requests with low wired RTT, then test whether an AP delivery drought coincides with the tail. The paper also derives microscopic access rate (MAR)—successful transmissions relative to observed idle slots—from Wi-Fi CCA as a shared signal of contention; BLADE uses MAR to adapt contention windows, which is an intervention rather than the attribution step.
why_it_works: The RTT comparison separates a healthy wired segment from delay at the Wi-Fi last hop, while the packet-count time window gives a concrete temporal signature of last-hop starvation. Their reported strong association between droughts and stalls supports that signature as a diagnostic clue. MAR offers additional evidence of shared-channel contention rather than relying only on a transmitter’s own collision history, though it does not identify particular competing flows.
root_seam: Attach request/frame identity and timestamps to robot-to-server and server-to-robot transport events; at the robot AP or NIC, retain per-interval successful delivery counts and available CCA/MAC contention counters. Compare transport RTTs and delivery gaps against server queue, GPU, and action-application timings. This could expose last-hop starvation and distinguish it from wired delay or server-side work, without assuming access to Reflex's private infrastructure.
experiment: On a robot-to-cloud testbed, inject controlled Wi-Fi contention, wired delay, server queueing, and GPU delay separately, including rare contention bursts. Compare request-level tail attribution using only end-to-end timing against attribution augmented with AP delivery counts, server-to-AP RTT, and (where available) CCA/MAR. Measure whether the added signals localize wireless droughts, avoid misattributing server/wired delays, and detect shared contention; separately test BLADE as a mitigation, not as evidence of diagnostic accuracy.
evidence_quote: In 86.19% of these stalled frames, the router failed to successfully transmit even a single packet during at least one 200 ms interval
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, §3 measurement discussion, “Packet Delivery Droughts: Root Cause of Frame Stalls”
reported_gain: Over 5× reduction in Wi-Fi packet transmission tail latency under heavy contention; over 90% reduction in cloud-gaming video stall rate.
baseline: Standard IEEE 802.11 contention control.
uncertainty: The paper studies cloud gaming rather than robot inference. The attribution evidence is interval-based and correlational, not packet-to-request causal reconstruction; 200 ms granularity may be too coarse for shorter robot-loop tails. MAR assumes sufficiently shared carrier-sense observations, which hidden terminals or partial visibility can undermine. Reported gains are the paper's results, not Root measurements.

title: Detecting Anomalous Topology, Routing Policies, and Congested Interconnections at Internet Scale
abstract: Separating mid-path Internet performance from edge effects remains a fundamental challenge in network measurement. This paper presents a methodology for detecting anomalous topology, routing policies, and congested interconnections using controlled A/B comparisons derived from Measurement Lab (M-Lab) data. The approach leverages M-Lab's uniform server selection policy: by comparing performance distributions from clients in the same access ISP to different nearby M-Lab servers, natural experiments are created that isolate mid-path effects while controlling for client-side variation, access network bottlenecks, and diurnal variation in test volume. This analysis is implemented in BigQuery using sparse multidimensional histograms enabling efficient computation of Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance and ratios of geometric mean throughput across many millions of measurements in a single pass. Differences in throughput suggest mid-path bandwidth bottlenecks or traffic management; excess differences in minimum RTT suggest suboptimal routing. These signals of interconnection problems are extracted from the noise deliberately suppressed by other measurement approaches. Public dashboards provide ongoing visibility into all M-Lab metropolitan regions with sufficient servers, with drill-down capability to individual ISP--server plots.
technical_mechanism: Use uniform assignment of measurements from the same access ISP to different nearby servers to form controlled A/B path comparisons; compare throughput and minimum-RTT distributions using KS distance and geometric-mean ratios. Throughput differences indicate mid-path capacity or traffic-management problems, while minimum-RTT differences indicate routing or path-length anomalies.
why_it_works: The server assignment is independent of network conditions, so the server groups have statistically comparable clients, access networks, and test-time distributions. Systematic performance differences are therefore evidence of differing mid-path behavior rather than client or access-edge variation. Minimum RTT and throughput provide complementary clues about path delay and capacity.
root_seam: At the request or transport-measurement layer, record the selected endpoint and per-request minimum RTT and throughput, then compare distributions across requests sent from the same robot/access network to alternate endpoints. This could indicate whether a regression follows a particular network path rather than the robot-side access edge. The method does not itself separate network delay from server queueing or compute, and its aggregate comparisons do not identify a particular packet-level cause.
experiment: Hold the robot workload and access network constant; randomly direct matched inference requests to two equivalent server endpoints or routes. Compare their request-level RTT and throughput distributions, including KS distance and geometric-mean ratios, and check whether a deliberately introduced path impairment changes these metrics while server-side queue and compute measurements remain stable. Separately test whether tail requests diverge from healthy requests within a route.
evidence_quote: This uniform test distribution, independent of network conditions, creates statistically equivalent measurement samples for each access ISP-server pair.
evidence_location: selected_pdf_text, methodology discussion of uniform server selection and natural A/B comparisons
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The paper studies aggregate Internet measurements, not remote robot inference or request-level tail-versus-healthy divergence. Applying its controlled endpoint comparison to Root requires comparable endpoints or routes and request-level measurements; the text does not establish that such controls are available in Root.

title: 1.5 Million Messages Per Second on 3 Machines: Benchmarking and Latency Optimization of Apache Pulsar at Enterprise Scale
abstract: This paper presents two independent contributions for Apache Pulsar practitioners. First, we validate 1,499,947 msg/s at 3.88 ms median publish latency on just three bare-metal Kubernetes nodes running Pulsar 4.0.8 with Java 21 and ZGC Generational garbage collection, and project a hardware-driven path to 15 million msg/s on 15 machines using five independent clusters with key-based partition routing. Hardware selection -- specifically dedicated NVMe journals achieving 0.02 ms fdatasync and 25 Gbps network interfaces -- is the primary determinant of throughput ceiling, not compute or software tuning. Second, we trace the complete latency optimization journey from 213 ms GC spikes and 13-18 ms median publish latency in production to 3.88 ms through Java Flight Recorder guided root cause analysis. Three independent root causes are identified and resolved: G1GC pauses eliminated by switching to ZGC Generational; journal fdatasync latency reduced from 5.1 ms to 0.02 ms through NVMe journal dedication; and a previously undocumented Linux kernel page cache writeback interaction inside BookKeeper's ForceWriteThread that degrades fdatasync from under 1 ms to 15-22 ms even across physically separate NVMe drives sharing the kernel block layer. This finding is undocumented in official Apache Pulsar and BookKeeper documentation and is relevant to all Pulsar operators experiencing unexplained P99.9 latency spikes. The combined optimizations achieve a 4.7x latency improvement at 50x higher throughput.
technical_mechanism: Correlate live runtime profiling with a latency-critical flush to attribute tail delay to time spent in a specific syscall, then relate it to concurrent writeback activity. For Root, the transferable operation is profiling endpoint runtime during slow requests to identify server-side blocking that could otherwise be mistaken for network delay.
why_it_works: The paper uses JFR during write-cache flushes to find that ForceWriteThread spends most of its time inside fdatasync while writeback activity rises. That turns a tail observation into a specific endpoint-side cause, helping Root distinguish at least some runtime/storage stalls from network delay. It does not isolate network time: the paper's latency breakdown combines broker and network.
root_seam: Attach request identity and timing to robot- or server-side runtime profiling around slow requests; correlate endpoint blocking or syscall time with transport timestamps for the same request. This could expose endpoint-side stalls without assuming access to Reflex infrastructure.
experiment: Replay matched requests under normal and induced endpoint writeback or syscall stalls. Collect request timings, JFR/runtime profiles, and transport timestamps; test whether profiling identifies endpoint-side delay and whether the remaining interval tracks network delay. Compare with healthy requests and report the network, endpoint, and unexplained portions separately.
evidence_quote: JFR profiling on a live bookie node during write cache flush identified the primary P99.9 driver.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section III.C, “Root Cause 3: Kernel Page Cache Writeback.”
reported_gain: 4.7× latency improvement at 50× higher throughput.
baseline: Production median publish latency of 13–18 ms; the abstract reports 213 ms GC spikes.
uncertainty: The profiling operation is concrete and transferable for endpoint-side diagnosis, supporting n14. The paper does not profile transport or separate network delay from server delay; its breakdown explicitly groups broker and network, so n15 is not promoted. The proposed Root experiment is not reported as a Root-measured result.

title: Hybrid Retrieval for COVID-19 Literature: Comparing Rank Fusion and Projection Fusion with Diversity Reranking
abstract: We present a hybrid retrieval system for COVID-19 scientific literature, evaluated on the TREC-COVID benchmark (171,332 papers, 50 expert queries). The system implements six retrieval configurations spanning sparse (SPLADE), dense (BGE), rank-level fusion (RRF), and a projection-based vector fusion (B5) approach. RRF fusion achieves the best relevance (nDCG@10 = 0.828), outperforming dense-only by 6.1% and sparse-only by 14.9%. Our projection fusion variant reaches nDCG@10 = 0.678 on expert queries while being 33% faster (847 ms vs. 1271 ms) and producing 2.2x higher ILD@10 than RRF. Evaluation across 400 queries -- including expert, machine-generated, and three paraphrase styles -- shows that B5 delivers the largest relative gain on keyword-heavy reformulations (+8.8%), although RRF remains best in absolute nDCG@10. On expert queries, MMR reranking increases intra-list diversity by 23.8-24.5% at a 20.4-25.4% nDCG@10 cost. Both fusion pipelines evaluated for latency remain below the sub-2 s target across all query sets. The system is deployed as a Streamlit web application backed by Pinecone serverless indices.
technical_mechanism: Precompute projected, fused document vectors in a separate index and retrieve with one dot-product query, replacing the two retrieval passes and rank-fusion step used by RRF.
why_it_works: The single-pass path avoids one Pinecone round-trip and the RRF fusion step. In Root, a controlled one-request versus two-request comparison with timestamps around each RPC could show whether an extra retrieval round-trip contributes to end-to-end latency; component timings would be needed to distinguish network delay from server-side work.
root_seam: Instrument request identity and timestamps at the robot/client and server around retrieval RPC send/response events; compare one-pass and two-pass retrieval while separately recording server processing time.
experiment: Replay comparable requests through one-pass and two-pass retrieval paths. Record end-to-end and per-RPC latency, including p50 and p95, and separate transport wait from server processing. Test whether removing a round-trip reduces the network component and tail latency.
evidence_quote: B5 is consistently faster because it requires only one Pinecone query vs. two for RRF.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section V-F, Latency Analysis
reported_gain: B5 averaged 847 ms versus RRF's 1271 ms on Expert 50 queries (33% faster); reported p95 was 1111 ms versus 1623 ms.
baseline: RRF two-pass retrieval: 1271 ms average latency and 1623 ms p95 on Expert 50 queries.
uncertainty: Latency is end-to-end through query encoding and retrieval; the paper does not report per-RPC transport versus server-processing timings. The measured gain is not a Root result and does not establish that the saved latency is specifically network tail.

title: Gleaner: A Semantically-Rich and Efficient Online Sampler for Microservice Diagnostics
abstract: Distributed tracing in microservices is critical for diagnostics but generates overwhelming data volumes, necessitating intelligent sampling. To maximize fidelity, state-of-the-art (SOTA) tail-based samplers analyze complete (or even log-enriched) traces by modeling them as graphs. However, this reliance on computationally expensive graph analysis creates a performance bottleneck that prohibits their use in online settings. To this end, we propose Gleaner, an online tail-sampling framework that breaks this trade-off. It is founded on the key insight that explicit graph structures are unnecessary for high-fidelity trace grouping. Instead, Gleaner represents each trace as a "bag-of-edges" augmented with log semantics, replacing slow graph algorithms with highly efficient set-based operations. It also employs an alarm-driven quota and a diversity-preserving strategy to prioritize anomalous and rare traces for downstream Root Cause Analysis (RCA). Experimentally, Gleaner processes traces at 0.74ms each, improving Trace Pattern Coverage by up to 128.7% and Shannon Entropy by up to 32.9% over baselines. At just a 1% sampling rate, Gleaner improves RCA accuracy by 42%-107% over the next-best sampler. Moreover, RCA on Gleaner's sampled data is more accurate than with the entire, unsampled dataset. This result reframes intelligent sampling from a data reduction technique to a powerful signal enhancement paradigm for automated operations.
technical_mechanism: After each trace completes, Gleaner encodes its inter-span event pairs and intra-span events as a lightweight event-pair set (EPS), scores trace relevance using signals including errors, logs, and latency, then uses external alarms to adapt sampling quotas and a diversity-preserving selector to retain diagnostically valuable traces. It is tail-aware sampling, not first-divergence diagnosis.
why_it_works: EPS and set operations preserve useful behavioral patterns without expensive graph analysis. Alarm-driven quotas concentrate the sampling budget on incident-relevant groups, while diversity selection avoids retaining only repeated examples. These retained traces can therefore provide more diagnostic signal per trace. The paper does not compare a tail request against a healthy request to find their first divergence.
root_seam: At the robot/server request-trace boundary, attach request identity and transport-event timestamps, then use an alarm or detected latency regression to trigger retention of complete traces and their EPS summaries. Include send/receive, queue, and ACK/loss events as trace events so retained data can distinguish network delay from server queueing or compute. The paper does not establish that its microservice trace signals or alarms are available in Reflex.
experiment: Replay matched healthy and network-tail robot inference requests with fixed trace-retention budgets. Compare random sampling against alarm-triggered quotas plus EPS-based diversity selection. Measure sampler runtime and retained-data volume, tail-request capture, and whether downstream analysis identifies network delay separately from server queueing and compute. Separately test whether EPS summaries retain enough information to rank the injected network cause as accurately as full traces.
evidence_quote: Instead, Gleaner represents each trace as a "bag-of-edges" augmented with log semantics, replacing slow graph algorithms with highly efficient set-based operations. It also employs an alarm-driven quota and a diversity-preserving strategy to prioritize anomalous and rare traces
evidence_location: Abstract; selected PDF text, Methodology overview
reported_gain: 0.74 ms per trace; up to 128.7% higher Trace Pattern Coverage and 32.9% higher Shannon Entropy over baselines; at 1% sampling, RCA accuracy gains of 42%–107% over the next-best sampler. These are paper results, not Root results.
baseline: For the abstract's coverage and entropy gains, the specific baseline is UNKNOWN. For the reported 1% RCA gains, the comparison is the next-best sampler; the paper also reports comparison with unsampled data.
uncertainty: The study concerns microservice traces and fault-injection cases, not remote robot inference or network-tail localization. It does not demonstrate packet/ACK/loss instrumentation, first-divergence diagnosis, or Root gains. Whether EPS can preserve the timing detail needed to isolate network delay is untested; the paper notes EPS is intentionally lossy and omits some timing and hierarchical information.

title: OCC: Physical-Layer Assisted Congestion Control for Real-Time Communications
abstract: Real-time communications (RTC) is a core technology for emerging applications in 6G, such as cloud gaming, teleoperation, and extended reality (XR), which require consistently low latency and high bitrates. Existing RTC solutions fundamentally struggle to maintain low latency while supporting high bitrates due to their reliance on trial-and-error-based mechanisms. These mechanisms fail to probe the available bandwidth (ABW) promptly and accurately, leading to a trade-off between latency reliability and bandwidth utilization. The tension becomes extremely more critical as the cellular bandwidth and application's demand fluctuate with a larger range in cellular networks nowadays. To address this trade-off, we propose OCC, a novel approach that utilizes physical-layer information to explicitly obtain the ABW in real time, enabling rapid adaptation to dynamic wireless network conditions. However, the unique characteristics of RTC, including traffic bursts, application (APP) limits, and encoder lag, make the physical-layer informed control non-trivial. OCC effectively addresses these issues through three innovative strategies: frame-aware bandwidth measurement, APP-limit-aware bandwidth estimation, and encoder-friendly rate control. Extensive over-the-air experiments on an open-source cellular testbed demonstrate that OCC significantly enhances the performance of mobile RTC, reducing tail network latency by 13% to 68% and improving video frame bitrate by 1.2× to 3.5×.
technical_mechanism: Use frame-aware cellular physical-layer measurements to estimate available bandwidth, then compare the wireless-link signal with end-to-end behavior to identify when the wireless hop is the bottleneck. The signal can expose a radio-capacity drop associated with a network-delay tail, rather than merely recording that delay occurred.
why_it_works: Base-station resource allocation and modulation/coding measurements reveal wireless capacity changes directly and faster than transport-layer trial-and-error. Aligning measurement with RTC frame bursts makes the estimate more reliable; the paper also describes detecting non-wireless bottlenecks and reverting to end-to-end control. This offers a way to associate a tail with wireless capacity variation while keeping network delay distinct from server queueing, GPU compute, and action application.
root_seam: At a cellular robot link, attach timestamped base-station radio metrics and flow identity to the robot-side and server-side packet timestamps. Correlate estimated available bandwidth and radio-capacity drops with one-way packet delay; this could localize a tail to the wireless hop. Root would need access to comparable RAN telemetry or an instrumented testbed; the paper does not establish access to Reflex infrastructure.
experiment: On a controlled cellular testbed carrying remote-inference requests, inject rare sharp radio-capacity drops and compare timestamped packet-delay tails with frame-aware base-station bandwidth estimates. Include non-wireless bottleneck episodes as controls. Test whether the signal distinguishes wireless-link tails from other network bottlenecks; separately measure server queueing, GPU compute, and action-application time. Treat any OCC rate-control change as a separate intervention from the diagnostic evaluation.
evidence_quote: OCC monitors RAN metrics at the cellular base station (BS) and calculates the ABW for an RTC client.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, design overview paragraph beginning “Motivated by this”; the same paragraph states that OCC detects bottleneck conditions and reverts to end-to-end solutions when the bottleneck is not wireless.
reported_gain: 13% to 68% reduction in network latency; video frame bitrate improved 1.2× to 3.5×.
baseline: GCC and PBE-CC.
uncertainty: The distinctive transferable value is the radio-layer capacity signal and its use in identifying whether the wireless hop is the bottleneck; OCC is primarily a congestion-control method, not a general tail-localization system. Root’s access to RAN telemetry is unknown, and the paper’s reported gains are not Root-measured gains.

title: Cloud Is Closer Than It Appears: Revisiting the Tradeoffs of Distributed Real-Time Inference
abstract: The increasing deployment of deep neural networks (DNNs) in cyber-physical systems (CPS) enhances perception fidelity, but imposes substantial computational demands on execution platforms, posing challenges to real-time control deadlines. Traditional distributed CPS architectures typically favor on-device inference to avoid network variability and contention-induced delays on remote platforms. However, this design choice places significant energy and computational demands on the local hardware. In this work, we revisit the assumption that cloud-based inference is intrinsically unsuitable for latency-sensitive control tasks. We demonstrate that, when provisioned with high-throughput compute resources, cloud platforms can effectively amortize network and queueing delays, enabling them to match or surpass on-device performance for real-time decision-making. Specifically, we develop a formal analytical model that characterizes distributed inference latency as a function of the sensing frequency, platform throughput, network delay, and task-specific safety constraints. We instantiate this model in the context of emergency braking for autonomous driving and validate it through extensive simulations using real-time vehicular dynamics. Our empirical results identify concrete conditions under which cloud-based inference adheres to safety margins more reliably than its on-device counterpart. These findings challenge prevailing design strategies and suggest that the cloud is not merely a feasible option, but often the preferred inference location for distributed CPS architectures. In this light, the cloud is not as distant as traditionally perceived; in fact, it is closer than it appears.
technical_mechanism: Inject controlled round-trip network delays at measured percentiles into the cloud inference path, then compare brake-actuation timing and safety outcomes against baseline conditions while holding the obstacle’s first-observation location constant.
why_it_works: The controlled delay changes communication timing without changing when the obstacle is first observed. Comparing frame-capture-to-brake timing therefore distinguishes a network-induced actuation delay from delayed detection, and the control-loop outcome shows whether that delay breaches the task’s safety margin.
root_seam: Attach timestamps to frame capture, remote request/response, and brake-command receipt; compare matched requests under baseline and injected or observed tail RTT. This can identify whether a late action arose in transport rather than detection or inference, though the paper does not separate network delay from server queueing at request level.
experiment: Replay the same robot perception-to-action workload with baseline and controlled RTT conditions, including rare tail delays. Hold inputs and compute configuration constant, record capture, response, and action timestamps, and compare end-to-end action latency and task safety outcomes.
evidence_quote: The obstacle is observed for the first time at the same location (★) in both baseline and adverse configurations. Only the timing of the actuation, specifically, the interval between frame capture (★) and brake signal reception (●), is affected by the added network delay.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section D, “Impact of High Network Latency”
reported_gain: Cloud deployment detected obstacles almost 20 m earlier than the device configuration under baseline conditions; this is a task outcome, not a Root gain.
baseline: Baseline cloud and on-device deployments; adverse cloud conditions use injected RTTs of 55–65 ms and more extreme p99-and-beyond latency.
uncertainty: The paper evaluates a simulated emergency-braking loop with synthetic latency injection, not a robot system or a diagnostic tool. It does not provide per-request network/queue decomposition, packet or ACK traces, or compact temporal signatures of packet droughts and loss recovery.

title: Enhancing Performance Insight at Scale: A Heterogeneous Framework for Exascale Diagnostics
abstract: As exascale systems reach unprecedented concurrency, traditional performance analysis tools struggle with the overhead of massive-scale telemetry. We present an accelerated infrastructure for the hpcanalysis framework that leverages a high-performance C++ API and GPU parallelism to enable high-throughput diagnostics. Our C++ API achieves a 9.69-second ingestion time for 100,000 MPI ranks on Aurora. Furthermore, our GPU-accelerated layer achieves up to 314x speedup over CPU-based processing when analyzing 100,000 execution traces. Finally, we implement a topology-aware workflow that maps logical performance outliers to physical Slingshot interconnect coordinates, localizing network congestion across 22 distinct racks on Aurora. We also demonstrate how the framework's advanced interface seamlessly integrates with external tools to provide sophisticated analytical models. We introduce a novel tri-dimensional performance model that "re-materializes" iterative behavior from execution traces; using this model, we identified a 32.28% potential speedup for a GAMESS workload on Frontier.
technical_mechanism: Cluster MPI ranks by communication-cost outliers, join those ranks to compute-node metadata, then map outlier nodes’ POSIX IDs to physical Slingshot coordinates to localize congestion.
why_it_works: Rank-level communication measurements identify which participants are unusually slow; comparison with the other ranks separates outliers from broadly shared delay. Mapping the outlier ranks to node identities and then interconnect coordinates shows whether the delay is associated with particular physical regions. This localizes correlated network congestion, though it does not distinguish network delay from other causes of MPI latency by itself.
root_seam: Attach at request or inference-phase timing that can be attributed to robot/server endpoints and network-facing transport events. Group comparable slow and healthy requests by endpoint or network path, then join outliers to available NIC, switch, or topology identifiers. Root could gain physical/path-level localization from sparse timing and metadata, but the paper does not establish that its MPI measurements transfer directly to robot inference.
experiment: On a controlled set of repeated inference requests, compare tail and healthy requests using phase-level communication timings and endpoint/path metadata. Test whether the outlier-grouping and topology-join workflow localizes an injected network impairment to its configured path or network region, while separately measuring server queueing, GPU, and action-application delays. Compare localization accuracy and collection overhead with full tracing.
evidence_quote: By mapping the 202 outlier compute nodes to the interconnect, we determined that the congestion was not confined to a single rack or chassis. The affected nodes were distributed across 22 different racks
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, section VI, “Interconnect Mapping and Congestion Analysis.”
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The paper reports MPI rank-level performance outliers correlated with compute nodes and maps them to Slingshot coordinates, but does not establish packet-level causality or separate network congestion from endpoint and application effects. The transfer to request-level robot inference is therefore unvalidated; the paper provides no Root experiment.

title: SprayCheck: Finding Gray Failures in Adaptive Routing Networks
abstract: Distributed machine learning (ML) training has become a dominant workload in modern data center networks, operating at massive scale with clusters comprising tens to hundreds of thousands of GPUs. The scale of these networks makes failures, and particularly gray failures, inevitable. Gray failures can significantly degrade both network and application performance, yet they are notoriously difficult to detect, localize, and debug. To meet the performance demands of ML workloads, adaptive routing is widely deployed to maximize network utilization by dynamically spreading traffic across many paths. While adaptive routing increases network utilization, it also greatly intensifies the effect of gray failures. Prior work has either dismissed gray failures as negligible or proposed detection mechanisms that fail to scale, rendering these approaches increasingly impractical for large-scale clusters. We present SprayCheck, a passive gray failure detection system that leverages the statistical properties of adaptive routing and network load balancing. By combining these properties with flow-level information, SprayCheck can identify failures before they significantly impact application performance, enabling preemptive rerouting and improving overall performance. Importantly, this is achieved through passive observation of traffic spraying, without introducing additional load on the network. We evaluate SprayCheck and show that it can detect and localize a single-link packet-drop-rate 1.5% within a single iteration and as little as 0.5% within 5 training iterations of Llama-3 70B in a 64 spine topology.
technical_mechanism: Passively count packets from each large flow arriving at a destination leaf from each spine, then compare each path’s count with the expected adaptive-routing distribution using a statistical threshold. A packet deficit identifies a suspect path; counting observed NACKs also provides a separate extension for localizing sending-access-link loss.
why_it_works: In a symmetric failure-free fabric, adaptive routing spreads enough packets from a large flow approximately evenly across paths. Loss on a path reduces its received count below expected variation, exposing gray packet loss without probes or per-packet tracing. NACK counts help distinguish source access-link loss when fabric and destination-side failures are excluded. This detects loss-related transport delay, but does not directly measure arbitrary delay or separate server queueing and GPU compute.
root_seam: At destination leaf switches, retain per-flow, per-spine packet counts and, where available, NACK counts; correlate those with request identity and robot/server transport timestamps. The resulting path deficit could localize transport loss while avoiding probe traffic and full packet traces. Transfer requires observable adaptive spraying, suitable switch counters, and a sufficiently large flow; the paper does not establish those conditions in Root’s network.
experiment: On a controlled multipath testbed, replay representative inference traffic and inject gray loss on one fabric link or access link. Compare per-flow path-count deficits and NACK-based localization with known fault location and request tail latency; measure detection time and healthy-path false alarms, and record server queueing and GPU compute separately. Include a non-spraying control to test the mechanism’s applicability boundary.
evidence_quote: By counting how many packets of a given flow arrive from each spine switch, a destination leaf switch can determine whether the expected even distribution remains intact, or if some paths suffered packet drops due to a gray failure.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, “Our approach” paragraph; access-link extension in the paragraph beginning “Detection of Access Link Faults.”
reported_gain: Detects/localizes 1.5% single-link packet-drop rate within one iteration and 0.5% within five Llama-3 70B training iterations in a 64-spine topology; this is the paper’s result, not a Root-measured gain.
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The fabric-path mechanism depends on adaptive packet spraying and sufficiently large flows; it does not directly expose delay absent loss. The paper sketches access-link localization using packet totals and NACKs, but Root’s transport and switch visibility are unknown.

title: Latency in Real-Time 3D Volumetric Streaming: A Comprehensive Study
abstract: Real-time 3D volumetric streaming is a transformative technology that enables the seamless transmission and rendering of high-fidelity 3D models, enhancing applications in virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), gaming, telepresence, and remote collaboration. However, latency remains a major challenge, affecting immersion, causing motion sickness, and disrupting real-time interactions. Addressing these latency issues is essential for improving user experience and ensuring system efficiency. This study conducts a comprehensive latency measurement and analysis within a real-time volumetric streaming environment. We systematically break down the streaming process into three key layers: the application layer, the transport protocol layer, and the network layer. By evaluating each layer in a real-world system, we identify latency bottlenecks, quantify their impact, and uncover the underlying causes of delay. Based on these findings, we propose targeted optimization strategies to mitigate latency and enhance system responsiveness. Through this research, we establish best practices and innovative solutions to improve the efficiency, scalability, and overall user experience of real-time 3D volumetric streaming. Our insights contribute to advancing the field, paving the way for more immersive and responsive digital environments.
technical_mechanism: Layered one-way latency decomposition: synchronize device clocks, timestamp frames and packets at send/receive boundaries, and measure kernel/NIC timing separately to distinguish application, transport, and network delay.
why_it_works: Boundary timestamps localize elapsed time to specific stages instead of treating end-to-end latency as one number. Packet-level kernel and NIC measurements can distinguish network-path delay from endpoint processing, while frame-level measurements expose transmission and application delays.
root_seam: Attach synchronized timestamps and request/frame identity at robot send, server receive/forward, and robot receive events. Where available, add packet-level kernel/NIC timestamps; compare the resulting stage timings to identify whether a tail arises on the network path, at an endpoint, or in server processing.
experiment: The paper measured a 30-fps stream over 300 frames, timestamping frame and packet boundaries and separately testing 300 packets at three IP packet sizes with kernel/NIC timing. A Root experiment could apply the same per-request stage timestamps, then compare tail-latency requests against typical requests and inspect packet/kernel/NIC timing for the implicated stage.
evidence_quote: To measure frame latency, a timestamp was added to the data structure of the transmission frame.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section IV.A, End-to-End Service and Frame Latency
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The paper reports measurements and localization across layers, but does not establish performance on remote robot inference or report tail percentiles. Its network-layer packet test is separate from service frames, so the method’s effectiveness for attributing Root tail events remains to be tested.

title: Identifying and Mitigating Systemic Measurement Bias in Production LLM Inference Benchmarks
abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) transition from research environments to production deployments, evaluating their performance against strict Service Level Objectives (SLOs) has become critical. However, current evaluation methodologies suffer from severe measurement bias at scale. We demonstrate that widely used benchmarking utilities rely on single-process, asyncio-driven architectures that introduce fundamental client-side queuing bottlenecks under high concurrency. By modeling the benchmarking client as an M/G/1 queue, we mathematically demonstrate how the Python Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) artificially inflates Time to First Token (TTFT) and Time Per Output Token (TPOT) metrics as request rates scale. To resolve this systematic inaccuracy, we propose an unbiased, multi-process evaluation framework that effectively distributes client-side load, ensuring negligible queuing overhead. Furthermore, we formalize a composite metric, Normalized Time Per Output Token (NTPOT), to robustly amortize end-to-end latency, including prefill and scheduling delays across sequence lengths. Our empirical evaluation demonstrates that this methodology successfully isolates pure serving engine performance, enabling accurate, reproducible profiling of LLMs at production scales exceeding thousands of queries per second.
technical_mechanism: Measure the delay from intended request dispatch to actual transmission, alongside successfully transmitted QPS. This exposes client-side scheduling-queue buildup separately from delay that occurs after transmission; multi-process workers reduce the client-side bottleneck.
why_it_works: If the load generator is saturated, dispatch delay rises and transmitted QPS falls even before the request enters the network. Comparing intended-dispatch, actual-send, and response-arrival times can therefore identify client-side queueing as a source of an apparent latency tail, rather than attributing all end-to-end delay to the inference service. The paper validates this attribution against a near-zero-server-latency simulator. It does not, by itself, distinguish network delay from server-side delay after transmission.
root_seam: At Root’s request-generation boundary, record request identity plus intended-dispatch, actual-send, and response-arrival timestamps, and track transmitted QPS. This adds a way to rule in or out client-side queueing without relying on private infrastructure; post-send delay still requires other signals to separate transport, server queueing, compute, and action application.
experiment: Replay a fixed request trace at increasing offered rates against a near-zero-latency simulator and a real inference endpoint. Record intended dispatch, actual transmission, and response arrival for each request. Test whether dispatch-delay tails and transmitted-QPS shortfalls identify generator saturation in the simulator, and whether subtracting pre-send delay changes the end-to-end tail observed against the real endpoint.
evidence_quote: The framework tracks the distribution of delays between a request’s intended dispatch time and its actual transmission.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section 6, “Scheduling Precision”; the following “Dispatch Throughput” bullet says actual transmitted QPS is monitored.
reported_gain: At 1,000 QPS against a near-zero-server-latency simulator, the paper reports 0.63 ms end-to-end overhead for Inference Perf versus 8 ms to 58 seconds for single-process utilities. This is a paper-reported benchmark result, not a Root-measured gain.
baseline: Single-process benchmarking utilities; the paper also compares its multi-process framework with alternative multi-process tools.
uncertainty: The mechanism diagnoses load-generator queueing and rate failure, not network-tail causes directly. No packet, ACK, loss, or network-arrival measurements are reported, so post-send network delay remains confounded with server-side queueing and processing.

title: AgentIR: A Workload-Adaptive Cascade Retrieval Substrate for Long-Term Conversational Memory
abstract: Long-term conversational memory is a retrieval workload classical IR was not built for: the index grows during the query stream, query types shift intra-session, and the latency budget per retrieval is sub-10 ms. Lucene-class engines treat the index as static and the query as stateless, leaving the workload's structure unexploited. AgentIR treats fusion as a per-query decision along two axes: which fusion to apply (BM25, Dense, RRF, or agent-aware RRF), and whether the 52 ms dense channel is worth running at all. The second axis is a confidence-triggered cascade router that decides from the BM25 top-k margin alone and re-tunes across workloads without retraining. On LongMemEval (n=500), where the dense channel does add information, the cascade skips 63% of queries at parity LLM-judged accuracy (2.67x faster under two judges, paired bootstrap p>=0.88); per-qtype thresholds extend this to 5.76x under 5-fold cross-validation. On LoCoMo (n=1,982), where BM25 alone is already the strongest single system, the same trigger auto-tunes to a 100% skip rate (132x faster, +0.089 Hit@5). Capacity on a shared 8-core VM rises from 154 to 1,400 concurrent agents (9x). Underneath the cascade, a time-partitioned index does O(log 1/epsilon) work independent of corpus size: 1234x corpus growth costs only 3.6x latency, ending in 1769x over sequential at sub-100 us p50 on 5M records. At parity quality with Lucene on 9 BEIR datasets up to 8.8M docs, the substrate runs 10x geo-mean over Pyserini 8T and 11x over PISA-1T BlockMax-WAND; an A100 reaches 1.8-39x over Pyserini 8T; chunked index build sustains 56.8K docs/sec on MS MARCO. Three subtle BM25/GPU correctness pitfalls that silently regress nDCG@10 by 6-8x are documented and fixed; post-fix CPU and GPU agree within 0.0002 nDCG@10 on all eight datasets that fit a single A100.
technical_mechanism: Partition the index into recency-ordered time windows and search only the recent partitions needed to meet a target miss probability, reducing retrieval work as the corpus grows.
why_it_works: The method exploits recency bias: when relevant records are concentrated in recent partitions, searching only a few partitions can preserve retrieval quality without scanning the full corpus. This makes it a concrete indexing mechanism for faster comparable retrieval, though it does not itself diagnose network delay.
root_seam: Attach the retrieval backend to the request timeline and compare its measured latency against a sequential or full-index baseline for the same query. This could help separate retrieval cost from transport, server queueing, GPU compute, and action-application delay; it would not identify which network segment caused a tail.
experiment: On matched requests, benchmark the recency-partitioned index against sequential full-index retrieval as corpus size grows; measure retrieval latency and answer/retrieval quality. In Root, separately record end-to-end request timing and retrieval-stage timing to test whether reducing retrieval work changes the observed tail.
evidence_quote: The temporal index partitions documents into time-window buckets (7-day intervals) sorted by recency.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, §4.3 Temporal Partitioned Index
reported_gain: At 5M records, 1769× over sequential at sub-100 μs p50; as corpus grows 1234×, temporal latency grows 3.6×.
baseline: Sequential retrieval over the full index.
uncertainty: The 5M-record scaling result uses a synthetic corpus with 80/20 recency-biased queries; the paper notes that a production trace at this scale would provide tighter validation. The mechanism concerns retrieval, not network-tail localization.

title: Wire-Level Interrupt-to-Decision Latency of On-Sensor MLC versus Host Inference on the NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano: A Pre-Registered Measurement Study
abstract: The Machine Learning Core (MLC) embedded in the STMicroelectronics LSM6DSOX IMU is widely cited as a low-latency alternative to host-side inference, yet wire-level decision-delivery latency is rarely measured. Using a Saleae Logic Pro 8 logic analyzer on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano, we measured interrupt-to-decision latency (sensor INT1 edge to host decision GPIO) for three pipelines (a host-side decision-tree classifier, the standard MLC bank-switch read protocol, and an MLC binary-fast variant) under idle, I2C bus contention, and CPU stress. The protocol was pre-registered with 12 externally-timestamped Zenodo amendments before confirmatory data collection (4,770 of 4,860 trials included, 98.15%, across nine cells). The host pipeline exhibits lower median latency than the MLC pipeline under all conditions: 321.7 vs 681.5 us at idle (2.1x faster) and 574.5 vs 1,325.4 us under I2C contention (2.3x faster). The three-transaction I2C read protocol, not the silicon's classification, is the dominant latency contributor. We additionally characterize a reproducible 706.5 ms MLC decision cadence that bounds full stimulus-to-decision latency. Code, data, and pre-registration: github.com/akulswami/sensor-mlc-latency.
technical_mechanism: Use two hardware-timestamped GPIO edges for interrupt-to-decision latency, then compare the standard decision path with a matched zero-I²C control under bus contention and CPU stress. The control isolates bus-protocol overhead from the interrupt/GPIO floor.
why_it_works: The paired wire timestamps avoid relying on software-clock timing, while the zero-transaction control removes the suspected I²C read path. Its much lower latency under contention, alongside a separate CPU-stress condition, localizes the observed delay to bus access rather than classifier computation or generic resource stress. This is a concrete minimal-signal and controlled-ablation method for n04; the paper does not itself separate network delay from server or GPU compute for n15.
root_seam: For Root, attach timestamps to request send/receive and response send/arrival, and compare matched requests with a controlled transport-bypassing or alternate-path condition where feasible. Pair these with server inference start/end timestamps. This would expose whether tail growth lies across the transport boundary or within server processing, without assuming access to Reflex infrastructure.
experiment: On matched robot inference requests, collect hardware- or monotonic-clock timestamps at robot send, server receive, inference start/end, server response send, and robot response arrival. Compare normal requests against a controlled alternate or bypass path; independently inject network contention and server/compute load. Check whether the transport interval's tail moves under network contention while server intervals remain stable, and whether the control path removes that effect.
evidence_quote: the mlc-binary pipeline, which performs zero I²C transactions on the decision path
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section VI.A, “The I²C read protocol dominates wire-level latency”
reported_gain: Under I²C contention, host median latency is 574.5 μs versus 1,325.4 μs for MLC; the zero-I²C MLC binary control has 49.4 μs median latency.
baseline: Standard MLC bank-switch read protocol with three I²C transactions; zero-I²C MLC binary pipeline is the control.
uncertainty: The study measures sensor I²C and CPU stress, not robot-server network transport, and provides no packet/ACK/loss sequence or direct network-versus-server/GPU timing. The n04 transfer is supported as an experimental pattern, not as a demonstrated Root result; n15 remains unresolved.

title: Waiting at the front door: Continuous monitoring of latency in the host network stack
abstract: With networking moving into the sub-millisecond latency domain, latency in the end host itself can become a significant barrier to achieving consistently low application latency. Both the physical interconnect between the network card and the CPU, the kernel network stack, and the scheduling of applications themselves can be considerable sources of latency. Previous work has studied host latency at various levels, yet there remains a lack of methods and tools to continuously monitor host latency in production. To remedy this, we present netstacklat, a monitoring tool that captures latency at several points in the host network, from the early parts of the Linux kernel network stack all the way until the application reads the data. We evaluate netstacklat in a testbed, demonstrating its ability to capture host latency across 144 variations of HTTP workloads for Nginx and Apache, while also showing how the low monitoring overhead does not inflate tail latency by more than 6%, where previous monitoring solutions increase it by over 100%. Furthermore, we share our initial findings from deploying netstacklat in Cloudflare's global CDN network.
technical_mechanism: Use eBPF probes at logical ingress-stack boundaries to read each packet's existing kernel timestamp, calculate cumulative latency at each boundary, and aggregate the measurements into per-stage latency histograms in kernel. TCP samples potentially inflated by head-of-line blocking are conservatively filtered.
why_it_works: Comparing latency distributions across successive boundaries localizes where ingress delay accumulates without exporting a full per-packet trace. The socket-read measurement additionally includes delays before the application reads, such as CPU scheduling, so it can help distinguish stack processing from later delivery-to-application delay. In-kernel aggregation keeps continuous monitoring overhead low.
root_seam: Attach analogous timestamps and request or packet identity at robot-side and inference-server transport boundaries. Stage-specific distributions could show whether a tail accumulates in host ingress processing or before the application reads, rather than attributing it to remote network delay. This method does not measure end-to-end path delay, server queueing, GPU compute, action application, or NIC-to-CPU delay; its demonstrated coverage is Linux ingress.
experiment: On a controlled remote-inference path, compare instrumented and uninstrumented runs while injecting network delay/loss and separately inducing host receive-stack load or application-read scheduling delay. Compare per-boundary latency distributions with end-to-end request tails and server/GPU timings; test whether the boundary deltas localize the injected cause without materially inflating tails.
evidence_quote: This selection has resulted in netstacklat recording the network stack latency at four different layers
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, section 4.2, “The netstacklat probe points”
reported_gain: In testbed evaluation across 144 HTTP workload variations, monitoring did not inflate tail latency by more than 6%; the abstract reports previous monitoring solutions increased it by over 100%. The conclusion reports 0.04% CPU utilization at peak hours in Cloudflare’s busiest data center location.
baseline: Unmonitored testbed runs and comparisons with lattrace, kyanos, retis, and pwru; the abstract also compares tail-latency inflation with previous monitoring solutions.
uncertainty: The evidence supports localization of host ingress-stack latency, not diagnosis of an end-to-end network tail in remote robot inference. Whether the same probes and timestamp semantics are available across the robot/server transport and runtime is unestablished. The method does not implement tail-triggered sampling or retention.

title: Certified Closed-Loop Control for Packet Networks: A Compositional Certification Framework
abstract: Packet networks are controlled dynamical systems with discontinuities, delayed observations, and partial state information. Adaptive or learning-driven proposers can improve performance, but an unsafe proposal may still cause starvation, tail-delay spikes, or unstable queue behaviour. This paper treats packet-network control as an executed-action certification problem. A certified operator sits between any proposer and the dataplane. At each control tick, the proposer emits an arbitrary candidate action u(t). The operator either projects it to an executable action u(t) that satisfies a configuration-compiled certificate, or reports INFEASIBLE and executes an always-defined fallback with quantified slack. The certificate also exports an auditable envelope z(t) for downstream composition. The guarantees are conditional and explicit. They apply on ticks where the operator reports CERTIFIED, the declared arrival envelope and backlog bound are valid, and the platform realises the assumed service lower bound. Under these conditions, one mechanism covers backlog caps, service floors, mitigation caps, Foster--Lyapunov drift constraints, and compositional envelope contracts. We prove operator-level safety, feed-forward compositional safety and stability using exported envelopes, and a cyclic closure result under a small-gain condition. We also define breach and infeasibility semantics, discuss calibration of the service-tracking factor that links certified targets to realised scheduler behaviour, and evaluate the design under delayed telemetry, delayed actuation, weak proposers, envelope mismatch, overload, and millisecond-scale certification. The present evaluation validates the certified execution boundary in a byte-level closed-loop backend; deployment-level scheduler tracking is left to future Linux or hardware experiments.
technical_mechanism: Reconstruct a conservative current-backlog bound from delayed queue counters using declared arrival envelopes and known scheduled or applied removals, then expose per-tick certification status and slack against backlog or drift constraints.
why_it_works: The reconstructed bound accounts for queue growth that may have occurred since the last counter sample, rather than treating stale occupancy as current state. Per-queue bounds and constraint status give Root evidence of queue buildup even when the tail occurs between telemetry samples. This identifies queue buildup as a contributor, not as the exclusive cause of a latency regression; transport delay, server queueing, GPU compute, and action-application delay still need separate measurements.
root_seam: Attach to timestamped robot- or server-side per-queue occupancy counters, arrival-envelope estimates, and records of scheduled/applied service actions. Retain the reconstructed backlog bound and certification status alongside request timing and independently measured transport, compute, and action-application intervals. This could avoid relying on a fresh high-frequency queue sample at every request, subject to valid envelope and action-accounting assumptions.
experiment: In a controlled Root replay, compare stale-counter backlog estimates with reconstructed bounds using identical requests and action records. Independently inject queue buildup, transport delay, GPU compute delay, and action-application delay. Test whether the bound rises under queue buildup despite delayed counters and whether non-queue perturbations are not incorrectly attributed to queue growth; report localization and false-positive rates against direct queue measurements.
evidence_quote: To obtain a bound at the current tick, we use two facts that are available to the controller: (i) the declared envelope upper-bounds arrivals between counter samples, and (ii) the controller knows the actions it has already scheduled to apply (including any actuation buffer).
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, section 5, “Backlog bounds from delayed counters and local accounting”
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: Direct execution of proposer actions; the delayed-telemetry stress passage also compares naive clipping.
uncertainty: The paper evaluates a byte-level closed-loop backend, not Root inference regressions. The method depends on valid arrival envelopes, usable queue counters, and accurate accounting of scheduled or applied removals. It bounds backlog but does not itself separate queueing delay from transport delay, server queueing, GPU compute, or action-application delay.

title: vla.cpp: A Unified Inference Runtime for Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: Deploying vision--language--action (VLA) models on robots requires adapting model-specific inference pipelines to heterogeneous processors and limited onboard memory. We present vla.cpp, a unified C++ inference runtime for eleven VLA models, with no PyTorch dependency for model execution. The runtime shares model loading, tensor execution, and serving while retaining architecture-specific attention, conditioning, and action heads. Iterative policies reuse observation-dependent computation across solver steps, while regression policies predict actions directly. We evaluate task success on LIBERO-Object and profile supported configurations on NVIDIA, Apple, and Intel hardware. BitVLA completes 200/200 LIBERO-Object episodes on an 8,GB Jetson Orin Nano. A ternary tensor-core kernel accelerates its client inference by 4.0--4.6× over the CUDA-core baseline on RTX 3060 and AGX Orin. A SmolVLA case study links positional-index precision to gripper commands and task success, showing why fixed-input numerical checks should accompany rollout evaluation. Deployments on UR10e and ALOHA demonstrate physical robot integration; delay and execution-horizon studies characterize synchronous chunked control. The results demonstrate a common deployment path across VLA architectures and hardware, with numerical validation and control settings guiding deployment alongside inference efficiency.
technical_mechanism: Inject a controlled delay after inference and before delivering each action chunk to the robot, holding hardware and precision fixed, then measure task outcomes and execution behavior.
why_it_works: The intervention emulates added delay in the chunk-delivery path while keeping inference hardware and precision unchanged, allowing Root to test how delivery delay affects a synchronous robot action loop without conflating it with those factors. It does not, by itself, distinguish network delay from other delivery-path delays.
root_seam: Attach the delay intervention and timestamps to the inference-complete and chunk-delivered events for each request, then compare robot-loop outcomes under controlled added delays. This tests sensitivity to delivery delay, but does not localize naturally occurring network tails.
experiment: On an RTX 4070 with ALOHA, the paper inserted artificial delays after GR00T-N1.7 inference and before delivering each chunk, reporting ten episodes per condition. A Root experiment could repeat this controlled intervention while recording the corresponding request and transport events.
evidence_quote: To isolate inference delay from hardware and precision changes, we insert an artificial delay after GR00T-N1.7 inference on an RTX 4070 and before delivering each chunk to ALOHA.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section IV-G(b), “Controlled latency injection”
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The study intervenes on delay but does not report packet-, ACK-, or transport-level signals, compare naturally occurring tail requests with healthy requests, or establish that the injected delay represents network delay specifically.

title: ARGUS: Production-Scale Tracing and Performance Diagnosis for over 10,000-GPU Clusters
abstract: Large-scale LLM training requires always-on, fine-grained observability for effective performance diagnosis at scale.
