Coarse resource monitors alone cannot localize root causes, and fine-grained profilers incur prohibitive (5%-30%) overheads and massive trace volumes, making always-on deployment impractical in large production clusters. We propose ARGUS, a low-overhead, fine-grained, always-on tracing and real-time analysis system for training workloads in 10,000+ GPU-scale production clusters. ARGUS decomposes observation along the training call hierarchy into CPU call stacks, framework semantics, and GPU kernel execution, with always-on collection under a combined overhead of less than 2%. It builds a unified data pipeline and compresses raw kernel events by approximately 3,700x from 10 MB to 2.7 KB per rank per step. Its progressive diagnosis framework automatically isolates anomalous windows, straggler ranks, and degraded kernels through iteration-time, phase-level, and kernel-level analysis. Deployed for over six months on a 10,000+ GPU production cluster, ARGUS has supported continuous fail-slow detection and performance optimization. Our case studies further demonstrate its effectiveness across representative anomalies, including compute stragglers, link degradation, pipeline-bubble amplification, FlashAttention JIT stalls, and compute stragglers masked by communication symptoms.
technical_mechanism: Continuously collect iteration, phase, and per-kernel timing signals; progressively narrow anomalous windows and straggler ranks with change-point/jitter detection and parallelism-group-aware cross-rank comparisons, then compare compressed per-kernel duration distributions across equivalent ranks. Retrieve detailed traces for the narrowed anomalous window to confirm the cause.
why_it_works: Cross-rank comparison among ranks with the same parallel role provides a healthy reference, while phase and kernel granularity helps distinguish slow computation from communication symptoms or secondary collective effects. This reduces the search from thousands of ranks to a small set of suspects without relying on out-of-band alerts alone. For Root, the comparison and narrowing workflow could identify whether a remote-inference tail is localized to a transport event or instead arises in another execution phase; the paper does not specify robot transport signals.
root_seam: Attach request identity and synchronized timestamps to robot-side and server-side transport events, queue/NIC signals, and inference phases. Compare tail requests with healthy requests and use progressive narrowing to separate network delay from server queueing, compute, and action application. ARGUS's cross-rank method transfers as a comparison strategy, but its training-specific signals do not directly provide robot transport evidence.
experiment: Replay the same remote-inference workload with controlled network delay/loss and separately injected server queueing or compute delays. Compare a baseline collector with progressive phase-level and per-request cross-layer comparisons, measuring cause classification, number of measurements/traces required, localization accuracy, tail-detection latency, and collection overhead.
evidence_quote: L2 performs cross-rank comparison on the phase durations recorded by framework semantics instrumentation within parallelism groups, using the coefficient of variation (CV) to quantify intra-group inconsistency and z-scores to identify straggler ranks.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, §6.1 Iteration-level Detection (L1) and Phase-level Attribution (L2)
reported_gain: ARGUS reports kernel-trace compression of approximately 3,700× (10 MB to 2.7 KB per rank per step), total collection overhead below 2%, and diagnosis narrowing to single-digit suspects. No Root gain is reported.
baseline: For the reported tracing overhead comparison, the baseline is training without ARGUS; the paper also compares against PyTorch Profiler and nsys. A Root-specific baseline is UNKNOWN.
uncertainty: The method is demonstrated for distributed GPU training, not remote robot inference. Its cross-rank healthy-reference assumption and training phase signals may not transfer directly; the context does not establish a concrete packet-, ACK-, or request-level network diagnostic operation.

title: Interference-Aware Cross-Application Placement: A Multi-Objective Optimization Approach for Microservice Clusters
abstract: In modern cloud architectures, multiple applications often run within the same clustered environment, sharing underlying resources. This resource sharing can cause interference among applications, leading to degraded latency and reduced system stability. As containerized microservices become increasingly central to cloud-native applications, their performance can suffer from complex interference scenarios related to resource competition. Meanwhile, most existing microservice approaches address interference either by detecting and localizing performance issues or by optimizing latency alone, without explaining why specific co-locations cause cross-application interference, and how this can inform service placement optimization. This work closes that gap by building a spatio-temporal data structure that captures the causal effects of cross-application interference. These causal effects are mathematically formalized as necessary and sufficient conditional probabilities that inform a multi-objective optimizer (Optuna). Cross-application profiling is used to simulate traces and estimate interference probabilities, while per-service latency baselines are provided by performance data, such as 95th-percentile response times (p95). Our approach supports network penalties, application isolation requirements, and adjustable weighting of necessary and sufficient causal metrics. Experimental results on real multi-application workloads show that interference-aware placements significantly reduce cross-application interference and improve response performance. Ultimately, the causality-driven multi-objective formulation gives cloud operators explicit control over interference, latency, and communication overhead when configuring service placements.
technical_mechanism: Estimate pairwise co-location interference using STIG structure and PN/PS/PNS probabilities, then correlate each pair's expected interference score with response-time degradation to identify interference-prone services.
why_it_works: The pairwise score links a shared-host relationship to service slowdown, which can expose a competing service as a contributor to a tail even when it is outside the request's call path. This diagnoses shared-resource contention; it does not attribute delay to network transport.
root_seam: Join request or service latency records with service-to-host placement, resource usage, and traces for other services on that host. Compare the pairwise interference score with transport, queueing, GPU, and action-application timings to see whether a co-located workload explains tail requests.
experiment: Replay a fixed Root inference workload while independently placing a competing service on and off the inference server or edge host. Use the paper's profiling and pairwise scoring approach to test whether it identifies the introduced contention and affected service. Record transport, server queueing, GPU compute, and action-application time separately; compare tail and healthy requests.
evidence_quote: The analyzer then correlates these scores with response-time degradation to identify interference-prone services
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section IV.A, Analyze phase
reported_gain: Interference decreased from approximately 1763 to 997 (about 43%) in the reported placement comparison; this is not a Root-measured gain.
baseline: Latency-only Optuna, genetic algorithm, and reinforcement-learning placement strategies under the same search budget.
uncertainty: The evidence supports identifying co-location interference, but not packet-level causes or separation of network delay from queueing and compute. The paper says its offline causal estimates may be biased by unobserved confounders.

title: Communication-Aware Robot Execution for Cloud Inference under Spatially Heterogeneous Connectivity
abstract: Cloud-hosted foundation models enable robots to use semantic reasoning beyond onboard computational limits. In this setting, the robot executes a currently available primitive generated by the cloud, and continued task progress requires the next cloud result before this primitive is exhausted. This execution becomes fragile under spatially heterogeneous connectivity, because the current primitive determines when the next result is needed, whereas the wireless environment determines where the next request can be submitted and where the response can be retrieved. Strategies that reduce latency or improve individual transmissions can shorten this dependency, but they do not determine a submission location that supports reliable upload and leaves a feasible opportunity for response retrieval. To address this problem, we introduce the request--response window, which characterizes the time required for the next cloud cycle, including uplink transmission, cloud inference, downlink retrieval, and inference uncertainty. Building on this window and an available communication map, the proposed framework treats the next request point as a motion decision during ongoing primitive execution, selecting it to provide sufficient communication quality for cloud request submission while preserving progress within the finite support of the current primitive. The selected request point is incorporated into a local planner, which guides the robot toward the request point before submission and then continues task execution while maintaining sufficient connectivity for retrieving the next cloud result. Experiments in an indoor wireless scenario built from measurements show that the proposed method achieves the best or tied-best task success among the compared methods, while using fewer request attempts and producing lower request failure rates.
technical_mechanism: Estimate a request–response window from recent inference and transmission observations, then use that window and a spatial communication map to select a communication-favorable request point along the robot’s remaining path. The robot moves to that point before submitting the cloud request, then plans to preserve connectivity while the response is pending.
why_it_works: Submission location and later retrieval location affect whether a cloud cycle succeeds when connectivity varies spatially. Selecting a request point couples the cycle’s estimated duration to the robot’s remaining primitive support and mapped connectivity, aiming to avoid failed uploads, missed downloads, and waiting without simply increasing request frequency. This is an execution-planning intervention, not packet-level tail diagnosis.
root_seam: A Root experiment could attach request IDs and timestamps to robot pose, mapped or measured connectivity, upload submission, response availability, and primitive expiry, then compare communication-aware request placement against nominal-path submission. This could test whether location-aware scheduling reduces network-related failures or blocking in robot-to-cloud loops. The paper does not provide packet/ACK/loss traces or a method to distinguish network delay from cloud inference delay at the request level, so it would not itself localize a network tail.
experiment: The paper evaluates measured indoor wireless connectivity with identical routes, waypoint sequences, delay model, robot limits, and communication map across methods. It compares communication-aware request placement against stop-and-wait, fixed-period asynchronous requests, and inference-time-based asynchronous requests; reported outcomes include task success, request attempts, failures, overlap, and waiting time. A Root replication could retain per-request transport timestamps and pose/connectivity data to separate network behavior from inference time.
evidence_quote: The planner then uses this estimate together with the communication map to select where the next request should be submitted.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section III.D, “Request Point Optimization”
reported_gain: At D_obs = 6.0 m, the proposed method achieves 100.0% task success with 15.3 ± 1.6 requests and no failed or overlapped requests; the fixed-period 5 s baseline achieves the same task success with 50.5 ± 3.4 requests and a 51.5 ± 0.7% overlap rate.
baseline: Stop-and-wait execution; fixed-period asynchronous requests at 5, 10, or 15 seconds; and inference-only asynchronous requests that use estimated inference time but do not select request location using the communication map.
uncertainty: The context reports an indoor measured-connectivity scenario and a shared inference/transmission delay model, but does not give packet-level measurements or isolate network transfer latency from cloud inference latency. The reported gains concern the paper’s task and request metrics, not a measured Root gain.

title: Inference Pipelines as Operating-System Objects: Priority Scheduling and Constant-Footprint Streaming for Microcontroller Neural Inference
abstract: Microcontroller runtimes treat the inference pipeline -- pre-processing, accelerator invocation, post-processing -- as application code: every project re-implements stage sequencing, buffer sizing, and completion signalling around a library call. We argue these are operating-system concerns and present the Phase 2 inference engine of SynapticOS, an open-source Zephyr-based runtime that makes the pipeline a first-class OS object. A pipeline is drawn from a static pool, validated against a canonical stage order, and executed by a priority job scheduler (realtime > normal > best-effort, FIFO per class) with cancellation and a bounded job table; no heap on the inference path. Stage buffers are sized exactly from configuration and tensor geometry for the nine built-in processors (bounded 4x fallback for user stages); all intermediates live in an ephemeral arena reset per frame, so streaming footprint is constant. We evaluate on the NXP FRDM-MCXN947 (Cortex-M33, 150 MHz) and the qemucortexm3 CI target, both running a deterministic stub NPU kernel: engine-overhead baselines, not silicon throughput. On the board the scheduler adds 92 us over the Phase 1 direct-HAL bracket (1,130 vs 1,038 us; dispatch 1 us); a 30-frame, six-stage face-detection pipeline averages 4.63 ms/frame (215.8 FPS, stub model included) vs 31.1 ms under QEMU soft-float, at a constant 2,784-byte arena peak returning to zero each frame. The PowerQuad DSP is routed and self-calibrated for FFT and Q15 matmul; end-to-end speedups are 5.51x (256-point FFT) and 1.66x (16x16 matmul), short of the plan's 10x target -- reported as missed, not re-scoped. Stage-boundary profiling now runs live on the board, closing a Phase 1 gap. The engine adds 3.8 KB flash on QEMU and 20.7 KB on FRDM. 99 tests across 13 ZTEST suites pass 100% under emulation. Released under Apache 2.0 at https://github.com/Dimitrios-Kafetzis/SynapticOS
technical_mechanism: Stage-boundary profiling: mark inference stages and derive per-stage and total durations, then compare the ordered timings of tail and healthy requests to find their first divergence.
why_it_works: Ordered stage durations can localize where a slow request first departs from a comparable healthy request, rather than merely flagging that total latency is high. The paper implements the profiling signal, not the comparison; Root would need to retain and correlate records by request.
root_seam: At the robot-side inference pipeline, associate stage-boundary timestamps and total duration with each request ID, alongside existing transport timestamps. This can distinguish delay within measured inference stages from delay outside that pipeline, but does not itself measure network delay or separate transport from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application.
experiment: For matched tail and healthy remote-inference requests, retain per-request stage timings and transport timestamps. Compare ordered stage durations to identify the first divergence, and check whether it falls inside local inference or outside the measured pipeline. Read each profile before the next inference completes, since the paper's profiler stores only the last completed result.
evidence_quote: From the four marks the profiler derives per-stage times, total time, the arena high-water mark, and an NPU utilisation ratio
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, section VI-B, Live stage-level profiling
reported_gain: The board profile reports 1,069 µs profiled inference, including a 1,068 µs stub model stage; no differential-diagnosis gain is reported.
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The method profiles local inference stages and retains only the last completed result. It does not perform tail-versus-healthy comparison, correlate profiles with request or transport events, or observe packet, ACK, loss, or network-queue signals. Diagnostic value for Root depends on adding per-request retention and correlation.

title: Modeling and Validation of Quality of Control for Edge-Offloaded Collaborative Navigation
abstract: Collaborative control in complex environments is severely challenged by stochastic wireless delay and reliability variations, which can degrade navigation, tracking, and collision avoidance. These network-induced uncertainties complicate the maintenance of energy efficiency during collaborative tasks, and can potentially lead to over-provisioning of resources. In this paper, for a navigation setup with dynamic collision avoidance, we address this challenge by expanding the quality of control (QoC) framework from prior works to practical robotic models. Our approach (i) models end-to-end network effects on closed-loop performance, (ii) systematically explores the impact of various control parameters dictating robotic motion on network latency-reliability (iii) validates these models through experiments on a private 5G testbed across varying delay, reliability and control configurations. Our analysis indicates the optimal control-communication co-design operating regimes for practical robots and also compares the QoC performance of standard ROS 2 quality of service (QoS) policies under real-world conditions and showing how RELIABLE QoS offers 51.5% better QoC than BEST-EFFORT under certain experimental settings.
technical_mechanism: Timestamp each control-relevant message at robot uplink send, edge receive, edge send, and robot downlink receive; compare the resulting end-to-end delay and reliability (including delay percentiles and packet deadline misses) with a disagreement-based QoC score, then evaluate how ROS 2 QoS and control settings change that outcome.
why_it_works: The stage timestamps expose where loop time accumulates across uplink, edge processing, and downlink, while the QoC metric connects late or missed updates to closed-loop disagreement. Comparing delay distributions and deadline misses across QoS policies can reveal whether delivery reliability or latency is associated with degraded robot behavior.
root_seam: Attach message identity and timestamps at the robot transport boundary and edge receive/send points, then correlate those events with command application and robot pose. This gives Root stage-specific timing and a behavioral outcome, helping distinguish network delay from edge processing time rather than relying only on end-to-end latency.
experiment: In a robot-to-cloud action loop, record per-request timestamps at robot send, server receive, server reply, and robot action application. Compute stage and end-to-end delay distributions, deadline misses, and a pose- or action-based disagreement score. Compare these under controlled network delay/loss and delivery-policy conditions while holding server workload fixed.
evidence_quote: For each run, we log: (i) commanded velocities, (ii) ROS 2 QoS settings, and (iii) timestamps at UL send, edge receive, edge send, and DL receive for all control-relevant messages.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section IV.A, “Testbed and Experimental parameters”
reported_gain: 51.5% higher QoC for RELIABLE QoS than BEST-EFFORT under certain experimental settings.
baseline: ROS 2 BEST-EFFORT QoS
uncertainty: The context reports stage timestamps and delay percentiles but does not demonstrate that the method isolates network tail causality from edge queueing or compute variability. The reported QoC gain is specific to the paper’s testbed and settings, not a Root result.

title: Enabling Multi-Dimensional Distributed Trace Comparison with Contrast
abstract: Diagnosis using distributed traces is fundamentally a comparative task: operators seek to understand how an anomalous execution differs from expected behavior, how a deployment changes system execution, or how two individual executions differ. Trace comparison is challenging because useful differences between executions can manifest across multiple dimensions, and no single diagnostic interface is effective at capturing all of them. Moreover, the relevant dimensions and comparison populations are often not known a priori; operators construct and refine comparison sets dynamically as they develop hypotheses about system behavior. This paper presents Contrast, a system for multi-dimensional comparative trace analysis. Contrast introduces the Trace Projection Object (TPO), a mergeable representation that captures structural, temporal, critical-path, and semantic properties of trace populations while enabling efficient construction of arbitrary comparison sets at query time. Unlike approaches that define a fixed notion of trace difference, Contrast separates trace representation from comparison semantics, allowing diverse interfaces to selectively reason about specific dimensions. This separation enables the composition of complementary interfaces, allowing operators to combine insights from multiple dimensions for more effective diagnosis. We demonstrate this capability through two complementary interfaces: (i) SpectroViz, a critical-path-based visual interface for localizing execution differences; and (ii) Parallax, a natural language interface for generating explanations of trace differences using LLMs. We demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of Contrast through controlled experiments on traces from DeathStarBench and evaluation on production traces from Uber.
technical_mechanism: Build mergeable trace-population representations containing structure, latency distributions, and critical-path occupancy; compare an anomalous request or population with a healthy one, overlaying critical-path differences in SpectroViz and summarizing population differences with Parallax.
why_it_works: The comparison exposes execution segments that are atypical or newly on the critical path, alongside missing branches, latency shifts, and semantic errors. The paper’s network-partition example shows that connectivity problems can appear as incomplete traces, timeouts, and divergent latency behavior. This can localize where a network-related delay enters the traced request, though it does not directly distinguish transport delay from server queueing or compute.
root_seam: Attach trace/request identity and timestamps to Root’s robot-side and server-side RPC spans; compare tail requests against healthy requests for critical-path shifts, missing or delayed calls, and latency distributions. This adds trace-level differential localization, not packet/ACK/loss reconstruction.
experiment: Replay or collect matched healthy and tail remote-inference requests under controlled network impairment and separately under server queueing or GPU-load impairment. Compare their trace populations using critical-path occupancy and structural/temporal differences; test whether the network-impaired cases show reproducible RPC-path divergences distinct from the non-network controls.
evidence_quote: We select one trace from the bad population and compare it against the good population of traces using SpectroViz.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, section describing Figure 11a and the network-partition trace comparison.
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: Good population of traces, compared with the bad population or an anomalous trace.
uncertainty: The context supports differential trace diagnosis and a network-partition example, but does not establish packet-level attribution or separation of network delay from server-side waiting. It also gives no quantitative diagnostic accuracy or Root-specific results.

title: Diagnose Before You Compress: Prediction-Independent Bottleneck Witness Refinement for LLM Serving Traces
abstract: Production LLM serving generates millions of diverse requests, making full-trace replay across serving configurations increasingly expensive. Existing trace reduction methods mainly preserve workload distributions or representative requests, but bottleneck-revealing workloads may be rare and non-representative. Moreover, evidence for one component cannot compensate for missing evidence in another, while using predicted bottlenecks as target truth creates circular evaluation. These limitations make it necessary to preserve evidence for every bottleneck component rather than rely on workload representativeness alone. We propose Bottleneck-Preserving Witnessing (BPW), a quality-constrained framework for compact and diagnostically reliable LLM serving replay suites. BPW first performs Workload Candidate Nomination using response-blind workload features and closed source-side measurements. This stage identifies workloads that may expose scheduler, prefill, decode, or KV-cache bottlenecks. Coverage-Priority Sequence Construction then organizes multi-component proposals as reusable hyperedges and prioritizes weak and uncovered dimensions. Finally, Bottleneck Truth Verification derives prediction-independent labels solely from direct target-system measurements. The verified results determine the earliest prefix satisfying the direct two-witness requirement for every component. Experiments on BurstGPT, ServeGen, and Mooncake show that BPW reaches the verified gate with a compact workload set and outperforms 16 policies, achieving relative improvements of 2.3% and 16.3% in Mean prefix Macro-F1 and WBRC-AUC, respectively. Stage-resolved and sensitivity analyses confirm the distinct contributions and local stability of its three stages. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/llmllmllm/BPW
technical_mechanism: Select and order a compact set of replay workloads to preserve per-component bottleneck witnesses: nominate candidates from response-blind features and source-side measurements, prioritize weak or uncovered components, then verify labels using direct target-system measurements and stop at the earliest prefix meeting the quality gate.
why_it_works: This is a witness-based diagnostic reduction, not merely representative sampling: evidence for one component cannot compensate for missing evidence in another, and direct target measurements avoid treating candidate predictions as truth. For Root, network-tail requests could be treated as a separate component and independently verified, making the compact suite a sufficient diagnostic witness set if it retains the required network evidence. It would expose rare tail cases that representative traffic might omit and avoid replaying the full request trace.
root_seam: Attach at Root's request identity and paired robot/server transport timestamps, supplemented where available by packet, ACK, or loss evidence. Use these signals to define network-tail truth independently of nomination; retain server queueing, GPU compute, and action-application delay as separate dimensions. The paper does not provide network features or labels, so these would need to be defined for Root.
experiment: From a fixed Root request pool, nominate candidate replays using response-blind request features and available source-side transport measurements; order them by weakest/uncovered diagnostic dimension. Verify network-tail labels only from direct target replay measurements using paired transport timestamps or packet/ACK/loss evidence. Compare the earliest prefix satisfying a predeclared two-witness-per-dimension gate with representative-subset and length/concurrency controls under identical candidate pools and replay budgets. Report network-tail recall, false positives, prefix cost, and stability across restarts, while measuring queueing, GPU, and action-application delays separately.
evidence_quote: The verified results determine the earliest prefix satisfying the direct two-witness requirement for every component.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Abstract; also Section 4, Methodology, Bottleneck Truth Verification and quality-gate descriptions.
reported_gain: Paper reports relative improvements of 2.3% in Mean prefix Macro-F1 and 16.3% in WBRC-AUC on average versus 16 policies across three traces; these are not Root network-tail results.
baseline: Sixteen reference policies, including traffic controls, geometric/design selection, information acquisition, and adapted trace-reduction policies; the strongest baseline varies by trace and metric.
uncertainty: The paper supports compact, non-compensatory diagnostic witness selection with independent target verification, but tests only scheduler, prefill, decode, and KV-cache bottlenecks. It does not define transport features, network-tail truth, or a network attachment point; Root transfer and any Root gain remain unmeasured.

title: Latency-Tolerant Cloud-Edge Collaborative Vision-Language-Action Models via Emergent Representational Specialization
abstract: Deploying billion-parameter Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies on mobile robots creates a systems conflict: semantic reasoning benefits from cloud GPUs, whereas closed-loop control must respond locally despite network delay and jitter. Existing hierarchical and asynchronous policies improve throughput, but their slow-path representations can still arrive stale or require explicit scheduling and delay cues. We introduce CloudEdgeVLA, a cloud-edge policy that treats temporal misalignment as a representation-learning problem. A cloud VLA encodes delayed observations into slowly varying task features, while a lightweight edge head combines the latest available cloud feature with current local vision. During training, current and randomly delayed frames are paired with the same current action target in fresh and stale paths. This objective encourages the cloud representation to preserve task-level information while the edge path supplies state-sensitive corrections, driving emergent specialization. Across four LIBERO suites, CloudEdgeVLA retains 63.8-78.0% success with a 40-step uniform-delay window, whereas VLASH reaches at most 6.4% and the evaluated single-path baselines at most 3.0%. By removing blocking synchronization from the control loop, the design offers a practical route to scalable VLA deployment in which cloud models can grow while edge computation remains lightweight and responsive.
technical_mechanism: Paired-frame dual-path training supervises cloud features computed from current and randomly delayed observations against the same current action target. At deployment, the edge never blocks for a cloud response: it fuses the latest received cloud feature with current local vision to produce actions.
why_it_works: Training encourages cloud features to retain task-level information that remains useful across observation ages, while current edge vision supplies state-sensitive corrections. This lets the robot continue its closed-loop action loop using stale cloud output rather than waiting for an update.
root_seam: Attach this mechanism at the cloud-feature-to-edge-action interface. Root could test the effect of stale cloud results by injecting controlled delay or replaying features of known age, while measuring action success and loop responsiveness. The method tolerates delay; it does not identify whether a tail came from transport, server queueing, or inference.
experiment: On the same robot task and cloud-edge setup, compare the paired-frame-trained controller with a single-path baseline under controlled uniform delay, including delay values beyond the training window. Measure task success and action-loop responsiveness; separately record transport and server-side timings if the goal is to localize network tails.
evidence_quote: The edge never blocks on a cloud response and uses the latest available feature.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, section 3.5, Emergent Representational Specialization
reported_gain: Under uniform delay up to 40 steps in LIBERO, success rates were 76.4% (Spatial), 75.6% (Object), 78.0% (Goal), and 63.8% (Long). In the real-robot pilot at 1000 ms added RTT, CloudEdgeVLA achieved 80%/70% static/dynamic success.
baseline: LIBERO comparison includes VLASH, which reached at most 6.4% under the 40-step delay condition; real-robot comparison includes VLASH, which achieved 0%/0% at 1000 ms added RTT.
uncertainty: The method demonstrates robustness to controlled or emulated delay, not diagnosis of naturally occurring network tails. The evidence does not separate transport delay from server queueing or model inference time.

title: TELLER: Non-intrusive Cross-Layer Root-Cause Analysis for LLM Inference
abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference has evolved from an offline workload into a continuously operated software service, yet root-cause analysis remains difficult because a single request spans the inference engine, Python/C++ backend, host CUDA APIs, GPU kernels, and distributed communication. Existing profilers expose raw timelines, while log-based diagnosis often misses cross-layer execution semantics and request-level structure. We present TELLER, a non-intrusive Trace- and Log-aware LLM inference Root-cause analysis framework. TELLER first collects NVTX/CUPTI traces and service logs without modifying model binaries, then reconstructs per-request call-chain trees and aligns log lines with the corresponding execution steps. We introduce a dependency-aware causal-context slice that preserves parent-child structure, temporal order, and communication relations, and a Trace Pair Encoding (TPE) tokenizer that compresses such slices into compact structural token sequences with parent, depth, and duration attributes. On top of these representations, TELLER combines numeric candidate localization with a multimodal root-cause model that jointly predicts abnormal steps, localizes suspicious operators, and generates natural-language explanations. Experiments on multi-node GPU inference workloads show a clear compression-accuracy trade-off: a moderate TPE vocabulary reduces per-step trace length by more than 80% while achieving the best overall performance on both horizontal (cross-node communication) and vertical (within-node execution stack) views, whereas more aggressive compression substantially degrades diagnosis quality. Further analyses under low-fault priors, strengthened baselines, modality ablations, explanation-quality checks, and tracing overhead show that TELLER provides a practical triage and evidence-localization substrate for LLM inference RCA.
technical_mechanism: Non-intrusive NVTX/CUPTI trace and service-log collection reconstructs per-request call-chain trees, aligns logs by request identity and time, then uses numeric candidate localization and dependency-aware causal-context slices to identify suspicious operators and communication events. The slices preserve parent-child structure, temporal order, communication relations, and durations for downstream diagnosis.
why_it_works: Request-level reconstruction connects communication events to execution context that raw timelines or detached logs lack. Comparing a faulty request's cross-layer path with a healthy request in the same batch can expose where behavior first diverges. Compact slices retain relevant structural and timing evidence for localization, but the method does not establish packet-level network causes.
root_seam: Attach request identity and timestamps to robot-side and server-side transport or communication events, then reconstruct each inference/action request's ordered path and compare tail requests with healthy counterparts. This could locate whether a delay first appears around communication or elsewhere in the execution path. TELLER does not itself provide packet/ACK/loss attribution or prove that a communication delay is network rather than endpoint or server queueing.
experiment: On a controlled remote-inference robot loop, collect request IDs and timestamps for client send/receive, server receive/dispatch, inference steps, and available transport events. Compare tail requests against healthy requests from the same workload using request-level reconstruction and first-divergence localization; validate localization against injected network delay/loss and separately injected server queueing or compute delay. Measure attribution accuracy and tracing overhead.
evidence_quote: TELLER first collects NVTX/CUPTI traces and service logs without modifying model binaries, then reconstructs per-request call-chain trees and aligns log lines with the corresponding execution steps.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Abstract.
reported_gain: Moderate TPE vocabulary reduces per-step trace length by more than 80%; the abstract reports best overall performance on horizontal (cross-node communication) and vertical views, without giving the metric values there.
baseline: Uncompressed trace length is the implied comparison for the reported trace-length reduction; the abstract does not specify the exact comparison baseline for diagnosis performance.
uncertainty: The supplied context supports request-level cross-layer communication-event diagnosis, but does not describe packet/ACK/loss sequences or a network-specific tail-localization evaluation. Robot/action-loop transfer and the proposed Root experiment remain unvalidated.

title: Uplink-Completion-Triggered Edge-GPU Inference for Multi-Agent Cooperative Perception
abstract: This paper investigates the coupling between wireless input completion and graphics processing unit (GPU) execution in centralized multi-agent cooperative perception. Specifically, beyond the conceptual treatment of completion-triggered overlap, a complete execution path is realized and validated on a physical GPU for a cooperative-perception deep neural network (DNN). Each encoder branch is released immediately upon completion of its corresponding input transmission, while the original fusion dependencies and inference mapping are preserved. The resulting release-triggered communication computation coupling (RTCC) propagates validated wireless completion events through host-to-device (H2D) staging, CUDA synchronization, and dependency-preserving branch dispatch, while remaining compatible with causal wireless schedulers. Experiments combining trace-driven wireless arrivals, physical GPU execution, and measured-DAG evaluation show that RTCC reduces complete-detection latency across different communication loads and schedulers, while preserving identical detection outputs and average-precision performance relative to conventional execution.
technical_mechanism: Completion-triggered branch execution with per-input completion-to-GPU timing: a validated wireless payload-completion event releases its corresponding encoder through H2D staging and CUDA dispatch, while a profiled dependency DAG records when computation can run and when the final join is ready.
why_it_works: The completion event makes the end of input delivery an explicit boundary, and GPU event timings expose subsequent staging and execution. Comparing these timestamps with the DAG’s expected service times can distinguish late input delivery from work that is ready but waiting on GPU execution, rather than treating end-to-end latency as one undifferentiated delay. The paper uses this chiefly to overlap computation and communication, not as an evaluated tail-diagnosis system.
root_seam: For each Root request or input, correlate robot/server transport-completion time with H2D start/end, encoder dispatch/completion, and downstream join/output timestamps. This would expose whether a slow request’s delay precedes input completion or follows it in GPU execution; it would not, by itself, distinguish transport delay from server queueing before the recorded completion event.
experiment: Replay matched request/input-arrival traces through completion-triggered execution and an all-arrival barrier, recording per-input transport completion, H2D, GPU branch start/end, and final output timestamps. Compare slow-request latency with the arrival gaps and measured GPU service times, and check whether the per-request decomposition identifies network-side versus post-completion delay. Keep server queueing and action-application timestamps separate where available.
evidence_quote: Once an input is validated as complete, it is asynchronously
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, RTCC physical-GPU realization paragraph; the supplied excerpt truncates the sentence after this phrase. Supporting description: “completion events generated by trace-driven wireless emulation [are connected] to pinned-memory H2D staging, CUDA-event synchronization, and encoder-branch dispatch.”
reported_gain: Mean complete-detection latency reduction of 64.96 ms (95% CI: 57.11–72.81 ms), versus Barrier execution.
baseline: Barrier execution: each encoder waits until all input transmissions are complete before execution.
uncertainty: Wireless completion times are trace-driven emulation, not over-the-air measurements. The paper demonstrates the completion-to-GPU execution path and latency overlap, but does not evaluate network-tail diagnosis or Root. Lane n13 is not promoted: transfer to robot-to-cloud action loops is plausible, but the supplied evidence is for multi-agent cooperative perception and does not establish direct applicability to action-loop requests.

title: Measuring Browser Webcam Gaze Honestly: A Capture-Clock Methodology and Open Reference Implementation
abstract: Browser-based webcam gaze trackers are increasingly used for crowd-scale data collection and in clinical settings where lab eye trackers are impractical, but the reported latency numbers may not represent real world functionality. The common practice of timestamping each gaze sample when it is emitted, rather than when its source frame was captured, makes the measured inference latency read about 0 ms no matter how slow the engine really is. We show how to measure it honestly, recovering a per-frame capture clock from the browser's re-quest-Video-Frame-Call-back (rVFC) API (captureTime where the browser exposes it for local camera streams, else presentationTime, in which case every recovered latency is a verifiable lower bound): exact source-frame pairing through a per-frame queue for engines that expose their inference pipeline, and a further lower bound for engines that do not, such as WebGazer. We release an open TypeScript implementation and benchmark harness, demonstrated on two interchangeable engines: WebGazer and a new FaceMesh+KRR pipeline.
technical_mechanism: Source-clock reconstruction with identity-based output pairing: recover each input frame’s source timestamp, then pair an inference result with the frame that produced it. When exact pairing is unavailable, tag the result with the latest known frame time and report the resulting latency only as a lower bound.
why_it_works: Emission-time timestamps can make a slow asynchronous pipeline appear to have near-zero latency. Measuring from the source clock to the correctly matched output exposes the elapsed request-to-result delay, including its tail. The method transfers to robot-cloud action loops as end-to-end latency measurement, but by itself does not separate network transport from server queueing or compute.
root_seam: Record a robot-side submission timestamp and request/frame identity, then match that identity to the server-side inference result and returned action. This provides a source-referenced end-to-end latency distribution and avoids falsely measuring only callback emission time. Additional transport and server-stage timestamps or events are required to attribute a tail specifically to the network.
experiment: On matched Root requests, compare callback/emission-time latency with source-timestamped, identity-matched request-to-result latency. Include both exact pairing and a documented lower-bound approximation if output identity is unavailable. Inject controlled network delay while separately recording transport and server-stage timings; check whether the corrected end-to-end p95/p99 reveals delayed requests and whether stage measurements distinguish network delay from queueing and compute.
evidence_quote: For engines that expose their inference pipeline at per-frame granularity, such as our FaceMesh+KRR engine, we keep a FIFO queue of frame timestamps and pair every gaze sample with the exact source frame it was computed from.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, §3.2, “Exact pairing via rVFC for queue-exposing engines”; lower-bound handling for opaque engines is described in §3.3.
reported_gain: Correct timestamping changes reported latency from approximately 0 ms to 22–34 ms median and 27–52 ms p95 in the browser gaze benchmark; this is not a Root or network gain.
baseline: Naive emission-time timestamping, which reports approximately 0 ms.
uncertainty: The paper measures browser capture-to-inference latency, not network transport or rare network delays. Source timestamps and identities must be preserved across Root’s transport, and stage-level evidence is needed to distinguish network delay from server queueing, compute, and action application.

title: DualPI2 Active Queue Management in ns-3: Implementation And Validation
abstract: The demand for ultra-low latency applications necessitates advanced network architectures like the Low Latency, Low Loss, and Scalable Throughput (L4S) standard. A core component of L4S is the DualPI2 Active Queue Management (AQM), which ensures the safe coexistence of scalable and classic traffic. Despite L4S's growing adoption, the ns-3 network simulator lacks a high-fidelity, up-to-date DualPI2 model. This paper presents a comprehensive implementation of the DualPI2 AQM in ns-3, while also mirroring the official Linux Kernel architecture. Our model incorporates representative mechanisms previously absent in simulation, such as credit-based Weighted Round Robin (WRR) scheduling, step-marking, and overload protection. To guarantee simulation accuracy, we validate our implementation against a physical Linux testbed across 25 diverse Bandwidth-Delay Product (BDP) scenarios. Results demonstrate that our ns-3 model replicates real-world behavior, ensuring strict throughput fairness and queue delay isolation. Ultimately, this validated model equips the research community with a robust tool to evaluate and advance L4S performance across diverse network topologies, ranging from data centers to wireless home and office environments.
technical_mechanism: Per-packet queue-sojourn measurement with queue-specific tracing: record how long packets reside in each sub-queue, and use that residence time to identify delay accumulating at the bottleneck queue.
why_it_works: Queue residence directly measures time spent waiting in a network queue, making it a concrete signal for distinguishing queue buildup from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application. Correlated with request timing, it could show whether network queue delay contributes to an inference tail. The paper also describes a secondary-threshold marking operation, but that is congestion control, not an independent diagnostic mechanism.
root_seam: Add enqueue/dequeue timestamps or equivalent sojourn-time telemetry at the robot or server transport bottleneck. Correlate packet/request identity and queue residence with end-to-end inference timestamps to separate network waiting from server-side queueing, GPU compute, and action application.
experiment: In a controlled Root setup, introduce bottleneck congestion while collecting per-packet sojourn times for the relevant queue and request-level inference timings. Check whether elevated queue residence coincides with request tails and whether it separates them from server queueing and compute delays.
evidence_quote: At the bottleneck router, native queue traces logged packet marks and drops, and a custom trace source was added to measure the sojourn time in each sub-queue.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section 5 Evaluation
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The paper validates an ns-3 DualPI2 implementation against a Linux testbed; it does not demonstrate request-level tail attribution or report a Root experiment. It supports the queue-residence signal and a controlled transfer experiment, but not a measured Root gain.

title: Static Pruning Across Sparse Retrieval Regimes: What Transfers, What Breaks, and What Still Helps
abstract: Static pruning is widely used to accelerate sparse neural retrieval, yet existing studies each validate their conclusions within a single custom pipeline, leaving it unclear which findings transfer to modern engines with different index organizations and dynamic pruning mechanisms. We present the first cross-engine pruning portability study, evaluating static pruning strategies across three engines - a controlled C++ pipeline (exhaustive inverted index), BMP (block-max pruning), and SEISMIC (clustered inverted indexes) - on two benchmarks (MS MARCO, Natural Questions) with two encoders spanning opposite query-density regimes (SPLADE: 44 avg. query terms; V3-GTE: 7 avg. query terms), totaling 1,140 experimental configurations, with an additional deep-judgment validation on TREC DL 2019/2020. We find that index-side pruning (document and posting-list) is portable: it consistently reduces latency (1.2-6.6×) and index size (18-82%) across all engines because sparse retrieval is memory-bound - a conclusion we support with cache-miss, TLB, and IPC profiling. In contrast, query pruning is already internalized by modern engines: it yields 4-11× speedup on the exhaustive pipeline but is subsumed by BMP's β and SEISMIC's querycut. Static pruning complements dynamic pruning: on BMP, combining document and query reduction yields 2.5× speedup with NDCG@10 within 0.003 of the exact baseline. Finally, NDCG@10 saturates while Recall@10 is still in the ∼85-95% range across all three engines, providing a portable stopping criterion: practitioners can push pruning to this knee without visible ranking degradation. Together, these findings answer what transfers (index-side pruning), what breaks (query pruning), and what still helps (static atop dynamic pruning).
technical_mechanism: Pair controlled changes to retrieval working-set size with per-query latency and hardware-counter profiling. Index-side pruning reduces posting-list traffic; cache-miss, TLB-miss, and IPC measurements test whether memory stalls explain latency changes. The diagnostic operation is counter-correlated latency profiling, not pruning alone.
why_it_works: The study reports sparse retrieval is memory-bound and correlates latency with memory locality, giving Root a way to test whether a slow request is delayed in server-side retrieval rather than on the network. A latency increase accompanied by increased cache/TLB misses supports a server memory-stall explanation; without that evidence, this method does not identify which network component caused delay.
root_seam: At the inference server, correlate request-ID-linked retrieval latency with cache-miss, TLB-miss, and IPC counters. Compare those measurements with robot/server transport timestamps so retrieval memory stalls can be separated from network transfer, server queueing, GPU compute, and action application. This uses ordinary host-side profiling and does not require Reflex-private infrastructure.
experiment: Replay the same inference requests under controlled network delay/loss and separately under retrieval working-set or memory-pressure changes. Collect transport timestamps, per-request retrieval latency, and cache/TLB/IPC counters. Test whether controlled memory pressure changes retrieval latency and counters while transport timing stays stable, and whether network impairment changes transport timing without the retrieval-counter signature. Compare against unprofiled request logging and report localization accuracy and overhead; do not attribute the paper's retrieval speedups to Root.
evidence_quote: Latency is tightly coupled to memory locality, not arithmetic throughput.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section 6.3, “Mechanistic Explanation: Memory-Bound Retrieval” (profiling discussion).
reported_gain: 1.2–6.6× retrieval latency reduction from index-side pruning; no Root-measured gain.
baseline: Unpruned/exact retrieval baseline for the reported retrieval speedups.
uncertainty: The paper supports profiling retrieval memory behavior, not diagnosing transport tails directly. Whether host counters can be reliably attributed to individual concurrent Root requests, and the diagnostic accuracy or overhead of this transfer, remain untested.

title: Affix Cache for Diffusion Large Language Models
abstract: Diffusion Large Language Models (DLLMs) enable non-autoregressive decoding and bidirectional context modeling, but efficient inference remains challenging. Unlike autoregressive systems, whose key-value (KV) cache can be reused for shared prefixes, DLLMs couple the KV states of shared context tokens with evolving generated tokens through bidirectional attention, making naive cache reuse stale while full recomputation is expensive. We present ACache, an affix-oriented cache reuse mechanism for shared text spans in DLLMs beyond prefixes. ACache identifies a small request-specific subset of critical affix tokens, called Anchor Tokens, by measuring their influence on masked generation tokens, and selectively recomputes the KV states of only these tokens while reusing the remaining affix cache. Built on Fast-dLLM, ACache recovers the accuracy loss caused by direct affix-cache reuse across different settings when recomputing around 20% of affix tokens. We also build a shared-prefix prototype on top of the Nano-vLLM engine, showing that ACache reduces recompute latency by up to 55.7% and improves end-to-end throughput by up to 1.68×.
technical_mechanism: ACache performs request-specific, one-shot anchor selection: it probes masked generation positions, ranks shared-affix tokens by attention received from those positions, recomputes the selected tokens’ KV states, and reuses the other shared-affix KV entries. A paged-cache read-slot map lets attention read the full logical context from shared and private cache slots.
why_it_works: The attention-based ranking identifies shared-token KV states most sensitive to the current request context. Refreshing those anchors limits stale-cache errors while retaining reuse for the remaining tokens. For comparable-baseline retrieval, this is a concrete cache-selection and reuse mechanism, though its experiments concern inference computation rather than network-tail diagnosis.
root_seam: For Root, the transferable attachment is request identity plus a shared-prefix or prompt-template cache key and cache-hit/recompute events. These could show whether a comparable healthy request’s cached baseline is reusable and separate cache recomputation cost from transport delay. The paper does not instrument network signals or diagnose network tails.
experiment: Controlled Root experiment: replay identical requests with and without a shared baseline cache, record cache key/hit status, selected/recomputed entries, and separate transport, server-queue, and inference timestamps. Compare tail latency and diagnostic localization while holding request mix and model work constant. The paper does not report such a Root experiment.
evidence_quote: ACache identifies a small request-specific subset of critical affix tokens, called Anchor Tokens, by measuring their influence on masked generation tokens, and selectively recomputes the KV states of only these tokens while reusing the remaining affix cache.
evidence_location: Abstract; selected PDF text, Section 3 mechanism description.
reported_gain: Up to 55.7% lower recompute latency and up to 1.68× end-to-end throughput in the shared-prefix Nano-vLLM prototype; not a Root or network-tail gain.
baseline: Fast-dLLM-based Nano-vLLM baseline.
uncertainty: Transfer to Root is indirect: the method optimizes DLLM KV-cache reuse, not baseline retrieval for network diagnosis, and provides no transport-level measurements. The prototype supports shared prefixes; end-to-end benefits for non-prefix affixes are not validated in a full runtime.

title: SchedBlame: Who Ran While You Waited? Culprit-Attributed CPU Contention for Containers on Stock Kernels
abstract: Containers that share a machine compete for CPU. When one slows down, the operator needs to know which co-tenant is responsible, and no deployed signal can say. Pressure stall information, per-cgroup wait counters, and run-queue latency histograms are all victim-side: they report that a container waited, never who it waited for. Recovering the culprit means a kernel patch, full scheduler tracing, or statistical inference: unportable, too costly to leave on, or unreliable when victims coexist. SchedBlame is an eBPF tracer that attributes CPU contention to the cgroups that caused it, on stock kernels, continuously. It inverts the accounting: instead of measuring how long a victim waited, it measures the CPU time every other cgroup consumed while that victim was runnable but not running on the same CPU. The mechanism is a per-CPU bitmap of which measured cgroups are waiting, maintained from the kernel's own runnable counts at four scheduler hooks. Every run slice carries that bitmap, so one 16-byte record charges CPU time to a full row of a competitor x victim blame matrix; the kernel stores no per-pair state. Three properties follow. Slices are self-describing, so userspace holds no waiting state and a lost record costs measurements, not correctness. The measured set is reconfigured by publishing an epoch, invalidating every cache and per-CPU bitmap in constant time while the hooks keep running. Sampling never touches waiting state, so rescaling by the inverse keep probability keeps the estimator unbiased. SchedBlame splits each container's per-second CPU demand into runtime, internal contention, external contention, and throttling, flags anomalies against a rolling 99th-percentile baseline, and names the competitors responsible. In production on unmodified 4.18 and 5.10 kernels, tracking 84 containers on a 96-core host, it costs about 1% of Redis throughput and 6% of one core.
technical_mechanism: At scheduler hooks, maintain a per-CPU bitmap of measured cgroups that are runnable but not running. Stamp each completed CPU run slice with that bitmap and charge its duration to the competitor–victim pairs it represents. Decompose victim demand into runtime, internal contention, external contention, and throttling; flag anomalies and rank competing cgroups.
why_it_works: It observes which cgroups consumed CPU while a victim was waiting, rather than inferring culprits from victim-side wait counters or isolated preemption events. Separately accounting for throttling helps distinguish scheduler contention from a victim's own quota limit. For Root, analogous scheduler measurements could identify server-side CPU queueing as distinct from transport delay, GPU compute, or action application.
root_seam: Attach to server-side scheduler events for the inference worker, keyed by request identity and timestamps; attribute runnable-but-not-running intervals to competing cgroups and separately record throttling. This could localize server CPU wait without mistaking it for network delay. The paper does not provide transport or robot-side signals.
experiment: On a controlled remote-inference workload, inject known server CPU contention and quota throttling while holding network conditions fixed, then inject network delay while server scheduling remains unconstrained. Compare per-request latency decomposition and culprit attribution against known injection windows and transport timestamps; measure tracer overhead.
evidence_quote: Instead of measuring how long a victim waited, it measures the CPU time every other cgroup consumed while that victim was runnable but not running on the same CPU.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Abstract
reported_gain: Production deployment tracking 84 containers on a 96-core host: about 1% Redis throughput cost and 6% of one core. The paper says detection quality has not been evaluated against a labelled set.
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The mechanism diagnoses CPU contention, not network tails directly; its transfer to Root would require adapting collection to inference requests and correlating scheduler intervals with transport events. The planned accuracy and overhead evaluations are not reported as completed.

title: Practical Zero-Trust for Mission-Critical Robotic Fleets via Hardware Attestation and Packet Timing Watermarking
abstract: Autonomous unmanned vehicles are vital to tactical missions, mission-critical public-safety operations like search and rescue and disaster response. However, their reliance on open wireless links and standard Robot Operating System (ROS 2) middleware exposes a broad cyber-physical attack surface. A compromise of these systems can disrupt real-time control loops, leading to mission failure or asset loss in high-stakes environments. This paper presents and empirically evaluates a layered, context-aware cybersecurity framework enforcing Zero-Trust principles for a multi-node robotic fleet over Wi-Fi. The framework integrates an active hardware root of trust (TPM 2.0), centralized in-band and out-of-band SIEM telemetry monitoring (ELK Stack and Kismet), and a non-cryptographic Inter-Packet Delay (IPD) timing watermark. Evaluated on a live ROS 2 mobile testbed under multi-layer exploits (OSI Layers 2-5), results demonstrate that while volume-based filters isolate brute denial-of-service floods, tracking the statistical sample kurtosis (K) of the embedded IPD watermark exposes stealthy Man-in-the-Middle command injections with complete detection accuracy without payload overheads.
technical_mechanism: Embed zero-mean Gaussian timing offsets in the controller’s packet-release intervals, then evaluate sample kurtosis over a rolling 5-second window at the robot; flag the flow when kurtosis leaves the expected watermark range.
why_it_works: The receiver knows the expected timing-distribution signature. An MITM relay’s queuing and user-space scheduling jitter perturbs that signature, so kurtosis can expose command injection even when ordinary packet jitter and loss remain near baseline. This is an integrity/anomaly signal, not a direct measurement separating network delay from relay or host scheduling delay.
root_seam: Attach watermark generation and receive timestamps to identified robot-to-cloud action-loop packets, retaining the rolling kurtosis result alongside request identity. This could reveal timing-distribution corruption hidden by aggregate jitter/loss metrics; Root would need to test whether the signal localizes network tails rather than merely detecting an on-path relay.
experiment: In a controlled robot-to-cloud loop, compare healthy traffic with injected network delay/tails and with relay or host-scheduling perturbations. Record packet/request timestamps and watermark kurtosis, and compare detection and localization against ordinary jitter/loss monitoring while separately measuring transport, server queueing, GPU compute, and action-application time.
evidence_quote: Because an active MITM relay introduces queuing dynamics and arbitrary OS task-scheduling jitter to intercept and parse topic payloads, an adversary inevitably corrupts this timing pattern.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section III-B, “Packet-Layer Inter-Packet Delay (IPD) Watermarking”; detection results in Section IV, Attack Scenario 4.
reported_gain: Complete 20/20 success rate identifying active injection attacks; 19/20 success under legitimate watermarked conditions.
baseline: Nominal watermark sample kurtosis 2.8–3.2; detector alerts at K < 2.0 or K > 4.5. Ordinary jitter and packet loss were reported as nearly indistinguishable from baseline during MITM.
uncertainty: The testbed is a local ROS 2 Wi-Fi fleet, not remote robot-to-cloud inference. The mechanism detects watermark perturbation but does not establish that the cause is network delay rather than relay queuing or host scheduling jitter; transfer to tail-latency localization remains to be validated.

title: Sharing a Fabric with Collective Communication: Two Storage Penalties in Deep Learning Training
abstract: Distributed DL training on HPC systems often shares one network fabric between NCCL/RCCL collective communication and parallel-filesystem I/O. Using a real GNN training workload on a Slingshot-11 system, we show that this sharing imposes two distinct costs. The primary cost is heavy-tailed DataLoader stalls: the typical DataLoader wait is just 15 ms at steady state, yet spikes to multiple seconds in 28% of Lustre iterations and 12% of VAST iterations. The secondary cost is traffic-class contention on collective communication: Lustre I/O stalls the all-reduce by up to 145× in an isolated benchmark. The two costs arise from different mechanisms. I/O stall latency affects any storage path that traverses the shared fabric, whereas all-reduce network contention occurs only when storage and collective communication share the same traffic class. Their common root cause is that storage I/O traverses the shared fabric. This work shows that node-local NVMe staging via DYAD (Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/flux-framework/dyad) eliminates both effects by keeping storage I/O off that path. Across a full training epoch, DYAD achieves a 7.4 times speedup over direct Lustre reads and a 1.06 times speedup over VAST. By the second epoch, once the local cache is fully warmed, DataLoader stalls are eliminated entirely, allowing DYAD to reach a 1.31 times speedup over VAST.
technical_mechanism: Use controlled storage-path and traffic-class substitutions, then compare per-iteration DataLoader wait and all-reduce tails: shared-fabric Lustre I/O, traffic-class-isolated VAST I/O, and node-local storage expose distinct effects of fabric latency and same-class contention.
why_it_works: Changing whether storage traffic traverses the fabric or shares the collective’s traffic class acts as a causal intervention. Stage-level tail measurements show that traffic-class isolation reduces all-reduce contention but leaves DataLoader stalls, while moving reads off the fabric removes both effects. This distinguishes shared-resource network delay from compute time and localizes the relevant resource to the storage path and, for all-reduce interference, the shared traffic class.
root_seam: For Root, correlate request-stage timestamps with transport or storage-path identity, then compare tails under a controlled path or traffic-class change. This could identify whether an off-path flow shares the relevant fabric resource without assuming access to Reflex’s private infrastructure.
experiment: Replay comparable robot inference requests while holding model, server load, and request mix constant; vary or tag the storage/background flow’s path or traffic class. Record request-stage latency and transport events, and compare tail latency with the flow present, isolated, and absent. Separate network-transfer time from server queueing, GPU execution, and action application.
evidence_quote: TC isolation (e.g., VAST on TC0) substantially reduces the secondary all-reduce effect, but it does not fix the primary DataLoader stall effect.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section II, “A. Mitigations”
reported_gain: DYAD achieved 7.4× speedup over direct Lustre reads and 1.06× over VAST in the first epoch; after the cache warmed, it achieved 1.31× over VAST.
baseline: Direct Lustre reads and direct VAST reads in the same training workload.
uncertainty: This is a training-storage study, not remote robot inference. Its controlled path comparisons support diagnosing shared-resource effects, but it does not identify individual off-path flows or provide Root measurements.

title: CARLAverse: A Highly Modular, Distributed, and Multimodal Framework for Human-in-the-Loop Simulation
abstract: The development of autonomous driving demands comprehensive testing in mixed-traffic scenarios involving vulnerable road users (VRUs), where purely artificial agents often fail to capture authentic human social negotiations. While human-in-the-loop (HITL) simulators enable safe investigation of these interactions, existing multi-agent platforms struggle with the network latency and synchronization constraints required for high-fidelity haptic feedback. To resolve this, we present CARLAverse, an open-source, multimodal simulation ecosystem. Extending modular hardware abstraction, CARLAverse integrates driving (DrivoCARLA), cycling (CycloCARLA), and pedestrian (WalkoCARLA) simulators into a shared virtual environment. Its core methodological contribution is a distributed physics architecture: latency-critical ego dynamics and high-frequency force feedback are computed locally on client nodes, while a central CARLA server orchestrates non-player character (NPC) physics and global traffic. By decoupling haptic control loops from network bottlenecks, CARLAverse enables scalable, cross-institutional HITL experiments without compromising physical immersion. Code and documentation: https://git.ieem-ka.de/simulator-environments/carlaverse
technical_mechanism: Move latency-critical ego physics and force-feedback control loops to each client node; keep global traffic and NPC physics on the central server, exchanging lightweight state updates and collision events.
why_it_works: The local control loop no longer waits for network transmission to or from the server. This can prevent WAN delay from affecting the action loop and, in a controlled comparison with centralized execution, help isolate the network contribution to loop latency.
root_seam: Attach timestamps to input, local physics execution, network state-update send/receive, and actuation events for the same action. Compare local-loop timing with a server-dependent loop to separate network delay from computation and actuation. The paper does not describe request identities or a method for detecting off-path flows or shared-resource contention.
experiment: Replay identical robot actions under centralized and client-local control while measuring input-to-actuation latency and separately timestamping network send/receive events. Inject controlled network delay or jitter and compare loop tails and action outcomes across the two configurations.
evidence_quote: the architecture inherently tolerates WAN latency
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section III, Distributed Architectures and Latency Management
reported_gain: UNKNOWN
baseline: UNKNOWN
uncertainty: The paper describes an architecture and intended latency benefits, but says quantitative validation is outside its scope. It does not report a controlled latency comparison or diagnose network tails, off-path flows, or shared-resource contention.

title: Hybrid Monitoring for Early Fault Detection in Cloud-Native 5G Systems
abstract: This paper presents the design implementation and evaluation of NetMon a hybrid network monitoring system designed for Kubernetes-based 5G packet core deployments specifically evaluated on Ericssons Access and Mobility Management Function AMF clusters NetMon combines eBPF-based passive kernel-level traffic observation with active TCP probing and centralized correlation to detect and localize network degradation within seconds The evaluation results demonstrate that the system detects faults as subtle as 10ms of added latency or 5 packet loss correctly attributes them to the affected infrastructure component and maintains this capability under application loads up to 50 simulated UE load The total resource overhead of 34 millicores CPU and 45 MiB memory per pod suggests that the approach is promising for further validation without impacting the monitored workload The hybrid approach addresses a gap in existing monitoring tools standard health checks cannot detect partial degradation scrape-based systems introduce detection delays measured in tens of seconds and purely passive tools cannot verify idle network paths By combining these complementary techniques and centralizing the analysis the system provides the early detection and fault localization capabilities required for maintaining service quality in cloud-native 5G infrastructure.
technical_mechanism: Combine kernel-timestamped active TCP round-trip probes with passive eBPF retransmission and traffic signals; detect deviations from per-peer baselines using statistical thresholds and CUSUM, then correlate anomalies across peers and workers to localize the affected component.
why_it_works: Active probes provide measurements even on idle paths, while passive kernel signals add evidence about retransmissions and traffic behavior. Per-peer baselines identify changes, and cluster-wide correlation turns individual anomalies into worker- or peer-level fault indications without requiring full application tracing. For Root, this could attach to request-linked transport events and provide sparse path and loss evidence alongside inference timings. The measured probe RTT includes remote peer processing, however, so it cannot by itself distinguish network delay from server queueing or compute.
root_seam: Add lightweight kernel transport timestamps and sparse active probes at robot/server communication endpoints, keyed to request or peer identity; correlate RTT shifts and retransmission/loss indicators with Root's inference-stage timings. This can expose path degradation without collecting full traces, but requires separate server-side timing to attribute RTT increases specifically to the network.
experiment: The authors evaluated NetMon on a live Kubernetes 5G AMF cluster with 10 pods across four workers. They injected controlled latency, jitter, loss, bandwidth throttling, partitions, link failures, pod termination, and gradual degradation using tc and iptables, repeated runs at 0%, 20%, and 50% simulated load, and measured detection and localization latency.
evidence_quote: The egress program timestamps outgoing SYN packets destined for the probe port, while the ingress program calculates latency when the first data-bearing reply segment arrives from the peer, emitting the RTT (in microseconds) via a ring buffer.
evidence_location: selected_pdf_text, §2.2, eBPF Passive Monitoring: TC Programs
reported_gain: Detected injected faults as subtle as 10 ms added latency or 5% packet loss; latency and jitter detection took 2–10 seconds and correct localization took 6–20 seconds. Full partitions were detected and correlated within 9–11 seconds. These are the paper's results, not Root measurements.
baseline: The paper reports comparison with typical Kubernetes liveness probes (10–30 second intervals) and Prometheus/Blackbox Exporter scrape cycles (commonly 15–60 seconds), and notes that purely passive eBPF cannot verify idle paths. It does not report a controlled head-to-head benchmark against those systems.
uncertainty: The tested system is Kubernetes 5G infrastructure rather than remote robot inference. Probe RTT includes remote peer application processing, and severe bandwidth throttling can starve monitoring reports. Baseline noise produced about 2,900 anomalies per hour in the virtualized test environment; softer correlations required operator judgment, and thresholds were tuned on preliminary baseline runs.

title: Scalable Packet Tracking on FPGAs for Erasure-Coded RDMA over Lossy WANs
abstract: Modern AI workloads increasingly rely on scale across architectures that interconnect multiple datacenters to form a single "AI factory", overcoming the power and cooling constraints of individual sites. However, extending Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) across wide area networks (WANs) introduces fundamental challenges: multi-path packet reordering, high latency, and packet loss that severely degrade performance. While erasure coding (EC) has emerged as a promising mechanism for loss recovery, its effectiveness critically depends on efficient packet arrival tracking implemented in hardware. We present COmpact Multi-path Erasure-coded Tracking (COMET), the first fully hardware-offloaded packet-arrival tracking design implemented on an FPGA-based network interface card (NIC) for multi-path RDMA over lossy WANs. COMET employs a scalable cache-based architecture that supports operation at high link rates. Our evaluation shows that COMET sustains line rate operation at 400 Gbps and beyond. Critically, COMET decouples on-chip memory footprint from link Bandwidth-Delay Product (BDP), and its cache-based architecture (COMET Cache) enables supporting 6 times more concurrent connections than state-of-the-art (SOTA) SoC-based designs. These results demonstrate that scalable, fully hardware-offloaded packet-arrival tracking is practical on FPGA-based NICs at current data rates, and its architectural scalability extends to emerging 1.6 Tbps NICs and beyond.
technical_mechanism: Per-path PSN-gap loss inference with jitter-bounded completion: infer missing packet counts from each path’s sequence progress, then use per-path progress and a timeout to complete a stripe and emit a path-specific drop bitmap.
why_it_works: The receiver turns sparse packet sequence and progress state into a per-path indication of which paths have not delivered expected packets, without retaining a full arrival bitmap. For Root, that could expose a lagging path or stalled network progress using compact NIC-side signals rather than full packet tracing. The signal localizes the path, but does not by itself establish whether a gap is loss or unusually late delivery.
root_seam: Attach at a robot-side or server-side NIC receive datapath: correlate request identity with packet sequence numbers, per-path arrival/progress state, and timeout events. This adds path-specific transport evidence to request latency diagnosis while leaving server queueing, GPU compute, and action application to be measured separately.
experiment: Replay identified requests across multiple paths while independently injecting path delay, jitter, loss, and path stalls. Compare per-path PSN-gap and timeout/drop-bitmap signals with packet captures and request-level latency. Test whether these signals identify the affected path and distinguish network delay from server queueing, GPU compute, and action application; specifically measure false loss indications when packets are delayed rather than dropped.
evidence_quote: If an arriving packet’s stripe offset is greater than the current eStripe, the Preprocessor infers that all intervening packets on that path have been lost.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Section IV.A, “Preprocessor”; timeout and completion behavior in the same section
