reported_gain: COMET Cache is reported to support 6 times more concurrent connections than state-of-the-art SoC-based designs, with line-rate operation at 400 Gbps and aggregate throughput exceeding 1.6 Tbps with 8 paths.
baseline: Bitmap-based tracking designs, including COMETBitmap and conventional bitmap tracking; SDR-RDMA on a BlueField-3 DPU is also compared.
uncertainty: The mechanism supplies a concrete per-path progress and inferred-loss signal, but the paper describes packet tracking and completion rather than network-tail diagnosis. Because an out-of-order gap is treated as loss and the timeout tolerates jitter, the signal alone may not distinguish a delayed packet from a lost one. The paper reports no Root-measured gain.

title: Accurate Distributed Tracing for Large-Scale AI Infrastructure: Time Synchronization as a Foundation for Reliable Observability
abstract: Distributed tracing in large-scale AI infrastructure fails silently when clock accuracy is insufficient: causal events are misordered, fault attribution is corrupted, and performance diagnoses are unreliable. We present TempoTrace, a system that co-designs IEEE 1588v2 PTP time synchronization with distributed tracing to preserve causal ordering across heterogeneous, multi-tenant GPU clusters. We formally prove that NTP-grade clocks produce causal inversions at 25-30% of directed operation pairs under WAN/cloud conditions (11.3% under LAN NTP). A Laplace heavy-tail noise model extends the analysis beyond Gaussian assumptions, giving a weighted expected misorder rate of 27.76% vs. 29.37% Gaussian, confirming robustness to tail shape. TempoTrace reduces GPU-to-host timestamp uncertainty from 2.1 us to a design target of 0.056 us residual standard deviation via GPUDirect RDMA hardware timestamping, with sub-100 ns PTP synchronization. A bounded Sketch Vector Clock tracks causal relationships with false-positive rate below 10⁻5 for up to four participants. A hybrid rule-based and XGBoost diagnosis engine achieves macro-F1 0.974 in controlled validation (1,800-incident corpus; McNemar p=1.25e-23). A formally proven multi-tenant model provides isolated logical clock domains. For RoCEv2/ECMP fabrics, P4-based in-band network telemetry corrects path-delay asymmetry, yielding 99.1% attribution accuracy. Application Confidence Policies let workloads specify precision requirements and degraded-mode fallback. Evaluation combines physical five-node measurements (NTP inversion rate 44.978%, Laplace fit preferred over Gaussian by AIC under congestion) and controlled synthetic validation with illustrative configurations from 512 to 16,384 H100 GPUs across InfiniBand and RoCEv2 fabrics.
technical_mechanism: Co-design PTP clock synchronization and distributed tracing: use GPUDirect RDMA hardware timestamps to reduce GPU-to-host timestamp uncertainty, bounded Sketch Vector Clocks to track causal relationships, and P4 in-band telemetry to correct RoCEv2/ECMP path-delay asymmetry. The operative diagnostic effect is more reliable cross-host event ordering and network-path attribution.
why_it_works: Accurate, comparable timestamps reduce false causal inversions that can corrupt attribution; the bounded sketch retains causal relationships compactly, while in-band telemetry provides path-delay information for asymmetric routes. For Root, this could make cross-host request and transport events meaningfully orderable and help attribute a tail to a path or link, rather than mistaking clock error for delay.
root_seam: Attach synchronized timestamps and request/span identity at robot-side send, server-side receive, and relevant server/GPU events; where supported, add network path telemetry. Compare event ordering and path delay for tail requests. The context does not establish direct packet-to-request reconstruction or prove separation of network transit from server queueing, GPU compute, and action application.
experiment: The context reports a five-node NTP causal-ordering validation using 100,000 known-causal probes across 20 directed host pairs, and describes controlled link-throttle and RoCEv2/ECMP attribution experiments. A Root experiment could inject known network delay or link throttling while separately recording robot send/receive, server queue, GPU, and action-application timestamps; compare attribution with and without synchronized clocks and path telemetry.
evidence_quote: TempoTrace reduces GPU-to-host timestamp uncertainty from 2.1 us to a design target of 0.056 us residual standard deviation via GPUDirect RDMA hardware timestamping, with sub-100 ns PTP synchronization. A bounded Sketch Vector Clock tracks causal relationships with false-positive rate below 10⁻5 for up to four participants.
evidence_location: CONTEXT abstract; validation details in passages on Exp 2.1–2.3 and Exp 3.1–3.2
reported_gain: Reported: NTP inversion rate was 44.978% in the five-node validation; the abstract reports 99.1% attribution accuracy for RoCEv2/ECMP with P4 in-band telemetry. These are paper results, not Root results.
baseline: NTP/Chrony for the causal inversion validation; the RoCEv2/ECMP passage describes comparison with and without in-band telemetry. UNKNOWN for a single overall baseline.
uncertainty: The context describes some claims as design targets, illustrative configurations, or proposed experiments, and notes that complete validation on real multi-node GPU clusters is still required. It does not provide sufficient implementation detail to establish request-to-packet linkage, per-request network-versus-compute decomposition, or direct applicability to a robot-to-cloud action loop.

title: DeltaINT: Toward General In-band Network Telemetry with Extremely Low Bandwidth Overhead
technical_mechanism: DeltaINT keeps per-flow embedded-state records in a programmable data-plane sketch, compares each packet’s current switch state with the most recently embedded state, and inserts that state into the packet only when the change exceeds a configured threshold.
why_it_works: Stable states need not be repeated, while significant changes—such as increased queue occupancy or latency—are carried in telemetry packets. For Root, this could expose switch-side network-state changes associated with slow inference requests while reducing telemetry bandwidth; it does not by itself distinguish network delay from server queueing, GPU compute, or action application.
root_seam: Attach telemetry to request-correlated robot/server transport packets or probes at programmable network devices. Compare recorded per-flow queue or latency state changes for slow requests against healthy requests, retaining states when changes exceed a threshold. The paper does not establish request-level correlation with remote robot inference.
experiment: On a controlled Root deployment, compare full INT with DeltaINT on the same request-correlated traffic. Measure telemetry bandwidth and packet overhead, and assess whether threshold-triggered queue or latency changes identify injected network-tail events without confusing them with server-side delays.
evidence_quote: DeltaINT embeds INT information into packets only when there exist significant state changes.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, Introduction; also Section III on DeltaINT’s delta-based update procedure.
reported_gain: Up to 93% bandwidth mitigation in gray failure detection: average per-packet bit cost falls from 112 bits with INT-Path to 8.1 bits for the reported configuration.
baseline: INT-Path, which inserts all four states into each packet at each node.
uncertainty: The reported gain is telemetry bandwidth reduction, not a Root latency or detection result. The method triggers on configured state changes, not explicitly on tail latency, and the context does not show evaluation on robot inference traffic.

title: Tales of the Tail: Hardware, OS, and Application-level Sources of Tail Latency
technical_mechanism: Instrument each request with fine-grained timestamps at packet arrival, network-stack processing, queue/wakeup, application processing, and packet transmission; compare the resulting per-stage tail distributions with a queuing-model ideal to distinguish queue buildup from other sources of tail latency.
why_it_works: Per-request stage durations localize where tail time accumulates rather than treating end-to-end latency as one value. The queuing model supplies an expected baseline for burst-induced queueing, while timestamp gaps expose excess delay in the stack, scheduling/wakeup, application, or transmit stages. Root could attach timestamps and request identity at robot/server transport and inference boundaries to separate network/queue delay from server queueing and compute.
root_seam: Add correlated timestamps at the robot-side send/receive and server-side NIC arrival, queue/wakeup, inference start/end, and response transmit events. This would let Root compare network transit with server queueing and inference time, and test whether observed queue delay matches a workload-based queuing baseline. The paper's measurements start and end at the server NIC, so it does not itself measure client or network-fabric delay.
experiment: The paper instruments three Linux servers and compares measured request-latency distributions against queuing-model predictions, then varies scheduling, core/interrupt placement, and other system configurations to identify sources of excess tail. A Root experiment could use the same per-request stage decomposition under controlled load and compare healthy and regressed runs, checking whether tail growth appears in transport, queue/wakeup, or inference intervals.
evidence_quote: T₁-T₂ is the network stack processing delay. T₂-T₃ is the queuing and wakeup delay. T₃-T₄ is the packet copy and return to user-level delay. T₄-T₅ is the user space application processing time. T₅-T₆ is the packet transmit delay.
evidence_location: Selected PDF text, section describing per-request timestamping and diagnostic intervals.
reported_gain: Memcached at 80% utilization improved from median 33 µs and 99.9th percentile 14 ms to median 11 µs and 99.9th percentile 32 µs after applying the paper's techniques.
baseline: Default configuration of a four-core computer with a 10 Gb/s NIC, Memcached at 80% utilization; the paper also compares measured distributions with an ideal queuing-model distribution.
uncertainty: The paper studies server-side NIC-to-NIC processing and excludes client and network-fabric latency in its principal measurements. It does not evaluate remote robot inference; transferring its instrumentation requires correlated timestamps across the robot and server.
